questions.question: A new startup called VeloPath Systems is rolling out a global fitness challenge leaderboard within its mobile app. The platform must ingest up to 320 thousand score submissions per minute from users spread across multiple regions, and rankings should refresh worldwide within just a few seconds. Analysts also need to keep detailed historical records for 5 years so they can study trends and seasonality. Which approach should you adopt to build the ingestion, processing, and analytics pipeline on Google Cloud?

options.text: Persist scores in Firestore, run a Cloud Function that recomputes rankings, and move historical submissions into Cloud Storage for archival
Publish each score event to Pub/Sub, calculate streaming rankings with Dataflow, land both raw and aggregated data in BigQuery, and surface dashboards with Looker Studio
Send every update to Bigtable, compute rankings using Dataflow, and export the results to Cloud SQL for reporting
Keep player scores in Memorystore, update rankings using Cloud Functions, and snapshot backups to Cloud Storage

questions.correct_text: Publish each score event to Pub/Sub, calculate streaming rankings with Dataflow, land both raw and aggregated data in BigQuery, and surface dashboards with Looker Studio
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Publish each score event to Pub/Sub, calculate streaming rankings with Dataflow, land both raw and aggregated data in BigQuery, and surface dashboards with Looker Studio.

This pipeline aligns with the throughput and latency targets. Pub/Sub can absorb hundreds of thousands of events per minute from multiple regions while buffering bursts and decoupling producers from consumers. Dataflow runs stateful windowed streaming computations, so it can maintain per player and global rankings with event time handling and elastic autoscaling. BigQuery accepts streaming inserts that become queryable within seconds and scales easily for both raw event storage and precomputed aggregates. You can partition and cluster tables to support 5 year retention with efficient queries. Looker Studio connects directly to BigQuery, providing near real time dashboards globally without copying data.

Persist scores in Firestore, run a Cloud Function that recomputes rankings, and move historical submissions into Cloud Storage for archival falls short for global high velocity ranking. Firestore triggers would fan out massive function invocations, and computing top rankings across a huge dataset requires heavy cross document aggregation that Firestore is not optimized to deliver. Archiving to Cloud Storage also fails to enable interactive SQL analytics over 5 years of history.

Send every update to Bigtable, compute rankings using Dataflow, and export the results to Cloud SQL for reporting matches services to the wrong roles. Bigtable is great for low latency key value lookups but not for ad hoc analytical queries spanning years of data. Pushing results into Cloud SQL adds an OLTP store that doesn't scale to large analytical reporting and would buckle under the volume and concurrency compared with BigQuery.

Keep player scores in Memorystore, update rankings using Cloud Functions, and snapshot backups to Cloud Storage uses a cache as the primary store, which isn't durable enough to act as system of record and cannot meet a 5 year retention need. Function based ranking updates would be tough to coordinate at this scale, and snapshot backups in Cloud Storage do not power interactive historical analytics.

questions.question: Your team has been tasked with launching an HTTP API for a publishing catalog at https://api.scrumtuous.com. The API will expose the paths https://api.scrumtuous.com/titles, https://api.scrumtuous.com/writers, and https://api.scrumtuous.com/categories. Each path needs to be dispatched to its own handler in your code, and the runtime must scale automatically with traffic. Which approach should you take on Google Cloud?

options.text: Build one Cloud Function that examines the request path and dispatches to the right handler
Deploy a single Cloud Run service whose application code implements several HTTP endpoints
Place API Gateway in front and have it route the three paths to three separate Cloud Functions backends
Deploy three independent Cloud Run services and map one URL path to each service

questions.correct_text: Deploy a single Cloud Run service whose application code implements several HTTP endpoints
questions.explanation:
The correct choice is Deploy a single Cloud Run service whose application code implements several HTTP endpoints.

Cloud Run is intended for containerized web applications that expose multiple routes, so you can implement /titles, /writers, and /categories as separate handlers using your preferred web framework. It scales automatically with incoming requests and supports mapping a custom domain such as api.scrumtuous.com to the single service, which keeps the deployment lean while still satisfying the requirement that each path map to its own handler.

Build one Cloud Function that examines the request path and dispatches to the right handler is a poor fit because it forces all routing through a single entry function rather than leveraging native framework routing. While it can work, it is less idiomatic for a multi endpoint HTTP API and offers fewer of the controls you usually want in a web service compared with a containerized app on Cloud Run.

Place API Gateway in front and have it route the three paths to three separate Cloud Functions backends piles on extra complexity and cost for this case. The requirement is a single API with multiple handlers in your code, which one Cloud Run service already satisfies without bringing in a gateway layer or multiple backends.

Deploy three independent Cloud Run services and map one URL path to each service fails the mapping requirement because Cloud Run custom domain mapping forwards every path of a mapped host to one service. Path based routing across services would require an additional routing layer that the question does not call for.

questions.question: In App Engine Standard running Python, how should an application handle termination so it safely closes database connections?

options.text: Use App Engine warmup requests to perform cleanup
Install a SIGTERM handler that stops accepting new requests and closes database connections before exiting
Set app.yaml so SIGTERM is ignored
Catch SIGTERM and immediately invoke sys.exit

questions.correct_text: Install a SIGTERM handler that stops accepting new requests and closes database connections before exiting
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Install a SIGTERM handler that stops accepting new requests and closes database connections before exiting.

App Engine Standard signals instance shutdown by sending SIGTERM. A correct handler should refuse new requests, allow in-flight work to wrap up within the available window, close any open database connections, and then exit. This sequence avoids connection leaks and prevents abrupt termination that could corrupt state or lose writes.

Use App Engine warmup requests to perform cleanup is wrong because warmup requests exist to prepare instances for serving traffic, not to handle shutdown. They give you no reliable or guaranteed window to release resources, and some newer runtimes do not even support warmup, which makes this an unreliable strategy.

Set app.yaml so SIGTERM is ignored is wrong because no supported app.yaml directive ignores termination signals. Ignoring SIGTERM would also risk an abrupt stop when the platform eventually terminates the instance.

Catch SIGTERM and immediately invoke sys.exit is wrong because exiting straight away skips stopping new traffic and closing connections. You need an orderly shutdown sequence that closes database connections before exit.

questions.question: A media streaming startup called AuroraStream Labs runs a microservices application on Google Kubernetes Engine, and customers complain that some endpoints become slow during busy periods. You need to pinpoint where the slowdown happens and identify which specific HTTP requests have the longest end to end latency across services. What should you do?

options.text: Emit structured HTTP request logs containing methods, paths, and latencies to STDOUT, route them with the logs router into Cloud Logging, and use log queries to compare slow endpoints
Instrument every microservice with OpenTelemetry and ship distributed traces to Cloud Trace, then use Trace views to examine slow spans and high latency requests
Capture packets with tcpdump on GKE nodes for a long window and later open the captures in Wireshark to investigate latency
Turn on GKE workload metrics and push Pod and container metrics into Cloud Monitoring, then build a custom dashboard to spot potential bottlenecks

questions.correct_text: Instrument every microservice with OpenTelemetry and ship distributed traces to Cloud Trace, then use Trace views to examine slow spans and high latency requests
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Instrument every microservice with OpenTelemetry and ship distributed traces to Cloud Trace, then use Trace views to examine slow spans and high latency requests.

Distributed tracing is designed to follow a single request as it travels through multiple services, recording spans and timings for each hop. Instrumenting with OpenTelemetry and sending traces to Cloud Trace lets you use Trace views to filter by service name, method, and URL, and sort by latency to find the slowest requests. From there you can drill into trace details to see which spans or downstream calls contribute most to the end to end latency.

Emit structured HTTP request logs containing methods, paths, and latencies to STDOUT, route them with the logs router into Cloud Logging, and use log queries to compare slow endpoints isn't enough because logs do not automatically correlate cross service calls into a single end to end view. Even with request IDs you would be stuck doing manual correlation and you would still lack the span timing and causal relationships that tracing offers.

Capture packets with tcpdump on GKE nodes for a long window and later open the captures in Wireshark to investigate latency is impractical and often ineffective because traffic is usually encrypted and packet captures do not cleanly map back to application endpoints. Long captures add overhead and do not give the service level span breakdown needed to find bottlenecks.

Turn on GKE workload metrics and push Pod and container metrics into Cloud Monitoring, then build a custom dashboard to spot potential bottlenecks gives you useful infrastructure and service metrics, yet it cannot tie together per request paths across services. Metrics can reveal saturation or errors but cannot point to which specific HTTP requests have the highest end to end latency.

questions.question: Your team at Solstice Tech is gearing up for a high traffic launch of several REST APIs on Cloud Run and you want to follow Google recommended practices to generate realistic distributed load that can scale quickly and coordinate many workers to reach roughly 1800 requests per second sustained over 45 minutes. How should you set up the load testing environment?

options.text: Launch a containerized load generator from Cloud Shell by starting several copies of the container one after another
Deploy a distributed load testing tool on a private Google Kubernetes Engine cluster and scale Pods to increase concurrent users
Create a managed instance group that runs a custom image with curl scripts on each VM to drive parallel requests from many IP addresses
Use Cloud Tasks to enqueue many HTTP calls against the Cloud Run endpoints to simulate client requests

questions.correct_text: Deploy a distributed load testing tool on a private Google Kubernetes Engine cluster and scale Pods to increase concurrent users
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Deploy a distributed load testing tool on a private Google Kubernetes Engine cluster and scale Pods to increase concurrent users.

This approach reflects Google guidance because a distributed load generator on GKE enables you to coordinate many workers, drive realistic user scenarios, and scale horizontally to hit and sustain a goal like 1800 requests per second over a 45 minute test window. A controller and worker pattern lets you synchronize test phases, ramp traffic up and down smoothly, and gather centralized metrics. Kubernetes lets you right size Pods and scale them rapidly, delivering predictable throughput and repeatable test runs.

Launch a containerized load generator from Cloud Shell by starting several copies of the container one after another is unsuitable for high traffic testing because Cloud Shell has strict resource and network limits and isn't built to coordinate many workers or hold high throughput for long.

Create a managed instance group that runs a custom image with curl scripts on each VM to drive parallel requests from many IP addresses is not advisable because improvised curl scripts do not deliver realistic user behavior, centralized coordination, or reliable metrics. The setup is operationally heavy and error prone, and it lacks the orchestration and scalability a purpose built distributed load testing framework provides.

Use Cloud Tasks to enqueue many HTTP calls against the Cloud Run endpoints to simulate client requests is incorrect because Cloud Tasks is a managed asynchronous work queue with rate limits and retry semantics that don't mirror client driven traffic. Its dispatch quotas and behavior aren't meant for load testing and would skew results rather than generate realistic load.

questions.question: Inside a GKE cluster, how do you let a specific Google Group create Kubernetes namespaces with least privilege through Kubernetes RBAC rather than wide Google Cloud IAM grants?

options.text: Create a Role granting namespace admin permissions and bind the group inside a single namespace
Grant the group the Kubernetes Engine Admin IAM role on the project
Define a ClusterRole that allows namespace create and bind the group through a ClusterRoleBinding
Bind the group to the cluster-admin ClusterRole via a ClusterRoleBinding

questions.correct_text: Define a ClusterRole that allows namespace create and bind the group through a ClusterRoleBinding
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Define a ClusterRole that allows namespace create and bind the group through a ClusterRoleBinding. Namespaces are cluster scoped resources in Kubernetes, so the permission to create them must be granted at the cluster level, which is what a ClusterRole combined with a ClusterRoleBinding does.

With this setup you define a ClusterRole that includes the create verb on the namespaces resource and bind the Google Group as the subject of a ClusterRoleBinding. In GKE you can use Google Groups directly as RBAC subjects, so the group can create namespaces without holding broader administrative permissions, satisfying least privilege.

Create a Role granting namespace admin permissions and bind the group inside a single namespace is wrong because a Role is namespaced and cannot grant permissions on cluster scoped resources like namespaces. It would only apply inside an existing namespace and wouldn't allow creating new ones.

Grant the group the Kubernetes Engine Admin IAM role on the project is wrong because Google Cloud IAM governs access to GKE resources at the project level and does not directly grant in cluster Kubernetes RBAC privileges. It is also far broader than required, breaking least privilege.

Bind the group to the cluster-admin ClusterRole via a ClusterRoleBinding is wrong because cluster-admin is a superuser level role that can do anything in the cluster. That far exceeds the need to create namespaces and violates least privilege.

questions.question: What does a Cloud Storage bucket retention policy enforce when set to 200 days?

options.text: It transitions objects to colder storage after 120 days
It blocks deletions and overwrites until the retention period elapses
It enables Object Versioning so prior versions are preserved

questions.correct_text: It blocks deletions and overwrites until the retention period elapses
questions.explanation:
The correct option is It blocks deletions and overwrites until the retention period elapses.

A Cloud Storage retention policy specifies a minimum time that objects must be kept. With a 200 day policy, objects cannot be deleted or replaced during that window, becoming effectively write once and read many until the period ends. This enforcement applies regardless of the requesting user's permission. When Object Versioning is enabled, the protected object generations also remain undeletable until retention has expired.

It transitions objects to colder storage after 120 days is incorrect because storage class transitions are governed by lifecycle rules and not by a retention policy. Retention does not change object storage classes, and the 120 day figure is unrelated to a 200 day retention configuration.

It enables Object Versioning so prior versions are preserved is incorrect because versioning is a separate feature that must be enabled on its own. A retention policy does not switch on versioning, although it does protect existing versions from deletion during the retention window.

questions.question: Which IAM role should a GKE pod's service account use to read and write Cloud Bigtable data without performing infrastructure administration?

options.text: Bigtable Viewer
Bigtable User
Bigtable Backup Admin
Bigtable Administrator

questions.correct_text: Bigtable User
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Bigtable User.

This role grants read and write permission to Bigtable tables and data while excluding instance and cluster administration. It is the right fit for a GKE pod service account that needs to interact with application data only and not manage infrastructure. You would bind the pod service account to this role on the project or Bigtable instance through Workload Identity.

Bigtable Viewer is read only and disallows writes, so it cannot satisfy a read and write requirement.

Bigtable Backup Admin focuses on creating and managing backups and restores. It does not grant the data read and write permissions an application needs against tables.

Bigtable Administrator grants broad administrative control over instances, clusters, and tables, which goes far beyond what an application pod needs and breaks the principle of least privilege.

questions.question: GoldenSky Retail at sample-shop.io is launching a stateless containerized API and the team wants automatic scaling from zero to handle roughly 1500 requests per minute at peak with very little operational work and an HTTPS endpoint immediately available with no certificate or load balancer to manage. Which Google Cloud service should you choose to run the container?

options.text: App Engine flexible environment
Cloud Run
Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)
Compute Engine

questions.correct_text: Cloud Run
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Cloud Run because it executes stateless containers with request driven autoscaling that can drop to zero and provides an HTTPS endpoint right away, with no certificates or load balancers for you to manage. This matches the requirement to serve about 1500 requests per minute with minimal operational effort.

Cloud Run deploys any container that listens on a port and scales instances up and down based on incoming requests, all the way down to zero when idle. You can tune concurrency so a single instance can serve multiple requests at the same time, which easily covers the described peak. It also issues a managed HTTPS URL at deploy time and lets you map a custom domain while Google manages the TLS certificates for you.

App Engine flexible environment isn't ideal because it does not scale to zero and usually keeps at least one instance running, which raises costs when idle. It also has slower startup times and does not provide the same request driven model that fits sudden bursts from zero.

Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) demands cluster and node management and you must configure an Ingress or Gateway along with certificates to expose HTTPS. It can autoscale pods and nodes, yet it doesn't remove the operational burden and it does not deliver instant scale to zero of the whole stack.

Compute Engine would require managed instance groups, a global HTTPS load balancer, and certificate management. It cannot scale to zero and entails the most operational effort of the options listed.

questions.question: Your team runs an HTTP Cloud Function that ingests analytics events from a single page web app and a native mobile app. The function is the public POST endpoint for every event upload. For historical reasons the function is hosted under a different hostname than the one the clients visit. The function is reachable at https://ingest.scrumtuous.com while web and mobile clients originate from https://app.scrumtuous.com. You need browsers to accept responses only when the request comes from the client origin and reject other sites. Which response header value should the Cloud Function return?

options.text: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://ingest.scrumtuous.com
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.scrumtuous.com
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://*.scrumtuous.com

questions.correct_text: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.scrumtuous.com
questions.explanation:
The right response header value is Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.scrumtuous.com. This matches the client origin making the requests and tells the browser to accept responses only for that site while rejecting others.

Browsers enforce CORS by comparing the Origin request header to the Access-Control-Allow-Origin value returned by the server. Returning the exact client origin ensures only that site is permitted. This configuration also works with credentialed requests because the value is explicit rather than a wildcard.

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://ingest.scrumtuous.com is wrong because it reflects the API host rather than the requesting site. The browser compares against the client Origin header and this value would not match requests originating from app.scrumtuous.com.

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * is wrong because it permits any origin, which fails the requirement to block other sites. It is also incompatible with credentialed requests, making it unsuitable for restricted access.

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://*.scrumtuous.com is wrong because CORS does not support wildcard subdomain patterns in this header. Only an exact origin or a full wildcard is valid, and a pattern like this will not match the browser Origin check.

questions.question: How should you release a redesigned API while keeping existing clients functional?

options.text: Use an Apigee proxy to rewrite legacy requests
Publish a new API version and keep the legacy one running until migration completes
Use App Engine traffic splitting
Have Cloud Endpoints enforce the new schema and retire the legacy version immediately

questions.correct_text: Publish a new API version and keep the legacy one running until migration completes
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Publish a new API version and keep the legacy one running until migration completes.

This follows established API versioning practice and preserves backward compatibility while you introduce breaking changes in a controlled way. You run the new version alongside the old one, allowing clients to migrate at their own pace. You communicate a clear deprecation timeline and monitor usage, then retire the legacy version once adoption is complete.

Use an Apigee proxy to rewrite legacy requests is not the best answer because a gateway can translate or normalize requests, yet it conceals breaking changes behind mappings and adds complexity. It can assist during migration but it should complement a versioned rollout rather than replace it.

Use App Engine traffic splitting controls how requests are routed between service versions for gradual deployments. It does not address API contract compatibility for external clients and provides no deprecation path.

Have Cloud Endpoints enforce the new schema and retire the legacy version immediately would break existing clients and violates backward compatibility best practices. In addition, Cloud Endpoints is in deprecation and being replaced by API Gateway or Apigee, making this choice less likely on newer exams.

questions.question: A digital publishing service on Google Cloud serves static images and large downloads from a single region, and readers in distant continents experience sluggish load times. What is the primary role of adopting a CDN in this design?

options.text: It automatically scans application code repositories for security flaws
It centralizes data storage to meet archival and compliance requirements
It speeds up delivery by caching frequently accessed content close to users across many regions
It governs east west service communication and enforces traffic policies within a cluster

questions.correct_text: It speeds up delivery by caching frequently accessed content close to users across many regions
questions.explanation:
The correct option is It speeds up delivery by caching frequently accessed content close to users across many regions.

A content delivery network caches static assets at edge locations that are physically closer to users, which lowers latency and shortens round trips to the single region origin. On Google Cloud this is achieved with Cloud CDN paired with global HTTP or HTTPS Load Balancing so cache hits are served from nearby points of presence and backend load and egress are reduced. This directly addresses the slow load times for readers on distant continents.

This design works well for static images and large downloads because the CDN can honor cache control headers and time to live settings and can efficiently serve large files from the edge while protecting origin capacity and improving user experience.

It automatically scans application code repositories for security flaws is unrelated to a CDN because that describes code or dependency scanning, a security function rather than content caching for performance.

It centralizes data storage to meet archival and compliance requirements describes long term storage and governance needs that would be met by storage services rather than an edge caching layer.

It governs east west service communication and enforces traffic policies within a cluster refers to a service mesh or networking controls inside a cluster and not to a global edge cache that improves content delivery to end users.

questions.question: A retail startup at sample-shop.io runs a production Java service on Google Kubernetes Engine that averages roughly 22,000 requests per minute, and the team needs continuous insight into CPU hot spots and method level execution with minimal overhead so they can evaluate runtime performance and resource usage without disrupting traffic. What should they implement?

options.text: Instrument the service with Cloud Trace to measure end to end request latency
Use Cloud Debugger to add snapshots and logpoints for investigating production errors
Enable Cloud Profiler on the Java service to continuously sample CPU and memory and surface method level timing with low overhead
Install the Ops Agent on the nodes to gather system CPU and memory metrics and build dashboards in Cloud Monitoring

questions.correct_text: Enable Cloud Profiler on the Java service to continuously sample CPU and memory and surface method level timing with low overhead
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Enable Cloud Profiler on the Java service to continuously sample CPU and memory and surface method level timing with low overhead.

Cloud Profiler is built for always on production profiling with very low sampling overhead, which fits a busy GKE based Java service handling around 22,000 requests per minute. It captures CPU and memory profiles and presents method level timing that helps locate hot spots and inefficient code paths without disrupting traffic. It supports Java on GKE and lets teams evaluate runtime performance and resource usage continuously.

Instrument the service with Cloud Trace to measure end to end request latency focuses on distributed tracing and request latency analysis. It helps locate slow requests and service interactions but does not provide CPU hot spot analysis or method level execution timing.

Use Cloud Debugger to add snapshots and logpoints for investigating production errors targets debugging through snapshots and logpoints rather than continuous performance profiling. It isn't designed to surface CPU or memory hot spots, and it has been retired, making it even less likely to be the right choice on newer exams.

Install the Ops Agent on the nodes to gather system CPU and memory metrics and build dashboards in Cloud Monitoring collects host level metrics and logs but does not capture application method level timing or profiling data. It is useful for infrastructure monitoring but will not reveal Java method hot spots.

HPA using the built in memory metric
Vertical Pod Autoscaler

The Vertical Pod Autoscaler adjusts container resource requests and limits and may restart pods to apply changes. It does not change the number of replicas, so it does not autoscale a Deployment based on memory utilization.

questions.question: At Cypress Outfitters a retail analytics group exposes an HTTP Cloud Function endpoint that accepts POST requests. Each request body is a flat JSON object containing only top level string and numeric fields. After each run the team requires that the combined dataset be ready for ad hoc analytics by many users within roughly 75 seconds. Which storage approach should you use to persist the incoming data so it supports this requirement?

options.text: Save each POST payload as a document in Firestore in Datastore mode
Insert parsed records into a regional Cloud SQL instance
Buffer events into Pub/Sub and archive them to Cloud Storage as hourly newline delimited JSON files for later analysis
Parse each POST payload and stream rows into BigQuery using the streaming API

questions.correct_text: Parse each POST payload and stream rows into BigQuery using the streaming API
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Parse each POST payload and stream rows into BigQuery using the streaming API.

This approach makes new rows available to query within seconds, which meets the requirement that the combined dataset be ready for ad hoc analytics within roughly 75 seconds. The flat JSON structure maps directly to table columns and the HTTP Cloud Function can parse and submit the data as rows with minimal transformation. BigQuery supports interactive and concurrent querying by many users, which fits the ad hoc analytics need.

Save each POST payload as a document in Firestore in Datastore mode is optimized for transactional document access and indexed lookups rather than large scale analytical SQL. You would need to export to an analytical store before querying, which would break the 75 second readiness requirement.

Insert parsed records into a regional Cloud SQL instance can store structured data, yet it is not designed for large scale ad hoc analytics by many users. Scaling ingestion and complex analytical queries in a relational instance adds operational overhead and is unlikely to meet the near real time requirement as volumes grow.

Buffer events into Pub/Sub and archive them to Cloud Storage as hourly newline delimited JSON files for later analysis is a batch ingestion pattern that delays availability. Hourly files would not be queryable within 75 seconds, failing the stated requirement.

Application Default Credentials
API key
OAuth 2.0 with user consent

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Application Default Credentials.

Client libraries for BigQuery and Secret Manager use these credentials by default, which means the function can call both services without any human approval at runtime. As long as the service account has the required IAM roles, access is automatic and secure with keyless rotation handled by the platform.

Service account with a JSON key is not appropriate because it depends on long lived keys that you must create, distribute, and rotate yourself. This raises risk and operational overhead and is unnecessary on Cloud Functions where the runtime can provide credentials automatically.

API key cannot authorize calls to BigQuery or Secret Manager because those services require IAM based OAuth tokens. API keys do not convey identity or permissions and therefore do not satisfy access controls for these services.

questions.question: Northwind Freight is building a telemetry platform on Cloud Bigtable to store streaming data from connected trucks. It must handle tens of thousands of writes per second while enabling fast retrieval of the latest readings per device without producing hotspotting. Which row key and schema approach should you implement?

options.text: Use the device ID as the entire row key and append every new reading as a separate column qualifier within a single wide row
Use the event timestamp as the row key so you can scan chronologically across the table
Create a composite row key of deviceId concatenated with a reverse timestamp and keep a minimal number of column families
Prefix the row key with a hash of the device ID then append the natural timestamp and place values in one column family

questions.correct_text: Create a composite row key of deviceId concatenated with a reverse timestamp and keep a minimal number of column families
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Create a composite row key of deviceId concatenated with a reverse timestamp and keep a minimal number of column families. This layout groups each device's data together while ordering the newest readings first per device, allowing you to read the latest value with a short prefix scan and a small limit. It spreads writes across devices so it avoids hotspotting, and keeping few column families reduces overhead and improves consistency of performance.

Bigtable stores rows in lexicographic order. Placing the device identifier first spreads load across tablets when many devices are writing. Using a reverse timestamp puts the most recent entries at the start of the device's row range so you can efficiently retrieve the latest reading without scanning through older data. Minimizing column families is a best practice because each family has its own resources and excessive families can hurt throughput.

Use the device ID as the entire row key and append every new reading as a separate column qualifier within a single wide row is not recommended because it creates very wide rows that can become a hotspot for that device, and it makes time ordering dependent on qualifier naming, which complicates efficient time range queries.

Use the event timestamp as the row key so you can scan chronologically across the table is incorrect because timestamps are monotonically increasing, which concentrates new writes in one key range and creates hotspotting. It also scatters a single device's readings across the table, making per device lookups inefficient.

Prefix the row key with a hash of the device ID then append the natural timestamp and place values in one column family does spread writes, yet the natural timestamp orders oldest first for each device, which makes fetching only the latest reading less efficient than using a reverse timestamp, and it adds complexity without improving the newest first retrieval pattern.

questions.question: Your team is deploying an HTTP API on a single Compute Engine VM in a production VPC. Several applications running on other instances in the same VPC must call this API without using any external connectivity. What should those clients use to obtain the service's IP address?

options.text: Create a Private Service Connect endpoint in the VPC and have clients connect to that private endpoint
Use the instance FQDN in Compute Engine internal DNS such as INSTANCE_NAME.ZONE.c.PROJECT_ID.internal
Attach a reserved static external IP to an external HTTP load balancer and publish a public Cloud DNS A record
Reserve a static internal IP for the VM and publish a private Cloud DNS A record in a private zone

questions.correct_text: Use the instance FQDN in Compute Engine internal DNS such as INSTANCE_NAME.ZONE.c.PROJECT_ID.internal
questions.explanation:
The correct choice is Use the instance FQDN in Compute Engine internal DNS such as INSTANCE_NAME.ZONE.c.PROJECT_ID.internal.

This internal DNS name is automatically created for each VM and resolves to the VM's primary internal IP for callers within the same VPC. It requires no extra configuration and ensures that traffic stays entirely within the VPC. Clients can use this name to reach the API privately and reliably, and the mapping updates automatically if the VM's internal IP changes, which simplifies operations.

Create a Private Service Connect endpoint in the VPC and have clients connect to that private endpoint is not appropriate because Private Service Connect is intended for privately consuming producer services that are exposed via service attachments or Google APIs. It is not used to directly target a single VM in your own project unless you re-architect the service behind a load balancer and publish a service attachment.

Attach a reserved static external IP to an external HTTP load balancer and publish a public Cloud DNS A record violates the requirement to avoid external connectivity. This would expose a public endpoint and route traffic through an external load balancer path rather than keeping it inside the VPC.

Reserve a static internal IP for the VM and publish a private Cloud DNS A record in a private zone could work but adds unnecessary management overhead. The built in internal DNS name already provides private name resolution to the VM's internal IP within the VPC without creating and maintaining private zones and records.

questions.question: On GKE, how do you restrict east west traffic so that only specific pod to pod connections are permitted and all other internal traffic is denied?

options.text: Cloud Armor
Private GKE cluster
Kubernetes NetworkPolicy rules
VPC firewall rules

questions.correct_text: Kubernetes NetworkPolicy rules
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Kubernetes NetworkPolicy rules.

Kubernetes NetworkPolicy rules let you declare which pods can communicate and on which ports using label selectors. On GKE you enable enforcement and create a default deny policy so all intra cluster traffic is blocked except the connections you explicitly allow. This provides fine grained east west control inside the cluster at the pod level.

Cloud Armor protects services at Google Cloud load balancers and focuses on external traffic and Layer 7 policies. It does not manage internal pod to pod communication inside a cluster, so it cannot enforce east west restrictions.

Private GKE cluster keeps nodes on private IP addresses and limits access to the control plane, but it does not provide policy controls between pods. It improves network exposure posture rather than governing which pods can talk to each other.

VPC firewall rules filter traffic at the virtual machine network interface and do not understand Kubernetes pod labels or policies. They cannot reliably govern pod to pod traffic on the same node and they are not the intended mechanism for application level isolation inside a cluster.

questions.question: VaultStream Capital is a small fintech that hosts its web tier on Google Kubernetes Engine, isolating its environments with three namespaces called prod, staging, and dev. The platform team wants each of those namespaces to be capped at a different ceiling for total compute consumption. What is the right way to configure this?

options.text: Apply a LimitRange in every namespace so the namespace-wide total of consumed resources is bounded
Author a separate ResourceQuota object and apply one to each namespace
Define a single cluster-scoped ResourceQuota and let it propagate automatically to every namespace
Lean on Google Cloud IAM roles to cap CPU and memory consumption on a per-namespace basis

questions.correct_text: Author a separate ResourceQuota object and apply one to each namespace
questions.explanation:
The right approach is to author a separate ResourceQuota object and apply one to each namespace.

Because a ResourceQuota is itself a namespaced object, it bounds the combined resource consumption of everything inside a single namespace. Creating an individual quota for prod, staging, and dev lets the control plane hold each environment to its own distinct CPU and memory request and limit ceilings, and that enforcement covers all pods and other objects living in that namespace.

Applying a LimitRange in every namespace does not work for this goal, since a LimitRange only establishes default request and limit values and optional per-pod or per-container maximums. It never sums up and caps the aggregate consumption of an entire namespace.

Defining a single cluster-scoped ResourceQuota is impossible because Kubernetes does not expose ResourceQuota at the cluster level. The object exists only as a namespaced resource, so achieving uniform limits requires one quota per namespace.

Leaning on Google Cloud IAM roles is the wrong tool, because IAM decides who is allowed to perform which actions. It has no influence over how much CPU or memory a workload actually burns at runtime, which is the job of Kubernetes policy objects such as ResourceQuota.

questions.question: A small fintech team at Cypress Analytics is building a web service that publishes and consumes events through Pub/Sub, and they want fast local feedback on every new build without sending traffic to the managed Pub/Sub service. How should they configure local integration testing so that developers can verify publish and subscribe behavior on their machines?

options.text: Add Cloud Code to the IDE and authenticate to a development project, then publish test messages to the managed Pub/Sub endpoint
Install the Pub/Sub emulator with gcloud and start it using a valid project ID, then run gcloud beta emulators pubsub env-init so the local app uses the emulator
Run a Pub/Sub emulator container on localhost on port 8687 and leave the application configuration unchanged
Enable the Pub/Sub API in the Google Cloud console and configure the local app to call pubsub.googleapis.com during tests

questions.correct_text: Install the Pub/Sub emulator with gcloud and start it using a valid project ID, then run gcloud beta emulators pubsub env-init so the local app uses the emulator
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Install the Pub/Sub emulator with gcloud and start it using a valid project ID, then run gcloud beta emulators pubsub env-init so the local app uses the emulator.

This approach runs a local Pub/Sub emulator so developers can publish and subscribe without sending traffic to the managed service. Running env-init exports the environment variables that point client libraries to the emulator, which gives fast feedback and avoids billing while keeping the workflow close to production by using the same APIs. Developers can create test topics and subscriptions against the emulator and iterate locally with confidence.

Add Cloud Code to the IDE and authenticate to a development project, then publish test messages to the managed Pub/Sub endpoint is wrong because it still sends traffic to the managed service. That doesn't deliver isolated local testing and can add latency and cost.

Run a Pub/Sub emulator container on localhost on port 8687 and leave the application configuration unchanged is wrong because client libraries must be routed to the emulator through environment variables such as the emulator host. Leaving configuration unchanged means the app will keep calling the managed endpoint. The suggested port is also not the standard default used by the official emulator.

Enable the Pub/Sub API in the Google Cloud console and configure the local app to call pubsub.googleapis.com during tests is wrong because it targets the managed service rather than a local emulator. This does not provide offline or isolated integration testing and can consume quota.

questions.question: A growing online ticketing startup runs its microservices on Google Compute Engine to keep control over VM types and networking. Traffic can spike by 30 times during 75 minute on sale windows so the system must scale rapidly, yet the team reports slower delivery pace and more engineering toil. Given this scenario, what is a likely trade off of choosing Compute Engine for this workload?

options.text: Greater risk of vendor lock in than managed platforms
Greater operational burden to provision and manage instances, networking, and patching
No support for multi zonal or regional high availability
Lack of native autoscaling for managed instance groups

questions.correct_text: Greater operational burden to provision and manage instances, networking, and patching
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Greater operational burden to provision and manage instances, networking, and patching.

Choosing Compute Engine grants the team granular control over VM types and networking, which suits bespoke microservice needs, yet it also means the team owns provisioning, capacity planning, image and template management, OS patching, firewalling, load balancing, health checks, and scaling policies. With traffic that can surge to 30 times in a short window, you can achieve rapid scale by configuring managed instance groups and autoscaling, but you must design and tune these pieces. That added setup and ongoing care explains the slower delivery pace and greater toil reported by the team, which lines up directly with this trade off.

Greater risk of vendor lock in than managed platforms is wrong because Compute Engine is baseline infrastructure that runs standard operating systems and containers, which are generally portable across cloud providers and on premises environments. It usually represents less lock in than highly opinionated fully managed platforms.

No support for multi zonal or regional high availability is wrong because Compute Engine supports zonal and regional managed instance groups and can place instances across multiple zones, and Google Cloud Load Balancing can distribute traffic across zones for resilient service delivery.

Lack of native autoscaling for managed instance groups is wrong because managed instance groups support native autoscaling using CPU utilization, load balancing capacity, and custom metrics, which can react quickly to surges when configured properly.

questions.question: An online retailer named PortsideCart runs its customer facing services on Google Kubernetes Engine across multiple zones. You need to keep users logged in during pod rescheduling and rolling updates, and session data must be reachable by all replicas and survive node restarts. What is the most effective way to manage and store user sessions so the experience stays consistent?

options.text: Store session data in Cloud Bigtable
Store session data in Google Cloud Firestore in Native mode
Store session data as a client side cookie
Store session state in a regional Cloud Spanner database

questions.correct_text: Store session data in Google Cloud Firestore in Native mode
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Store session data in Google Cloud Firestore in Native mode.

This choice provides a fully managed, regional or multi region document database that every pod across zones can reach. It persists independently of your cluster so sessions survive pod rescheduling and node restarts. It offers strong consistency for document reads and writes, simple document modeling for per session records, and built in features like TTL policies that automatically expire stale sessions. Its high availability and automatic replication keep the user experience consistent during rolling updates.

Store session data in Cloud Bigtable is optimized for very large analytical or time series workloads and lacks the simple transactional and query patterns that session storage benefits from. It also adds unnecessary operational complexity for small per user session documents.

Store session data as a client side cookie puts state on the client, which is size constrained and prone to loss or tampering. Sensitive session state should be validated and stored server side, so this does not meet security and manageability needs even though it would be available to all replicas.

Store session state in a regional Cloud Spanner database can satisfy durability and consistency requirements but is significantly more complex and costly than needed for simple session documents. Latency and operational overhead are higher and features like TTL based expiration are more straightforward with a document store.

questions.question: A Cloud Run service crashes after deployment although the container runs fine locally. What should you do first to begin troubleshooting?

Inspect Cloud Logging for errors and stack traces
Raise the service memory limit
Enable Error Reporting in Cloud Operations

Inspecting Cloud Logging for errors and stack traces is the best first step because Cloud Run automatically sends request and container logs to Cloud Logging. Starting with Cloud Logging gives you concrete evidence so you can identify the root cause before making any configuration changes.

Raise the service memory limit might be appropriate only after logs confirm an out of memory condition. Increasing memory without evidence is guesswork and does not constitute a sound first troubleshooting action.

questions.question: How should you configure identities and IAM so a Cloud Function can read Cloud Storage and publish to Pub/Sub while applying least privilege at both runtime and deployment?

options.text: Use the default Cloud Functions service account with Storage Admin and Pub/Sub Admin and assign the deployer Cloud Functions Admin
Use a dedicated service account with a minimal custom role and allow the deployer to impersonate it
Create a dedicated service account with a custom role and have the deployer use user managed service account keys

questions.correct_text: Use a dedicated service account with a minimal custom role and allow the deployer to impersonate it
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Use a dedicated service account with a minimal custom role and allow the deployer to impersonate it.

This setup honors least privilege at runtime because the function operates under its own service account holding only the permissions required to read objects in Cloud Storage and publish to Pub/Sub. You can implement that with a minimal custom role containing just storage object read and topic publish permissions, or with the smallest predefined roles that cover the need. It also honors least privilege at deployment time because the person or CI system performing the deployment is granted only the right to act as the service account through impersonation. That avoids handing out broad administrative roles and eliminates the need to manage long lived keys while preserving auditability and tight scope.

Use the default Cloud Functions service account with Storage Admin and Pub/Sub Admin and assign the deployer Cloud Functions Admin is wrong because it grants far more permissions than required. The default service account is shared across workloads, which weakens isolation, and the Admin roles allow full control over Storage and Pub/Sub, breaking least privilege. Giving Cloud Functions Admin to the deployer also provides excessive capability beyond what is needed to deploy a single function.

Create a dedicated service account with a custom role and have the deployer use user managed service account keys is wrong because user managed keys raise risk and operational burden. Keys can be leaked, must be rotated, and are harder to audit. Google Cloud recommends using impersonation to obtain short lived credentials rather than distributing keys.

questions.question: You handle roughly 750 thousand log entries per hour containing a customer ID and an amount, and you need to aggregate totals per customer ID in one pass with fast lookups. Which data structure should you use?

options.text: Skip list
Linked list
Hash table
Balanced binary search tree

questions.correct_text: Hash table
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Hash table.

A Hash table maps each customer ID to a running total and offers expected constant time inserts and lookups. This lets you process the stream in a single pass by updating the total for the key as each log entry arrives, satisfying the need for fast lookups and efficient aggregation at the stated scale.

Skip list maintains ordering and delivers logarithmic time operations, which adds overhead you do not need when the goal is only fast key based aggregation in one pass.

Linked list requires linear time to find a customer ID, so lookups would be too slow for efficient one pass aggregation.

Balanced binary search tree offers logarithmic lookups and updates and maintains order, which is slower than the expected constant time behavior needed here and provides ordering that isn't required.

questions.question: For real time Pub/Sub message processing with very low latency, automatic scaling, minimal operations, and pay per use compute, which service should you use?

options.text: Dataflow streaming pipeline
Pub/Sub triggered Cloud Functions
App Engine Standard with Pub/Sub push
Cloud Run jobs

questions.correct_text: Pub/Sub triggered Cloud Functions
questions.explanation:
The correct choice is Pub/Sub triggered Cloud Functions because it delivers event driven execution with very low latency, automatic scaling to handle bursts, minimal operations, and genuine pay per use billing.

With Pub/Sub triggered Cloud Functions you pay only while your function code runs and Google manages all infrastructure. Cloud Functions scales from zero to many instances driven by Pub/Sub message volume and starts quickly, supporting real time processing.

Dataflow streaming pipeline is built for long running streaming analytics and uses worker resources that remain allocated, which raises operations effort and cost. Dataflow does not scale to zero and is not pay per use per invocation, so it isn't the best fit for very low latency event handling.

App Engine Standard with Pub/Sub push can receive push requests, yet you must manage an application along with its versions and instance settings. Pricing and scaling are instance oriented rather than pure pay per use, and cold starts can add latency compared with Cloud Functions.

Cloud Run jobs is designed for finite batch workloads that run to completion and is not intended for continuously processing Pub/Sub messages. For Pub/Sub event driven processing you would use a Cloud Run service rather than Cloud Run jobs, so this choice does not meet the requirement.

questions.question: Sapphire Bay Analytics is building a client portal on Google Cloud that connects to the Google Sheets API so customers can read and update their own spreadsheets. The application must authenticate as the signed in user with an explicit consent screen and limit permissions to only the specific sheet the customer is working with. Which approach should you implement?

options.text: Configure Workload Identity Federation so the application calls the Sheets API using a Google service account
Use an OAuth Client ID and the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/spreadsheets.readonly scope to obtain a user access token for each session
Use an OAuth Client ID and the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/spreadsheets scope to obtain a user access token for each session
Use a service account with domain wide delegation and the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/spreadsheets scope to impersonate users across the Workspace domain

questions.correct_text: Use an OAuth Client ID and the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/spreadsheets scope to obtain a user access token for each session
questions.explanation:
The correct approach is Use an OAuth Client ID and the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/spreadsheets scope to obtain a user access token for each session.

This uses the standard OAuth 2 user flow with a consent screen so the app acts as the signed in user. The spreadsheets scope grants read and write access, which fulfills the requirement to support both reading and updating. You can keep access tightly bounded in practice by only operating on the specific spreadsheet ID the user is working with.

Configure Workload Identity Federation so the application calls the Sheets API using a Google service account is not appropriate because it authenticates as a service account rather than the signed in user. It does not present a user consent screen and requires sharing user spreadsheets with the service account, which does not meet the per user consent requirement.

Use an OAuth Client ID and the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/spreadsheets.readonly scope to obtain a user access token for each session fails the update requirement because the readonly scope prevents write operations.

Use a service account with domain wide delegation and the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/spreadsheets scope to impersonate users across the Workspace domain is intended for administrator approved server to server impersonation. It bypasses individual user consent and is overly broad for a customer portal that should authenticate as the signed in user.

questions.question: Your team manages a GKE cluster for a retail platform at sample-shop.io and you must ensure that only the pod named checkoutpod in the payments namespace can connect to the pod ledgerapi in the finance namespace on TCP port 9443 and that every other inbound connection to ledgerapi is blocked. What should you use?

options.text: VPC firewall rules
Kubernetes Network Policies
Google Cloud NAT
Istio Service Mesh

questions.correct_text: Kubernetes Network Policies
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Kubernetes Network Policies.

Kubernetes Network Policies let you select the destination pod with labels and then explicitly allow only the desired sources and ports. You can create a policy in the finance namespace that selects the ledgerapi pod by label and permits ingress on TCP 9443 only from the payments namespace and the pod labeled checkoutpod. Because a policy selects the ledgerapi pod, any traffic not explicitly allowed is denied, blocking all other inbound connections. On GKE you must have network policy enforcement enabled so the rules take effect in the data plane.

VPC firewall rules operate at the VPC and instance level and don't understand Kubernetes pods or namespaces. They match node IPs rather than pod identities, so they cannot allow only a single pod in one namespace to reach a specific pod and port while blocking all others inside the cluster.

Google Cloud NAT provides outbound internet connectivity for private resources. It doesn't control east west traffic inside the cluster and can't filter inbound connections to a pod.

Istio Service Mesh can enforce fine grained policies but it adds significant operational overhead and requires sidecars. Native Kubernetes Network Policies satisfy this layer four restriction directly and more simply for this use case.

questions.question: In Apigee, what does adding the API Key policy to an API proxy do?

options.text: OAuth 2.0 token verification
API key validation
Request quota enforcement

questions.correct_text: API key validation
questions.explanation:
The correct option is API key validation.

Adding the API Key policy to an Apigee API proxy validates an API key that a client provides. The policy checks the key against keys issued to registered developer apps and can verify that it is associated with the required API product. It extracts the key from the configured location such as a header or query parameter and rejects the request if the key is missing, expired, revoked, or not authorized.

The option OAuth 2.0 token verification is wrong because OAuth access token validation is performed by the OAuthV2 policy, not by the API Key policy. API keys and OAuth tokens are different credential types verified by different policies.

The option Request quota enforcement is wrong because rate limiting and quota enforcement are implemented by the Quota policy. The API Key policy doesn't track or enforce call counts and only verifies the client key.

questions.question: A payment service at mcnz.com uses a Cloud Firestore transaction to decrease a user's wallet balance and to add a ledger entry. If one of the operations inside this transaction fails, what will Cloud Firestore do?

options.text: Firestore converts the attempt into a batch write and keeps the successful writes
Firestore commits the successful changes and skips only the failing step
The transaction is aborted and none of the operations are committed
The failed step is placed on Cloud Tasks for a later retry

questions.correct_text: The transaction is aborted and none of the operations are committed
questions.explanation:
The correct option is The transaction is aborted and none of the operations are committed.

Cloud Firestore transactions are atomic, meaning either every operation in the transaction succeeds and the commit applies or any failure causes a full rollback. Nothing is partially written, and changes are only made visible if the entire transaction function completes successfully. The client SDK may retry the whole transaction when there are contention or transient errors, but if it ultimately fails then nothing is committed.

Firestore converts the attempt into a batch write and keeps the successful writes is wrong because transactions and batched writes are different APIs and Firestore does not convert one into the other. A failed transaction never keeps partial results and there is no automatic fallback to a batched write.

Firestore commits the successful changes and skips only the failing step is wrong because that would violate the all or nothing guarantee of transactions. If one operation fails, the entire set of operations is rolled back.

The failed step is placed on Cloud Tasks for a later retry is wrong because Firestore does not enqueue failed operations into Cloud Tasks. Any retry behavior is handled by the SDK retrying the whole transaction or by your application logic.

questions.question: Your team at Lakeshore Artworks is building a Cloud Function that responds to Cloud Storage object finalize events for a bucket that receives uploads from sample-shop.io. You want to cut the development feedback loop to under five minutes while following Google recommended practices so developers can test quickly and iterate safely. What should you do?

options.text: Configure Cloud Audit Logs to trigger a new Cloud Function when the original function source changes and test the new function with synthetic requests
Edit a duplicate of the function in the console editor and route the production web application to it to validate changes live
Refactor the function into an HTTP triggered variant and test it by calling the endpoint with mock payloads during development
Run the storage triggered function locally using Functions Framework and emulate Cloud Storage events with curl to localhost

questions.correct_text: Refactor the function into an HTTP triggered variant and test it by calling the endpoint with mock payloads during development
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Refactor the function into an HTTP triggered variant and test it by calling the endpoint with mock payloads during development.

This approach shortens the feedback loop because an HTTP function can be invoked instantly with representative request bodies that mirror Cloud Storage event payloads. Google recommends separating business logic from the trigger and exercising that logic through fast, repeatable calls, which an HTTP entry point enables during development and CI. Developers can validate parsing and error paths quickly without waiting for real object finalize events and without touching production buckets.

Configure Cloud Audit Logs to trigger a new Cloud Function when the original function source changes and test the new function with synthetic requests is not appropriate because Audit Logs are not designed to react to source edits in order to spin up test functions. Source changes should flow through a proper build and deploy pipeline, and this method would not deliver fast or reliable iteration on event handling.

Edit a duplicate of the function in the console editor and route the production web application to it to validate changes live is risky and not recommended. Editing in the console bypasses version control and code review, and sending production traffic to validate changes endangers reliability and user experience.

Run the storage triggered function locally using Functions Framework and emulate Cloud Storage events with curl to localhost is not the recommended fastest path. While you can run HTTP functions locally with the Functions Framework, accurately producing Cloud Storage CloudEvents requires extra tooling. Simply curling localhost doesn't faithfully emulate storage event metadata and envelopes, so this won't provide reliable or streamlined feedback for development.

questions.question: Birchwood Logistics runs ten containerized microservices on Compute Engine virtual machines. Traffic surges by roughly 15 times during a 90 minute marketing window and then drops to near idle levels for about 10 hours overnight. The team wants to redesign the system to improve elasticity and performance while minimizing cost when demand is low, and they prefer a managed approach to cut operational burden. Which platform should they adopt?

options.text: Replatform to App Engine standard environment
Increase the fixed pool of Compute Engine instances
Migrate the services to Cloud Run
Deploy on GKE Autopilot with Horizontal Pod Autoscaler

questions.correct_text: Migrate the services to Cloud Run
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Migrate the services to Cloud Run.

This service runs container images without requiring you to manage servers, and it automatically scales up quickly to absorb brief marketing surges. It can also scale to zero when idle, which minimizes cost during the long overnight lull. It bills on actual usage rather than provisioned capacity and it lowers operational burden while delivering strong elasticity and performance for HTTP driven microservices.

Replatform to App Engine standard environment is not a great fit for arbitrary containerized workloads because standard relies on specific language runtimes rather than custom containers. It would likely require code and deployment changes to fit the sandbox constraints and offers less flexibility for existing container images.

Increase the fixed pool of Compute Engine instances wouldn't be elastic and would force you to overprovision for the 15 times peak, which wastes money during the long idle period. It also leaves you with ongoing instance and configuration management that the team wants to avoid.

Deploy on GKE Autopilot with Horizontal Pod Autoscaler reduces some node management but still requires Kubernetes expertise and ongoing tuning. It commonly keeps baseline capacity running and introduces extra operational complexity compared with a fully managed request driven platform, so it is usually less cost efficient than a scale to zero service for spiky traffic.

questions.question: PineMutual Media runs its mobile API on App Engine Standard, and the growth team wants to run an A and B experiment on a new recommendation feature to measure user engagement. The platform must serve two live API versions with a 70 to 30 traffic split and capture request metrics, and the team cannot modify application code. What should you do?

options.text: Migrate the backend to Cloud Run and deploy two revisions with percent based traffic splitting
Deploy two versions on App Engine and configure built in traffic splitting for the desired percentages
Recreate the service on Compute Engine and place an NGINX reverse proxy in front to route users by cookie
Place an External HTTP(S) Load Balancer in front and use URL maps to distribute 70 and 30 percent to two backends

questions.correct_text: Deploy two versions on App Engine and configure built in traffic splitting for the desired percentages
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Deploy two versions on App Engine and configure built in traffic splitting for the desired percentages.

With App Engine traffic splitting you can run two live versions and route seventy percent to one and thirty percent to the other without touching application code. The platform supports random, cookie, or IP based splits, which enables clean A and B experiments. Request logs and metrics are captured per version in Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging so you can measure engagement without any code changes.

Migrate the backend to Cloud Run and deploy two revisions with percent based traffic splitting is unnecessary for an app already on App Engine Standard and likely requires containerization and operational changes that conflict with the constraint to avoid modifying the application. Although Cloud Run supports percent based traffic splitting, migrating offers no benefit over the native capability already available.

Recreate the service on Compute Engine and place an NGINX reverse proxy in front to route users by cookie introduces heavy operational overhead and complexity when the platform already provides built in percentage based routing. Cookie management, proxy configuration, and metrics correlation would all become custom work and none of it is required to meet the stated needs.

Place an External HTTP(S) Load Balancer in front and use URL maps to distribute 70 and 30 percent to two backends does not meet the requirement because URL maps route by host or path rather than by percentage. It also adds an extra layer that does not improve on the native version level splitting available in the service.

questions.question: A regional credit union must keep application audit logs for 7 years to satisfy regulatory controls. The logs are seldom accessed during normal operations, yet auditors may request them on short notice and the team must retrieve them quickly. Which Google Cloud service is the most appropriate for storing these logs?

options.text: Cloud Firestore
Cloud Storage Coldline storage class
Cloud Storage Standard storage class
Cloud Bigtable

questions.correct_text: Cloud Storage Coldline storage class
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Cloud Storage Coldline storage class because it provides low cost long term storage for data that is rarely accessed while still offering fast retrieval when auditors request it.

This storage class is designed for multi year retention and provides immediate access with high availability, satisfying the need to retrieve logs quickly. It minimizes ongoing storage costs and applies retrieval and early deletion charges only when you access the data, which aligns with seldom read audit logs. You can also enforce compliance with retention policies and bucket lock, so the seven year requirement can be met reliably.

The Cloud Storage Standard storage class is optimized for frequently accessed data and would be unnecessarily expensive for storing rarely accessed logs for seven years even though it delivers fast retrieval.

Cloud Firestore is a transactional document database for application data and is not intended for bulk log archiving. It lacks the cost profile and lifecycle controls that make object storage suitable for long term compliance retention.

Cloud Bigtable is a managed NoSQL database for high throughput and low latency workloads such as time series processing and is not an archival storage solution. Keeping inactive logs there for seven years would be costly and operationally unnecessary.

The security team requires every container image in use to be scanned for known vulnerabilities with as little operational overhead as possible, and they prefer a solution that integrates natively with Google Cloud and runs automatically when images are pushed. Run a scheduled GKE CronJob that pulls images in use and scans them with open source tools like Trivy or Clair
Turn on vulnerability scanning in Artifact Registry and enable the Container Analysis API so images are scanned automatically on push
Rely on a Binary Authorization policy to block images and use it as your only control for vulnerability checks

questions.question: Your team is building a SaaS platform for BirchValley Creative that needs to send email from each user's Gmail account. The application must authenticate each individual user and request only the least privilege needed to send messages without reading or managing drafts or inboxes. Which approach should you implement for authentication and authorization?

options.text: Create an OAuth client ID and request the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.compose scope to obtain a per user access token
Create an OAuth client ID and request only the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.send scope to acquire an access token per user
Configure a service account with domain wide delegation and the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.compose scope
Use an API key with HTTP referrer restrictions to call the Gmail API

questions.correct_text: Create an OAuth client ID and request only the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.send scope to acquire an access token per user

It also ensures each user explicitly consents and receives their own access token, which fits a multi-tenant SaaS pattern where users authenticate individually.

Create an OAuth client ID and request the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.compose scope to obtain a per user access token is too permissive because the compose scope grants permission to manage drafts in addition to sending. That exceeds the requirement to send email without reading or managing inboxes or drafts.

Configure a service account with domain wide delegation and the https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.compose scope is not appropriate for a SaaS app that must authenticate each individual user because domain wide delegation relies on an administrator granting organization wide impersonation. It also requests a broader compose scope than needed.

Use an API key with HTTP referrer restrictions to call the Gmail API does not work because Gmail requires user authorization with OAuth and API keys cannot access user data or send mail as a user.

questions.question: OvertureLive operates an online box office for a chain of concert halls, and demand spikes sharply the moment a popular show goes on sale. As soon as a particular seat is locked in, the customer's browser should receive an instant confirmation, and the platform has to absorb those peaks gracefully. How would you architect the booking flow to satisfy both goals?

options.text: Persist each booking as an object in Cloud Storage and use an object finalize trigger to fire a Cloud Run service that finalizes the order
Publish each booking as a message onto a Pub/Sub topic and wire Eventarc to invoke a GKE service that handles the booking
Enqueue the booking in Cloud Tasks, which kicks off a Workflows orchestration to carry out the booking
POST the booking over HTTP to an external Application Load Balancer that hands it to a Compute Engine managed instance group for handling

questions.correct_text: Publish each booking as a message onto a Pub/Sub topic and wire Eventarc to invoke a GKE service that handles the booking
questions.explanation:
The best fit is to publish each booking as a message onto a Pub/Sub topic and wire Eventarc to invoke a GKE service that handles the booking.

Decoupling the web tier from the booking processor through a message broker keeps the front end responsive and lets the system push very high volume. During an on-sale rush the broker absorbs the burst so that stateless workers can fan out horizontally and clear the backlog quickly. A worker claims the seat with a transactional write, emits the result, and the browser surfaces an immediate confirmation, whether by briefly awaiting the outcome or receiving a push over a web socket. Pairing an ordering key per seat with idempotent handlers guarantees a single winner and prevents retries from double booking.

Persisting each booking as a Cloud Storage object and reacting to a finalize trigger is a poor fit, because object storage is not a transactional booking queue. Writing one file per request adds latency and offers no clean per-seat ordering or contention-safe way to stop double bookings.

Enqueuing in Cloud Tasks to drive a Workflows orchestration layers on orchestration latency and suits rate-limited background jobs more than a very high fan-in event stream. It lacks native per-key ordering and does not handle the bursty streaming throughput an on-sale event generates.

POSTing directly to an external Application Load Balancer fronting a Compute Engine managed instance group couples synchronous processing to VMs and depends on instance autoscaling that can lag a sudden surge. With no buffering layer, overload and contention become likely and safe seat locking is harder to build at scale.
