questions.question: FieldLink Robotics runs its application on Google Cloud against a MySQL relational schema with heavy read and write traffic. The team wants automated backups and guidance for growing capacity, and while they can handle light maintenance, they do not want to operate the database from top to bottom. How should they deploy the database?

options.text: Spin up MySQL from Google Cloud Marketplace on Compute Engine and import the schema
Stand up Cloud Spanner and load the relational schema
Run MySQL on Cloud SQL and import the schema
Move the data into Firestore and host it there
Provision Bigtable and load the data into a new table

questions.correct_text: Run MySQL on Cloud SQL and import the schema
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to run MySQL on Cloud SQL and import the schema.

Cloud SQL is a fully managed MySQL service with automated backups and point-in-time recovery, high-availability configurations, read replicas to scale reads, and automatic storage growth. It surfaces performance metrics and Query Insights that aid capacity planning and right-sizing, and you can set maintenance windows and rely on automatic patching, which trims operational effort while still letting the team handle light maintenance.

Spinning up MySQL on Compute Engine leaves you running MySQL on VMs, meaning you own backups, replication, failover, patching, and capacity planning. That clashes with the requirement to avoid operating the database end to end.

Standing up Cloud Spanner brings in a different distributed relational service that is not MySQL compatible. It excels at global scale but would demand significant schema and application changes the scenario never asks for.

Moving the data into Firestore switches to a document store rather than a relational engine. It does not match a MySQL relational schema or support joins the same way and would require a major redesign.

Provisioning Bigtable uses a wide-column NoSQL database built for very low-latency key-value and time series workloads. It offers no relational SQL features or transactional behavior that MySQL applications expect.

questions.question: PineLoop is a neighborhood engagement app that helps residents coordinate meetups and lets small businesses reach nearby customers. The company plans to open service in additional continents, and investors expect a surge in traffic with a similar experience whether members are 25 or 14,000 miles away. PineLoop's stack combines an on premises data center with Google Cloud where APIs run on Compute Engine and a single instance MySQL database stores state. Releases currently require manual evening deployments, there is no centralized logging, and uptime signals are minimal which causes frequent alerts when APIs go silent. Leadership wants to shorten release cycles, adopt Google recommended SRE practices, and comply with regional regulations while scaling to support 15x more concurrent users. As the team prepares new regions, they need to increase API development velocity while keeping the QA environment stable and aligned with the QA team's feature acceptance criteria. Which approach should they take?

options.text: Require unit test coverage in every change and stop QA deployments unless all unit tests pass
Migrate the APIs to Cloud Run and use traffic splitting for QA to hold back traffic from new revisions when errors are detected
Integrate automated performance tests into the CI pipeline and block promotion to QA until all performance checks meet defined thresholds
Configure HTTP health checks for the QA environment and redeploy the APIs later if the environment is reported as unhealthy

questions.correct_text: Integrate automated performance tests into the CI pipeline and block promotion to QA until all performance checks meet defined thresholds
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Integrate automated performance tests into the CI pipeline and block promotion to QA until all performance checks meet defined thresholds.

This approach enforces performance gates before any build reaches QA, which keeps the QA environment stable and aligned with acceptance criteria. It catches latency and throughput regressions early, supporting the goal to scale for much higher concurrency while maintaining a consistent experience across regions. It also advances SRE practices by turning performance expectations into automated checks tied to promotion, which shortens release cycles and reduces noisy alerts later.

Require unit test coverage in every change and stop QA deployments unless all unit tests pass is insufficient because unit tests validate functional correctness rather than capacity, latency, or resource efficiency. Relying on unit tests alone will not protect QA from performance regressions and will not ensure readiness for the expected traffic surge.

Migrate the APIs to Cloud Run and use traffic splitting for QA to hold back traffic from new revisions when errors are detected addresses runtime platform and production canary techniques rather than stabilizing QA. Traffic splitting is designed for progressive delivery in production and does not create a deterministic QA gate that validates performance before promotion.

Configure HTTP health checks for the QA environment and redeploy the APIs later if the environment is reported as unhealthy is reactive and focuses on liveness checks rather than enforcing performance thresholds. This would allow problematic builds into QA and increase toil because redeploying after failures slows releases and does not prevent regressions upfront.

questions.question: Solstice Media is deploying an App Engine application that must upload files to Cloud Storage and execute SQL queries in BigQuery within the same project. You plan to use a single service account and want to grant only the least permissions those tasks require. Which roles should you assign to that service account?

Assign Storage Admin and BigQuery User
Assign Storage Object Creator and BigQuery Job User

questions.correct_text: Assign Storage Object Creator and BigQuery Job User
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to assign Storage Object Creator and BigQuery Job User. This pairs Storage Object Creator for uploading objects to Cloud Storage with BigQuery Job User for running SQL query jobs, holding permissions to the minimum the tasks need.

Storage Object Creator lets the application upload new objects to buckets without listing, reading, or deleting existing ones, which matches the upload-only requirement and follows least privilege.

BigQuery Job User lets the service account create and run query jobs in the project and manage those jobs. If the app also has to read from particular datasets, you can layer on dataset-level access such as Data Viewer on those datasets. Among the choices, this is the minimal role for running queries.

Assigning Storage Object Viewer and BigQuery Data Viewer is wrong because Object Viewer cannot upload objects and Data Viewer cannot create or run query jobs, so it does not cover the stated tasks.

Assigning Storage Admin and BigQuery User is wrong because these roles are broader than needed. Storage Admin can manage buckets and objects, and BigQuery User can create datasets and do more than run queries, which violates least privilege.

Assigning Storage Object Admin and BigQuery Admin is wrong because both grant full administrative control, far more access than uploading files and running queries requires.

questions.question: How should a single page app load a noncritical metrics panel so it never blocks rendering and gracefully handles timeouts or failures?

options.text: Render a spinner until the request completes no matter how long
Use an asynchronous request and hide the optional panel on timeout or error
Send a synchronous request and remove the panel if it fails
Retry with exponential backoff until a successful response

questions.correct_text: Use an asynchronous request and hide the optional panel on timeout or error
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Use an asynchronous request and hide the optional panel on timeout or error. This ensures the page renders immediately and the optional panel never blocks the user experience, even when the network is slow or unavailable.

Loading the panel asynchronously lets the single page app render core content first. You can set a reasonable timeout and use a cancellation mechanism so that if the request exceeds the limit or fails, the panel is simply hidden or omitted. This is a graceful degradation pattern that keeps the interface responsive and avoids distracting the user with prolonged loading states.

Render a spinner until the request completes no matter how long is not suitable because it does not handle failure or timeout conditions gracefully. It can spin indefinitely and mislead users into waiting for nonessential data, which harms the experience.

Send a synchronous request and remove the panel if it fails is wrong because synchronous requests block the main thread and can delay rendering. Synchronous XHR on the main thread is deprecated and should not be used for UI work in modern browsers.

Retry with exponential backoff until a successful response is not appropriate for optional content because it can waste client resources and prolong visual distraction. For noncritical UI, it is better to stop quickly on failure and proceed without the panel rather than retrying indefinitely.

questions.question: Driftwood Apps is building a cross-platform checklist product that has to keep each user's tasks in sync across their phones and tablets. It must keep working when the network is down and must reflect changes instantly on every signed-in device. The team wants the least operational overhead and almost no custom synchronization code. Which database approach should they choose?

options.text: Provision a Bigtable cluster, model rows to dodge write hotspots, and emit updates with Bigtable change streams
Use Firestore in Native mode, enable client offline persistence, and subscribe to snapshot listeners for live updates
Provision Cloud SQL for MySQL, design a relational schema for to-do items, and add indexes for common lookups
Embed a SQLite database on each device and run a periodic job that syncs dumps to Cloud Storage

questions.correct_text: Use Firestore in Native mode, enable client offline persistence, and subscribe to snapshot listeners for live updates
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to use Firestore in Native mode, enable client offline persistence, and subscribe to snapshot listeners for live updates.

This option provides built-in offline persistence on supported clients, so reads and writes still work while the network is down and automatically reconcile once connectivity returns. Snapshot listeners push near-real-time updates to every signed-in device, satisfying the requirement for immediate visibility of changes. It is serverless and scales on its own, keeping operational overhead low, and it minimizes custom synchronization code because the client SDK handles caching, queuing, and merge behavior.

Provisioning a Bigtable cluster with change streams is a poor fit, because it is not a client-facing synchronization system and change streams target backend consumers rather than mobile clients. You would have to build and run a custom pipeline and conflict-resolution logic, and there is no built-in device offline persistence.

Provisioning Cloud SQL for MySQL would require custom APIs, polling or push infrastructure, and client-side caching to achieve real-time sync. It also lacks built-in offline support and adds operational work for maintenance and scaling compared with a serverless document database.

Embedding SQLite on each device with periodic dumps to Cloud Storage fails the immediacy requirement and creates messy conflict resolution. Periodic dumps are not real time, and Cloud Storage is object storage, not a synchronization database.

questions.question: A fintech startup is delivering a containerized microservice to GKE Autopilot using a CI/CD pipeline built with Cloud Build and Cloud Deploy. The environments are Development, UAT, and Live. You want the pipeline to advance a release from UAT to Live automatically only after the UAT rollout completes verification. What should you do?

options.text: Configure a Cloud Build trigger on the clouddeploy-operations Pub/Sub topic that runs a build step to call the Cloud Deploy API and promote from UAT to Live
Set up Cloud Scheduler to run every 10 minutes to poll Cloud Deploy for UAT rollout status and invoke a promotion to Live when the rollout is successful
Create a Cloud Function that subscribes to SUCCEEDED events on the clouddeploy-operations Pub/Sub topic and invokes the Cloud Deploy API to promote the release from UAT to Live
Configure Eventarc to listen for GKE audit log events indicating rollout completion in UAT and trigger a service to promote the release to Live

questions.correct_text: Create a Cloud Function that subscribes to SUCCEEDED events on the clouddeploy-operations Pub/Sub topic and invokes the Cloud Deploy API to promote the release from UAT to Live
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Create a Cloud Function that subscribes to SUCCEEDED events on the clouddeploy-operations Pub/Sub topic and invokes the Cloud Deploy API to promote the release from UAT to Live.

Cloud Deploy publishes Pub/Sub notifications for rollout and verification state changes. By subscribing to SUCCEEDED events on the clouddeploy-operations topic, the function runs as soon as the UAT rollout verification completes successfully and then calls the Cloud Deploy API to promote the release to the Live target. This provides event driven automation with low latency and avoids fragile polling.

You can grant the function only the required Cloud Deploy permissions and parse the event payload to confirm the UAT target before invoking the promotion. This ensures promotions occur only after verification success in UAT and keeps the pipeline deterministic and auditable.

Configure a Cloud Build trigger on the clouddeploy-operations Pub/Sub topic that runs a build step to call the Cloud Deploy API and promote from UAT to Live is not ideal because Cloud Build is optimized for building and testing artifacts rather than acting as a general event handler. It adds unnecessary build overhead and does not natively filter for Cloud Deploy SUCCEEDED rollout events as cleanly as a lightweight subscriber.

Set up Cloud Scheduler to run every 10 minutes to poll Cloud Deploy for UAT rollout status and invoke a promotion to Live when the rollout is successful is wrong because polling introduces delay and wasted calls. It cannot guarantee immediate promotion after verification completion and is less reliable than reacting to the exact SUCCEEDED event.

Configure Eventarc to listen for GKE audit log events indicating rollout completion in UAT and trigger a service to promote the release to Live is wrong because rollout completion is a Cloud Deploy event rather than a GKE audit log event. While Eventarc can consume Cloud Deploy events, watching GKE audit logs would not reliably indicate that the UAT rollout verification has succeeded.

questions.question: A travel booking startup called Wayfare Junction is launching a web portal on Google Cloud that serves dynamic pages to users on three continents. The team wants a single global HTTP(S) load balancer using Google-managed SSL certificates for portal.example.com, and they must enforce user authentication at the load balancer layer with no changes to the application code. What should they configure?

options.text: Deploy the application to App Engine standard and rely on the platform's load balancing and built-in authentication settings
Run the service on GKE and turn on Identity Aware Proxy on a Google Cloud external HTTP(S) Load Balancer with Google-managed SSL certificates
Host the workload on GKE, manage certificates with cert-manager, and authenticate using an in-cluster sidecar
Use a global external HTTP(S) Load Balancer with Google Cloud Armor policies and Google-managed certificates for access control

questions.correct_text: Run the service on GKE and turn on Identity Aware Proxy on a Google Cloud external HTTP(S) Load Balancer with Google-managed SSL certificates
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to run the service on GKE and turn on Identity Aware Proxy on a Google Cloud external HTTP(S) Load Balancer with Google-managed SSL certificates. This gives a single global entry point with managed certificates and enforces user authentication at the load balancer, so the application code never has to change.

Identity Aware Proxy integrates with the external HTTP or HTTPS Load Balancer and makes users authenticate before requests reach the backend. It supports OAuth 2.0 based access and sits in front of the application, satisfying the requirement to enforce authentication without modifying the service. Google-managed SSL certificates are provisioned and renewed automatically for the load balancer, and the global external load balancer offers worldwide anycast reach behind a single IP, meeting the need to serve users across continents. The pattern works well with GKE through Ingress and container-native load balancing.

Deploying to App Engine standard and using its built-in authentication is not the best fit, because the requirement is to enforce authentication at the external global load balancer with Google-managed certificates. App Engine standard uses its own front end, and its built-in authentication is tied to the platform, which would mean adopting App Engine and would not explicitly meet the external load balancer requirement.

Hosting on GKE with cert-manager and an in-cluster sidecar does not meet the requirement, because the certificates would not be Google-managed and authentication would happen inside the cluster rather than at the load balancer. It also introduces sidecar changes and fails to centralize access control at the edge.

Using a global external load balancer with Google Cloud Armor policies cannot satisfy user authentication, because Cloud Armor provides web application firewall and IP or geo filtering. It does not authenticate users or integrate with identity providers to gate access.

questions.question: Harbor Analytics keeps stateless services on Cloud Run alongside Compute Engine batch workers in a shared VPC, and the Cloud Run service accepts internal ingress only. Scheduling time-based calls to it returns HTTP 403 Permission Denied. Without loosening that internal exposure, what is the managed and secure way to drive these jobs?

options.text: Run a cron script on the Compute Engine VMs that calls the Cloud Run endpoint on the desired schedule
Use Cloud Tasks to send authenticated HTTP requests bearing an OIDC token straight to the Cloud Run URL
Use Cloud Scheduler with Pub or Sub to publish a message that triggers the Cloud Run service
Switch the Cloud Run ingress setting to "Internal and Cloud Load Balancing" so scheduled requests can reach the service

questions.correct_text: Use Cloud Scheduler with Pub or Sub to publish a message that triggers the Cloud Run service
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to use Cloud Scheduler with Pub or Sub to publish a message that triggers the Cloud Run service.

This works because Cloud Scheduler can publish a message to Pub or Sub on a schedule, and that message can trigger Cloud Run through a managed event-delivery path such as an Eventarc Pub or Sub trigger. Your Cloud Run service keeps its internal ingress setting while the trigger delivers requests authenticated with a service account, which preserves security and avoids exposing the service to the internet. The approach is fully managed and reliable, and it cleanly separates scheduling from request handling.

Running a cron script on the Compute Engine VMs is not a managed solution and adds operational overhead and reliability risk. It also forces you to handle IAM authentication and private networking to reach an internal Cloud Run service, increasing complexity and missing the requirement for a secure managed approach.

Using Cloud Tasks to send authenticated HTTP requests straight to the Cloud Run URL still fails, because the service allows only internal ingress. Cloud Tasks sends requests from Google infrastructure outside your VPC, so the traffic is blocked unless you relax ingress, which the question forbids.

Switching the Cloud Run ingress to "Internal and Cloud Load Balancing" violates the requirement to leave the internal exposure unchanged. It would also need extra load balancer configuration, when a managed event path from scheduling through Pub or Sub to Cloud Run already satisfies the need without widening exposure.

questions.question: Your team at HarborWest Media is building a backend service to compute live engagement metrics for an interactive video platform. The service requires persistent WebSocket connections for each viewer session, and a single connection can remain open from 15 minutes to 4 hours. Traffic surges on weekday evenings and during weekend premieres. The platform must scale automatically with demand while keeping cost and operational effort low. Where should you deploy this backend service?

options.text: GKE Autopilot
Cloud Functions
App Engine flexible environment
Cloud Run

questions.correct_text: App Engine flexible environment
questions.explanation:
The correct option is App Engine flexible environment because it supports long lived WebSocket connections that can remain open for hours, provides automatic scaling for traffic surges, and keeps operational effort low with a fully managed platform.

App Engine flexible environment supports native WebSockets and does not impose short request deadlines, so a single viewer session can stay connected for up to four hours without being terminated by the platform. It offers automatic scaling that adjusts instance counts based on load, which handles evening spikes and premiere events while you avoid managing servers or clusters.

GKE Autopilot can host WebSocket workloads and can scale, yet it still requires you to design and operate Kubernetes deployments, services, and autoscalers. This increases operational complexity compared with a fully managed application platform and does not meet the goal of keeping operational effort as low as possible.

Cloud Functions is not suitable for persistent WebSocket sessions and is designed for short lived event driven execution with request timeouts. Long lived connections from 15 minutes to 4 hours do not fit its execution model.

Cloud Run supports WebSockets, however each connection is still subject to the service request timeout, which has an upper bound of 60 minutes. Sessions that need to stay open for up to four hours would be terminated and therefore it cannot meet the requirement.

questions.question: Which type of Cloud Storage bucket keeps data near users around the globe and helps satisfy response times under 150 milliseconds?

options.text: A dual-region bucket
A Coldline bucket
A multi-region bucket
A regional bucket

questions.correct_text: A multi-region bucket
questions.explanation:
The right answer is a multi-region bucket.

This option stores objects across several geographically separated locations inside a broad location that spans many regions. It is designed to serve content to users worldwide and keep data close to them, which raises availability and lowers latency. That distribution helps meet demanding response-time goals such as under 150 milliseconds for global access.

A dual-region bucket places data in exactly two specified regions. It improves durability and can reduce latency for users near those two locations, but it does not spread data broadly near users everywhere, so it is weaker when you need global low-latency targets.

A Coldline bucket is a storage class for infrequent access with lower storage cost and retrieval charges. It defines no global placement and is not tuned for low-latency delivery to a worldwide audience.

A regional bucket holds data in a single region. It fits well when your compute runs in the same region and you want local performance, but it does not keep data near users globally.

questions.question: Which Google Cloud compute and datastore pairing should you use for a REST API that spikes to about 3200 requests per second during 48 hour events and scales to zero when idle with minimal operations?

options.text: GKE Autopilot with Cloud Bigtable
App Engine standard with Cloud SQL
Cloud Run with Firestore
Cloud Run with Cloud SQL

questions.correct_text: Cloud Run with Firestore
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Cloud Run with Firestore because it provides serverless compute and a serverless datastore that handle spiky traffic to about 3200 requests per second and scale to zero when idle with very little operations.

This pairing is fully managed and needs almost no infrastructure to provision or maintain. The compute layer autosizes quickly to absorb bursty workloads and can return to zero instances when idle, which satisfies the requirement to scale to zero. The datastore is also serverless and automatically scales read and write throughput without manual capacity planning, which keeps operational effort low and costs aligned to usage.

GKE Autopilot with Cloud Bigtable is not a good fit because the cluster and the database require provisioned capacity and don't scale to zero when idle. This choice also demands more configuration and ongoing tuning, which conflicts with minimal operations.

App Engine standard with Cloud SQL is less suitable because the database in this choice is not serverless and does not scale to zero. Managing connections and sizing for spikes adds operational overhead, which goes against the goal of minimal operations.

Cloud Run with Cloud SQL partially meets the compute requirement since the service can scale to zero, yet the database does not. The need for connection management and fixed database capacity makes this option harder to operate for sharp spikes compared with a fully serverless datastore.

questions.question: The team at mcnz.com runs a customer facing API on Google Kubernetes Engine and wants to release a new version while keeping the ability to switch back to the previous release within 75 seconds if issues appear. They also want to validate the new version under real production traffic before sending all requests to it. Which deployment strategy should they use?

options.text: Rolling update with maxSurge 1 and maxUnavailable 0
Recreate deployment strategy
Blue/green deployment using separate environments and a controlled traffic switch
Canary release with progressive traffic shifting

questions.correct_text: Blue/green deployment using separate environments and a controlled traffic switch
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Blue/green deployment using separate environments and a controlled traffic switch.

With Blue/green deployment using separate environments and a controlled traffic switch, you keep two identical environments running and you route production traffic to only one at a time. You can validate the new version with real production traffic in a controlled manner while keeping the previous version fully available. If a problem appears you can switch traffic back immediately, which comfortably meets the 75 second rollback requirement.

On GKE this approach maps well to using separate Services or backends that sit behind the same load balancer so you can flip or gradually steer traffic in a controlled way. Because the previous version remains warm and ready, there is no need to reschedule pods during rollback which keeps the switch fast and predictable.

Rolling update with maxSurge 1 and maxUnavailable 0 replaces pods in place inside a single environment. It does not give you an instantaneous traffic switch, and a rollback is another rollout which may exceed the 75 second target. It also does not clearly separate validation traffic from full production traffic.

Recreate deployment strategy stops the old version before starting the new one, which causes downtime. It does not allow validating the new version under real production traffic and it cannot offer a rapid fallback because the prior version is not kept running.

Canary release with progressive traffic shifting is useful for gradual exposure to production traffic, yet it does not maintain two fully separate environments ready for an immediate flip. Restoring all traffic to the previous version is not as instantaneous as with Blue/green deployment using separate environments and a controlled traffic switch, which makes meeting a strict 75 second rollback objective less reliable.

questions.question: You are a developer at a photo sharing startup called LakeView Lens that is migrating from PostgreSQL to Cloud Firestore to manage member profiles and the posts they publish. How should you model the collections to enable scalable queries and a clear one to many relationship between each member and their posts?

options.text: Create separate top level collections named members and posts and link them by a userId field
Store each member with all of their posts embedded as an array field inside the member document
Keep a top level collection for members and create a posts subcollection under each member document
Use a single posts root collection and create a subcollection named profile under each post document

questions.correct_text: Keep a top level collection for members and create a posts subcollection under each member document
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Keep a top level collection for members and create a posts subcollection under each member document.

This subcollection pattern cleanly models the one to many relationship because each post is a separate document stored under its parent member. It scales for high write rates since posts are independent documents, and it avoids hot spotting on a single member document. It also supports efficient queries because you can read a specific member's posts by targeting that member's posts subcollection, and you can query across all members using a collection group query on posts. This design keeps documents within size limits and enables pagination and indexing over individual post fields.

Create separate top level collections named members and posts and link them by a userId field can work but does not encode the hierarchy in the document path, which makes the relationship less explicit. It relies solely on a field join for scoping and rules and does not provide the natural parent child organization that subcollections offer when you want a clear one to many structure.

Store each member with all of their posts embedded as an array field inside the member document is not scalable because the member document can grow without bound and hit the document size limit. It also causes write contention on a single document and prevents efficient querying and pagination of individual posts.

Use a single posts root collection and create a subcollection named profile under each post document inverts the relationship and duplicates or fragments profile data. It does not help you query a member's posts and it does not reflect the intended parent to child structure from member to posts.

questions.question: A media platform run by scrumtuous.com will be built on Google Cloud and it must store tens of petabytes of unstructured assets such as high resolution images and 8K video. The content will be accessed and updated frequently and it must be kept with very high durability. Which Google Cloud storage service should be selected?

options.text: Cloud Bigtable
Cloud Storage
Cloud Spanner
Filestore

questions.correct_text: Cloud Storage
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Cloud Storage.

This service is Google Cloud object storage that handles unstructured content at massive scale. It supports tens of petabytes and offers up to eleven nines of annual durability. It offers regional and multi regional locations and the Standard storage class is designed for frequent access and updates. Cloud Storage also integrates well with content delivery workflows and supports lifecycle management and object versioning for protection and control.

Cloud Bigtable is a wide column NoSQL database for large scale analytical or operational workloads and time series data. It is not an object store and it is not intended for large binary media like high resolution images or 8K video and it does not provide the global object durability and distribution that Cloud Storage offers.

Cloud Spanner is a distributed relational database for structured transactional data. It is not optimized or cost effective for storing very large unstructured blobs at petabyte scale or for media delivery.

Filestore provides managed NFS file shares for Compute Engine and GKE. Its capacity is typically measured in terabytes rather than petabytes and it targets POSIX file system workloads rather than internet scale object storage with very high durability.

questions.question: You need a fully managed relational database on Google Cloud that keeps strong consistency and SQL while spreading reads and writes horizontally across regions at roughly 600,000 operations per second. Which one qualifies?

options.text: Cloud Bigtable
Cloud Spanner
Firestore
AlloyDB for PostgreSQL

questions.correct_text: Cloud Spanner
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Cloud Spanner, because it is the only fully managed relational database on Google Cloud that combines strong consistency and SQL with horizontal scaling across regions to handle around 600,000 reads and writes per second.

Cloud Spanner offers ANSI SQL, true relational semantics, and externally consistent transactions across regions. It is built for global horizontal scalability with synchronous replication in multi-region configurations, which lets it sustain very high throughput while preserving strong consistency for both reads and writes.

Cloud Bigtable is a wide-column NoSQL database that thrives at massive scale for key-value and time series workloads, but it is not relational and provides neither SQL nor multi-row transactional guarantees, so it does not meet the requirements.

Firestore is a NoSQL document database that gives strong consistency for document reads and transactions within its model, yet it is not a relational SQL database and was not designed for the described cross-regional relational workload at this throughput.

AlloyDB for PostgreSQL is a managed PostgreSQL-compatible service offering high performance and read pooling, but it does not provide globally distributed horizontal scaling with synchronous cross-regional strong consistency for writes as the question demands.

questions.question: Your team manages a Go web API on Google Kubernetes Engine for mcnz.com, and in the past 120 minutes you have seen a sharp rise in CPU usage and memory allocations across several pods. What should you do to identify which functions are using the most CPU time and allocating the most memory so that you can prioritize optimizations?

options.text: Instrument the service with OpenTelemetry and export spans to Cloud Trace, then review request latency and span timelines on the Trace overview
Add the Cloud Profiler agent to the Go service and enable profiling, then analyze the CPU and heap flame graphs in the Google Cloud console
Use Cloud Debugger to capture snapshots during high load and inspect code lines and local variables when requests are processed
Insert detailed log statements around function entry and exit and redeploy, then parse the logs with a Python script to approximate the longest running functions

questions.correct_text: Add the Cloud Profiler agent to the Go service and enable profiling, then analyze the CPU and heap flame graphs in the Google Cloud console
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Add the Cloud Profiler agent to the Go service and enable profiling, then analyze the CPU and heap flame graphs in the Google Cloud console.

Cloud Profiler provides continuous production profiling for Go services on GKE with low overhead, which is exactly what you need to identify code hotspots. By enabling Cloud Profiler you can view CPU and heap flame graphs that attribute time and allocations to specific functions, which lets you quickly see which functions consume the most CPU and which ones allocate the most memory so you can prioritize optimizations.

Instrument the service with OpenTelemetry and export spans to Cloud Trace, then review request latency and span timelines on the Trace overview is not suitable because tracing shows request latency and span timing rather than CPU consumption or memory allocation by function. Traces help diagnose distributed latency but they do not reveal which functions are the hottest for CPU or allocation.

Use Cloud Debugger to capture snapshots during high load and inspect code lines and local variables when requests are processed is wrong because that tool was designed for snapshot debugging rather than performance profiling and it has been retired, so it is not appropriate for identifying CPU or heap hot paths in production.

Insert detailed log statements around function entry and exit and redeploy, then parse the logs with a Python script to approximate the longest running functions is unreliable and risky because it adds overhead, measures wall time rather than CPU time, and provides no visibility into memory allocation hot spots. This method is noisy and inferior to the precise information that Cloud Profiler gives you.

questions.question: A platform team at example.com runs a single Google Kubernetes Engine cluster that runs many microservices. They need to separate workloads for staging, qa, and prod so that compute resources and network traffic are isolated between environments while staying within the same cluster. Use dedicated Kubernetes namespaces for each environment together with quotas and network policies
Provision a separate GKE cluster for each environment
Set up separate VPC networks and use VPC Network Peering for each environment

questions.correct_text: Use dedicated Kubernetes namespaces for each environment together with quotas and network policies
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Use dedicated Kubernetes namespaces for each environment together with quotas and network policies. This satisfies the need to isolate compute resources and network traffic while remaining within a single GKE cluster.

You can also apply NetworkPolicy to restrict which pods can communicate, which delivers network isolation between environments. GKE supports enforcing these policies, so the combination aligns directly with the requirements for staging, qa, and prod.

Assign taints and tolerations on dedicated node pools for each environment primarily influences scheduling and keeps pods on certain nodes, yet it does not provide network isolation and it does not enforce per environment resource limits. Without quotas and network policies, this approach does not meet the full isolation requirements.

Provision a separate GKE cluster for each environment would achieve isolation, but it contradicts the requirement to stay within the same cluster and it adds unnecessary operational overhead and cost.

Set up separate VPC networks and use VPC Network Peering for each environment is not compatible with a single cluster because a GKE cluster is created in one VPC and subnet. Peering does not segment workloads inside the cluster and it does not provide pod level policy controls, so it does not address the stated need.

questions.question: Birchwood Freight has just finished lifting its customer web application into Google Cloud, and you have about two weeks to gather actionable metrics and pitch ideas to your engineering lead for improving database performance and cost efficiency while keeping operations simple and low risk. options.text: Spin up a Compute Engine VM, install PostgreSQL and MongoDB, migrate to PostgreSQL, then copy the data into MongoDB
Load the database into BigQuery, then move the records into Firestore in Native mode
Migrate the database to Cloud SQL, then import the data into Firestore in Native mode
Move the database to Cloud Spanner, then track performance and cost metrics with Cloud Monitoring

questions.explanation:

This lets you stand up a managed relational database fast with minimal risk and overhead. You can use Database Migration Service to move data into Cloud SQL with little effort, then lean on Cloud SQL features and Query Insights to collect performance metrics such as query latency, CPU and memory usage, and connection counts. Because Cloud SQL ties into Cloud Monitoring and billing data, you can quickly gather actionable performance and cost signals inside the two-week window.

Importing into Firestore in Native mode adds a serverless document store that scales automatically with simple operations. Firestore exposes usage and latency metrics in Cloud Monitoring and a pay-for-what-you-use cost model, making it easy to evaluate cost efficiency for the parts of the app that fit a document model. Together these services keep the footprint simple and managed while giving you clear metrics to guide improvements.

Spinning up a VM and self-managing PostgreSQL and MongoDB is wrong, because operating databases on VMs raises operational complexity for patching, backups, and high availability. Adding two engines also increases risk and effort, which does not suit a short timeline focused on low risk and quick insights.

Loading into BigQuery first is wrong, because BigQuery is built for analytics rather than transactional workloads. Pushing operational data into BigQuery adds needless steps, fails to produce the runtime performance metrics you need for a production database, and complicates the path to Firestore.

Moving to Cloud Spanner is wrong, because Spanner targets planet scale and strong consistency across regions, which raises cost and migration complexity. It is not the simplest or lowest-risk path when you have only two weeks to gather metrics and propose improvements.

questions.question: Your team at a video startup is building a thumbnail generation microservice on Google Kubernetes Engine, and all callers will run inside the same GKE cluster. You want client pods to reliably discover and reach this API without hardcoding IP addresses. What should you implement so that clients can obtain and use a stable address for the service inside the cluster?

options.text: Configure an Ingress resource and have clients use the Ingress hostname to call the API inside the cluster
Create a Service of type LoadBalancer and publish an A record in Cloud DNS that points to the provisioned IP
Create a ClusterIP Service and have clients call the workload by its Kubernetes service name via cluster DNS
Use Cloud Endpoints and provide the endpoint URL to clients via a ConfigMap or environment variable

questions.correct_text: Create a ClusterIP Service and have clients call the workload by its Kubernetes service name via cluster DNS
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Create a ClusterIP Service and have clients call the workload by its Kubernetes service name via cluster DNS.

A ClusterIP Service gives the API a stable virtual IP that is reachable only within the cluster, which matches the requirement that all callers run in the same GKE cluster. Kubernetes adds DNS records for the service name so client pods can make reliable calls using the service name without hardcoding any pod or node IPs. This also decouples clients from pod churn because the ClusterIP Service continuously routes to healthy pods behind it.

Configure an Ingress resource and have clients use the Ingress hostname to call the API inside the cluster is not a good fit because Ingress is intended to expose HTTP or HTTPS services through a load balancer and is typically used for traffic entering the cluster. For in-cluster communication, using a service and cluster DNS is simpler and avoids unnecessary hops.

Create a Service of type LoadBalancer and publish an A record in Cloud DNS that points to the provisioned IP is unnecessary and counterproductive here. A LoadBalancer service allocates a network load balancer and an external or regional IP which is for north south traffic. Clients that already run inside the cluster should use a ClusterIP Service and the built-in Kubernetes DNS rather than relying on Cloud DNS and an external address.

Use Cloud Endpoints and provide the endpoint URL to clients via a ConfigMap or environment variable is not a fit for in-cluster discovery. Cloud Endpoints focuses on API management and external access patterns and placing the URL in a ConfigMap still requires hardcoded addressing. Kubernetes already offers automatic service discovery through a ClusterIP Service and cluster DNS.

questions.question: Engineering teams at sample-shop.io use Cloud Build to produce container images and they want to push them during CI. The operations group requires that every image be stored in a single secure registry that they administer in a separate project and they want to avoid distributing static credentials while following least privilege. How should you configure this so the requirement is met?

options.text: Configure Binary Authorization with a policy that only allows deployments from the operations registry while letting teams push images wherever they choose
Enable Artifact Registry in every development project and grant the operations team access to all of those registries

Set up a centralized operations project with Artifact Registry and grant each development project's Cloud Build service account writer access to the required repositories and push images to this registry
Create an operations project with Artifact Registry and issue a dedicated service account and JSON key per team and store the keys in source to authenticate docker pushes

questions.correct_text: Set up a centralized operations project with Artifact Registry and grant each development project's Cloud Build service account writer access to the required repositories and push images to this registry
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Set up a centralized operations project with Artifact Registry and grant each development project's Cloud Build service account writer access to the required repositories and push images to this registry.

This method meets the requirement to keep every image in a single secure registry that the operations team controls. Each development project uses its Cloud Build service account and you grant only the Artifact Registry writer role on the specific repositories in the centralized operations project. Builds then authenticate with short lived tokens through the Cloud Build service account which avoids distributing static credentials and follows least privilege.

To implement this, identify the Cloud Build service account in each development project and grant it the Artifact Registry writer role on the target repository in the operations project. Configure the build steps to authenticate to Artifact Registry using the gcloud credential helper so pushes go to the centralized repository endpoint. This gives the operations team full administrative control of the registry while developers only have the minimum permissions needed to push.

Configure Binary Authorization with a policy that only allows deployments from the operations registry while letting teams push images wherever they choose is wrong because Binary Authorization governs what can be deployed rather than where images are pushed. It would not ensure that all images are stored in a single registry and it does not solve CI push authentication.

Enable Artifact Registry in every development project and grant the operations team access to all of those registries is incorrect because it spreads images across many registries and violates the requirement to store every image in one secure registry managed by operations.

Create an operations project with Artifact Registry and issue a dedicated service account and JSON key per team and store the keys in source to authenticate docker pushes is incorrect because distributing and storing static service account keys is insecure and does not follow least privilege or the requirement to avoid static credentials.

questions.question: A Cloud Function in project A must write objects into a Cloud Storage bucket that sits in project B. You want the function's runtime identity to stay in project A and to grant only least privilege. What is the right setup?

options.text: Use the default Compute Engine service account in the function's project and grant it roles/storage.objectCreator on the bucket
Create a dedicated service account in the function's project, grant it roles/storage.objectCreator on the target bucket, and run the function as that account
Have the function generate a signed URL and upload to the bucket without any cross-project IAM
Create a dedicated service account in the bucket's project and run the function as that account

questions.correct_text: Create a dedicated service account in the function's project, grant it roles/storage.objectCreator on the target bucket, and run the function as that account
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to create a dedicated service account in the function's project, grant it roles/storage.objectCreator on the target bucket, and run the function as that account.

This keeps the runtime identity anchored in the function's own project, which satisfies the ownership and auditability requirement. You then grant only roles/storage.objectCreator on the destination bucket, so the function can upload objects but cannot read or delete them, aligning with least privilege because access is scoped to the minimal role and to the specific bucket in the other project.

In practice you create the service account in the same project as the function, configure the function to run as it, and add an IAM binding on the target bucket in the other project granting that account roles/storage.objectCreator. The result is clean cross-project separation with clear audit trails and minimal permissions.

Using the default Compute Engine service account in the function's project and granting it roles/storage.objectCreator is not ideal, because the default account is shared and often carries broader permissions than needed. It can work technically but violates least privilege and recommended workload isolation.

Having the function generate a signed URL without cross-project IAM does not preserve the function's runtime identity for authorization or audit and adds key-management and signing complexity. It also bypasses bucket IAM, contradicting the goal of granting least privilege to the function's identity.

Creating a dedicated service account in the bucket's project and running the function as it fails the requirement to keep the runtime identity in the function's project. Running as an identity from the destination project reduces separation of duties and makes auditing along project boundaries harder.

questions.question: A fintech startup named Sandhill Ledger uses Cloud Pub/Sub to broadcast events across its microservices. One service exposes a public REST API for partners and must prevent any unauthorized calls while providing centralized authentication and request governance. What should you implement to protect this service?

options.text: Enable IAM access control on the Pub/Sub topic
Place Cloud Endpoints in front of the API to enforce authentication and validate requests
Set up Cloud VPN between environments
Use Identity-Aware Proxy in front of the service

questions.correct_text: Place Cloud Endpoints in front of the API to enforce authentication and validate requests
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Place Cloud Endpoints in front of the API to enforce authentication and validate requests. This puts a managed control point in front of the public REST interface so only authenticated partner calls are allowed and policies are enforced consistently.

Cloud Endpoints acts as an API gateway that verifies API keys or JWTs, supports Google service accounts and third party identity providers, enforces quotas and request validation using an OpenAPI specification, and offers centralized logging and monitoring. These capabilities prevent unauthorized access while giving you unified governance across partner requests.

Enable IAM access control on the Pub/Sub topic does not protect an external HTTP API. Pub or subscribe IAM permissions secure message publishing and consumption on a topic, not inbound requests to a separate REST service.

Set up Cloud VPN between environments provides encrypted network connectivity between networks, which does not authenticate callers to a public API or enforce request validation and policy. It solves private connectivity, not API security and governance.

Use Identity-Aware Proxy in front of the service is designed to gate user access to applications behind Google load balancers and is best for interactive user authentication tied to identities. It is not an API management layer for partner-facing REST endpoints and it does not provide API key management, request validation with OpenAPI, or per method quotas in the way an API gateway does.

questions.question: Your team at Cascade Insights is launching a streaming analytics platform on Google Kubernetes Engine made up of several microservices that must each scale on their own as load shifts. The services should communicate only inside the cluster, and you want to rely on Kubernetes-native DNS so you never manage external DNS records. What should you implement?

options.text: Deploy each microservice as a StatefulSet and expose it through an Ingress for internal traffic
Set up a private Cloud DNS zone and add DNS records for each backend so services call one another by those names
Run each microservice as a Deployment, expose it with a ClusterIP Service, and use the Service DNS name for in-cluster communication
Deploy each microservice as a Deployment, expose it with a LoadBalancer Service, and call it by its external IP

questions.correct_text: Run each microservice as a Deployment, expose it with a ClusterIP Service, and use the Service DNS name for in-cluster communication
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to run each microservice as a Deployment, expose it with a ClusterIP Service, and use the Service DNS name for in-cluster communication. This lets every microservice scale independently, keeps traffic inside the cluster, and relies on Kubernetes-native DNS for simple name-based discovery.

Deployments are the standard controller for stateless microservices and let you scale each service on its own. A ClusterIP Service exposes the pods on a stable virtual IP reachable only within the cluster, and Kubernetes DNS automatically creates a resolvable name for each Service, so other services call it as service-name.namespace with no external DNS to manage.

Deploying each microservice as a StatefulSet behind an Ingress is not appropriate, because StatefulSets are meant for workloads needing stable identities and storage, which is atypical for stateless microservices. Ingress is for inbound traffic from outside the cluster into Services rather than east-west traffic among Services inside it.

Setting up a private Cloud DNS zone with records for each backend adds needless complexity, because Kubernetes already provides built-in DNS for Services. Service IPs can change and Kubernetes DNS handles that automatically, whereas Cloud DNS records would be external to the cluster and require ongoing upkeep.

Exposing each Deployment with a LoadBalancer Service and calling it by external IP would push each service externally and force clients onto external addresses. That violates the requirement to keep communication inside the cluster and bypasses the simple in-cluster Service DNS names.

questions.question: Your team at Larkspur Analytics is building a microservice that publishes and consumes messages, and you need to run integration tests on developer laptops without using any managed resources. You want to simulate Google Cloud Pub/Sub locally so that developers can test the system offline. What should you do?

options.text: Use Pub/Sub Lite instead during development
Start the local Pub/Sub emulator using the gcloud beta emulators pubsub start command
Use a third-party message broker to replicate the Pub/Sub API
Use Google Cloud Console to run a Pub/Sub emulator

questions.correct_text: Start the local Pub/Sub emulator using the gcloud beta emulators pubsub start command
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Start the local Pub/Sub emulator using the gcloud beta emulators pubsub start command. This gives developers a local Pub/Sub endpoint so they can publish and consume messages on developer laptops while staying completely offline and avoiding any managed resources.

The Pub/Sub emulator is provided with the Cloud SDK and can be started locally with the gcloud command. Client libraries can target it by setting the emulator host environment variable, which allows realistic end to end tests of publishers and subscribers without incurring cloud charges. The emulator mirrors key Pub/Sub behaviors closely enough for integration testing and is the supported path for local development.

Use Pub/Sub Lite instead during development is wrong because Pub/Sub Lite is still a managed Google Cloud service and cannot run locally. It requires provisioning resources in a project and therefore does not meet the requirement to test offline without managed resources.

Use a third-party message broker to replicate the Pub/Sub API is incorrect because third party brokers do not match Pub/Sub APIs and semantics and can lead to differences in acknowledgments, ordering, and authentication that mask production issues. The question asks to simulate Pub/Sub which the official emulator already does.

Use Google Cloud Console to run a Pub/Sub emulator is incorrect because there is no emulator available in the Console. Emulators are started locally through the Cloud SDK on the developer machine.

questions.question: MoorPark Labs ingests application logs into a Cloud Storage bucket every 18 hours. Authenticated security analysts must be able to review high priority events from the most recent 30 days, and an external auditor must be able to access the complete log history once each year. You need to minimize storage costs while meeting these review requirements. Which configuration choices should you implement?

options.text: Configure a lifecycle rule to move objects older than 30 days to Nearline storage
Lock a retention policy on the bucket using Bucket Lock with 400 days
Use a scheduled job to rewrite objects into a Coldline class after 30 days
Configure a lifecycle rule that transitions objects older than 30 days to Coldline storage
Enable Object Versioning on the log bucket

questions.correct_text: Configure a lifecycle rule that transitions objects older than 30 days to Coldline storage
questions.explanation:
The correct choices are Lock a retention policy on the bucket using Bucket Lock with 400 days and Configure a lifecycle rule that transitions objects older than 30 days to Coldline storage.

The first choice guarantees that no log objects can be deleted or overwritten for one year, which preserves the complete history for the annual audit. This meets the governance requirement by enforcing a minimum hold period at the bucket level.

The second choice minimizes cost by keeping the most recent 30 days in the default hot class for frequent analyst access, then automatically moving older data to a low cost archive tier that is designed for very infrequent reads. This aligns storage class with the access pattern and relies on automated transitions rather than manual processes.

Configure a lifecycle rule to move objects older than 30 days to Nearline storage is not optimal because the access pattern for older logs is annual rather than monthly, so a colder tier is more cost effective for this use case.

Use a scheduled job to rewrite objects into a Coldline class after 30 days adds operational complexity and extra request costs, and it can conflict with a one year retention lock. Native lifecycle transitions already perform this action reliably without custom jobs.

Enable Object Versioning on the log bucket is unnecessary for the stated requirements and would increase storage costs by retaining multiple versions. The retention policy already guarantees the data needed for audit is preserved.

questions.question: Your Cloud Functions backend is hitting all its performance numbers, yet shipping new features feels slower than it would on containers. Which inherent FaaS trade-off is the most plausible culprit?

options.text: Variability in cold starts
Limits on automatic scaling during bursts
Restricted control of the runtime and environment
Strict execution-time and memory ceilings

questions.correct_text: Restricted control of the runtime and environment
questions.explanation:
The right answer is restricted control of the runtime and environment.

This trade-off slows feature delivery because the platform owns the operating system, base image, and runtime. Teams cannot freely select unsupported language versions or install arbitrary system packages or background processes. Building features that need native extensions, custom binaries, or specialized networking often takes longer or becomes infeasible, whereas a containerized workload would let you package exactly what you need and move ahead.

Variability in cold starts affects request latency rather than development pace, and the scenario says performance goals are already met, so it is not the factor slowing feature delivery.

Limits on automatic scaling during bursts are not the usual bottleneck for Functions, since the service is designed to scale automatically to demand. With performance objectives already satisfied, scaling during bursts is unlikely to be the reason delivery slows.

Strict execution-time and memory ceilings are genuine constraints, but they mainly determine workload fit and performance characteristics. When the application already meets its performance goals, these limits are not the chief cause of slower iteration compared with containers.

questions.question: At mcnz.com your engineering team shifted its microservices onto a Container as a Service platform on Google Cloud. The services scale smoothly through traffic spikes, yet the release cadence has slipped from roughly every 4 days to about every 12 days. Which trade-off of adopting a CaaS platform most likely explains this slowdown?

options.text: Higher platform cost for the managed control plane
Trouble integrating the platform with CI or CD pipelines
Slower feature delivery from the added complexity of container orchestration workflows
An inability to cope with heavy traffic volumes

questions.correct_text: Slower feature delivery from the added complexity of container orchestration workflows
questions.explanation:
The right answer is slower feature delivery from the added complexity of container orchestration workflows.

Moving to a managed container platform improves scalability and reliability, but it brings orchestration constructs and processes that demand more coordination. Teams must manage cluster resources, write and review manifests, configure rollouts and rollbacks, and keep policies consistent across environments. These extra steps raise cognitive load and governance, which often lengthens lead time for changes and explains the shift from four days to about twelve.

Higher platform cost for the managed control plane is not the best explanation, because higher costs do not directly slow deployment frequency. Cost is a financial trade-off, not a process or workflow constraint that delays releases.

Trouble integrating with CI or CD pipelines is unlikely, because Google Cloud offers well-documented integrations for building and deploying to Kubernetes, and many teams use Cloud Build and similar tools successfully. Integration is a solved path and rarely becomes the primary bottleneck when cadence slips after adopting containers.

An inability to cope with heavy traffic clearly does not fit, since the services are scaling smoothly during spikes. With scale working as intended, it is not the reason releases slowed.

questions.question: You need a managed database that speaks ANSI SQL, grows by scaling out rather than up, and guarantees externally consistent transactions even when they reach across regions. On Google Cloud, which service fits that bill?

options.text: AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
Cloud Spanner
BigQuery
Cloud SQL

questions.correct_text: Cloud Spanner
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Cloud Spanner. It is the only managed relational database on Google Cloud that provides horizontal scaling and ANSI SQL alongside externally consistent transactions across multiple regions.

This service is globally distributed and scales reads and writes by automatically partitioning data while holding strong consistency. It uses TrueTime to guarantee external consistency for distributed transactions, supports ANSI SQL, and offers multi-region configurations with synchronous replication for high availability.

AlloyDB for PostgreSQL centers on PostgreSQL compatibility and high performance with read-pool scale-out. It does not provide horizontally scalable writes or externally consistent transactions across multiple regions.

BigQuery is an analytics data warehouse rather than a managed relational OLTP database. It supports ANSI SQL for analytical queries but offers no transactional semantics with externally consistent multi-region transactions.

Cloud SQL is a managed MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server service that mainly scales vertically and uses read replicas for limited read scaling. It does not deliver global horizontal scale or externally consistent transactions across multiple regions.

questions.question: Vellum Interactive is taking a single-VM legacy app built from Nginx, MariaDB, and PHP-FPM and moving it to Google Kubernetes Engine. You need a containerization plan that matches Google's guidance for high availability and dependable health checks. Which plan should you adopt?

options.text: Pack the entire Nginx, MariaDB, and PHP-FPM stack into one container and run supervisord to manage the processes
Put each service in its own container but sequence their startup with a custom shell script
Place Nginx, MariaDB, and PHP-FPM in separate containers and set readiness and liveness probes on every container
Use a single image for all components with an entrypoint script that backgrounds each daemon

questions.correct_text: Place Nginx, MariaDB, and PHP-FPM in separate containers and set readiness and liveness probes on every container
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to place Nginx, MariaDB, and PHP-FPM in separate containers and set readiness and liveness probes on every container.

This plan follows Kubernetes design by running one main process per container and lets the platform manage health predictably. Readiness probes ensure traffic only reaches a container once it is ready, and liveness probes let Kubernetes restart unhealthy containers, improving availability. Separating the services also enables independent scaling and lifecycle management. You can run stateless tiers like Nginx and PHP-FPM as Deployments and address database needs with dedicated configurations, all while keeping per-container health checks.

Packing the whole stack into one container with supervisord is wrong, because multiple daemons in a single container hide individual health and prevent Kubernetes from probing and restarting components independently. It creates a single point of failure and complicates signal handling and graceful shutdown.

Putting each service in its own container but sequencing startup with a custom shell script is wrong, because startup-ordering scripts provide no ongoing health management. Kubernetes should use readiness and liveness probes to gate traffic and recover from failures rather than depend on brittle boot sequencing.

Using a single image with an entrypoint that backgrounds each daemon is wrong, because backgrounding multiple daemons in one image causes PID 1 and signal-propagation problems and blocks per-service health checks and targeted restarts.

questions.question: MapleLearn is an online training platform whose web application runs on Compute Engine and must answer over both HTTP and HTTPS. Engineers occasionally need to open an SSH session from their laptops to do routine maintenance. What configuration follows Google best practices while keeping the instances secure?

options.text: Give every web VM an external IP and allow inbound HTTP, HTTPS, and SSH through broad firewall rules
Keep the web servers on private IPs behind a global HTTP(S) load balancer and add a bastion VM with a public IP plus restricted firewall rules for SSH
Use Identity Aware Proxy for TCP forwarding to reach SSH and keep the web servers on private IP addresses behind an HTTP(S) load balancer
Remove external IPs from the web VMs and depend on Cloud NAT so administrators can SSH in from the internet

questions.correct_text: Use Identity Aware Proxy for TCP forwarding to reach SSH and keep the web servers on private IP addresses behind an HTTP(S) load balancer
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to use Identity Aware Proxy for TCP forwarding to reach SSH and keep the web servers on private IP addresses behind an HTTP(S) load balancer.

IAP for TCP forwarding lets authorized engineers open SSH sessions to private instances without assigning external IPs or exposing SSH to the internet. IAM governs the access and the connection is proxied through Google, so you can pare firewall rules down to only what IAP and health checks require. That shrinks exposure while keeping administrative access secure and auditable.

Keeping the web servers behind the external HTTP(S) load balancer leaves them on private addresses while still serving HTTP and HTTPS to users. The load balancer terminates client connections and forwards to the private backends, which matches Google's recommendations for public web services on private instances.

Giving every web VM an external IP and broad firewall rules is not a best practice, because it widens the attack surface and exposes SSH straight to the internet. Least privilege argues against broad rules and against external IPs on servers when a load balancer and IAP can do the job more securely.

Adding a bastion VM with a public IP can work but is not preferred when IAP is available. A bastion is one more public endpoint to manage and patch, and Google recommends IAP to eliminate the jump host and centralize access control through IAM.

Removing external IPs and relying on Cloud NAT will not work, because Cloud NAT supports only outbound connections from private instances. It does not permit inbound connections such as SSH from the internet.

questions.question: At Northwind Fitness your platform team operates four regional Google Kubernetes Engine clusters. Each cluster runs the same Deployment, which yields several replicas of the same Pod, and the containers write application logs to stdout. You want to pull those logs for every replica across all four clusters with a single command from your terminal. Which command should you use?

options.text: kubectl logs -l app=myapp --all-containers
gcloud compute ssh [NODE] --command='sudo journalctl -u kubelet'
gcloud logging read [FILTERS]
gcloud container clusters get-credentials [CLUSTER] [FLAGS]

questions.correct_text: gcloud logging read [FILTERS]
questions.explanation:
The right answer is gcloud logging read [FILTERS].

When cluster logging is enabled, GKE forwards container stdout and stderr to Cloud Logging by default, centralizing logs from every cluster in the project. With gcloud logging read you query those aggregated logs using filters that select the Kubernetes container resource type and labels for the Deployment or Pod, which retrieves entries from all replicas across all four clusters in a single command from your terminal.

kubectl logs -l app=myapp --all-containers operates only against the current kubeconfig context and usually a single namespace unless you extend it, so it cannot aggregate logs across multiple clusters in one invocation.

gcloud compute ssh [NODE] --command='sudo journalctl -u kubelet' connects to one node and reads kubelet service logs, which are not your container application logs, and you would have to repeat it per node.

gcloud container clusters get-credentials [CLUSTER] [FLAGS] only points kubectl at one cluster by updating your kubeconfig and retrieves no logs at all.

questions.question: You are building a Python service at Emberlight Labs and you use PyTest for unit tests. A helper function fetches rows from a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance. You want the unit tests to be fast and dependable and to isolate external dependencies so your suite of 400 tests can finish in about 4 minutes. What approach should you take to test this function?

options.text: Point unit tests at a separate Cloud SQL instance dedicated to testing
Run tests against the real database and remove test rows after each run
Use mocking to simulate the Cloud SQL client so tests run without a database
Use Cloud SQL Auth Proxy and connect tests to a short lived database

questions.correct_text: Use mocking to simulate the Cloud SQL client so tests run without a database
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Use mocking to simulate the Cloud SQL client so tests run without a database.

Unit tests should be fast, deterministic, and isolated. This method replaces the real Cloud SQL client with a fake or stub in memory and removes network latency and Cloud SQL startup overhead. It lets you verify query building and result handling with predictable fixtures and it avoids flakiness and makes it feasible to run 400 tests in about three minutes using PyTest.

You can implement this with Python's unittest.mock or the PyTest monkeypatch fixture to stub the client methods and have them return predefined rows or raise controlled exceptions. This keeps your tests focused on business logic while leaving database integration to separate integration tests.

Point unit tests at a separate Cloud SQL instance dedicated to testing adds network and service dependency which slows tests and introduces flakiness from instance availability and quotas. It also increases cost and operational burden and it is better suited to integration tests than unit tests.

Run tests against the real database and remove test rows after each run couples tests to stateful cleanup which is brittle and slow. Failures or interruptions can leave residue and cause non deterministic results and parallel runs can collide on data.

Use Cloud SQL Auth Proxy and connect tests to a short lived database still relies on an external database and requires provisioning and teardown which hurts speed and reliability. It is a fine integration test setup but it does not meet the requirement for fast and dependable unit tests.

questions.question: Skyline Seats is lifting its old ticketing system onto Google Kubernetes Engine. Five services must read and write the same shared POSIX directory at once, and you would rather not rewrite how the code touches the filesystem. What is the right way to give the pods shared storage in GKE?

options.text: Mount a bucket into each pod with the Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver and write the logs through the mounted path
Provision Filestore and present an NFS share to the cluster by creating a PersistentVolume with "ReadWriteMany" access for the pods
Create one persistent disk and use a StatefulSet so every replica mounts the same volume for log writes
Write logs to a Cloud Storage bucket by integrating the services with the Cloud Storage API

questions.correct_text: Provision Filestore and present an NFS share to the cluster by creating a PersistentVolume with "ReadWriteMany" access for the pods
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to provision Filestore and present an NFS share to the cluster by creating a PersistentVolume with ReadWriteMany access for the pods. This matches the need for a shared POSIX path that several services read and write concurrently, and it lets you mount the same network file system into each pod without touching the application code.

This approach delivers NFS-backed storage with POSIX-style file operations and supports the ReadWriteMany access mode in GKE. You can mount the volume at the exact path the legacy app expects, so the migration stays simple while five pods read and write simultaneously.

Mounting a bucket with the Cloud Storage FUSE CSI driver is not suitable, because Cloud Storage is object storage and the FUSE layer does not offer full POSIX semantics or strong multi-writer behavior for concurrent file operations. That can break workloads that rely on file locks, atomic renames, or directory semantics.

Creating one persistent disk and using a StatefulSet will not work, because Persistent Disk does not support mounting the same volume read-write across multiple nodes. A StatefulSet does not change those storage access limits.

Writing logs to a Cloud Storage bucket through the Cloud Storage API would require code changes and presents no POSIX filesystem path, so it fails the requirement to keep the application writing to a shared filesystem unchanged.
