questions.question: At BlueSky Outfitters you are building a loosely coupled, event-driven microservices platform. It needs to consume Cloud Storage object finalize events, Pub/Sub messages, and Admin Activity audit logs, then fan those out to several Cloud Run services running in two regions with as little custom integration as possible. Which Google Cloud service best provides a unified way to capture these events and route them to Cloud Run?

options.text: Pub/Sub
Eventarc
Workflows
Cloud Tasks

questions.correct_text: Eventarc
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Eventarc, because it gives you a single eventing layer that can ingest Cloud Storage object finalize events, Pub/Sub messages, and Admin Activity audit logs and route them to Cloud Run services across regions with minimal custom integration.

Eventarc ships with built-in providers for Cloud Storage and for Cloud Audit Logs, which covers Admin Activity, and it also supports triggers for Pub/Sub topics. You define triggers with attribute filters and send events straight to Cloud Run services, avoiding glue code and keeping the platform loosely coupled.

Eventarc supports regional triggers and destinations, so you can create triggers in each region and route to the Cloud Run services running there. That satisfies the requirement to trigger services across two regions while keeping a unified control plane for event routing.

Pub/Sub is a messaging service that can deliver to subscribers, but it does not natively unify Cloud Storage and Admin Activity audit events into one routing layer for Cloud Run. You would need extra log sinks and custom wiring, which clashes with the minimal-integration requirement.

Workflows orchestrates and sequences calls to services and APIs, but it offers no native event ingestion from Cloud Storage or Admin Activity audit logs and is not an event-routing service to Cloud Run.

Cloud Tasks is built for asynchronous task dispatch and rate limiting to HTTP targets, not for capturing and routing events from Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub, or Audit Logs, so it does not meet the unified event ingestion requirement.

questions.question: BrightWave Analytics runs an API on Cloud Run behind the Google Cloud external HTTP load balancer. The service emits structured JSON application logs, and the team wants those entries correlated with the load balancer logs in Cloud Logging so both show up under the same trace during investigations. What should they implement?

options.text: Turn on Cloud Trace for the Cloud Run service and rely on automatic correlation in Cloud Logging
Send all application logs to Cloud Logging and later join them with load balancer logs using a Log Analytics query
Parse the X-Cloud-Trace-Context header on each request and set logging.googleapis.com/trace on your structured log entries
Write a random UUID to logging.googleapis.com/labels on each log line

questions.correct_text: Parse the X-Cloud-Trace-Context header on each request and set logging.googleapis.com/trace on your structured log entries
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to parse the X-Cloud-Trace-Context header on each request and set logging.googleapis.com/trace on your structured log entries. This makes your application logs carry the same trace identifier that the external HTTP load balancer propagates, so Cloud Logging groups both log sets under one trace during investigations.

With this approach you extract the trace ID from the incoming trace context header and write it to the special trace field on each structured log entry in the format projects/PROJECT_ID/traces/TRACE_ID. You can also include spanId and trace_sampled to sharpen trace and log correlation. When the trace field matches the value the load balancer uses, Cloud Logging automatically links your application entries with the load balancer access logs in the trace view.

Turning on Cloud Trace and relying on automatic correlation is insufficient, because correlation requires that each log entry explicitly carry the trace field matching the load balancer trace ID. Simply enabling tracing does not guarantee your custom logs include the correct value.

Sending all application logs to Cloud Logging and joining them later with a Log Analytics query does not produce a single trace. Queries can analyze and join data, but trace correlation in Cloud Logging depends on the trace field on each entry and cannot be created after the fact by a query.

Writing a random UUID to logging.googleapis.com/labels does not work, because labels are not used for trace correlation and a random value will never match the load balancer trace identifier. The trace field must hold the exact projects/PROJECT_ID/traces/TRACE_ID value to link entries correctly.

questions.question: You need to design a REST API for a library cooperative where the API must publish paths on a single domain using HTTPS such as https://api.example.com/books, https://api.example.com/members, and https://api.example.com/loans. Each path must invoke a distinct function in your application and you need a single centralized entry point to control routing for all inbound requests. How should you deploy this API?

options.text: Build a single Cloud Function that inspects the request path and invokes code branches for each path
Deploy an API Gateway and set up three routes that forward to separate Cloud Functions backends
Create one Cloud Run service with multiple URL mappings configured in the service
Use Cloud Endpoints with a single wildcard path that proxies all traffic to one backend Cloud Function

questions.correct_text: Deploy an API Gateway and set up three routes that forward to separate Cloud Functions backends
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Deploy an API Gateway and set up three routes that forward to separate Cloud Functions backends. This meets the need to publish multiple paths under one HTTPS domain and offers a single centralized entry point to control routing for every request.

This gateway lets you define explicit routes such as books, members, and loans that each forward to a distinct backend. It integrates directly with serverless functions which keeps each endpoint isolated and versioned while keeping one public host name. It also enables consistent authentication, authorization, quotas, and logging in one place which satisfies the requirement for centralized control.

Build a single Cloud Function that inspects the request path and invokes code branches for each path is not ideal because it pushes routing into application code rather than a managed control plane. It limits per route configuration, complicates security and observability, and couples all endpoints to one deployment and scaling unit which reduces agility.

Create one Cloud Run service with multiple URL mappings configured in the service is not feasible because a single service does not provide built in path based routing to different backends. To route by path under one domain you still need an external router such as a gateway or load balancer which this option does not include.

Use Cloud Endpoints with a single wildcard path that proxies all traffic to one backend Cloud Function would forward everything to one backend and would not invoke distinct functions per path without custom logic. It also does not define centralized routes for each path. This product is treated as a legacy choice and newer exams favor the managed gateway approach for new designs.

questions.question: A news analytics startup is rolling out several microservices on GKE to run its platform. Each service must scale on its own, communicate only inside the cluster, and keep a steady network identity so service discovery stays reliable. Which approach should you implement?

options.text: Run each microservice as a Deployment, expose it with a headless Service, and have callers reach it by pod IP addresses
Run each microservice as a Deployment, front it with an Ingress backed by a LoadBalancer, and have services call one another by HTTP hostnames
Run each microservice as a Deployment, expose it with a ClusterIP Service, and have callers use the Service DNS name
Run each microservice as a StatefulSet with a LoadBalancer Service and have other services call the LoadBalancer's external IP

questions.correct_text: Run each microservice as a Deployment, expose it with a ClusterIP Service, and have callers use the Service DNS name
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to run each microservice as a Deployment, expose it with a ClusterIP Service, and have callers use the Service DNS name.

This keeps traffic inside the cluster while giving each service a stable virtual IP and DNS name for discovery. A Deployment lets each microservice scale on its own through replicas and rolling updates, and the Service abstraction fronts the shifting set of pods so clients never track pod IP changes. Service DNS provides a consistent identity that other services can call reliably.

The Service type here is internal only, which satisfies the requirement that communication stay within the cluster. As the Deployment scales, pods come and go while the Service continues routing to healthy endpoints, preserving availability and scalability without exposing anything externally.

Running each microservice as a Deployment with a headless Service and calling pod IPs is not suitable, because a headless Service allocates no virtual IP and leaves clients to resolve and pick individual pod IPs. Pod IPs change as pods reschedule or scale, breaking the requirement for a consistent identity and complicating client logic.

Fronting each Deployment with an Ingress backed by a LoadBalancer is aimed at exposing services to external clients. It adds external load balancers and public routing that internal service-to-service calls do not need and violates the internal-only requirement.

Running each microservice as a StatefulSet with a LoadBalancer Service is a poor fit, because StatefulSets target stateful workloads needing stable pod identities and storage. A LoadBalancer exposes an external IP, sending traffic outside the cluster path and risking hairpinning or extra cost. This fails the internal-only requirement and is the wrong pattern for typical stateless microservices.

questions.question: BlueLake Insights runs a production Cloud Run service that reads from the Pub/Sub topic orders-in, processes the messages, and then publishes to the topic orders-out. Over the past 45 minutes failures have spiked, and you want to reproduce the issue safely with mock messages so you can find the root cause. What should you do?

options.text: Use the gcloud CLI to publish mock messages to the live orders-in topic, raise the service logging level to DEBUG or INFO, and review the logs in Cloud Logging
Open the Google Cloud console, publish sample messages to the orders-in topic, raise the application logging level to DEBUG or INFO, and inspect the resulting logs
Install the Pub/Sub and Cloud Run emulators on your workstation, run the service locally with DEBUG or INFO logging, publish mock messages to orders-in, and review the local logs
Start a local Pub/Sub emulator, repoint the production Cloud Run service at it, then send mock messages and read the logs

questions.correct_text: Install the Pub/Sub and Cloud Run emulators on your workstation, run the service locally with DEBUG or INFO logging, publish mock messages to orders-in, and review the local logs
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to install the Pub/Sub and Cloud Run emulators on your workstation, run the service locally with DEBUG or INFO logging, publish mock messages to orders-in, and review the local logs, because it lets you reproduce the failure safely and in isolation without touching production.

Running the service locally with emulators lets you craft mock payloads, control timing and volume, and enable verbose logging without affecting live subscribers or producers. The Pub/Sub emulator mimics the API so client libraries can send and receive messages via the PUBSUB_EMULATOR_HOST setting. Local logs are easy to inspect, and you can iterate quickly while leaving production queues and services untouched.

Using the gcloud CLI to publish mock messages to the live orders-in topic drives test traffic into production, which can worsen the incident and distort metrics. It also mixes debugging changes with live traffic and offers no isolation, making root cause analysis harder.

Publishing sample messages from the Google Cloud console has the same problems, because you are still exercising the live system and risk triggering retries and side effects on downstream consumers.

Starting a local Pub/Sub emulator and repointing the production Cloud Run service at it is neither practical nor safe. The emulator is meant for local testing and is not reachable from a managed Cloud Run service in production, and changing production configuration to point at an emulator adds risk during an incident and should be avoided.

questions.question: A team at scrumtuous.com is about to publish a public REST API on Google Cloud for outside partners and wants the docs to be both interactive for developers and indexable by search engines. Which tool should they pick to define and publish it?

options.text: API Gateway with OpenAPI
Cloud Endpoints
API Gateway with gRPC
Service Directory

questions.correct_text: Cloud Endpoints
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Cloud Endpoints, because it ships with a developer portal that generates interactive documentation from your OpenAPI specification, and that portal is a public site search engines can index.

Cloud Endpoints provides an Endpoints Portal that renders rich, try-it-style documentation from the underlying API definition. The portal is customizable, hosted as a public website, and crawlable by search engines, which fits the need for both interactive docs and discoverability for external partners. Note that Cloud Endpoints is in maintenance mode, and although newer solutions like Apigee offer modern portals, among these options it is the only service that natively provides the requested developer portal and SEO-friendly publication.

API Gateway with OpenAPI manages and secures APIs from an OpenAPI configuration, yet it includes no built-in developer portal or interactive documentation, so you would have to build and host those separately and would not get SEO discoverability out of the box.

API Gateway with gRPC focuses on managing gRPC backends and optional HTTP JSON transcoding and offers no developer portal or public interactive documentation for REST consumers.

Service Directory is a service registry for service discovery within environments and is not used to publish public APIs or provide documentation, so it does not meet the requirement.

questions.question: Riverbend Health Insurance is migrating its policyholder system to Cloud Spanner. The dataset is projected to reach about 60 million records, and each policyholder can have several phone numbers on file. Support agents need to look up a policyholder fast by typing in any phone number. How should you model the schema so phone-number searches stay fast as the data scales?

options.text: Create a "Policyholders" table with an array column named "phone_numbers" and build a secondary index on that array
Keep a single "Policyholders" table where phone numbers live in a JSON field and add a secondary index on that JSON field
Create an interleaved child table named "PolicyholderPhones" under "Policyholders" and add a secondary index on the phone number column
Store phone numbers in Cloud Bigtable keyed by their E.164 values and keep "Policyholders" in Cloud Spanner with the application joining results

questions.correct_text: Create an interleaved child table named "PolicyholderPhones" under "Policyholders" and add a secondary index on the phone number column
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to create an interleaved child table named "PolicyholderPhones" under "Policyholders" and add a secondary index on the phone number column. This keeps phone-number lookups efficient as the data grows, because the index supports direct point queries and the child table models the one-to-many relationship without duplication.

This design stores each phone number as its own row keyed to the parent policyholder. The secondary index on the phone column lets Spanner seek straight to matching numbers rather than scanning large parent rows. Interleaving preserves locality between parent and child data for common access patterns, while the index gives global lookup performance for agent searches.

Creating a "Policyholders" table with an array column and indexing the array is not valid, because Spanner does not support secondary indexes on ARRAY columns. Queries would have to unnest arrays, blocking efficient index-backed lookups and forcing scans as the dataset grows.

Keeping phone numbers in a JSON field with a secondary index on that field is not correct, because Spanner does not support secondary indexes directly on JSON columns. You would need generated columns to extract normalized values for indexing, and even then a single JSON blob is a poor fit for fast equality lookups across many phone numbers.

Storing phone numbers in Cloud Bigtable keyed by E.164 while keeping policyholders in Spanner adds cross-system complexity for no benefit here. Spanner already handles this access pattern with a child table and index, and an application-level join across systems would sacrifice transactional simplicity and raise operational overhead.

questions.question: Your team at Northwind Bikes is shifting a legacy service off Compute Engine onto Google Kubernetes Engine. You want Cloud Build to turn the application code into a container image and publish it to Artifact Registry so the cluster can deploy it. Which actions make Cloud Build build and push the image to the right repository?

options.text: Run gcloud container images add-tag us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/svc-registry/app-svc us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/svc-registry/app-svc:stable

Create a file named "cloudbuild.yaml" that contains steps: - name: 'gcr.io/cloud-builders/docker' args: ['build', '-t', 'us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/svc-registry/app-svc', '.'] - name: 'gcr.io/cloud-builders/docker' args: ['push', 'us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/svc-registry/app-svc']
Run gcloud run deploy app-svc --image us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/svc-registry/app-svc
Execute gcloud builds submit from the application's source directory
Create a file named "cloudbuild.yaml" that contains steps: - name: 'gcr.io/cloud-builders/cloud' args: ['app', 'deploy'] timeout: '1800s'

questions.correct_text: Execute gcloud builds submit from the application's source directory
questions.explanation:
The correct actions are to create a file named "cloudbuild.yaml" that contains steps: - name: 'gcr.io/cloud-builders/docker' args: ['build', '-t', 'us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/svc-registry/app-svc', '.'] - name: 'gcr.io/cloud-builders/docker' args: ['push', 'us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/svc-registry/app-svc'], and to execute gcloud builds submit from the application's source directory.

The first action defines a Cloud Build configuration that runs the Docker builder to build the image and tag it with the Artifact Registry repository path in us-central1, then pushes that image to the same path. That directly fulfills the requirement to have Cloud Build create the image and publish it to Artifact Registry for later deployment to your GKE cluster.

The second action triggers Cloud Build from the source directory. Running the submit command in the directory holding the build file makes Cloud Build upload the source, read the configuration, and run the build and push steps. This is the standard workflow for creating and publishing an image with Cloud Build.

Running gcloud container images add-tag is not correct, because it only adds a new tag to an image that already exists. It neither builds nor pushes the image with Cloud Build, and it is tied to Container Registry workflows, which has been deprecated in favor of Artifact Registry, making it less likely on newer exams.

Running gcloud run deploy is not correct, because it deploys the image to Cloud Run rather than preparing an image for a GKE cluster, and it does not have Cloud Build build and push the image.

Creating a cloudbuild.yaml with an App Engine deploy step is not correct, because it targets App Engine deployment and does not build and push a container image to Artifact Registry for GKE.

questions.question: Helix Visuals has to push static assets like images and JavaScript to a worldwide audience, and the team wants very high availability, low latency, and almost no operations to run. Which storage-and-delivery setup on Google Cloud meets those aims?

options.text: Build a managed instance group that serves the files from VMs and place it behind an external HTTP(S) load balancer with Cloud CDN enabled
Deploy a Standard class regional Cloud Storage bucket for the static files and configure an external HTTP(S) load balancer with a backend bucket and Cloud CDN
Store the static content in a Standard class multi-regional Cloud Storage bucket and front it with an external HTTP(S) load balancer using a backend bucket with Cloud CDN enabled
Package the static site into a Cloud Run service and place it behind an external HTTP(S) load balancer with Cloud CDN enabled

questions.correct_text: Store the static content in a Standard class multi-regional Cloud Storage bucket and front it with an external HTTP(S) load balancer using a backend bucket with Cloud CDN enabled
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to store the static content in a Standard class multi-regional Cloud Storage bucket and front it with an external HTTP(S) load balancer using a backend bucket with Cloud CDN enabled.

This configuration gives you a serverless origin replicated across multiple geographically separate locations, which raises availability. Pairing a Cloud Storage backend bucket with an external HTTPS load balancer integrates directly with Cloud CDN, so assets are cached at edge locations and served with low latency worldwide. You also skip managing VMs or application runtimes, keeping operational overhead minimal while still providing a global anycast entry point.

Building a managed instance group that serves files from VMs is not ideal, because you must manage instances, operating systems, and scaling policies. Cloud CDN can cache, but the origin is still a fleet of VMs, which adds operational work and reduces simplicity compared with a storage bucket.

Deploying a Standard class regional bucket with a load balancer and Cloud CDN can work in many cases, but the origin lives in a single region. For very high availability you want a multi-regional or dual-region origin so that cache misses or invalidations can still be served from another location if a region has issues.

Packaging the static site into a Cloud Run service adds an unnecessary compute layer for purely static assets. You would pay for and manage a service runtime and would not gain the inherent multi-regional replication that Cloud Storage provides as a static-content origin.

questions.question: What is the right way to package a Java service straight from its source, leaving behind any VM operating-system baggage, and then ship it to Google Kubernetes Engine?

options.text: Deploy to Cloud Run
Migrate to Containers
Use Jib to build an image from source, push it to Artifact Registry, then deploy to GKE
Import the VM disk as an image on Compute Engine

questions.correct_text: Use Jib to build an image from source, push it to Artifact Registry, then deploy to GKE
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to use Jib to build an image from source, push it to Artifact Registry, then deploy to GKE. This builds a container directly from your Java project carrying no VM operating-system artifacts and aligns with the requirement to deploy on Google Kubernetes Engine.

Jib builds an OCI image from Maven or Gradle without a Dockerfile or a local Docker daemon. The image is layered so dependencies and application classes are separated, keeping only application artifacts in the image and avoiding VM remnants. You then push the image to Artifact Registry so GKE can pull it, and create a Deployment or other workload in GKE to run it.

Deploy to Cloud Run is not correct, because the target platform in the question is GKE. Cloud Run is a serverless container platform and the option does not address building from source for GKE.

Migrate to Containers focuses on turning existing VMs into containers for lift-and-shift, which can preserve OS dependencies and is not meant for building from application source. The question emphasizes starting from source and avoiding VM OS artifacts for GKE.

Import the VM disk as an image on Compute Engine moves a VM disk into Compute Engine, which is not containerization, would carry OS artifacts, and deploys nothing to GKE.

questions.question: At Nimbus Trail Media you are rolling out a new set of services on Compute Engine, and one virtual machine will not finish booting, so you need to pinpoint the cause and recover it quickly. Which actions should you take first?

options.text: Review the VPC firewall rules and custom routes that affect the instance
Check whether the boot disk has run out of space
Try connecting to the VM with a different SSH username
Verify and repair the root file system using the interactive serial console
Check whether inbound or outbound traffic to the instance is being dropped by the network

questions.correct_text: Verify and repair the root file system using the interactive serial console
questions.explanation:
The correct actions are to check whether the boot disk has run out of space and to verify and repair the root file system using the interactive serial console.

A full boot disk is a common reason a VM fails to finish starting, because the operating system and services cannot write temporary files or logs. Checking utilization quickly confirms the problem, and you can resolve it by removing unneeded files, resizing the persistent disk, and growing the filesystem so the instance can finish booting.

The interactive console gives you access even when SSH is unavailable, letting you read boot messages and run recovery commands directly. Repairing the root filesystem with tools such as fsck, or fixing fstab issues, addresses corruption or misconfiguration that stops the OS from mounting and starting, which makes it an effective first recovery step.

Reviewing VPC firewall rules and custom routes is unrelated to an operating-system boot failure. Networking rules can block connectivity but they do not stop the VM from booting.

Trying a different SSH username will not help when the VM has not finished booting or the SSH service is not running. You need out-of-band access instead.

Checking whether network traffic is being dropped focuses on connectivity rather than the root cause of a failed boot. Network drops do not prevent the guest operating system from starting.

questions.question: NeighborNet helps neighbors plan meetups, set up pick-up games, and connects small shops with nearby customers. Heading into a global launch, the company wants a uniform experience for travelers and remote communities, tighter security, and less infrastructure toil, all in line with Google's recommendations. Its setup straddles on-premises systems and Google Cloud: public APIs run on Compute Engine VMs, state lives in a single MySQL instance, data is shipped to a legacy warehouse, and analytics run on an on-premises Hadoop cluster. Logging is thin and uptime signals are noisy, so they want usage dashboards, solid API authentication and authorization, richer logs, and cloud-native analytics, plus a move to serverless for elastic scale and secure internal access. As they get ready to publish their APIs to the public in new regions, which public API service on Google Cloud should they pick?

options.text: Apigee X
Cloud Functions
Cloud Endpoints
Cloud Armor

questions.correct_text: Cloud Endpoints
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Cloud Endpoints.

Cloud Endpoints is a managed public API service that suits a serverless architecture and supplies authentication and authorization, usage dashboards, and rich logging through Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring. It supports OpenAPI and gRPC, so the team can define APIs cleanly and apply consistent policies. By running the ESPv2 proxy on services such as Cloud Run or Compute Engine, Cloud Endpoints scales elastically and can sit in multiple regions to give a consistent global experience while keeping infrastructure toil low. It also supports API keys and JWT validation and offers quota and monitoring features that strengthen security and provide clear operational signals.

Apigee X is a full-lifecycle API management platform with advanced capabilities such as monetization and a developer portal, which can be more than is needed for simply exposing public APIs with lightweight management. It adds complexity that is unnecessary for a serverless migration focused on straightforward API management and observability.

Cloud Functions is a compute service for running code in response to events or HTTP requests. It is not an API management service and does not provide centralized authentication and authorization policies, quotas, or comprehensive API analytics across multiple backends.

Cloud Armor is a web application firewall and DDoS protection service that secures applications behind load balancers. It does not offer API definition, routing, usage analytics, or developer-focused API management.

questions.question: You are writing a TypeScript single-page app that runs wholly in the browser and, from app.example.com, must save documents into each signed-in user's own Google Drive, asking for only the smallest Drive scopes and letting users grant or pull back access. Which authorization approach follows Google API best practices for reaching user data?

options.text: Use an API key to call the Drive API from the browser
Generate an OAuth client ID for a web application
Create and use a service account for Drive access
Firebase Authentication

questions.correct_text: Generate an OAuth client ID for a web application
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to generate an OAuth client ID for a web application.

This method uses Google Identity Services with OAuth so the app can obtain user consent and short-lived access tokens right in the browser. You configure a Web application client with app.example.com as an authorized JavaScript origin and request only the minimal Drive scopes such as drive.file. It supports incremental authorization and lets each user grant or revoke access through their Google Account, which aligns with best practices for accessing user data.

Using an API key to call the Drive API from the browser is wrong, because API keys only identify the calling project and are meant for access to public data. They provide no user consent or secure access to private Drive files.

Creating and using a service account for Drive access is incorrect, because a service account represents the application rather than the end user. It is designed for server-to-server scenarios, would require exposing credentials in the browser, and would not act on behalf of each user unless using domain-wide delegation, which does not fit this use case.

Firebase Authentication is not sufficient, because it establishes user identity for your app but does not by itself grant Drive API scopes or tokens. You would still need an OAuth consent flow to obtain the proper Drive access, so it does not meet the requirement.

questions.question: As scrumtuous.com's platform team brings workloads onto Google Kubernetes Engine, they want a clear definition of what a Kubernetes Pod is inside a cluster. Which statement is correct?

options.text: A virtual machine that Kubernetes creates
An abstraction that exposes an application behind a stable IP and DNS name in the cluster
The smallest deployable unit that groups one or more containers sharing the same IP address and storage volumes on a node
A YAML file that defines how to roll out an application

questions.correct_text: The smallest deployable unit that groups one or more containers sharing the same IP address and storage volumes on a node
questions.explanation:
The right answer is the smallest deployable unit that groups one or more containers sharing the same IP address and storage volumes on a node. This accurately describes a Kubernetes Pod within a cluster.

A Pod is the fundamental workload unit in Kubernetes. It can run a single container or several tightly coupled containers that need to share a network namespace and volumes. All containers in a Pod share one IP address and port space inside the cluster and are scheduled together onto the same node.

A virtual machine that Kubernetes creates is incorrect. Kubernetes schedules Pods onto nodes, which are machines or virtual machines from the underlying infrastructure. Kubernetes does not create virtual machines when it creates Pods, because Pods run containers on existing nodes.

An abstraction that exposes an application behind a stable IP and DNS name is incorrect. That describes a Kubernetes Service, which provides stable virtual IPs and DNS names to route to Pods. A Pod itself does not handle stable service discovery.

A YAML file that defines how to roll out an application is incorrect. Rollout behavior comes from higher-level controllers such as a Deployment, which you typically declare in YAML. A Pod manifest defines a Pod but does not handle rollout strategies.

questions.question: Which Cloud Build feature lets builds reuse previously downloaded dependencies to shorten build time, with no changes to your code or repository structure?

options.text: Use smaller base images
Artifact Registry remote repositories
Cloud Build named caches
The Docker no-cache flag

questions.correct_text: Cloud Build named caches
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Cloud Build named caches, because it lets you reuse downloaded dependencies across builds without changing your code or repository layout.

Cloud Build named caches persist specific directories between builds by assigning each cache a name and a path. Cloud Build restores the cached content on later builds, which speeds up package-manager operations such as npm, Maven, Gradle, or pip installs. You configure it in the build configuration, so you do not alter your source tree or modify application code.

Using smaller base images can shorten image pull times and reduce image size, but it offers no mechanism to reuse dependency downloads across different builds, and it usually means changing your Dockerfile rather than using a Cloud Build caching feature.

Artifact Registry remote repositories can proxy and cache external dependencies at the registry level, but they are not a Cloud Build feature and generally require changing dependency sources or client configuration. The question asks for a Cloud Build capability needing no code or repository changes, which this does not satisfy.

The Docker no-cache flag disables build caching and forces every step to run fresh, increasing build duration and preventing reuse of previously downloaded dependencies, which is the opposite of what is needed.

questions.question: Pixellium Retail is launching a global storefront on Google Cloud and expects spikes of up to roughly 300 thousand concurrent users during big promotions. You need session persistence designed so the site stays highly available through zone outages and keeps working even if an entire region goes down. Which approach should you implement?

options.text: Keep session data in the memory of each Compute Engine virtual machine
Use Memorystore for Redis Standard tier in a single region
Store session information in Firestore using a multi-region location
Persist sessions in a single-region Cloud SQL instance

questions.correct_text: Store session information in Firestore using a multi-region location
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to store session information in Firestore using a multi-region location.

This uses Firestore multi-region replication, so session data is synchronously replicated across independent regions and stays available during zone failures and even if an entire region becomes unavailable. Firestore is fully managed and horizontally scalable, so it can handle very high request rates during large promotions. It provides strong consistency and automatic failover, letting application instances in different regions share one session store without relying on sticky sessions.

You can set time-to-live policies and simple document schemas in Firestore, keeping session data lightweight and easy to expire. Global applications benefit because Firestore multi-region locations are designed for low-latency access and durable storage through infrastructure disruptions.

Keeping session data in each VM's memory fails, because state is tied to individual instances and is lost on restart, autoscaling, or load balancing to a different instance. A zone outage or regional failover would drop user sessions and break continuity.

Using Memorystore for Redis Standard tier in a single region is regional only, and while it can fail over across zones it does not survive a regional outage. That creates a single regional dependency for a global storefront and raises latency for users served from other regions.

Persisting sessions in a single-region Cloud SQL instance keeps the write primary in one region, so a regional outage would block writes and invalidate sessions. In-region high availability and cross-region read replicas exist, but they do not provide multi-region write availability, and the relational overhead may not suit the high write rate of session updates at peak.

questions.question: A fintech startup named Maple Ledger is preparing a production service that must achieve 99.95% (this remains a contractual target) uptime. The containers will run on Google Kubernetes Engine and the application will store transactional data in Cloud SQL. Which deployment approach should you implement to satisfy this availability objective while following Google Cloud best practices?

options.text: Create a single zonal GKE cluster and use a zonal Cloud SQL instance
Run two independent zonal GKE clusters in one region and attach a primary Cloud SQL instance with read replicas
Provision a GKE regional cluster that spans three zones and deploy a Cloud SQL instance with high availability enabled in the same region
Place GKE and Cloud SQL in the same zone to reduce latency

questions.correct_text: Provision a GKE regional cluster that spans three zones and deploy a Cloud SQL instance with high availability enabled in the same region
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Provision a GKE regional cluster that spans three zones and deploy a Cloud SQL instance with high availability enabled in the same region.

This method aligns with Google Cloud reliability guidance because a regional GKE cluster spreads the control plane and nodes across three zones which protects against a single zone failure. Cloud SQL high availability places a standby instance in a different zone and offers automatic failover which meets the higher availability requirement for a production transactional database. Keeping both services in the same region maintains low latency while still avoiding a zonal single point of failure. Together these capabilities are designed to achieve the 99.95 percent uptime target.

Create a single zonal GKE cluster and use a zonal Cloud SQL instance concentrates both the application and the database in one zone which creates a single point of failure and does not meet a 99.95 percent availability objective.

Run two independent zonal GKE clusters in one region and attach a primary Cloud SQL instance with read replicas does not provide seamless failover because Cloud SQL read replicas do not automatically promote on failure and multi cluster failover would require custom orchestration. This design risks downtime during failover and does not match Google managed high availability patterns.

Place GKE and Cloud SQL in the same zone to reduce latency reduces latency but increases risk because a zonal outage would take down both tiers which fails the required uptime goal.

questions.question: Oakline Finance has taken on a new regulation requiring that a copy of certain application logs from the payments project be delivered to a locked-down security project that only the security operations team can access. You must leave the payments project's current logging behavior untouched and use a managed solution that scales. What should you do?

options.text: Edit the _Default log bucket configuration to forward matching logs into the security project's log bucket
Schedule a Cloud Dataflow job that reads from the _Required log bucket and writes those entries to the security project's log bucket
Create a user-defined log bucket named sec-logs-archive in the security project and configure a Cloud Logging sink in the payments project to route the required logs to that bucket
Export only System Event logs from the _Required log bucket into a bucket in the security project

questions.correct_text: Create a user-defined log bucket named sec-logs-archive in the security project and configure a Cloud Logging sink in the payments project to route the required logs to that bucket
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to create a user-defined log bucket named sec-logs-archive in the security project and configure a Cloud Logging sink in the payments project to route the required logs to that bucket.

This uses Cloud Logging routing, which is fully managed and scales automatically. A sink on the payments project can match the specific application logs and deliver a duplicate to a log bucket in the locked security project while the original logs keep flowing to the existing buckets in the payments project. You can restrict access to the duplicated logs with IAM on the destination log bucket and project so only the security operations team can read them. This keeps current logging behavior unchanged and provides near-real-time delivery without custom pipelines.

Editing the _Default log bucket configuration to forward matching logs is not correct, because forwarding is configured with sinks on the resource rather than by editing a log bucket. Changing the _Default bucket would also risk altering the payments project's existing behavior, which the requirement forbids.

Scheduling a Cloud Dataflow job to read from the _Required log bucket is not correct, because it introduces needless custom processing and scheduling and is not the managed Cloud Logging routing solution. Log buckets are not meant to be read by external batch jobs, and this would not provide the simple scalable duplication that sinks offer.

Exporting only System Event logs from the _Required log bucket is not correct, because the requirement is to duplicate specific application logs, and the _Required bucket holds audit logs rather than application logs. It also suggests sending to a generic bucket, often meaning Cloud Storage, which would not preserve Cloud Logging features or meet the stated need.

questions.question: A retail platform stores transactional data in Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL, and you must surface analytics that stay only seconds behind the operational data while leaving the production instance unburdened. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Point analytical queries at a Cloud SQL read replica
Take a Cloud SQL clone and refresh it on a 30 minute cycle
Replicate Cloud SQL to BigQuery with Datastream
Schedule Cloud Functions through Cloud Scheduler to dump CSV files every 3 hours

questions.correct_text: Replicate Cloud SQL to BigQuery with Datastream
questions.explanation:
Replicate Cloud SQL to BigQuery with Datastream is the right answer.

Datastream relies on change data capture, so every insert, update, and delete in Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL is streamed into BigQuery within seconds. Because the reporting workload then executes inside BigQuery, demanding scans and joins never touch the transactional instance, which removes contention on operational resources. The pipeline is fully managed, scales as volume grows, and keeps the analytical copy fresh without adding load to the primary database.

Pointing analytical queries at a Cloud SQL read replica falls short because a replica is still backed by the transactional engine. Large analytical scans there create replica lag and resource pressure, and the replica cannot match BigQuery's columnar engine or its elastic scale for big analytical workloads.

Taking a Cloud SQL clone and refreshing it on a 30 minute cycle is a batch pattern, not a near real time one. It adds moving parts and cost, and the data goes stale between refresh windows.

Scheduling Cloud Functions through Cloud Scheduler to dump CSV files every 3 hours is an even coarser batch flow that sits far from near real time. The export and load steps add latency and fragile glue code, and the export itself can pressure the source.

questions.question: While investigating higher than normal request latency in a service with Cloud Profiler, you need a profile that reports the full clock time elapsed through each code path. Which profiling type fits?

options.text: Heap profiling
Contention profiling
Wall time profiling
CPU time profiling

questions.correct_text: Wall time profiling
questions.explanation:
Wall time profiling is correct because it records the total elapsed time through each code path, which is precisely what users perceive as request latency.

A wall time profile counts end to end duration, combining time spent executing on the CPU with time spent waiting. Those waits include I O, network round trips, lock acquisition, thread scheduling, and any other blocking. Diagnosing elevated latency demands visibility into the full clock time per code path, and this profile delivers exactly that.

Heap profiling tracks memory allocation and retention rather than time. It is the tool for chasing leaks or heavy allocators, but it says nothing about how long requests take.

Contention profiling reports how long threads block on locks and monitors, which helps locate synchronization hot spots. It ignores non lock waits and on CPU execution, so it does not represent total elapsed time.

CPU time profiling counts only the intervals when the CPU is actively running code. Because it omits I O and other blocked periods, it understates request latency and never captures the full elapsed time.

questions.question: CityConnect is a community networking platform that helps residents organize local events and lets neighborhood businesses reach nearby audiences, and it is opening in new regions staffed by teams in their own time zones. Backers want fast growth and a uniform experience for users whether they sit 8 miles or 16,000 kilometers apart, plus clear availability reporting, useful logs, and quick incident handling. Today the architecture is hybrid across on-premises systems and Google Cloud, with APIs running on Compute Engine and a lone MySQL instance in Google Cloud holding state, while releases are done by hand and logging is sparse. The roadmap requires supporting 15x more concurrent users, satisfying rules like GDPR, securing the on-premises to cloud link, introducing metrics and monitoring, hardening APIs, speeding feature validation, and scaling elastically. To cut global latency the team has already stood up database read replicas in user regions and routes reads there. With the least engineering effort, what is the most effective way to lower latency for every database operation?

options.text: Move the services to Google Kubernetes Engine and front application traffic with a global HTTP load balancer
Convert the database to Firestore in Datastore mode and serve all users from it
Migrate the database to Cloud Spanner and serve all global user traffic from a multi-region instance
Switch the database to Bigtable and use it for worldwide requests

questions.correct_text: Migrate the database to Cloud Spanner and serve all global user traffic from a multi-region instance
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Migrate the database to Cloud Spanner and serve all global user traffic from a multi-region instance.

Cloud Spanner is a managed relational database that replicates across regions automatically while preserving strong consistency, so both read and write latency drop for users on different continents and you still operate one logical database. A multi-region instance positions replicas near users and handles quorum and failover for you, so there is no need for custom sharding, hand managed replication, or invasive rewrites. Since Cloud Spanner speaks SQL and supports schemas, moving off MySQL requires far less redesign than adopting a NoSQL engine, yet it still delivers the global scale and availability the business needs with minimal engineering effort.

Moving the services to Google Kubernetes Engine and fronting application traffic with a global HTTP load balancer mainly improves request routing and compute elasticity, leaving the database as the bottleneck. With a single primary MySQL instance, writes still cross long distances and accumulate latency, so end to end database latency is not reduced.

Converting the database to Firestore in Datastore mode would force a heavy redesign away from relational schemas and SQL toward an entity based NoSQL model. Even with multi region locations, Firestore lacks the relational semantics and global transactional guarantees this workload needs, so it does not satisfy the minimal effort goal.

Switching the database to Bigtable for worldwide requests would likewise demand a major rewrite, since Bigtable is a wide column NoSQL store with no SQL or relational features. Its cross cluster replication is eventually consistent, which is unsuitable for globally consistent transactional access.

questions.question: A payments startup running on Google Cloud must connect to many external partner APIs whose owners frequently revise request and response shapes that you cannot influence. You want a client-server style that stays flexible as those contracts shift and that is widely interoperable across platforms. Which approach should you pick?

options.text: gRPC with Protocol Buffers
REST with JSON
REST with XML
gRPC with JSON

questions.correct_text: REST with JSON
questions.explanation:
REST with JSON is the correct pick because it interoperates broadly across platforms and absorbs evolving contracts without tightly binding clients to servers.

Partners and tool ecosystems adopt it nearly everywhere, so it is simple to call from browsers, mobile apps, and backend services alike. JSON is readable and lenient, letting clients ignore unfamiliar fields and keep functioning as providers add or rearrange payload elements. REST over HTTP also supports clean versioning and gradual rollout of changes, which matters when many third parties integrate at varying speeds.

gRPC with Protocol Buffers is built for performance and strong typing, but it depends on a shared Interface Definition Language and tighter coordination between teams. Frequent contract churn across many external partners becomes harder to manage, and it is not as universally supported across every client environment.

REST with XML is uncommon for modern public APIs and is more verbose. Most developers and client platforms favor JSON, which makes XML a less interoperable and less convenient option for broad partner integration.

gRPC with JSON is an unusual combination because gRPC is designed around Protocol Buffers. JSON transcoding exists, yet you still author proto contracts and take on operational overhead, and you forfeit the ubiquity and simplicity that plain REST with JSON gives heterogeneous partners.

questions.question: During traffic spikes your application receives HTTP 429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED responses from Firestore. Which approach best reduces these limit errors when load surges?

options.text: Introduce Memorystore caching while leaving the current retry policy in place
Optimize data access and use jittered exponential backoff retries
Request a Firestore quota increase and depend on standard exponential backoff
Optimize data access and use fixed interval retries

questions.correct_text: Optimize data access and use jittered exponential backoff retries
questions.explanation:
Optimize data access and use jittered exponential backoff retries is correct.

An HTTP 429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED means Firestore is throttling requests during bursts. Adding jitter to exponential backoff staggers retries so clients no longer all retry in lockstep. That breaks the thundering herd, gives the service room to recover, and still lets pending operations make progress.

Refining your access patterns then cuts the odds of hot documents and concentrated index updates. You can spread reads and writes by sharding counters, distributing keys across prefixes, batching where it helps, and pruning unnecessary indexes. Such design decisions reduce contention and smooth traffic, which directly lowers 429 occurrences during spikes.

Introducing Memorystore caching while leaving the current retry policy in place is partial: a cache may relieve some read pressure but does nothing for write throughput or for synchronized retries. The unchanged retry behavior can still produce aligned retry storms that trigger more 429 errors.

Requesting a Firestore quota increase and depending on standard exponential backoff misses the real cause of burst driven 429 errors. Some limits do not move with quota increases, and backoff without jitter can still synchronize client retries and extend the throttling.

Optimize data access and use fixed interval retries keeps a poor retry strategy. Fixed intervals tend to align clients, repeatedly overloading Firestore during surges and producing continued 429 responses.

questions.question: A Node.js web app your team is developing has to reach Google Cloud APIs while acting for users who have logged in with their Google Accounts. To obtain the tokens needed for those API requests, which authentication and authorization flow is the one to build?

options.text: Gather each user's Google username and password and forward the credentials to Google over HTTPS to obtain an access token
Put the app behind Identity-Aware Proxy and depend on IAP headers to call Google Cloud APIs as the signed in user
Use the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow by redirecting to the Google consent screen then exchange the returned code on the server for access tokens used to call Google Cloud APIs
Save the short lived authorization code in a browser cookie and pass that code directly when calling Google Cloud APIs

questions.correct_text: Use the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow by redirecting to the Google consent screen then exchange the returned code on the server for access tokens used to call Google Cloud APIs
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Use the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow by redirecting to the Google consent screen then exchange the returned code on the server for access tokens used to call Google Cloud APIs.

This is the standard web server flow for a Node.js backend that must act for signed in users. The app sends the user to the consent screen and gets back a one time authorization code, which the server exchanges for access and refresh tokens. Keeping that exchange on the server limits credential exposure and lets you refresh tokens later without prompting the user again, all while calling Google Cloud APIs with the scopes the user approved.

Gathering each user's Google username and password and forwarding the credentials to Google is wrong because Google prohibits third party apps from collecting Google Account passwords, and doing so violates security best practices. OAuth exists precisely to grant delegated access without sharing passwords.

Putting the app behind Identity-Aware Proxy and depending on IAP headers is wrong because IAP gates access to your app and can assert user identity to your backend, but it does not mint OAuth tokens for Google Cloud APIs. You still need a user OAuth flow to obtain those tokens for delegated calls.

Saving the short lived authorization code in a browser cookie and passing it directly is wrong because authorization codes are single use and short lived and must be exchanged on the server for tokens. They are not valid bearer credentials, and storing them in cookies raises the risk of interception.

questions.question: SummitPay runs a regional Google Kubernetes Engine cluster spanning three zones. You need to deploy a payment validation microservice that retains roughly 100 GiB of persistent data, survives individual pod restarts, and scales automatically with load without anyone intervening. How should you deploy it?

options.text: Run it as a DaemonSet with a Compute Engine persistent disk attached so each node hosts one pod
Create a Deployment that mounts a PersistentVolumeClaim and configure a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler to scale replicas based on metrics
Use a StatefulSet with hostPath volumes and depend on a Vertical Pod Autoscaler to adjust CPU and memory for pods
Deploy a Deployment backed by an emptyDir volume and attach a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler to absorb traffic spikes

questions.correct_text: Create a Deployment that mounts a PersistentVolumeClaim and configure a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler to scale replicas based on metrics
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Create a Deployment that mounts a PersistentVolumeClaim and configure a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler to scale replicas based on metrics. It is the only choice that delivers both durable storage across pod restarts and automatic, metric driven horizontal scaling.

A Deployment suits a microservice, and a PersistentVolumeClaim keeps the 100 GiB of data intact when individual pods restart. On GKE the claim can be backed by a Compute Engine persistent disk, and in a multi zone cluster a regional persistent disk raises availability while still attaching to one node at a time. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler then adjusts replica count from CPU or custom metrics, so the service scales on its own with no manual steps.

Running it as a DaemonSet with a Compute Engine persistent disk so each node hosts one pod is wrong because a DaemonSet places one pod on every node, which suits node level agents rather than a demand driven microservice. It cannot autoscale replica count, and a single persistent disk cannot attach to many nodes at once.

Using a StatefulSet with hostPath volumes and a Vertical Pod Autoscaler does not meet the requirements because hostPath stores data on the node filesystem, so the data is lost if the pod reschedules elsewhere. VPA only tunes resource requests and limits and does not scale the number of replicas.

Deploying a Deployment backed by an emptyDir volume fails the persistence requirement because emptyDir is wiped when the pod restarts or moves. Even though HPA would scale replicas, the service would lose its 100 GiB of data on restart.

questions.question: Your team is relocating several backend services to Google Cloud. One of them runs today on a virtual machine and has no special operating system requirements. You authored a Dockerfile, built the container, and pushed the image to Artifact Registry. You want the simplest way to serve HTTP requests while cutting infrastructure and operational effort to a minimum. Which platform should you choose?

options.text: Compute Engine
Cloud Run
GKE Autopilot
App Engine flexible environment

questions.correct_text: Cloud Run
questions.explanation:
Cloud Run is the correct option.

Cloud Run is a fully managed platform for stateless containers that scales automatically with incoming HTTP traffic and hides servers and clusters entirely. It deploys straight from Artifact Registry with little configuration and hands you a secure HTTPS endpoint by default. That matches the goal of the simplest path that minimizes infrastructure and operations while serving HTTP requests.

Compute Engine would make you provision and manage virtual machines, set up instance groups and load balancing, and own patching and autoscaling. That is far more operational work than Cloud Run for a simple containerized service.

GKE Autopilot removes node management, yet you still manage Kubernetes objects such as Deployments and Services and must reason about cluster and networking concepts. For a straightforward HTTP container that is more complex than Cloud Run.

App Engine flexible environment can run containers but carries longer startup times and instance lifecycle management and is less streamlined for generic containers. For new container based HTTP workloads, Cloud Run is the simpler and more modern choice.

questions.question: An events company called EventBridge runs its API on Cloud Run, and that API must read from a relational database. The workload is read dominant at about 95% reads and can spike to roughly 18,000 requests per second. You want the lowest possible latency and solid throughput with the least operational overhead for the connection. Which Google Cloud data store should you pick, and how should Cloud Run connect to it?

options.text: Cloud SQL, connecting through the instance public IP with the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy
Cloud Bigtable, connecting with the Bigtable client libraries
Cloud SQL and connect over private IP using the Cloud SQL connector
Cloud Spanner, connecting with the Spanner client libraries

questions.correct_text: Cloud SQL and connect over private IP using the Cloud SQL connector
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Cloud SQL and connect over private IP using the Cloud SQL connector.

The workload needs a relational database, and Cloud SQL offers managed MySQL or PostgreSQL with minimal operational effort. A private IP keeps traffic on your VPC, avoiding public egress and typically trimming latency. The Cloud SQL connectors handle secure connections with IAM and TLS and simplify configuration on Cloud Run; from Cloud Run you attach a Serverless VPC Access connector to keep that path private and simple.

A read heavy profile at this request rate can be served by Cloud SQL when you right size the instance, manage connections in the application, and optionally add read replicas for extra read throughput. That meets the throughput goal while keeping the connection method simple and dependable.

Connecting Cloud SQL through the instance public IP with the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy does work, but it runs an extra process inside your container and depends on public IP networking. That adds overhead under heavy traffic and can raise latency compared with a private IP path managed by the connector.

Cloud Bigtable with the Bigtable client libraries does not fit because Bigtable is a NoSQL wide column store while the requirement calls for a relational database.

Cloud Spanner with the Spanner client libraries is a powerful relational service for large global workloads, but it is unnecessary here and brings higher cost and adoption complexity. Cloud SQL fits the latency and throughput needs with lower operational complexity.

questions.question: InkBoard, a design studio, is launching a collaborative whiteboard service on Google Kubernetes Engine. It must hold user session state only while a session is active and drop it when the session ends, and that state must stay available even if application pods restart. Which storage approach should you choose?

options.text: Bigtable
Run Redis as an in-memory store in the GKE cluster
Cloud Firestore in Native mode
A Kubernetes emptyDir volume per pod

questions.correct_text: Run Redis as an in-memory store in the GKE cluster
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Run Redis as an in-memory store in the GKE cluster. It covers the need for short lived session data that can expire or be deleted at session end while staying reachable by new or restarted application pods, because the store lives outside the app pod lifecycle.

Running Redis in the cluster gives very low latency access and supports key expirations, so the application can set a TTL or explicitly delete keys when a session finishes. Because Redis runs as a shared service behind a Kubernetes Service, multiple pods read and write the same session data, and a restarted application pod simply reconnects to Redis and continues using the active session keys.

Bigtable is a durable wide column database for large analytical or time series workloads, not for ephemeral session data that should vanish at session end. It would keep data longer than needed and add needless operational and cost overhead.

Cloud Firestore in Native mode is a durable document database optimized for persistent data and offline synchronization. It does not offer the in memory semantics and simple key expiration model typically wanted for transient session state.

A Kubernetes emptyDir volume per pod holds data only for the pod's lifetime and is not shared across pods. The data is removed when the pod is deleted or rescheduled, which contradicts the requirement that session data survive pod restarts.

questions.question: Cobalt Imaging Labs is building a photo analysis workflow on Cloud Functions second generation. Because the chosen language has no Google Cloud client libraries, the code calls the Cloud Vision API directly over REST. The team wants those HTTP calls to authenticate as the function's attached service account and wants to avoid managing long lived keys. What is the correct way to authenticate these requests?

options.text: Create an API key for the Cloud Vision API and place it in the Authorization header
Request an OAuth 2.0 access token from the metadata server for the function's service account and include it as a Bearer token in the Authorization header
Store a service account JSON key file in Cloud Storage and load it at runtime to sign the REST requests
Obtain an identity token from the metadata server with the Vision API as the audience and place it in the Authorization header

questions.correct_text: Request an OAuth 2.0 access token from the metadata server for the function's service account and include it as a Bearer token in the Authorization header
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Request an OAuth 2.0 access token from the metadata server for the function's service account and include it as a Bearer token in the Authorization header.

This relies on the runtime's attached service account and the metadata server to mint short lived OAuth 2.0 access tokens, so rotation is automatic and you never handle long lived secrets. The token goes into the Authorization header as a Bearer token, and Google Cloud APIs such as Vision validate it against the service account's IAM permissions. It works even with no client library available, since you only need an HTTP call to the metadata server followed by the API call.

Creating an API key for the Cloud Vision API and placing it in the Authorization header is wrong because API keys are long lived and carry neither the function's identity nor its IAM permissions. API keys are not used in the Authorization header, and this would not meet the requirement to avoid managing long lived keys.

Storing a service account JSON key file in Cloud Storage and loading it at runtime is wrong because it requires creating and managing a long lived service account key. That raises risk and is unnecessary when the platform can supply short lived tokens through the metadata server.

Obtaining an identity token from the metadata server with the Vision API as the audience is wrong because identity tokens are for authenticating to services that accept OpenID Connect tokens, such as Cloud Run services and HTTP endpoints. Google APIs like Vision expect OAuth 2.0 access tokens, not identity tokens.

questions.question: A media company keeps its asset files in a Cloud Storage bucket and applies two lifecycle rules to them. The first removes any object once it reaches 150 days, while the second shifts objects into Coldline at the 120 day mark. Suppose an object has now reached 160 days, making both rules eligible during the very same evaluation pass. Which action does Cloud Storage carry out?

options.text: The storage class is switched to Coldline first, and deletion is handled on a later run
The delete action is applied to the object
The most recently created rule takes precedence
The action producing the lowest monthly cost is chosen

questions.correct_text: The delete action is applied to the object
questions.explanation:
The correct option is The delete action is applied to the object.

Cloud Storage lifecycle management evaluates every matching rule for an object and, when several actions are eligible at once, applies the one with the highest precedence. Deletion holds the highest precedence, so when an object qualifies for both deletion and a storage class transition on the same run, the object is deleted and no transition happens. At 160 days both rules qualify, so the object is removed.

The storage class is switched to Coldline first with deletion on a later run is wrong because Cloud Storage does not transition the class when deletion is also eligible. The object is removed rather than transitioned.

The most recently created rule takes precedence is wrong because creation time does not factor into lifecycle evaluation. Precedence comes from the action type, not from rule order or recency.

The action producing the lowest monthly cost is wrong because lifecycle decisions are deterministic and are not cost driven. The platform applies the predefined precedence of actions rather than computing costs.

questions.question: At Lumina Broadcasting your team uses Cloud Build to build, test, and deploy a microservices application whose code lives in several repositories split between Cloud Source Repositories and GitHub. You need every push in any repository to kick off an automated build while leaving the multi repository layout intact. What should you configure?

options.text: Set Cloud Scheduler to invoke Cloud Build on a frequent schedule
Define a single Cloud Build trigger that uses a wildcard pattern spanning all repositories
Create a separate Cloud Build trigger for each repository
Use Pub/Sub to capture repository change events and route them to one trigger

questions.correct_text: Create a separate Cloud Build trigger for each repository
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Create a separate Cloud Build trigger for each repository.

A Cloud Build trigger is bound to a single repository and listens for events such as pushes or pull requests there. When the codebase spans many repositories, you create one trigger per repository so each push starts its own automated build without disturbing the multi repository layout. This works for both Cloud Source Repositories and GitHub and lets you keep branch or tag filters and build configurations tailored to each service.

Setting Cloud Scheduler to invoke Cloud Build on a frequent schedule is wrong because a scheduler fires on time based intervals rather than on push events, so it would miss commits and could launch needless builds when nothing changed.

Defining a single Cloud Build trigger with a wildcard spanning all repositories is wrong because wildcards in triggers filter branches or tags within one repository, and a trigger cannot span multiple repositories.

Using Pub/Sub to capture repository change events and route them to one trigger is wrong because this is not the native integration for source pushes from Cloud Source Repositories or GitHub. It would require custom eventing that alters the architecture and adds complexity without meeting the requirement as cleanly as per repository triggers.

questions.question: You are a backend developer at a ticketing platform that records purchases in Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. The analytics team's heavy reporting queries are slowing the live checkout path. You must give analysts fresh order data without hurting production performance. What should you do?

options.text: Change the application to write each transaction to both Cloud SQL and Bigtable, and give the analytics team access to Bigtable
Spin up a cloned Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance for analytics and run a job every 20 minutes to sync recent changes
Create a BigQuery dataset and use Datastream to continuously replicate selected Cloud SQL tables into BigQuery
Have Cloud Scheduler invoke a Cloud Function every 2 hours to export order data as CSV files to a Cloud Storage bucket

questions.correct_text: Create a BigQuery dataset and use Datastream to continuously replicate selected Cloud SQL tables into BigQuery
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Create a BigQuery dataset and use Datastream to continuously replicate selected Cloud SQL tables into BigQuery. It supplies fresh data for analytics while isolating production traffic, so reporting no longer slows checkouts.

This uses change data capture from Cloud SQL, streaming only inserts, updates, and deletes with low latency. Analysts then query a serverless warehouse that scales for heavy scans and joins, decoupling reporting compute from the transactional database. You get near real time updates without custom sync scripts and avoid contention on production tables.

Changing the application to write each transaction to both Cloud SQL and Bigtable is unsuitable because dual writes add complexity and risk to transactional integrity. Bigtable targets large scale key value and wide column workloads rather than interactive SQL analytics and ad hoc joins.

Spinning up a cloned Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance with a 20 minute sync job is brittle and lagging. A clone is a point in time copy, and scheduled syncs add delay and operational overhead. Even kept current, it keeps analytics on a relational instance that does not scale like a warehouse and can still be resource intensive.

Having Cloud Scheduler invoke a Cloud Function every 2 hours to export CSV files yields data that is too stale, and CSV files have no query engine. This adds batch latency and forces extra pipelines before analysts can run efficient SQL.

questions.question: Granite Insights hosts workloads on Google Cloud for one of its domains and needs centralized control over customer managed encryption keys for data at rest across multiple projects. The team requires key lifecycle management with automatic rotation every 90 days, and the keys must work with Cloud Storage, BigQuery, and Compute Engine disks. Which Google Cloud service should they adopt?

options.text: Cloud Storage
Cloud Key Management Service
Cloud HSM
Secret Manager

questions.correct_text: Cloud Key Management Service
questions.explanation:
Cloud Key Management Service is the correct answer.

Cloud Key Management Service centralizes the creation and governance of customer managed encryption keys across many projects. It handles key lifecycle management, including automatic rotation on a schedule you can set to 90 days, and it integrates directly with Cloud Storage, BigQuery, and Compute Engine disks so you can enforce CMEK consistently for data at rest across those services.

Cloud HSM provides hardware security modules for hardware backed keys and acts as a protection level within KMS. By itself it does not deliver broad lifecycle management, rotation policies, or the seamless integrations across Cloud Storage, BigQuery, and Compute Engine; you still use KMS to manage and rotate keys.

Secret Manager stores application secrets such as API keys and passwords and is not used to manage CMEK for data at rest in storage systems or disks. It lacks the required integrations and automated key rotation for those services.

questions.question: Which Google Cloud logging storage approach satisfies a 6 month internal retention plus a 5 year compliance retention, keeps logs easy to search right after ingestion, and demands the least operational work?

options.text: A BigQuery export with a 5 year expiration
Cloud Logging custom bucket with 5 year retention

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Cloud Logging custom bucket with 5 year retention, because it keeps logs immediately searchable in Logs Explorer and lets you set a five year retention that covers compliance while still allowing easy search of the most recent six months with almost no operational effort.

With a custom log bucket set to five year retention, you configure retention on the managed bucket and continue using Logs Explorer for fast searches right after ingestion. This avoids export pipelines and extra storage systems, and you can shape access with log views to highlight the most recent six months for internal users while retaining the full five years for compliance.
