questions.question: An online ticketing platform runs its backend on Cloud Run, and a major release introduces a redesigned checkout that you worry may contain hidden defects. You want to direct only a small slice of live users to the new build at first while everyone else stays on the stable version, the rollout must avoid noticeable disruption, and you need to watch latency and error metrics for the new code during the trial. Which approach meets these goals?

options.text: Stand up an external HTTP load balancer with two serverless network endpoint groups pointing at separate Cloud Run services and weight a small slice of traffic to the service running the new build
Use Cloud Run revision traffic splitting to route about 10% of requests to the new revision and then raise the share as metrics remain healthy
Push the new build straight to production and keep watching logs for errors
Create a separate Cloud Run service for the new version and switch the domain mapping to it after testing

questions.correct_text: Use Cloud Run revision traffic splitting to route about 10% of requests to the new revision and then raise the share as metrics remain healthy
questions.explanation:
The correct approach is Use Cloud Run revision traffic splitting to route about 10% of requests to the new revision and then raise the share as metrics remain healthy.

Cloud Run can send a controlled percentage of requests to a new revision while the rest stay on the stable one. The service URL stays the same, so users notice no change and disruption is avoided. You can start at ten percent and ramp up gradually as latency and error rates stay healthy. Cloud Monitoring provides per revision metrics, so you can observe the canary's latency and error ratios independently before promoting it.

Standing up an external HTTP load balancer with two serverless network endpoint groups pointing at separate Cloud Run services is unnecessary and adds operational complexity. It splits traffic across different services rather than revisions, making it harder to attribute and compare metrics for a single code revision. Cloud Run already supports percentage based rollouts within one service, which better fits a low disruption canary.

Pushing the new build straight to production and watching logs does not satisfy sending only a fraction of users first and risks broad impact if defects exist. Logs alone do not give the clear per revision performance view needed for a safe trial.

Creating a separate Cloud Run service and switching the domain mapping after testing is a hard cutover rather than a gradual rollout. It can cause noticeable disruption at switchover and prevents side by side comparison of latency and errors between new and stable versions.

questions.question: You run the subscription billing platform at Vellum Media on Google Cloud. Legal policy requires that certain application access logs be kept 9 months for internal reviews while a different set must be kept 4 years for regulatory audits. You want to reduce on-premises storage and keep the logs easy to search while minimizing operational effort. How should you store incoming logs on Google Cloud?

options.text: Place logs in a Cloud Storage bucket with a 4 year retention policy
Write logs to Cloud Storage with 9 month retention, then schedule transfers to a second bucket that retains them for another 3 years and 3 months
Use Cloud Logging with two log buckets that have custom retention settings and configure a sink to route the relevant logs to each bucket
Export all logs to BigQuery with partitioned tables and set a default table expiration of 4 years

questions.correct_text: Use Cloud Logging with two log buckets that have custom retention settings and configure a sink to route the relevant logs to each bucket
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Use Cloud Logging with two log buckets that have custom retention settings and configure a sink to route the relevant logs to each bucket.

This lets you give one log bucket a retention of roughly nine months and a second bucket a retention of four years. Inclusion filters on sinks route only the required log streams to each destination, so each policy is enforced automatically. The logs stay in Cloud Logging, remaining indexed and searchable in Logs Explorer with minimal operational effort.

Placing logs in a single Cloud Storage bucket with a 4 year retention policy cannot satisfy two distinct retention requirements with one bucket, and Cloud Storage lacks the integrated search and querying experience for logs without extra tooling.

Writing logs to Cloud Storage with 9 month retention then transferring to a second bucket for another 3 years and 3 months adds needless complexity and does not keep logs easy to search. Scheduled transfers create copies and do not turn object storage into a log search solution, and managing two retention phases in object storage is operationally heavier and error prone.

Exporting all logs to BigQuery with partitioned tables and a single 4 year default expiration does not meet the nine month requirement because it assigns one four year expiration to everything. BigQuery is searchable, but you would need separate tables or datasets with different expirations, which is not what this option proposes.

questions.question: At a fintech startup named Tidelock Pay you run many microservices on Google Kubernetes Engine, each exposing a REST API through its own Kubernetes Service. You must ship new API versions without breaking current consumers and without disrupting third party integrations on your domain. You also want one managed entry point that routes to the right backend by versioned URL paths such as /v1 and /v2, following Google's recommended approach. How should you set up the client connection?

options.text: Adopt a Service Discovery system so clients pick the backend matching the requested version
Configure an Ingress with path rules that direct /v1 and /v2 traffic to their corresponding Services
Run a separate GKE cluster per API version and use DNS records to steer traffic to each versioned backend
Publish multiple API versions behind one Service and require the POST body to carry the version

questions.correct_text: Configure an Ingress with path rules that direct /v1 and /v2 traffic to their corresponding Services
questions.explanation:
The correct choice is Configure an Ingress with path rules that direct /v1 and /v2 traffic to their corresponding Services. This gives one managed entry point on your domain and routes each request to the right backend by versioned path.

On GKE an Ingress provisions a Google Cloud HTTP(S) Load Balancer that terminates TLS and supports path based routing. URL maps that match /v1 and /v2 forward traffic to the appropriate Kubernetes Services while clients keep using a single hostname. This follows Google guidance to version APIs in the URI and lets you introduce new versions without breaking existing consumers or changing client integrations.

Adopting a Service Discovery system so clients pick the backend is unsuitable because it pushes version selection to clients, increasing coupling and removing the single managed entry point on your domain.

Running a separate GKE cluster per API version with DNS steering adds needless complexity and cost, and DNS cannot route by URL path. It also brings propagation delays and makes controlled cutovers harder than edge path routing.

Publishing multiple API versions behind one Service and requiring the POST body to carry the version is wrong because load balancers match on host, path, and headers rather than request bodies. Versioning in the URI is the recommended approach, and body based routing would not work at the edge.

questions.question: A retail analytics team needs to invoke external partner APIs that require mutual TLS on outbound calls, and it must also validate API keys and enforce request rate limits. The traffic path runs Web application, then Cloud Load Balancing, then a managed component, then the partner APIs. Which Google Cloud component belongs in that managed position to satisfy these needs?

options.text: Anthos Service Mesh
Cloud Armor
Cloud Endpoints
Cloud VPN

questions.correct_text: Cloud Endpoints
questions.explanation:
Cloud Endpoints is the correct choice for the managed component between Cloud Load Balancing and the partner APIs.

Cloud Endpoints validates API keys and enforces quota based rate limiting through Google Service Control, which covers the key validation and rate limiting needs. With ESPv2, Cloud Endpoints can also establish mutual TLS toward upstream services, so it can securely call external partner APIs that demand client certificates. It sits naturally behind Cloud Load Balancing and acts as a managed API proxy for outbound calls.

Anthos Service Mesh centers on service to service communication inside a mesh and is mainly for east west traffic within clusters or across services. It is not the right managed edge component to validate API keys for a web application or to front outbound calls to external partner APIs.

Cloud Armor is a web application firewall and DDoS protection service for inbound requests to your load balancer. It neither validates API keys for applications nor performs mutual TLS as a client to external partner APIs.

Cloud VPN provides network layer site to site connectivity. It offers no application level features such as API key validation, request rate limiting, or mutual TLS to specific external APIs.

The findings need to integrate smoothly into the existing Google Cloud deployment workflow so other teams are not affected. Which approach should you take?

options.text: Connect your Aqua Security deployment with Artifact Registry to perform image scans
Turn on the Container Scanning capability in Artifact Registry and scan the images that Cloud Build pushes
Activate Binary Authorization and require an attestor that certifies the image has no vulnerabilities
Push the built images to Docker Hub and execute vulnerability scans there

The option Push the built images to Docker Hub and execute vulnerability scans there relocates artifacts outside Google Cloud and modifies existing workflows. It adds permission and egress concerns and does not blend cleanly with native deployment phases in Google Cloud.

questions.question: At Cascade Courier, a microservice on Google Kubernetes Engine reads from a Pub/Sub subscription and processes messages. The publish rate is very uneven, and roughly every 30 minutes there are brief surges where up to 65,000 messages arrive at once. You need to keep processing latency low by automatically adjusting the number of pods based on the backlog rather than CPU. Which GKE feature should you configure to adapt the workload automatically?

options.text: Vertical Pod Autoscaler in Auto mode
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler with an external metric from Cloud Monitoring
Cluster Autoscaler on the node pool
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler based on average CPU utilization

questions.correct_text: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler with an external metric from Cloud Monitoring
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Horizontal Pod Autoscaler with an external metric from Cloud Monitoring.

With the Cloud Monitoring adapter, the HPA can use the Pub/Sub subscription backlog metric to drive replica counts. You configure a target such as undelivered messages per pod, and the HPA rapidly increases pods during the 65,000 message bursts and scales them back down once the queue drains. This keeps processing latency low because scaling decisions are tied directly to backlog instead of resource usage.

Vertical Pod Autoscaler in Auto mode tunes CPU and memory requests for existing pods and may restart them to apply changes. It does not change the number of pods and cannot react to a Pub/Sub backlog metric, so it will not satisfy the requirement.

Cluster Autoscaler on the node pool only adds or removes nodes when pods are pending due to insufficient capacity. It does not determine how many replicas of your workload should run, and it cannot scale based on a queue backlog on its own.

Horizontal Pod Autoscaler based on average CPU utilization reacts to CPU rather than message backlog. A pull based Pub/Sub consumer can show low CPU while a sizable queue builds up, which would fail to keep latency low.

Around 250 external developers at brighttrail-dev.io are expected to integrate within the first 75 days, and you must provide usage metrics while blocking any unauthorized calls. Which Google Cloud service configuration should you choose?

options.text: Cloud Endpoints with Identity and Access Management (IAM)
API Gateway integrated with Identity and Access Management (IAM)
API Gateway only
API Gateway with Cloud Logging

questions.correct_text: API Gateway integrated with Identity and Access Management (IAM)
questions.explanation:
The right pick is API Gateway integrated with Identity and Access Management (IAM). This combination delivers built in authentication and authorization to stop unauthorized calls, and it provides out of the box usage metrics through Cloud Monitoring and logs through Cloud Logging, which fits a public mobile API consumed by hundreds of external developers.

This ensures only authenticated and authorized callers reach your backend, while the gateway automatically emits request counts, latency, and error metrics to Cloud Monitoring along with detailed request logs to Cloud Logging. The combination satisfies both the need for usage visibility and strong access control for a public API.

Cloud Endpoints with Identity and Access Management (IAM) is not the preferred option for new designs. Google recommends moving to API Gateway, and there is dedicated guidance to migrate. While it can enforce auth and provide metrics, it is an older solution and is less likely to be the best answer on current exams.

API Gateway only does not satisfy the need to prevent unauthorized calls because it lacks an authentication and authorization layer in this configuration. You must pair the gateway with IAM or another supported auth method to restrict access.

API Gateway with Cloud Logging emphasizes collecting logs, which helps troubleshooting, but logging by itself does not block unauthorized requests and is not a replacement for authentication and authorization. You still need IAM or another auth control to secure the API, and metrics need Cloud Monitoring rather than logs alone.

questions.question: Brookdale Outfitters is rolling out a checkout service on Google Kubernetes Engine and needs each pod that is being terminated during a rolling update to stop receiving new traffic and finish any in flight work before it is removed. Which practice should they adopt to ensure a graceful shutdown of each pod?

options.text: Define a Pod Disruption Budget for the Deployment
Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds to allow sufficient time for graceful shutdown
Use a liveness probe
Add a readiness probe

questions.correct_text: Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds to allow sufficient time for graceful shutdown
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds to allow sufficient time for graceful shutdown.

When a Pod is terminated, Kubernetes sends SIGTERM to the containers and waits for the duration you set in terminationGracePeriodSeconds before sending SIGKILL. This grace period lets the application stop accepting new work and finish any in flight requests during a rolling update. You can also pair this with a preStop hook or signal handling so the service drains cleanly while terminationGracePeriodSeconds guarantees there is enough time to complete the shutdown.

Define a Pod Disruption Budget for the Deployment is not correct because a disruption budget only limits how many Pods can be voluntarily disrupted at one time and it does not control the shutdown behavior of an individual Pod or grant time to finish in flight work.

Use a liveness probe is not correct because liveness triggers restarts when a container is unhealthy and it does not manage graceful termination or traffic draining during updates.

Add a readiness probe alone is not correct because that probe only controls whether new traffic is sent to a Pod and it does not ensure the Pod gets enough time to finish existing requests without terminationGracePeriodSeconds.

questions.question: Marlowe Logistics is migrating its event tracking workload to Cloud Bigtable, and the team needs row keys that operators can easily read while also spreading traffic evenly across the cluster to prevent hotspots, so which row key strategy should they choose?

options.text: Use a truncated SHA256 of the full row contents as the row key
Build row keys by joining several human readable attributes and place the most high cardinality attribute first
Use a Unix epoch timestamp in microseconds as the entire row key
Use monotonically increasing integers as the primary key for each new row

questions.correct_text: Build row keys by joining several human readable attributes and place the most high cardinality attribute first
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Build row keys by joining several human readable attributes and place the most high cardinality attribute first.

This approach matches how Cloud Bigtable stores data because rows are sorted lexicographically by the key. Placing a high cardinality attribute first spreads keys across tablets, which evens out write and read traffic and reduces hotspots. Joining human readable attributes keeps the key understandable for operators while still letting you order the fields to support common range scans and locality.

Use a truncated SHA256 of the full row contents as the row key would distribute keys well, but it fails the human readable requirement and removes the ability to perform natural range scans. Tying the key to the entire row contents is also risky because any change to the data would change the key.

Use a Unix epoch timestamp in microseconds as the entire row key produces a strictly increasing key that concentrates writes on the most recent tablet and causes hotspots. It also does not naturally group related entities for efficient scans.

Use monotonically increasing integers as the primary key for each new row has the same hotspot problem because inserts always land at the end of the keyspace.

questions.question: Crestline Analytics is moving its microservices onto Google Kubernetes Engine with container images in Artifact Registry, and a Cloud Build pipeline pushes about 25 images per day. The security team requires that workloads with known critical CVEs never reach any cluster. What should you implement in the build workflow and at deployment time to enforce this?

options.text: Run Web Security Scanner against the staging service URL and block the release if critical issues appear while using Binary Authorization to gate the rollout

Turn on Artifact Analysis scanning in Artifact Registry, then have Cloud Build query the Container Analysis API for critical findings and create an attestation that is required by a Binary Authorization policy before GKE deployment
Review vulnerability reports for images in the Cloud Console and have a release engineer manually create an attestation that Binary Authorization will require before deployment
Deploy an OPA Gatekeeper admission policy in the clusters that denies images unless they carry a specific label indicating no critical CVEs

questions.correct_text: Turn on Artifact Analysis scanning in Artifact Registry, then have Cloud Build query the Container Analysis API for critical findings and create an attestation that is required by a Binary Authorization policy before GKE deployment
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Turn on Artifact Analysis scanning in Artifact Registry, then have Cloud Build query the Container Analysis API for critical findings and create an attestation that is required by a Binary Authorization policy before GKE deployment.

This approach automates vulnerability detection during the build stage and enforces admission control at deploy time. Artifact Registry vulnerability scanning produces findings in Container Analysis that include severity and package details. A build step can query for critical issues and fail early or move on to create a signed attestation only when the image is clean. A Binary Authorization policy on the clusters requires that attestation, which prevents images with critical CVEs from being admitted. This forms a reliable and scalable gate that fits a pipeline that pushes dozens of images daily.

Run Web Security Scanner against the staging service URL and block the release if critical issues appear while using Binary Authorization to gate the rollout is wrong because Web Security Scanner tests web application endpoints after deployment rather than image CVEs before deployment. It does not provide the authoritative image vulnerability metadata needed for admission control, and it does not integrate to create attestations bound to container images.

Review vulnerability reports for images in the Cloud Console and have a release engineer manually create an attestation that Binary Authorization will require before deployment is wrong because a manual process is error prone and does not scale to frequent image pushes. The requirement demands a reliable automated gate, so human review could let vulnerable images slip through.

Deploy an OPA Gatekeeper admission policy in the clusters that denies images unless they carry a specific label indicating no critical CVEs is wrong because labels can be forged or omitted and do not represent verified vulnerability status. Gatekeeper rules on labels alone cannot authoritatively evaluate CVE findings. Binary Authorization with attestations based on Container Analysis data offers a stronger integration purpose built for this control.

You want to deploy the application on Google Cloud with minimal operations overhead and restrict access to people signed in with their company Google accounts, and you prefer a serverless platform that integrates with Google identity. Which actions should you take to meet these requirements?

options.text: Provision a managed instance group on Compute Engine and run the web app behind an HTTP load balancer
Package the application into a container image and run it on Cloud Run
Configure Identity Aware Proxy and grant roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor to the employee group
Protect the service with Identity Aware Proxy and grant roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor to the workforce group
Build a custom sign in flow using a Cloud SQL table of users and password hashes

questions.explanation:
The correct actions are Package the application into a container image and run it on Cloud Run and Protect the service with Identity Aware Proxy and grant roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor to the workforce group.

Packaging the application into a container image and running it on Cloud Run meets the serverless and minimal operations requirement, since the platform handles scaling, patching, and availability for you. It comfortably serves an internal audience of this size and integrates cleanly with Google identity controls for secure access.

Protecting the service with Identity Aware Proxy and granting roles/iap.httpsResourceAccessor to the workforce group ensures only users signed in with company Google accounts can reach the app. IAP enforces Google identity in front of HTTPS resources, and assigning the workforce group the HTTPS IAP access role provides the intended gated access for employees.

Provisioning a managed instance group on Compute Engine behind an HTTP load balancer is a poor fit because it is not serverless and adds operational work to manage instances, images, autoscaling, and patching. It also does not by itself integrate with Google identity for per user access control.

Configuring Identity Aware Proxy and granting roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor to the employee group is wrong because that role applies to IAP TCP forwarding rather than to web applications over HTTPS, so it would not grant access to an IAP protected HTTPS endpoint.

Building a custom sign in flow with a Cloud SQL table of users and password hashes contradicts the requirement to integrate with Google identity and increases operational and security burden. It needlessly duplicates identity management already provided by Google Workspace and IAP.

questions.question: A travel booking startup is launching a microservices platform on Cloud Run with supporting workflows in Cloud Functions. The platform now spans roughly 25 services, and frequent blue green releases trigger endpoint changes. Managing environment variables for service URLs has become brittle and hard to scale. You want a managed approach where services register at deploy time and clients can discover them at runtime. What should you implement?

options.text: Publish service endpoints in Cloud DNS private zones with SRV or TXT records and have clients resolve them with DNS lookups
Call the Cloud Run Admin API and Cloud Functions API on startup to enumerate deployed services in the project and cache their URLs
Create a Service Directory namespace and register Cloud Run and Cloud Functions services during deployment, then query them through the API at runtime
Run a HashiCorp Consul cluster on GKE, register each service with Consul during deployment, and have clients query Consul for locations

questions.correct_text: Create a Service Directory namespace and register Cloud Run and Cloud Functions services during deployment, then query them through the API at runtime
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Create a Service Directory namespace and register Cloud Run and Cloud Functions services during deployment, then query them through the API at runtime.

This approach offers a fully managed service registry that fits microservices on serverless platforms. You register endpoints at deploy time, and clients can discover them at runtime by calling an API or using DNS. It handles frequent blue green releases because the registry becomes the single source of truth for current endpoints and metadata, which removes brittle environment variable wiring and reduces configuration drift.

It also aligns with the requirement for a managed solution. You avoid running your own discovery infrastructure while gaining features like regional namespaces, access control, endpoint health and attributes, and consistent lookups across services and languages.

Publish service endpoints in Cloud DNS private zones with SRV or TXT records and have clients resolve them with DNS lookups is not ideal for dynamic service discovery. DNS records are not a purpose built registry for serverless endpoints, record management is manual or scripted, propagation is governed by TTLs, and SRV or TXT records do not provide the richer metadata or lifecycle integration needed for frequent blue green changes.

Call the Cloud Run Admin API and Cloud Functions API on startup to enumerate deployed services in the project and cache their URLs is brittle and not scalable. It requires custom code, elevated permissions, caching and staleness handling, and it still lacks a canonical registry with attributes or health. Startup enumeration does not satisfy ongoing runtime discovery when endpoints change during releases.

Run a HashiCorp Consul cluster on GKE, register each service with Consul during deployment, and have clients query Consul for locations contradicts the requirement for a managed approach. It adds operational overhead to deploy, scale, secure, and upgrade a discovery cluster and complicates networking for serverless clients. A native managed registry is the intended solution on this platform.

questions.question: The fintech startup Crescent Ledger is launching a globally reachable set of about 15 APIs running on Cloud Run and GKE in multiple regions across two continents. Several services use gRPC while the rest use OpenAPI. You need a managed control plane that provides fine grained access control with API keys and JWTs, enforces per client quotas, supplies rich usage analytics, and uses an efficient proxy to keep latency low. Which Google Cloud product should you adopt to manage these APIs?

options.text: Cloud Run
Cloud Endpoints
API Gateway
Cloud Functions

questions.correct_text: Cloud Endpoints
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Cloud Endpoints.

Cloud Endpoints provides a managed control plane for APIs and supports both OpenAPI and gRPC, which matches the mix in the scenario. It enforces API keys and JWT authentication, applies per client quotas through Google Cloud Service Control, and offers rich usage analytics through Cloud Monitoring and Logging. Its efficient Cloud Endpoints ESPv2 Envoy based proxy can be deployed alongside services on Cloud Run and GKE, which keeps latency low and scales well across regions.

Cloud Run is a serverless compute platform for running containers. It does not provide full API management with fine grained access control, per client quotas, or dedicated API analytics, so it does not satisfy the requirements.

API Gateway is a fully managed gateway that works well for simple serverless backends, yet it adds an extra network hop and offers less flexibility for colocating the proxy with your services. The question emphasizes an efficient proxy and detailed controls across gRPC and OpenAPI workloads on GKE and Cloud Run, which better aligns with Cloud Endpoints.

Cloud Functions is an event driven compute service and not an API management product. It does not provide the required API keys and JWT enforcement, per client quotas, or rich analytics for managing multiple external APIs.

questions.question: You are building microservices for a retail analytics startup called Summit Retail Labs, and everything runs in containers. Your Cloud Build pipeline builds images, runs a full regression test stage, and pushes the artifacts to Artifact Registry. You have already enabled Binary Authorization on your GKE clusters. You must guarantee that only images that have successfully passed regression tests can be admitted to the clusters. What should you do?

options.text: Turn on Container Analysis vulnerability scanning and in the build pipeline generate an attestation for images with no high or critical findings
Use Cloud Deploy with a manual approval gate that approves a release only when the regression stage passes
Create a Binary Authorization attestor and policy and have the Cloud Build pipeline write an attestation only when the regression tests succeed
Apply the Restricted Pod Security Admission profile to the namespaces and sign passing images with cosign in the pipeline

questions.correct_text: Create a Binary Authorization attestor and policy and have the Cloud Build pipeline write an attestation only when the regression tests succeed
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Create a Binary Authorization attestor and policy and have the Cloud Build pipeline write an attestation only when the regression tests succeed.

This approach uses Binary Authorization admission control in GKE. You define a policy that requires an attestation from a trusted attestor, and the pipeline writes that attestation only when the regression suite succeeds. The cluster admits only images that carry the required attestation, which directly enforces that only passing builds can run.

Turn on Container Analysis vulnerability scanning and in the build pipeline generate an attestation for images with no high or critical findings is wrong because vulnerability severity does not prove that regression tests passed. Scanning results are about known issues in dependencies, and without a policy tied to test pass attestations you cannot guarantee admission only for tested images.

Use Cloud Deploy with a manual approval gate that approves a release only when the regression stage passes is wrong because a manual approval is a release workflow control and not a cluster admission control. It does not integrate with admission decisions at deploy time and it can be bypassed outside that pipeline.

Apply the Restricted Pod Security Admission profile to the namespaces and sign passing images with cosign in the pipeline is wrong because Pod Security Admission enforces workload security settings and not image provenance or test outcomes. Cosign signatures alone do not restrict admission unless verified by an admission policy, and this option does not establish such enforcement.

questions.question: A GKE cluster hosts a photo sharing service that experiences irregular surges during marketing pushes. The service must grow capacity quickly to maintain high availability during bursts and then reduce usage when traffic is light to control costs. Which autoscaling configuration should you use?

options.text: Use a custom metric for pending request count and scale pods via a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler
Create a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler that scales on CPU and memory utilization
Rely only on Cluster Autoscaler to add and remove nodes
Enable Vertical Pod Autoscaler to adjust CPU and memory requests during peaks

questions.correct_text: Create a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler that scales on CPU and memory utilization
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Create a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler that scales on CPU and memory utilization. This configuration matches the requirement to rapidly increase capacity during marketing surges and to scale back down when traffic subsides, which keeps availability high and costs controlled.

CPU and memory utilization are native resource metrics in GKE that are available without extra setup. This approach increases pod replicas quickly when containers are under pressure and then reduces replicas when usage falls. It is simple to configure, reacts well to bursty traffic, and avoids the overhead of managing additional metrics pipelines.

Use a custom metric for pending request count and scale pods via a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler is unnecessary for the scenario as described and adds complexity. Custom metrics require instrumentation and publishing as well as careful threshold tuning, and they are best used when resource usage does not correlate with demand which is not indicated here.

Rely only on Cluster Autoscaler to add and remove nodes is insufficient because it changes node count rather than pod replicas. Without scaling the number of pods, your service may not add capacity quickly enough during a surge even if more nodes become available.

Enable Vertical Pod Autoscaler to adjust CPU and memory requests during peaks is not appropriate for sudden bursts because it rightsizes requests and can cause pod restarts rather than quickly adding replicas. It also conflicts with using a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler on CPU or memory for the same workload in GKE.

questions.question: A service hosted on Cloud Run depends on a backend that has become sluggish, and you want to harden the service against that slowness while continuing to run it on Cloud Run. Which technique is the better fit?

options.text: Configure client timeouts and retries with exponential backoff
Client circuit breaker
Increase Cloud Run vCPU and memory
Enable Cloud Run automatic retries

questions.correct_text: Client circuit breaker
questions.explanation:
Client circuit breaker is the correct option.

This pattern notices when a dependency turns slow or error prone and fails fast once thresholds are crossed. It keeps Cloud Run instances from being tied up waiting on long downstream calls and sheds load so the dependency can recover. You implement it in your service code with a library and keep the workload on Cloud Run while improving overall resilience and latency.

Configuring client timeouts and retries with exponential backoff is not enough on its own for a slow dependency, because repeated retries can amplify pressure downstream and prolong saturation. Timeouts are necessary hygiene, but without a breaker you keep pushing work into a system that cannot respond promptly.

Increasing Cloud Run vCPU and memory does not address the root cause, which is downstream slowness. More resources can even raise concurrency and generate more requests against the struggling dependency, making things worse.

Enabling Cloud Run automatic retries applies to retrying requests that clients make to your Cloud Run service and does not make your service more resilient to a slow dependency it calls. It can also cause duplicate work if requests are not idempotent and does nothing to short circuit slow downstream calls.

questions.question: Picture an organization where a dozen development squads each operate inside their own dedicated Google Cloud project. You have been asked to design an access scheme that is uniform, scales as the company expands, and reflects what Google recommends. How would you grant each squad's developers access to their project?

options.text: Grant access at the folder to all developers with roles assigned directly to each user and give them the project number
Create one shared service account per team with Owner on the project and hand out the key file to team members
Create a Google Group for each team, add the developers to the group, grant the required roles to the group on the project, and share the project ID
Add each developer directly to the project with the needed roles and send them the project ID

questions.correct_text: Create a Google Group for each team, add the developers to the group, grant the required roles to the group on the project, and share the project ID
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Create a Google Group for each team, add the developers to the group, grant the required roles to the group on the project, and share the project ID.

This centralizes membership in a group and binds IAM roles to that group on the specific project. It honors least privilege because you grant only the roles each team needs on its own project. It scales as teams grow and change, since onboarding and offboarding become adding or removing group members rather than editing project policies per person. Sharing the project ID is appropriate because it is the human friendly identifier developers use to find the project.

Granting access at the folder to all developers with per user role assignments and the project number is overly broad, because it spreads access across every project in the folder and breaks least privilege. Assigning roles directly to individuals does not scale across many teams with frequent personnel changes, and the project number is not what users normally need since the project ID is used in the Console and most tools.

Creating one shared service account per team with Owner and distributing the key file is insecure and against guidance. Humans should not use shared service account keys, distributing keys raises compromise risk, and the Owner basic role grants far too broad permissions for routine access.

Adding each developer directly to the project with the needed roles and the project ID can work for a tiny team but does not scale. Per user bindings increase operational overhead and lead to stale access when people change teams or leave, while groups simplify management and improve security and auditability.

questions.question: Your microservices workload runs on a managed Containers as a Service offering, and the platform team you head is small. Latency and throughput SLOs are all green, but over the last six weeks the rate at which you ship features has slipped by roughly a third. Among the inherent compromises of choosing a CaaS model, which one is the likeliest explanation for this slower release pace?

options.text: Longer container image build and vulnerability scanning cycles in Cloud Build and Artifact Registry delay merges and deployments
The team has a limited ability to implement DevOps and continuous delivery practices
Engineers are spending more time on container orchestration and cluster lifecycle operations than on feature work
The platform has a smaller ability to serve heavy traffic bursts

questions.correct_text: Engineers are spending more time on container orchestration and cluster lifecycle operations than on feature work
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Engineers are spending more time on container orchestration and cluster lifecycle operations than on feature work.

A managed Containers as a Service platform still leaves substantial operational responsibility with the team. Cluster design, upgrades, node and workload autoscaling, network and security policy configuration, observability, cost management, and incident troubleshooting all demand ongoing effort. That operational toil competes directly with product development and can lower feature throughput even while the application meets its latency and throughput objectives.

Longer container image build and vulnerability scanning cycles in Cloud Build and Artifact Registry is not an inherent trade off of a CaaS platform. Build and scan times can be reduced with caching, parallelization, and targeted policies, and scanning can run asynchronously or be tuned, so this would not typically cause a sustained drop in delivery rate.

The team having a limited ability to implement DevOps and continuous delivery practices is inaccurate. Kubernetes based platforms are designed to enable CI and CD and GitOps workflows and usually strengthen DevOps practices rather than restrict them.

The platform having a smaller ability to serve heavy traffic bursts does not match the scenario. The SLOs are being met and managed CaaS platforms provide robust autoscaling, so burst capacity is unlikely to be the cause of slower releases.

questions.question: You are rolling out four microservices onto one regional GKE cluster. The constraints are that every service comes up with three replicas and that callers elsewhere in the cluster always address it through a fixed name that survives scaling events. Which Kubernetes design meets both constraints?

options.text: Expose each microservice with an Ingress and have internal callers use the Ingress IP while the microservice runs as a Deployment
Run each microservice as a single Pod, create a ClusterIP Service, then reference the Pod addresses from other services
Create a Deployment per microservice and expose each one with a ClusterIP Service then use the Service DNS name for interservice communication
Use a StatefulSet for each microservice with a headless Service so callers connect to individual Pod hostnames

questions.correct_text: Create a Deployment per microservice and expose each one with a ClusterIP Service then use the Service DNS name for interservice communication
questions.explanation:
The correct design is Create a Deployment per microservice and expose each one with a ClusterIP Service then use the Service DNS name for interservice communication.

A Deployment lets each microservice start with the required three replicas because it manages replica sets and rolling updates. Exposing it through a ClusterIP Service yields a stable virtual IP and DNS name that persist as Pods are rescheduled or scaled. Other services call that Service DNS name, which provides built in load balancing across healthy Pods and keeps callers decoupled from ephemeral Pod IPs.

Exposing each microservice with an Ingress and having internal callers use the Ingress IP is inappropriate because Ingress is intended for HTTP or HTTPS traffic entering the cluster from outside. Using an Ingress IP for in cluster calls bypasses Kubernetes service discovery and does not give the simple stable service name internal clients should use.

Running each microservice as a single Pod with a ClusterIP Service and referencing Pod addresses fails the replica requirement and is fragile. A single Pod cannot provide three replicas, and Pod IPs change on rescheduling, so referencing Pod addresses is not stable.

Using a StatefulSet per microservice with a headless Service is unnecessary for typical stateless microservices and provides no single stable name with automatic load balancing. StatefulSets and headless Services suit workloads needing stable Pod identities and direct Pod addressing, which complicates callers and is not needed here.

questions.question: Crimson Fox Apps is preparing the backend for a single player mobile game that will see long idle periods and sudden traffic bursts. The engineers want to minimize operations work, and they want to lower costs during quiet times while still scaling rapidly when demand rises. Which Google Cloud compute platform best fits these requirements?

options.text: App Engine flexible environment
Compute Engine managed instance groups
Cloud Run
Google Kubernetes Engine with cluster autoscaling

questions.correct_text: Cloud Run
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Cloud Run.

This service is fully managed and container based, so there is very little to operate. It scales automatically with incoming requests and can scale to zero during long idle periods, which reduces costs when the game is quiet. When traffic spikes, it rapidly creates more instances to handle the burst, which matches the pattern of a single player mobile game backend with sudden surges.

App Engine flexible environment is not ideal here because it keeps instances running and does not scale to zero in practice, which means you continue paying during idle periods. It also has longer startup times, so it is less responsive to sudden bursts compared to a serverless option.

Compute Engine managed instance groups can autoscale, but you still manage virtual machines, images, and patching. Instance startup is slower than on a serverless platform, and the operational burden is higher than needed for this scenario.

Google Kubernetes Engine with cluster autoscaling can scale nodes and pods, but you still operate a Kubernetes cluster and its components. There is more complexity and some baseline costs, so it is not as simple or cost efficient during idle times as a serverless platform.

questions.question: Westlake Logistics moved a set of services into Google Cloud, and their long established on premises monitoring suite that also ingests cloud data is slow to raise high priority alerts for the new deployments. What should the team do to obtain timely visibility without forcing an abrupt tooling change?

options.text: Export application logs to BigQuery and create scheduled queries and alerts to detect incidents
Adopt Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring for collection, dashboards, and alerting, and route alert notifications into the existing monitoring platform
Install the Ops Agent on the Compute Engine virtual machines to enhance metrics and log collection
Retire the legacy monitoring suite and perform a complete cutover to Cloud Monitoring

questions.correct_text: Adopt Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring for collection, dashboards, and alerting, and route alert notifications into the existing monitoring platform
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Adopt Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring for collection, dashboards, and alerting, and route alert notifications into the existing monitoring platform.

This approach uses Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring to collect metrics and logs natively in Google Cloud, which gives near real time dashboards and alerting policies so the team can detect incidents quickly. By forwarding alert notifications to the existing platform through supported channels such as webhooks, Pub/Sub, or email, the team preserves current workflows and gains timely visibility without a disruptive change.

It supports hybrid environments and scales across virtual machines, containers, and serverless services. The team can define metric and log based alerts with appropriate thresholds and notification strategies, then deliver those notifications to both the legacy suite and on call destinations to ensure continuity.

Export application logs to BigQuery and create scheduled queries and alerts to detect incidents is primarily an analytics pattern, and scheduled queries introduce delay, so it does not meet the need for timely alerts. It also increases operational overhead compared with using built in alerting from the native monitoring stack.

Install the Ops Agent on the Compute Engine virtual machines to enhance metrics and log collection improves data collection on virtual machines but does not address the slow alerting path, and it leaves other Google Cloud services uncovered. Without moving alert evaluation to a faster system, high priority alerts will still be delayed.

Retire the legacy monitoring suite and perform a complete cutover to Cloud Monitoring conflicts with the requirement to avoid an abrupt tooling change. A gradual integration that routes notifications into the existing platform is safer and provides timely visibility now.

questions.question: Aurora FinTech runs a microservice on GKE across three environments: development, UAT, and production, with UAT pipelines executing in Cloud Build. Artifact Analysis is already wired into Cloud Build and Binary Authorization is enabled across all the related Google Cloud projects. You have created an attestor and must guarantee that only container images passing the UAT checks can roll out to the production cluster. What should you do next?

options.text: After UAT completes, sign the attestation with a key stored as a Kubernetes secret then add a GKE cluster specific rule in Binary Authorization on the production project policy
After UAT completes, sign the attestation with a key managed in Cloud KMS then add a GKE cluster specific rule in Binary Authorization on the production project policy
After UAT completes, sign the attestation with a key managed in Cloud KMS then configure a default rule in Binary Authorization on the UAT project
Use Cloud Deploy with a manual approval gate to promote the image to production

questions.correct_text: After UAT completes, sign the attestation with a key managed in Cloud KMS then add a GKE cluster specific rule in Binary Authorization on the production project policy
questions.explanation:
The correct option is: After UAT completes, sign the attestation with a key managed in Cloud KMS then add a GKE cluster specific rule in Binary Authorization on the production project policy.

This ties the UAT success signal to a cryptographic attestation created with a secure KMS managed key and then enforces that signal exactly where it matters, the production cluster. Binary Authorization evaluates policy in the project that owns the target cluster, and a cluster specific rule on the production project policy admits only images carrying the required attestation. A KMS managed key is the recommended and supported way to manage attestor keys and gives strong key protection with IAM based control.

Signing the attestation with a key stored as a Kubernetes secret then adding a cluster specific rule on production is wrong because storing private keys in Kubernetes secrets is insecure and not the recommended way to manage attestor keys. Binary Authorization supports and recommends Cloud KMS managed keys or other supported providers for signing.

Signing the attestation with a KMS managed key but then configuring a default rule on the UAT project is wrong because enforcement must occur where deployment happens. A default rule on the UAT project does not protect the production cluster and would not stop untrusted images from reaching production.

Using Cloud Deploy with a manual approval gate is wrong because a manual approval is a process control, not a cryptographic guarantee. Without a Binary Authorization policy requiring the attestation, an approval gate cannot ensure only UAT validated images reach the production cluster.

questions.question: Smart meters stream telemetry into your platform at around 7,500 messages each second, and you have a dozen separate microservices, each of which has to see every single event for its own task, whether that is enrichment, raising alerts, or long term archival. The services must scale independently and stay loosely coupled from whatever is producing the data. Which Google Cloud building block should you put in place?

options.text: Cloud SQL with a table for incoming events that each service queries for new rows
Cloud Pub/Sub with a single topic and one subscription per microservice so each service receives all messages
Cloud Storage where the producer writes objects that services periodically read
Cloud Tasks with a shared queue that pushes tasks to service endpoints

questions.correct_text: Cloud Pub/Sub with a single topic and one subscription per microservice so each service receives all messages
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Cloud Pub/Sub with a single topic and one subscription per microservice so each service receives all messages.

Cloud Pub/Sub provides true fan out, since every subscription attached to a topic receives every published message. You create twelve subscriptions so each microservice gets the full event stream. Each subscriber scales independently with its own pull or push configuration and acknowledgement flow, which keeps the producer decoupled from consumers. A rate of 7,500 messages per second sits well within the managed capacity of Cloud Pub/Sub, and at least once delivery with retention aids reliability and replay.

Cloud SQL with a table for incoming events that each service queries is not a messaging solution and would force inefficient polling and contention at this write and read rate. It lacks per consumer delivery tracking and acknowledgements and tightly couples schema and retry logic in application code.

Cloud Storage where the producer writes objects for periodic reads is optimized for object storage and batch processing rather than high rate event streaming. Writing many tiny objects is inefficient, latency is higher, and there is no built in way to ensure every service reliably processes every event without complex polling and coordination.

Cloud Tasks with a shared queue that pushes tasks to endpoints is designed to dispatch a task to a single handler and does not natively broadcast the same item to multiple independent consumers. It also adds queue level throttling and limits that do not fit a requirement where all twelve services must process every event.

questions.question: You are the only engineer on call during a long holiday weekend at Beacon Robotics and your lead asks you to ship a small fix to the public website within the next two hours. Your toolchain uses Google Cloud services such as Cloud Storage and Cloud Build, and your repository is managed with Git. You do not have your work laptop, and company policy forbids storing source code on any personal or public device. How should you configure a secure development environment to complete the change?

options.text: Use Cloud Workstations in your project and make the edits in the browser, then push a "pull request"
Copy the repository into a Cloud Storage bucket, then mount it with gcsfuse on the public computer and edit with a local editor
Open Cloud Shell and develop with the built-in editor, then send the updates as a "pull request"
Create a Compute Engine VM and SSH to it from the public computer, then clone the repo and push a "pull request"

questions.correct_text: Open Cloud Shell and develop with the built-in editor, then send the updates as a "pull request"
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Open Cloud Shell and develop with the built-in editor, then send the updates as a "pull request".

This approach provides a ready to use browser based development environment that runs entirely on Google managed infrastructure, so no source code is stored on the public computer. You can clone the repository inside the session, use the preinstalled editor and Git, and rely on your Google credentials for secure access. You can push a branch and create a pull request without provisioning any new infrastructure, which fits the two hour constraint.

Use Cloud Workstations in your project and make the edits in the browser, then push a "pull request" is secure and powerful when it is already provisioned, yet it often requires creating a workstation cluster, configurations and IDE images which adds setup time and permissions steps. With a tight deadline and no prior setup, this is not the fastest or simplest option.

Copy the repository into a Cloud Storage bucket, then mount it with gcsfuse on the public computer and edit with a local editor violates the policy that forbids storing source code on personal or public devices because editing locally places code on that machine. A bucket is not a Git working directory, and gcsfuse does not offer full POSIX semantics which can make Git operations unreliable.

Create a Compute Engine VM and SSH to it from the public computer, then clone the repo and push a "pull request" keeps code off the public device but it requires provisioning a VM, managing access, and installing tools which takes time and increases the attack surface. A prehardened ephemeral browser based environment is faster and simpler for an urgent fix.

questions.question: Running its site on App Engine standard, a media startup wants to pit a reworked landing page against the existing one over a two week trial. The goal is to route a tunable fraction of visitors to each variant, do it without editing application code, and retain the ability to shift the split or roll everything back fast. On Google Cloud, what is the best way to run this A or B test?

options.text: Create an external HTTP load balancer with two backend services, each serving a different homepage build
Deploy two separate App Engine services and place one homepage version in each
Configure App Engine traffic splitting to send a percentage of requests to each deployed version
Migrate to Cloud Run and split traffic between two revisions

questions.correct_text: Configure App Engine traffic splitting to send a percentage of requests to each deployed version
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Configure App Engine traffic splitting to send a percentage of requests to each deployed version. It satisfies the need to run a two week experiment without code changes, lets you tune the percentage in real time, and lets you revert instantly by routing all traffic back to the stable version.

With this feature you deploy both versions under the same App Engine service and allocate a controllable share of incoming requests to each. Cookie based assignment can keep users consistently on one variant, which is ideal for A or B experiments. You can adjust the split at any time in the console or with gcloud and roll back in a single change.

Creating an external HTTP load balancer with two backend services is unnecessary and adds complexity. The external load balancer does not target individual App Engine versions directly, so you would have to rearchitect with serverless network endpoint groups or extra routing. App Engine already provides a native capability that is simpler and safer here.

Deploying two separate App Engine services with one version in each does not meet the requirement for percentage based splitting within App Engine. Traffic splitting is managed per service, and splitting across services would need extra routing or code logic, conflicting with the goal of no code changes and easy split adjustment.

Migrating to Cloud Run and splitting traffic between two revisions is not best for a time boxed experiment. Cloud Run supports weighted traffic across revisions, but migrating platforms adds effort and risk and is unnecessary when App Engine already offers a built in way to do the same thing.

questions.question: A microservice at SwiftCargo runs on Cloud Run and must send event messages to a Pub/Sub topic named "shipments-feed". You want to assign only the minimal permissions needed to the Cloud Run service account so it can publish messages and nothing more. Which role should you grant to that service account?

options.text: Pub/Sub Admin
Pub/Sub Publisher
Pub/Sub Editor
Pub/Sub Subscriber

questions.correct_text: Pub/Sub Publisher
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Pub/Sub Publisher.

This role grants only the permissions required to publish messages to a Pub/Sub topic, and it does not allow creating, deleting, or modifying topics or subscriptions. It aligns with the principle of least privilege for a Cloud Run service that only needs to send events to the shipments-feed topic.

Pub/Sub Admin is overly broad because it allows full administrative control of Pub/Sub resources which goes far beyond publishing and is not aligned with least privilege.

Pub/Sub Editor also provides wide edit capabilities across topics and subscriptions which is more access than needed for simple publishing.

Pub/Sub Subscriber is for receiving messages from subscriptions and it does not include the ability to publish to a topic.

questions.question: A GKE cluster you operate is built from private nodes that carry no external IP addresses. Routine database maintenance requires the applications on those nodes to reach the Cloud SQL Admin API, yet your security team has mandated that none of this traffic may travel over the public internet. What is the right way to give the private nodes secure access to the Cloud SQL API?

options.text: Configure Cloud NAT for the cluster to provide internet egress while keeping nodes without public IPs
Enable Private Google Access for GKE so node IPs can privately reach Google APIs including the Cloud SQL API
Set up Dedicated Interconnect to Google Cloud to create a private physical link to the Cloud SQL API
Assign public IP addresses to the GKE nodes so they can contact the Cloud SQL API directly

questions.correct_text: Enable Private Google Access for GKE so node IPs can privately reach Google APIs including the Cloud SQL API
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Enable Private Google Access for GKE so node IPs can privately reach Google APIs including the Cloud SQL API.

Private Google Access lets nodes without external IP addresses reach Google APIs over Google's private network paths rather than the public internet. In a GKE private cluster you enable Private Google Access on the VPC subnet that hosts the nodes, which allows them to call the Cloud SQL Admin API securely while satisfying the requirement to avoid public internet egress.

Configuring Cloud NAT for the cluster is not appropriate because NAT still sends traffic to public internet endpoints. The nodes would remain without external IPs, but the egress path would not be private to Google APIs, so it does not meet the security constraint.

Setting up Dedicated Interconnect is unnecessary and does not solve the problem. Dedicated Interconnect connects on-premises networks to Google Cloud and is not required for private access from GKE nodes to Google APIs inside Google Cloud.

Assigning public IP addresses to the GKE nodes violates the requirement that nodes must not use the public internet and should therefore be avoided.

questions.question: The product team is launching a ticketing site where customers sign in, drop seats into a basket, and get signed out after 45 minutes of inactivity. When they return and sign in again, their basket must still be there. Following Google Cloud best practices, how should you handle session state and basket persistence?

options.text: Use Cloud Spanner for both session state and basket items
Store session identifiers in Cloud Pub/Sub and save basket records in Cloud SQL
Keep session data in Memorystore for Redis or Memorystore for Memcached and persist basket data in Firestore
Store basket JSON in Cloud Storage objects where the object name is the session identifier

questions.correct_text: Keep session data in Memorystore for Redis or Memorystore for Memcached and persist basket data in Firestore
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Keep session data in Memorystore for Redis or Memorystore for Memcached and persist basket data in Firestore.

Sessions are ephemeral and belong in a low latency cache. Memorystore for Redis or Memorystore for Memcached lets you set a 45 minute time to live that matches the inactivity timeout while keeping the application tier stateless. This supports horizontal scaling and fast lookups for session validation.

The shopping basket must persist across sign outs and new sessions. Storing the cart as documents in Firestore and keying it to the user rather than the session gives durable storage with strong consistency at the document level and automatic scaling. Firestore supports transactional updates, which is handy for adding items and adjusting quantities, and it fits a cart document model well.

Using Cloud Spanner for both session state and basket items is a poor fit because keeping short lived session data in a global relational database adds cost and complexity for no benefit. Session data needs neither the relational schema nor the cross regional consistency Spanner provides.

Storing session identifiers in Cloud Pub/Sub and basket records in Cloud SQL is wrong because Pub/Sub is a messaging service, not a session store or database. Cloud SQL can hold cart tables but can become a bottleneck under large scale web traffic and does not match the flexible document shape of a cart.

Storing basket JSON in Cloud Storage objects named by session identifier is unreliable for a frequently updated cart. Object storage is for large immutable objects, and tying the cart to a session identifier risks losing it when the session expires or changes, with no transactional updates for item counts and merges.

questions.question: For a monthly audit, your platform team wants a lightweight script that enumerates every Cloud Bigtable instance, Memorystore for Redis instance, and Cloud SQL database within one Google Cloud project, and whoever runs it should be able to narrow the results with their own filter expression. Which technique gives you the cleanest way to collect those listings?

options.text: Use Cloud Asset Inventory with a project wide search and a single filter expression
Use gcloud bigtable instances list, gcloud redis instances list, and gcloud sql databases list and pass --filter to each command before aggregating the results
Call the HBase API, the Redis REST API, and connect to MySQL to enumerate resources, then merge and filter in the script
Run gcloud bigtable instances list, gcloud redis instances list, and gcloud sql databases list without filters and apply a custom filter in code

questions.correct_text: Use gcloud bigtable instances list, gcloud redis instances list, and gcloud sql databases list and pass --filter to each command before aggregating the results
questions.explanation:
The correct choice is Use gcloud bigtable instances list, gcloud redis instances list, and gcloud sql databases list and pass --filter to each command before aggregating the results.

This uses the supported listing commands for each service and applies the same user supplied filter expression consistently with the gcloud filtering syntax. It keeps the utility simple because each command returns exactly the resource type you need, and filtering happens before aggregation, which reduces data handling and makes the script faster and easier to maintain.

Using Cloud Asset Inventory with a single project wide filter is not the best fit because one filter must span different asset types whose fields differ, making user provided filters harder to express. It also adds an extra dependency and permissions that are unnecessary when the service specific commands already provide the listings.

Calling the HBase API, the Redis REST API, and connecting to MySQL to enumerate resources, then merging and filtering, is overly complex and uses the wrong interfaces. The supported approach is the Cloud admin and gcloud tooling rather than connecting to databases or using the HBase API for Bigtable, and it would require credentials and network paths to every database and would not scale well.

Running the list commands without filters and filtering in code works but is suboptimal, because it pulls more data than needed and duplicates filtering logic gcloud already provides. Pushing filters to the commands is simpler and more efficient.

questions.question: At Pinecone IoT Labs you created a Python Cloud Function that ingests live device telemetry, and the source is stored in a Git repository hosted at pineconeiot-dev.io. A Cloud Build workflow deploys the function, then replays roughly 650 test messages per second for 10 minutes, and finally deletes the function to avoid extra cost. During a failed test run you notice that the cleanup step does not execute and the temporary function remains, so what change should you make to the Cloud Build configuration to ensure the deletion step still runs even when the test step fails?

options.text: Set the cleanup step to waitFor the test step so it only runs after the test completes
Create a separate Cloud Build trigger that runs on build failure to perform the cleanup
Add an if condition on the cleanup step so it always runs regardless of prior step status
Configure the test step with onError ABORT and place the deletion step immediately after it

questions.correct_text: Add an if condition on the cleanup step so it always runs regardless of prior step status
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Add an if condition on the cleanup step so it always runs regardless of prior step status. This relies on the step level conditional in Cloud Build so the deletion executes even when the test step fails.

Cloud Build supports an if expression on each step. By setting the cleanup step to use an expression that always evaluates to true, such as an always function, the deletion will run no matter whether the test succeeds, fails, or is cancelled. This is the most direct and reliable way to guarantee resource cleanup after test runs.

Set the cleanup step to waitFor the test step so it only runs after the test completes is incorrect because waiting on the test step does not force execution after a failure. When a step fails, dependent steps are skipped by default, so the cleanup would still not run.

Create a separate Cloud Build trigger that runs on build failure to perform the cleanup is not appropriate because triggers are designed to start builds from repository events or schedules rather than directly from other build failures. While you could engineer a workaround with notifications, it adds complexity and is unnecessary when a simple conditional on the step solves the problem.

Configure the test step with onError ABORT and place the deletion step immediately after it is wrong because aborting on error stops the build and prevents subsequent steps from running. That would block the cleanup rather than ensure it.

questions.question: You need one central place to create, govern, and rotate the encryption keys that protect applications spread across Google Kubernetes Engine and Compute Engine. The solution has to rotate keys automatically on a 90 day cadence and produce audit logs spanning several projects. Which Google Cloud service fits?

options.text: Secret Manager
Cloud Key Management Service
Cloud Functions
Certificate Authority Service

questions.correct_text: Cloud Key Management Service
questions.explanation:
Cloud Key Management Service is the correct option.

Cloud Key Management Service centrally creates and manages cryptographic keys for workloads on Google Kubernetes Engine and Compute Engine. You can configure automatic key rotation on a fixed schedule such as every 90 days. It integrates with Cloud Audit Logs for both admin activity and key usage, and you can host keys in a dedicated security project while granting cross project access so multiple projects share the same governed keys.

Secret Manager stores and serves application secrets such as API keys and passwords. It does not generate or centrally manage encryption key material for customer managed encryption and provides no native key rotation for CMEK use cases.

Cloud Functions is a serverless compute platform for event driven code. It neither generates, stores, nor rotates encryption keys and is not a key management service.

Certificate Authority Service issues and manages X.509 certificates for workloads and devices. It manages certificates rather than data encryption keys and does not fulfill centralized key generation and rotation for CMEK.

questions.question: A microservice that runs on Compute Engine for a boutique travel firm named Skyward Voyages encounters an elusive failure roughly every 75 minutes that is difficult to reproduce. You plan to rely on Cloud Logging to investigate the problem. What is the most effective way to monitor the application logs for this intermittent behavior?

options.text: Set a log sink to BigQuery and investigate with SQL
Open Cloud Logging Log Explorer and apply filters to isolate suspected errors
Build a Cloud Monitoring dashboard to chart the application logs
Use Cloud Error Reporting to group and view exceptions

questions.correct_text: Open Cloud Logging Log Explorer and apply filters to isolate suspected errors
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Open Cloud Logging Log Explorer and apply filters to isolate suspected errors. This provides an interactive way to narrow the time window and conditions, test different filters, and watch entries as they arrive so you can catch the elusive failure when it occurs.

This option is designed for rapid investigation. You can filter by resource type, instance labels, severity, text, and structured fields in jsonPayload. You can adjust the time range and use live streaming of new entries to monitor the service while you reproduce the issue. Once you discover a pattern, you can save the query or create log based metrics and alerts to track future occurrences.

Set a log sink to BigQuery and investigate with SQL is better for historical analysis and large scale aggregation. It is not ideal for real time monitoring of an intermittent issue because export adds delay and the SQL workflow is slower for quick, iterative filtering of raw logs.

Build a Cloud Monitoring dashboard to chart the application logs does not directly visualize raw logs. You would first need to create log based metrics, and only then could you chart them. That adds setup time and can hide the detailed context you need to diagnose a sporadic failure.

Use Cloud Error Reporting to group and view exceptions focuses on grouping stack trace based exceptions in supported runtimes. It may miss failures that do not emit exceptions or that log custom error messages, and it does not provide the flexible ad hoc filtering needed to investigate varied log patterns.

questions.question: brightorbit.io is introducing a microservices platform that must run in their on premises data center and in Google Cloud. The team wants very high scalability and prefers managed offerings over running infrastructure themselves. Which deployment strategy should they choose?

options.text: Adopt multiple GKE clusters managed by Anthos and install and operate open source Istio as the multicluster service mesh for all microservices
Use only Cloud Run fully managed in Google Cloud and call on premises systems through a Cloud VPN or Private Service Connect link
Provision a GKE cluster in each location and register them with Anthos and deploy each microservice as a Cloud Run for Anthos service into its local cluster
Create a managed GKE cluster in Google Cloud and keep open source Kubernetes on premises without Anthos and use a global external load balancer to spread user traffic across both environments

questions.correct_text: Provision a GKE cluster in each location and register them with Anthos and deploy each microservice as a Cloud Run for Anthos service into its local cluster
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Provision a GKE cluster in each location and register them with Anthos and deploy each microservice as a Cloud Run for Anthos service into its local cluster.

This approach lets you run the same platform in the on premises data center and in Google Cloud while keeping a consistent control and management experience through Anthos. Registering the clusters into a single fleet provides unified policy, configuration, and visibility. Deploying microservices as Cloud Run for Anthos services delivers a serverless developer experience with rapid scaling on top of Kubernetes while workloads stay local to each environment, which aligns with the preference for managed capabilities rather than self running infrastructure.

Note that Cloud Run for Anthos is deprecated. This means it is less likely to appear on newer exams, although in the context of this scenario it historically represented the managed path to run the same serverless model in both environments.

Adopt multiple GKE clusters managed by Anthos and install and operate open source Istio as the multicluster service mesh for all microservices is not preferred because it requires you to install and operate open source Istio yourself. That contradicts the stated preference for managed offerings when a managed service mesh is available.

Use only Cloud Run fully managed in Google Cloud and call on premises systems through a Cloud VPN or Private Service Connect link does not meet the requirement to run the platform in the on premises data center. It only places workloads in Google Cloud and merely reaches back to on premises systems.

Create a managed GKE cluster in Google Cloud and keep open source Kubernetes on premises without Anthos and use a global external load balancer to spread user traffic across both environments fails the preference for managed offerings on premises and lacks unified management across environments. Relying on a global external load balancer to span cloud and on premises can be complex and does not make the on premises Kubernetes environment managed or consistent with the cloud.
