questions.question: Each tenant object in your Cloud Storage bucket is encrypted under its own distinct customer supplied key. A storage client library upgrade went out last week, and since then a portion of object reads come back with an HTTP 4xx error. Of the following, which is the most probable reason these reads are failing?

options.text: The object is protected by a Cloud KMS key and the calling service account lacks the required CryptoKey Decrypter role
The read request did not include the base64 encoded SHA256 hash of the customer supplied encryption key
The client encoded the customer supplied key in base64 before sending it with the request
The bucket's storage class prevents reads of objects encrypted with customer supplied keys

questions.correct_text: The read request did not include the base64 encoded SHA256 hash of the customer supplied encryption key
questions.explanation:
The correct option is The read request did not include the base64 encoded SHA256 hash of the customer supplied encryption key.

With customer supplied encryption keys in Cloud Storage, every read must include the encryption algorithm, the base64 encoded key, and the base64 encoded SHA256 hash of that key. If the client upgrade stopped sending the hash header, the service cannot verify the key and the read fails with an HTTP 4xx response. That fits intermittent failures after a client change, because only requests missing the hash would be rejected.

The object being protected by a Cloud KMS key with a missing CryptoKey Decrypter role is incorrect because the scenario uses customer supplied keys, not Cloud KMS. The KMS Decrypter role applies to customer managed keys, not to CSEK reads.

The client encoding the customer supplied key in base64 before sending it is incorrect because base64 encoding of the key is required for CSEK requests and would not, by itself, cause failures.

The bucket's storage class preventing reads of CSEK encrypted objects is incorrect because storage class does not restrict the ability to read objects encrypted with customer supplied keys.

questions.question: A Go service deployed as a Cloud Function handles photo uploads, with its source kept in Cloud Source Repositories and a Cloud Build trigger firing on every commit to main. Each build deploys the function, runs an integration test that mimics an HTTP upload, then tries to tear the function down again. The snag is that a failing test stops the pipeline before the teardown step, leaving an orphaned function behind. Which change to the Cloud Build configuration guarantees that teardown still happens after a failing test?

options.text: Give each deployed function a unique timestamped name and schedule a recurring job to remove functions older than 48 hours
Use the ignoreExitStatus parameter set to true for the test step and add the deletion step after it
Move the cleanup logic into a finally block inside the test script so it always runs even when the test fails
Reduce the test step timeout to a small value so the build moves on to the cleanup step if the test hangs or fails

questions.correct_text: Use the ignoreExitStatus parameter set to true for the test step and add the deletion step after it
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Use the ignoreExitStatus parameter set to true for the test step and add the deletion step after it.

In Cloud Build, a step that exits with a nonzero status normally halts the build and prevents later steps from running. Setting ignoreExitStatus to true on the test step lets the build continue to the next step even when the test fails. Placing the deletion step right after the test guarantees cleanup runs while the failure stays visible in the logs for diagnosis.

This keeps the test failure signal intact while ensuring cleanup executes, and it keeps lifecycle control in the Cloud Build configuration rather than in ad hoc logic inside a test script.

Giving each deployed function a unique timestamped name and scheduling a recurring job to remove functions older than 48 hours is inappropriate because it adds operational overhead and does not guarantee timely cleanup when a test fails. It can leave stray functions for long periods and does not address cleanup within the same build.

Moving cleanup into a finally block inside the test script couples cleanup to the test implementation and can still be unreliable if the process terminates abruptly. It also hides lifecycle control inside the test code rather than the build pipeline where step ordering and failure handling belong.

Reducing the test step timeout is incorrect because a timeout still produces a failing step, which stops later steps from running. It also risks aborting valid tests and does not ensure cleanup always runs.

questions.question: Your team operates a payments microservice on Google Kubernetes Engine for a startup named LumaPay. The service depends on third party API tokens that rotate every 45 days. Those tokens must reach pods only at runtime and must never be stored in the pod manifest or the container image. Which approach supplies these tokens most securely?

options.text: Keep the tokens in Cloud KMS and have the application call the KMS API at startup to read them
Store the tokens in Secret Manager and grant the pod access through Workload Identity to fetch them at runtime
Create a Kubernetes Secret with the tokens and expose them as environment variables in the pod spec
Set the tokens directly as environment variables in the Deployment configuration

questions.correct_text: Store the tokens in Secret Manager and grant the pod access through Workload Identity to fetch them at runtime
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Store the tokens in Secret Manager and grant the pod access through Workload Identity to fetch them at runtime.

This uses Secret Manager for centralized storage with versioning, IAM, and audit logging, and Workload Identity so pods authenticate to Google APIs without long lived keys. The application fetches the secret only at runtime, so nothing is embedded in the image or manifest. Rotation every forty five days is simple, because you publish a new version in Secret Manager and the pod retrieves the latest version the next time it reads the secret without a redeploy.

Keeping the tokens in Cloud KMS and calling the KMS API at startup is not a fit because a key management service manages encryption keys and cryptographic operations rather than storing and serving plaintext secrets. You would still need separate storage for ciphertext and extra decryption and rotation logic, adding complexity and not meeting the requirement cleanly.

Creating a Kubernetes Secret and exposing it as environment variables in the pod spec is weaker, because the secret is referenced in the pod spec and may be exposed through environment variables that can leak via logs or crash reports. It also complicates rotation, since updating environment variables requires a rollout to propagate changes.

Setting the tokens directly as environment variables in the Deployment configuration is insecure because the values sit in plaintext in the manifest and the container environment, are not delivered at runtime, and are not easily rotated.

questions.question: You run a regional managed instance group that autoscales on average CPU utilization and sits behind a global HTTP load balancer. To make the group add capacity earlier in a spike and bring down p95 latency, which autoscaling adjustments should you make?

options.text: Use HTTP load balancing utilization as the autoscaling metric
Shorten the autoscaler cooldown period
Raise the target CPU utilization threshold
Lower the target CPU utilization threshold

questions.correct_text: Lower the target CPU utilization threshold
questions.explanation:
The correct options are Shorten the autoscaler cooldown period and Lower the target CPU utilization threshold.

When you scale on average CPU, the autoscaler adds instances whenever measured utilization exceeds the target. A lower target means the group crosses that threshold sooner during a spike, triggering scale out earlier and preserving headroom that helps reduce p95 latency.

The cooldown period sets how long the autoscaler waits for new instances to stabilize before counting their metrics and making further decisions. Shortening that window lets the autoscaler reassess more quickly after an initial resize and add capacity sooner if utilization stays high during a sharp surge, which helps contain tail latency.

Using HTTP load balancing utilization as the autoscaling metric is not the right tuning here. The question already specifies CPU based autoscaling, and you can achieve earlier scale out by adjusting the CPU target and timing. Switching metrics would require backend capacity settings and does not directly address earlier CPU triggered scale out for this group.

Raising the target CPU utilization threshold would delay scale out because instances would run hotter before capacity is added. That typically increases queueing and worsens p95 latency during spikes.

questions.question: The reliability engineers responsible for your APIs need to study 90 days of request volume, latency, and error trends, focused specifically on the payments-live and accounts-live environments, which together make up the entire api-hub-prod environment group. Staying within Google's recommended practices, how should you set this up?

options.text: Assign the Apigee API Reader role to the site reliability team for both environments and review traffic with Cloud Monitoring
Grant the Apigee Analytics Viewer role to the site reliability team for both environments and analyze traffic using Apigee API Analytics
Grant the Apigee Analytics Viewer role to the site reliability team for both environments and review metrics in Cloud Monitoring
Enable Apigee to export request logs to Cloud Logging and stream them to BigQuery then create dashboards in Looker Studio

questions.correct_text: Grant the Apigee Analytics Viewer role to the site reliability team for both environments and analyze traffic using Apigee API Analytics
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Grant the Apigee Analytics Viewer role to the site reliability team for both environments and analyze traffic using Apigee API Analytics.

Apigee API Analytics is the native place to study request volume, latency, and error trends. It provides out of the box reports and flexible filtering by environment and time window, so the team can focus on the payments-live and accounts-live environments and review 90 days of data. The Apigee Analytics Viewer role at the environment scope grants read access to these analytics without broader administrative permissions, which aligns with least privilege and Google recommended practice.

Assigning the Apigee API Reader role and reviewing traffic in Cloud Monitoring is insufficient because the API Reader role does not grant permission to view analytics data. Cloud Monitoring can surface some Apigee metrics but is not the primary tool for deep Apigee analytics and trend exploration.

Granting the Apigee Analytics Viewer role but reviewing metrics in Cloud Monitoring is not ideal because that role is intended for Apigee Analytics, and the richest analytics views live in the Apigee UI and APIs. Cloud Monitoring is better for operational dashboards and alerting than for detailed traffic analytics across proxies and dimensions.

Enabling Apigee to export request logs to Cloud Logging, streaming them to BigQuery, and building Looker Studio dashboards adds unnecessary complexity and cost here. Logs do not replace built in analytics, and this pipeline is not needed when Apigee Analytics already provides the required trends and reports.

questions.question: At Blue Harbor Media your BigQuery project contains the "CoreLedger" dataset holding employee travel and expense records, and each record names the department that owns it. You want a simple, maintainable security model so employees see only the rows for their own department while avoiding any data duplication. What should you implement?

options.text: Build data pipelines that copy filtered rows from the "CoreLedger" dataset into separate per department datasets and grant access to those departmental datasets
Create per department views in the "CoreLedger" dataset that filter by department and grant employees access only to those views
Apply Cloud IAM Conditions on the BigQuery tables to let users read only the rows for their department
Create a separate table per department within the "CoreLedger" dataset and grant users access to their department table

questions.correct_text: Create per department views in the "CoreLedger" dataset that filter by department and grant employees access only to those views
questions.explanation:
The correct choice is Create per department views in the "CoreLedger" dataset that filter by department and grant employees access only to those views.

BigQuery views expose a filtered query result while keeping a single source of truth in the base tables. With authorized views you grant access to the view rather than the underlying table, enforcing row filtering without copying data. That keeps the model simple and maintainable and ensures employees see only their department's rows without duplication.

BigQuery also supports row level security through row access policies, which would satisfy the requirement in a modern design, although it is not among the presented options, so views are the best fit here.

Building data pipelines that copy filtered rows into separate per department datasets is wrong because it duplicates data, raises cost and operational complexity, and risks drift between copies. It also violates the requirement to avoid data duplication.

Applying Cloud IAM Conditions on the tables is incorrect because IAM Conditions operate at the resource and request level and do not provide row level filtering for BigQuery tables. Row restrictions in BigQuery come from authorized views or row access policies.

Creating a separate table per department fragments the data model, complicates queries and maintenance, and duplicates schema and storage, so it is not appropriate.

questions.question: BrightHarbor Market runs a worldwide storefront on Cloud Run and wants to evaluate a refreshed color theme with real production users while keeping risk low. The product team needs rigorous evidence about changes in completed checkouts derived from concurrent live traffic. What approach on Google Cloud should you implement to run this experiment and measure the outcome?

options.text: Roll out the new theme as a canary to 5% of traffic for 36 hours using Cloud Deploy then shift to 100% and compare sales afterward
Use a feature flag in the frontend to show the new theme to 40% of signed in users and track their purchase rates
Configure an external HTTP(S) load balancer to send 30% of requests to a Cloud Run service with the new theme and 70% to the current theme while you compare conversion rates
Enable traffic mirroring on the external HTTP(S) load balancer to duplicate live requests to the new theme service and analyze differences in sales

questions.correct_text: Configure an external HTTP(S) load balancer to send 30% of requests to a Cloud Run service with the new theme and 70% to the current theme while you compare conversion rates
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Configure an external HTTP(S) load balancer to send 30% of requests to a Cloud Run service with the new theme and 70% to the current theme while you compare conversion rates.

This approach implements a true concurrent experiment with live traffic. It lets you split production requests between the current and new theme at the same time, which removes time based effects and provides a clean comparison of completed checkouts. You can instrument checkout events and attribute them to each variant so you can analyze conversion rates with confidence and adjust the split as results emerge.

Roll out the new theme as a canary to 5% of traffic for 36 hours using Cloud Deploy then shift to 100% and compare sales afterward is sequential and compares different time periods. It does not provide concurrent control and treatment, which weakens the evidence, and it removes the control once you shift to full traffic.

Use a feature flag in the frontend to show the new theme to 40% of signed in users and track their purchase rates limits the sample to signed in users which introduces selection bias and may not reflect all shoppers. It is also an application level toggle rather than a platform level traffic split, so it does not best satisfy the requirement to evaluate with unbiased concurrent live traffic.

Enable traffic mirroring on the external HTTP(S) load balancer to duplicate live requests to the new theme service and analyze differences in sales does not work for conversion measurement because mirrored responses are not returned to users and mirrored backends should not change state. Mirroring is intended for safe validation and not for experiments that require real user outcomes.

questions.question: On Google Cloud, a sports media startup is putting together a mobile feed service written in TypeScript. Its backing datastore has to be resilient across zones out of the box, serve quick reads and writes to mobile clients, honor ACID transactions, and permit clients to talk to it directly so that a middle tier is not mandatory. It also has to store semi structured documents and ship client libraries that keep operating through network partitions and reconcile data offline. Which managed database should they pick?

options.text: Set up Bigtable and integrate the Bigtable client in the app
Create Cloud SQL and connect using the Cloud SQL connectors
Deploy Firestore in Native mode and use the Firestore client SDK from the app
Adopt BigQuery and call the BigQuery API from the application

questions.correct_text: Deploy Firestore in Native mode and use the Firestore client SDK from the app
questions.explanation:
The correct choice is Deploy Firestore in Native mode and use the Firestore client SDK from the app.

Firestore is a managed document database that stores semi structured data as documents and collections, which fits this use case. It provides strong consistency and supports ACID transactions, so it can enforce correctness for mobile reads and writes. With a regional or multi region location, Firestore replicates across zones for resilience, and multi region locations add cross region redundancy. Mobile and web client SDKs connect directly to Firestore using security rules, so the app can run without a mandatory middle tier. Those SDKs support persistence and synchronization, so apps keep reading and writing during network partitions and automatically sync when connectivity returns, satisfying the offline requirement.

Setting up Bigtable and integrating the Bigtable client is not appropriate because Bigtable is a wide column store built for large scale throughput with single row transactions only, and it does not provide ACID transactions across multiple documents. It also offers no mobile client SDKs or offline synchronization for direct app access.

Creating Cloud SQL with the Cloud SQL connectors is a poor fit because Cloud SQL is relational and expects a fixed schema rather than semi structured documents. Direct mobile client access is unsupported, connectors target trusted server environments, and Cloud SQL lacks client side offline sync and conflict resolution.

Adopting BigQuery and calling the BigQuery API is incorrect because BigQuery is an analytical warehouse optimized for large scale queries rather than low latency transactional reads and writes. It provides no ACID transactions for app level OLTP, no mobile client SDKs, and no offline synchronization.

questions.question: You are architecting a public image delivery API for Rivertown Media. The twin goals are minimal storage spend and very low latency image downloads for users scattered across multiple regions, and during big launches the request rate can climb to 150000 per minute. Which architecture on Google Cloud gets you there?

options.text: Run a web server on Compute Engine and store images on Persistent Disk
Use Cloud CDN in front of Cloud Storage buckets that hold the images
Use Transfer Appliance to load data and serve from Cloud Filestore
Use Cloud Run to generate signed URLs for Cloud Storage without any caching layer

questions.correct_text: Use Cloud CDN in front of Cloud Storage buckets that hold the images
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Use Cloud CDN in front of Cloud Storage buckets that hold the images.

This pairing puts a global content delivery network in front of durable object storage, giving low latency downloads from edge locations near users while keeping origin egress and storage costs low. Edge caching absorbs sudden traffic spikes, so the system comfortably handles bursts to 150000 requests per minute with no server scaling on your part. You also gain cache controls and invalidation to tune freshness for image content while the origin stays simple and inexpensive.

Running a web server on Compute Engine with images on Persistent Disk relies on a VM and block storage that lack global edge caching and become a bottleneck under extreme read surges. It demands significant operational work to scale and still delivers higher latency to users far from the VM.

Using Transfer Appliance to load data and serve from Cloud Filestore misuses an offline ingestion device for ongoing delivery and places images on an NFS file service meant for POSIX workloads rather than internet scale static distribution. It offers no edge caching and would be costly and complex to scale globally.

Using Cloud Run to generate signed URLs for Cloud Storage without a caching layer secures access but does not improve latency or offload the origin. Without an edge cache, every request still reaches the origin, raising latency for distant users and risking hot object throttling during surges.

questions.question: When an application needs globally consistent reads and writes across regions to back real time shared state, which Google Cloud database is purpose built for that requirement?

options.text: Cloud Bigtable
Cloud Spanner
AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
Cloud Firestore

questions.correct_text: Cloud Spanner
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Cloud Spanner, because it provides globally strong consistency for reads and writes across regions for real time shared state.

Cloud Spanner uses TrueTime to deliver external consistency for both transactions and reads. In a multi region configuration it synchronously replicates data across regions, so any read after a write returns the most recent committed data from anywhere. It supports distributed ACID transactions, which makes it well suited to shared state that must stay consistent worldwide.

Cloud Bigtable is tuned for large scale throughput and low latency, but its cross region replication is asynchronous and therefore eventually consistent, so it does not provide globally strongly consistent reads and writes.

AlloyDB for PostgreSQL is a regional relational service whose cross region read replicas use asynchronous replication, so it cannot offer globally strong consistency for writes across regions.

Cloud Firestore offers strong consistency within a chosen region or multi region location, but replication is confined to that location, so it does not provide globally strong consistency across arbitrary regions.

questions.question: A customer portal you maintain on GKE is fronted by an external HTTP load balancer. For the past 45 minutes a handful of users browsing the site have intermittently seen 502 Bad Gateway errors, so you turn to Cloud Monitoring to triage. To begin narrowing down the source, which metric is the right one to inspect first?

options.text: Ingress request latency p95
Current number of running pods in the GKE workload
HTTP response code metrics on the external HTTP or HTTPS load balancer
CPU utilization percentage on the GKE node pool

questions.correct_text: HTTP response code metrics on the external HTTP or HTTPS load balancer
questions.explanation:
The correct option is HTTP response code metrics on the external HTTP or HTTPS load balancer.

Response code metrics at the load balancer immediately confirm the presence and timing of 502 errors and quantify their rate. This is the fastest way to decide whether the problem sits at the edge or in the backends, since these metrics show the distribution of 2xx, 4xx, and 5xx. Because a 502 means the proxy could not get a valid response from a backend or the connection failed, starting here gives you a precise anchor for the incident and guides next steps such as reviewing backend health checks and service logs.

Ingress request latency p95 is not the best first metric, because latency can stay normal while errors rise. It does not reveal whether the edge is returning errors or a particular backend is failing, so it gives limited direction for initial triage of 502s.

Current number of running pods can look healthy even when readiness is failing or the load balancer returns errors due to backend issues. Pod count does not correlate directly with transient 502s and is more useful after you confirm error rates at the edge.

CPU utilization on the GKE node pool is an indirect signal not specific to HTTP error conditions. Nodes can show normal CPU while clients see 502 from timeouts, connection resets, or misconfiguration, so this is not the first place to look.

questions.question: On a Compute Engine virtual machine you operate a data processing service whose job involves reading and writing objects through the Cloud Storage API. The goal is to grant it exactly the permissions it requires, in a way that is both secure and low maintenance, and crucially without handing out any long lived secrets. What is the right approach?

options.text: Use the Compute Engine default service account and assign it the Storage Admin role
Authenticate with a user account that has the required IAM roles and pass the user's OAuth refresh token to the VM
Attach a custom service account to the VM and grant only the required Cloud Storage roles, then let the application fetch short lived tokens from the metadata server
Create a service account key and store the JSON key in Secret Manager for the app to load at startup

questions.correct_text: Attach a custom service account to the VM and grant only the required Cloud Storage roles, then let the application fetch short lived tokens from the metadata server
questions.explanation:
The correct choice is Attach a custom service account to the VM and grant only the required Cloud Storage roles, then let the application fetch short lived tokens from the metadata server.

This follows least privilege by granting only the specific Cloud Storage IAM roles the workload needs. The application uses Application Default Credentials to obtain short lived access tokens from the Compute Engine metadata server, removing any need to manage or distribute secrets. Tokens rotate automatically, and the setup is low maintenance and secure for a long running service.

Using the Compute Engine default service account with the Storage Admin role is too permissive and breaks least privilege. The default service account is shared across workloads, and granting broad admin permissions expands blast radius, whereas a dedicated service account scoped to only the required roles is the recommended pattern.

Authenticating with a user account and passing the user's OAuth refresh token to the VM relies on human credentials and introduces long lived secrets that must be stored and rotated. Workloads on Compute Engine should use service accounts and the metadata server rather than user credentials.

Creating a service account key and storing the JSON key in Secret Manager still uses a long lived key that can leak or needs rotation. Although Secret Manager protects storage, Google recommends avoiding service account keys when the platform can supply short lived credentials through the metadata server.

questions.question: You are about to expose a set of new REST APIs to roughly 180 partner developers, with the endpoints fronted by Google Cloud API Gateway. From a security standpoint, what is the principal role that API Gateway plays?

options.text: Cloud Build
Provide a managed front door that centralizes authentication, authorization, and request policy enforcement for APIs
Cloud Armor
Cloud Firestore

questions.correct_text: Provide a managed front door that centralizes authentication, authorization, and request policy enforcement for APIs
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Provide a managed front door that centralizes authentication, authorization, and request policy enforcement for APIs.

API Gateway gives your REST APIs a single entry point and centralizes identity and access control. It can verify API keys and JSON Web Tokens and integrates with Google Cloud IAM to control who may invoke your services. It also lets you define request policies such as required headers and request validation, so you consistently enforce security and governance for all partner traffic.

Cloud Armor provides web application firewall features and DDoS protection for external HTTP traffic. While it protects at the edge, it does not provide API authentication and authorization or the centralized policy enforcement an API gateway supplies.

Cloud Firestore is a NoSQL document database for storing and querying data. It is not used to front APIs or enforce API security policies.

questions.question: Wavefront Sports Analytics uses Cloud Build to run linting, unit tests, integration checks, and a container image build for a service that deploys to Cloud Run. You notice that linting and unit tests do not depend on the image build, and the integration checks only need the unit tests. You want to shorten total build time by adjusting cloudbuild.yaml while keeping the same steps. Which configuration approach should you use?

options.text: Enable Cloud Build caching to skip repeated downloads and rebuilds across runs
Define every task in the steps list so they always run one after another
Use the waitFor field to express dependencies and allow independent steps to start together by setting waitFor to ["-"] where appropriate
Lower each step timeout to end long tasks sooner if they exceed limits

questions.correct_text: Use the waitFor field to express dependencies and allow independent steps to start together by setting waitFor to ["-"] where appropriate
questions.explanation:
The right approach is Use the waitFor field to express dependencies and allow independent steps to start together by setting waitFor to ["-"] where appropriate.

Cloud Build runs steps sequentially by default, and waitFor lets you describe which steps truly depend on others so independent work can start at the same time. In this scenario you can start linting and unit tests immediately by setting their waitFor to ["-"]. You can then configure the integration checks to run only after unit tests by setting their waitFor to the unit test step name. The image build can also run in parallel by using waitFor: ["-"]. This reduces the total wall clock time while keeping the same steps.

Enable Cloud Build caching to skip repeated downloads and rebuilds across runs does not change the order of execution or introduce concurrency within a single build. Caching can help across repeated builds, but it does not parallelize independent steps.

Define every task in the steps list so they always run one after another forces a fully serial pipeline, which prevents independent tasks from running concurrently and increases overall duration.

Lower each step timeout to end long tasks sooner if they exceed limits does not make steps complete faster. Timeouts only abort steps after a threshold and can cause unnecessary failures without improving normal build times.

questions.question: A development team at Westbrook Ledger uses Cloud Build to compile a containerized service, and each run spends significant time downloading a large set of third party libraries which slows the pipeline. You want to cut the build duration without altering the application code or repository layout. What should you do?

options.text: Use smaller base images in your Dockerfiles
Enable caching of dependency directories in Cloud Build
Use the no cache flag in Docker build steps
Move your dependency artifacts to a Cloud Storage bucket and download them during each build

questions.correct_text: Enable caching of dependency directories in Cloud Build
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Enable caching of dependency directories in Cloud Build.

This approach lets Cloud Build persist package manager caches and dependency directories across builds so repeated runs skip most downloads. By storing locations such as the Maven local repository, the npm cache, the pip cache, Gradle caches, or the Go module cache, subsequent builds can reuse previously fetched artifacts and significantly reduce build time.

You can implement this by configuring a cache in the Cloud Build configuration so paths that hold downloaded libraries are retained between runs. This change is applied in the build pipeline configuration and does not require altering application code or the repository layout, which meets the requirement in the scenario.

Use smaller base images in your Dockerfiles is not targeted at dependency download time and would require changing Dockerfiles in the repository. Even if image pulls are smaller, the repeated third party library downloads would still slow the build.

Use the no cache flag in Docker build steps would disable caching and force redownloading and rebuilding on every run. That would make builds slower rather than faster.

Move your dependency artifacts to a Cloud Storage bucket and download them during each build still performs network downloads on every run and adds operational overhead. It does not provide the automated reuse and invalidation that Cloud Build caches offer.

questions.question: To lower the risk of a microservice release, you want a staged approach in which only users coming from a single geographic region land on the new build while everyone else keeps hitting the existing one, and you need the ability to back out instantly the moment a serious issue surfaces. Which combination of GCP service and capability supports this?

options.text: Cloud Armor with a geo policy that forwards requests from a selected region to a backend running the new build
GKE with Anthos Service Mesh using a VirtualService that matches the X-Geo-Region header and routes a canary subset with quick rollback
Cloud Run with percentage based traffic splitting that inspects a location header to route requests
Compute Engine managed instance groups with an external HTTP(S) Load Balancer using a URL map that matches the Location header for routing

questions.correct_text: GKE with Anthos Service Mesh using a VirtualService that matches the X-Geo-Region header and routes a canary subset with quick rollback
questions.explanation:
The correct option is GKE with Anthos Service Mesh using a VirtualService that matches the X-Geo-Region header and routes a canary subset with quick rollback. A VirtualService can match a request header that represents the user's region and send only those requests to a canary subset while everyone else stays on the stable version. If a critical problem appears, you revert instantly by updating the configuration to send one hundred percent of traffic to stable.

This uses service mesh traffic management to match on headers and route to named subsets that map to different versions of the same service. You can localize the rollout to one geography when a client location header is injected by the edge, and you can shift traffic between subsets without redeploying workloads, enabling a very fast rollback.

Cloud Armor with a geo policy is incorrect because it is a web application firewall and DDoS defense that can allow, deny, or rate limit traffic by geography but does not forward requests to different backends. Routing and canary splitting belong to a load balancer or a service mesh.

Cloud Run with percentage based traffic splitting is incorrect because Cloud Run splits traffic only by percentage across revisions and does not support request header based routing between revisions. The Location header is a response header rather than a client request attribute, so this cannot target a single region without another routing layer.

Compute Engine managed instance groups with an external HTTP(S) Load Balancer matching the Location header is incorrect because URL maps evaluate request attributes and the Location header is a response header not present in client requests. While advanced rules can match on request headers clients send, this design does not provide an easy canary subset with instant rollback at the microservice level.

questions.question: Driftwood Travel operates about fifteen microservices on Google Kubernetes Engine, and one service must connect to a partner's on premises database over a private connection. You need to keep the database credentials secure and support rotation every 60 days while following Google Cloud best practices. What should you do?

options.text: Mount an encrypted PersistentVolume containing the credentials into the application Pod
Use the Secret Manager CSI driver to mount secrets from Secret Manager into the Pod
Store the credentials in a Kubernetes Secret and use the Cloud KMS plugin for encryption and decryption
Configure a service mesh to govern traffic between the microservice and the external database

questions.correct_text: Store the credentials in a Kubernetes Secret and use the Cloud KMS plugin for encryption and decryption
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Store the credentials in a Kubernetes Secret and use the Cloud KMS plugin for encryption and decryption. This keeps credentials encrypted at rest in etcd using customer managed keys and aligns with GKE best practices. You can meet the 60 day rotation requirement by updating the Secret on that schedule and by rotating the KMS key according to your key management policy.

This approach provides centralized key control and auditability through Cloud KMS while Kubernetes RBAC governs who and what can read the Secret. Rotation can be automated with a pipeline or a Kubernetes CronJob that writes a new Secret version and triggers a rollout so Pods pick up the updated value. This keeps credentials off local disks and avoids embedding them in images or code.

Mount an encrypted PersistentVolume containing the credentials into the application Pod is not appropriate because a volume is file storage and not a secret distribution mechanism. It complicates rotation and increases exposure risks through snapshots or node disks and it does not integrate with native Secret access controls.

Use the Secret Manager CSI driver to mount secrets from Secret Manager into the Pod can work, but it is not the best fit here. It adds another external dependency and policy boundary, and you still need to orchestrate rotation and pod reloads. The question emphasizes GKE best practices for in cluster secret storage which are satisfied by Kubernetes Secrets protected with Cloud KMS.

Configure a service mesh to govern traffic between the microservice and the external database does not address storing or rotating database credentials. A mesh focuses on traffic policy and mTLS between services and it does not manage secret material or rotations.

You decide to run a targeted Cloud Storage performance diagnostic and capture its results as a JSON file to attach to a support case. options.text: gcloud storage cp ~/sample.bin gs://mediaarchive93
gsutil perfdiag -o diag2025.json gs://mediaarchive93
gsutil stat gs://mediaarchive93/**
gcloud compute scp app-vm:~/data gs://mediaarchive93

The correct option is gsutil perfdiag -o diag2025.json gs://mediaarchive93. It runs a focused Cloud Storage performance diagnostic against the named bucket and writes the structured results to a JSON file called diag2025.json, which is exactly what a support case needs.

This command measures end to end throughput and latency for Cloud Storage. It exercises uploads and downloads with controlled parameters and records network and I O characteristics. The -o flag writes the diagnostic output to the given JSON file so you can archive and share it. The tool is part of gsutil, the correct utility for Cloud Storage diagnostics.

gcloud storage cp ~/sample.bin gs://mediaarchive93 only copies a local file into the bucket and runs no performance tests and produces no JSON report.

gsutil stat gs://mediaarchive93/** retrieves object metadata and can list details but does not run performance diagnostics and does not emit a JSON diagnostic file.

gcloud compute scp app-vm:~/data gs://mediaarchive93 copies files between your local machine and Compute Engine VMs; it does not target Cloud Storage buckets and produces no diagnostic output.

questions.question: On GKE you are deploying a containerized workload whose Pods must read and write objects in a Cloud Storage bucket called data-archive-93. Following least privilege, you want the Kubernetes service account behind those Pods to be able to manipulate objects but never to administer the bucket. Which IAM role should you assign?

options.text: Storage Admin
Storage Viewer
Storage Object Admin
Project Owner
Storage Object Viewer

questions.correct_text: Storage Object Admin
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Storage Object Admin, because it grants read and write permissions on objects in a bucket without allowing bucket management, which fits least privilege for the Kubernetes workload.

This role permits creating, updating, deleting, reading, and listing objects. It does not include permissions to create or delete buckets or to change IAM policies on the bucket. You grant it on the specific bucket to the Google service account the Pods use, so they can access only the objects they need.

Storage Admin is too broad here because it grants full control over buckets and objects and allows changing IAM policies, exceeding least privilege.

Storage Viewer is read only and cannot write objects, so the Pods could not upload or modify data.

Project Owner grants administrative permissions across the entire project, far beyond what the workload requires.

Storage Object Viewer only allows reading and listing objects and cannot support writing or deleting objects.

questions.question: Your GKE workloads run inside an Istio mesh that enforces a strict AuthorizationPolicy alongside a NetworkPolicy. You notice that roughly 30 percent of the requests going from "inventory-api" to "billing-api" come back as 403, while the remaining requests go through fine. What most likely accounts for this?

options.text: A Kubernetes NetworkPolicy is blocking pod to pod traffic between "inventory-api" and "billing-api"
The AuthorizationPolicy is missing allow rules for specific HTTP methods or paths from "inventory-api" to "billing-api"
The Envoy sidecar is not injected in some pods which causes inconsistent policy enforcement
An Istio RequestAuthentication or JWT rule is rejecting some tokens from "inventory-api"

questions.correct_text: The AuthorizationPolicy is missing allow rules for specific HTTP methods or paths from "inventory-api" to "billing-api"
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is The AuthorizationPolicy is missing allow rules for specific HTTP methods or paths from "inventory-api" to "billing-api".

Under strict enforcement in Istio, an AuthorizationPolicy that allows only certain HTTP methods or paths will permit some requests and reject others. A subset of calls returning 403 indicates routing and connectivity are fine and that the proxy received the request but the policy did not match the method or path for those requests. That matches about 30 percent of calls failing while others succeed.

A Kubernetes NetworkPolicy blocking pod to pod traffic is unlikely because NetworkPolicy operates at layers 3 and 4 and would consistently allow or drop traffic. Drops would appear as timeouts or connection resets rather than 403 responses from the application layer.

The Envoy sidecar not being injected in some pods would not produce 403 responses. A missing sidecar bypasses Istio policy and would not cause the proxy to deny requests; you would see unfiltered success or network level behavior rather than authorization denials.

An Istio RequestAuthentication or JWT rule rejecting some tokens typically surfaces as 401 for authentication failures. A 403 usually means the request was authenticated and then blocked by authorization, which points back to the AuthorizationPolicy method or path conditions rather than token validation.

questions.question: A travel booking startup hosts its customer portal on App Engine Standard. It needs scheduled jobs that periodically clear out stale records and assemble weekly booking summaries, and the team is adamant about not standing up any additional servers or bolting on separate managed services to do it. Which approach should they take?

options.text: Build a Cloud Workflows pipeline that invokes the app's HTTP endpoints on a schedule
Create App Engine cron.yaml entries that call application endpoints to run the cleanup and report routines
Provision a Compute Engine virtual machine and configure a Linux cron to trigger the tasks
Use Cloud Functions with Cloud Scheduler to execute the maintenance and reporting jobs

questions.correct_text: Create App Engine cron.yaml entries that call application endpoints to run the cleanup and report routines
questions.explanation:
The correct approach is Create App Engine cron.yaml entries that call application endpoints to run the cleanup and report routines.

This uses the built in scheduling capability of the App Engine environment to call specific URLs at defined times. It requires no extra servers and adds no separate managed service, because scheduling is part of the application configuration. You define cron entries in a cron.yaml file and implement handlers that perform the deletions and generate the weekly summaries. The service can run at minute level frequency or on weekly schedules and respects your app authentication and version routing.

Building a Cloud Workflows pipeline that invokes the app's HTTP endpoints on a schedule is inappropriate because it introduces an additional managed service just to orchestrate simple periodic calls when the platform already provides built in scheduling.

Provisioning a Compute Engine VM with a Linux cron violates the requirement to avoid new servers and adds unnecessary operational overhead for a task the platform already supports.

Using Cloud Functions with Cloud Scheduler adds multiple separate managed services and extra moving parts, which is unnecessary given the native scheduling features in the existing environment.

questions.question: A containerized microservice your team is shipping to Cloud Run produces request and error logs as it runs. You want those logs surfaced in Cloud Logging for centralized observability, all while keeping the implementation effort minimal and staying aligned with best practices. What is the right move?

options.text: Call the Cloud Logging API from the application code and post log entries directly
Write all application logs to standard output and standard error so Cloud Run ships them to Cloud Logging automatically
Use Cloud Scheduler to trigger a Cloud Run job that parses container log files and uploads them to Cloud Logging every 12 hours
Bundle a fluent-bit agent inside the container to tail files and forward entries to Cloud Logging

questions.correct_text: Write all application logs to standard output and standard error so Cloud Run ships them to Cloud Logging automatically
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Write all application logs to standard output and standard error so Cloud Run ships them to Cloud Logging automatically.

This is the recommended approach for Cloud Run, because the platform automatically captures anything written to standard output and standard error and forwards it to Cloud Logging with useful context. Using stdout and stderr keeps engineering effort low, avoids extra dependencies, and supports structured JSON so you can enrich entries with fields like severity and trace.

Calling the Cloud Logging API from the application code adds needless complexity and coupling, since Cloud Run already exports stdout and stderr to Cloud Logging automatically. This approach requires client libraries, authentication, retries, and error handling and can still miss helpful automatic context.

Using Cloud Scheduler to trigger a Cloud Run job that parses container log files every 12 hours is inappropriate because Cloud Run containers do not persist log files and observability should be near real time. This delays visibility and adds operational work without benefit.

Bundling a fluent-bit agent inside the container is unnecessary on Cloud Run, since the platform already collects logs from stdout and stderr. Packing an agent increases image size and complexity, and file tailing is unreliable in an ephemeral container environment.

questions.question: Your REST endpoint at LuminaStream stores viewer comments by writing them into Cloud Firestore in Native mode. A 12 minute load test surfaces a bug: whenever Firestore answers with HTTP 429 Too Many Requests, the comment is never saved yet your endpoint still returns HTTP 200 OK to the caller. You want callers to be told clearly whenever a write actually fails. How should you change the behavior?

options.text: Queue the write with Cloud Tasks and return HTTP 202 Accepted
Add exponential backoff retries for Firestore writes and if all retry attempts fail then respond with HTTP 500 Internal Server Error
Return HTTP 503 Service Unavailable
Return HTTP 200 OK with an error message in the response body

questions.correct_text: Add exponential backoff retries for Firestore writes and if all retry attempts fail then respond with HTTP 500 Internal Server Error
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Add exponential backoff retries for Firestore writes and if all retry attempts fail then respond with HTTP 500 Internal Server Error.

Firestore may throttle writes during bursts and respond with HTTP 429, which signals that the request should be retried. The robust pattern is to retry with exponential backoff and jitter inside a bounded retry budget. Your service should acknowledge success only when the write is confirmed, and if all retries are exhausted it should return HTTP 500 to signal failure clearly rather than masking it with a success status.

This aligns with Google API error handling guidance and Firestore best practices for rate limits. It gives the server the first chance to absorb transient throttling and gives the caller an unambiguous error when the write ultimately fails.

Queueing the write with Cloud Tasks and returning HTTP 202 Accepted is incorrect because it acknowledges the request before the write occurs. That hides immediate failures, and the caller cannot tell the write did not persist, which violates the requirement for a clear failure response.

Returning HTTP 503 Service Unavailable is not the best choice because you should first implement retries to handle transient throttling, and only if those retries fail should you signal an error. Here, returning 500 after exhausting retries accurately conveys that the server could not complete the operation.

Returning HTTP 200 OK with an error message in the body is incorrect because 200 indicates success and many clients treat it that way. This obscures the failure and breaks standard HTTP semantics.

questions.question: During a peak season stress test for a new release at SunWave Apps, a previously quiet Cloud Storage bucket spikes to 2500 writes per second and 8000 reads per second within the first 60 seconds. Your service starts receiving intermittent 5xx and 429 responses from the Cloud Storage JSON API as the traffic bursts. You must reduce failed responses when warming up this cold bucket without changing your storage topology. What should you do?

options.text: Use the XML API instead of the JSON API for all Cloud Storage operations
Add client and server retries with exponential backoff and jitter when HTTP errors occur
Throttle client traffic so the request rate ramps up gradually to the idle bucket
Distribute uploads across several separate Cloud Storage buckets

questions.correct_text: Throttle client traffic so the request rate ramps up gradually to the idle bucket
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Throttle client traffic so the request rate ramps up gradually to the idle bucket. This approach smooths the transition from an idle state to a high workload which reduces transient 5xx and 429 responses while preserving your existing bucket layout.

A gradual ramp allows Cloud Storage to adapt to the new traffic profile and allocate resources as load increases. Sudden spikes from a cold bucket can trigger temporary throttling and backend saturation which lead to intermittent errors. By increasing request rates over a short warm up window, you give the service time to scale and you minimize initial failures while still reaching the target throughput.

The option Use the XML API instead of the JSON API for all Cloud Storage operations is incorrect because switching APIs does not change backend capacity or rate limiting behavior, and it does not address burst induced errors.

The option Add client and server retries with exponential backoff and jitter when HTTP errors occur is insufficient because it helps recover after errors but it does not prevent the initial failures during a burst. Retries can also amplify traffic during a surge which can prolong the problem.

The option Distribute uploads across several separate Cloud Storage buckets is not appropriate because it changes the storage topology which the question explicitly prohibits.

questions.question: A catalog service you are developing runs on Cloud Run with Firestore in Datastore mode behind it, and one endpoint returns the list of available items to the web app. Once concurrency climbs to roughly 900 users you start seeing HTTP 500 responses, and the Cloud Run logs reveal instances pinned at a 1 GB memory ceiling as Firestore entity reads spike. You want to rework the listing query so the instances stay healthy and the UI can keep paging through results smoothly. What should you do?

options.text: Increase the Cloud Run service memory limit
Use integer offsets for pagination in the query that retrieves the listing
Use Firestore query cursors to paginate and retrieve the listing in smaller batches
Use projection queries to return only the necessary fields for each item in the listing

questions.correct_text: Use Firestore query cursors to paginate and retrieve the listing in smaller batches
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Use Firestore query cursors to paginate and retrieve the listing in smaller batches.

This returns only the next page anchored to the last document from the previous page and avoids scanning past results. By limiting each page and advancing with a cursor, the service reduces entity reads and memory pressure on each Cloud Run instance. That keeps instances from hitting memory limits during peaks and lets the UI fetch additional pages smoothly and predictably.

Increasing the Cloud Run service memory limit addresses the symptom rather than the cause. It does not reduce the number of Firestore reads or the data processed per request, so instances can still face heavy load during peaks while costs rise.

Using integer offsets for pagination forces the backend to read and discard skipped entities before returning the page, which amplifies reads and memory use as page numbers grow. Under high concurrency this quickly spikes entity reads and can exhaust instance memory.

Using projection queries to return only necessary fields can reduce payload size in Datastore mode, but it does not fix the inefficiency of scanning or skipping large result sets. It also brings limitations and still requires an efficient pagination strategy, so it will not stabilize instances during spikes by itself.

questions.question: A new customer portal at Orion Media must allow sign in through three or more external identity providers, for example Google, Facebook, and GitHub. The team is after a managed offering that speaks OIDC or SAML, scales into the millions of accounts, and plugs into the web front end. Which Google Cloud service should handle authentication?

Cloud Identity Platform
Cloud Identity and Access Management
Firebase Authentication

questions.correct_text: Cloud Identity Platform
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Cloud Identity Platform. It is a fully managed customer identity service on Google Cloud that supports standards based federation with OIDC and SAML, integrates cleanly with web front ends through SDKs and REST, and is built to scale to millions of user accounts.

It ships with out of the box connectors for common social identity providers such as Google, Facebook, and GitHub, and it also supports generic OIDC and SAML so you can add more providers as needed. It offers user management APIs, multi tenancy, and configurable authentication flows, which makes it a strong fit for a large scale customer portal.

Cloud Identity-Aware Proxy secures access to applications running on Google Cloud by enforcing access for authenticated users, but it is meant for protecting internal or employee facing apps rather than serving as a customer identity provider for public sign up and sign in.

Cloud Identity and Access Management controls permissions for Google Cloud resources for workforce users and service accounts. It is not an end user authentication system and does not handle federation with external identity providers for your application.

Firebase Authentication focuses on developer friendly auth for mobile and web apps, and while it supports popular social logins, it does not provide the full enterprise federation capabilities and controls emphasized here, such as direct SAML and generic OIDC connectors with governance and SLAs in standard Firebase projects.

questions.question: BrightLedger develops a Google Cloud service with its pipeline built on Cloud Build and Cloud Source Repositories. What the team wants is a dependable, repeatable way to push releases to production that leans on automation together with code review. Which workflow fits that goal?

options.text: Commit straight to the production branch in Cloud Source Repositories and start a Cloud Build manually
Maintain separate repositories for development, staging, and production and run manual builds for each environment
Work in feature branches and merge into the main production branch through review and set a Cloud Build trigger on main to build and deploy automatically
Create one Cloud Build trigger that deploys to production for any branch pattern so any push can release

questions.correct_text: Work in feature branches and merge into the main production branch through review and set a Cloud Build trigger on main to build and deploy automatically
questions.explanation:
The correct option is Work in feature branches and merge into the main production branch through review and set a Cloud Build trigger on main to build and deploy automatically.

This workflow gives a predictable, repeatable release path because all changes are developed in isolated branches, reviewed through pull requests, and merged into main only after approval. A Cloud Build trigger on main then automatically builds and deploys, removing manual steps and ensuring consistent automation with an auditable history of what shipped and why.

It also aligns with common CI and CD practices on Google Cloud, since Cloud Build triggers can filter on the main branch and run pipelines that test, build, and deploy. Although the question references Cloud Source Repositories, which has been retired on newer timelines, the same branch and trigger pattern applies with other supported Git providers.

Committing straight to the production branch and starting a Cloud Build manually is unsuitable because it bypasses code review and relies on manual starts, undermining predictability, auditability, and repeatability.

Maintaining separate repositories for development, staging, and production with manual builds complicates traceability and increases manual work. A single repository with branches or controlled release mechanisms is simpler and more reliable for promoting changes.

Creating one Cloud Build trigger that deploys to production for any branch removes necessary control and review. Allowing any branch to release to production increases risk and does not enforce the required approval gates.

questions.explanation:
The right pick is Use Jest module mocks and spies to replace HTTP and Pub/Sub clients with fakes during testing.

This choice ensures your unit tests are fast and deterministic because the code under test does not make any real network calls. By mocking the HTTP client and the Pub/Sub publisher, you can simulate responses and verify interactions such as which methods were called and with what data. This approach isolates the module so failures clearly indicate code defects rather than flaky network conditions or external system issues.

Run the tests for scheduleHandler.js in an isolated GKE namespace is not appropriate for unit tests because the code would still reach the network and external services. This is closer to an integration or system test and would be slower and more brittle than an isolated unit test.

Configure Cloud Build to run tests against a staging Google Cloud project with test credentials still hits external systems and requires cloud resources. That turns unit tests into integration tests and adds latency and potential flakiness, which contradicts the requirement for quick tests that avoid external dependencies.

Redesign scheduleHandler.js so it no longer depends on any external services at all is unnecessary and unrealistic for a module that must call third party APIs and publish events. A better practice is to keep the design but inject dependencies and use mocks in tests so the production behavior remains intact while tests stay fast and isolated.

questions.question: Cobalt Commerce Analytics runs a large fleet of microservices on Google Kubernetes Engine. Its platform engineers want every call between services encrypted with mutual TLS, they want one place to apply consistent traffic rules, and they want fine grained per-request telemetry, all of it achieved without touching the source of any application. Which technology should they roll out?
questions.correct_text: Istio
questions.explanation:
Istio is the right answer. As a service mesh layered onto GKE, it turns on mutual TLS between workloads, gives the platform team a single control point for traffic policy, and emits granular per-request telemetry, none of which requires editing application code.

The mesh works by injecting Envoy sidecar proxies alongside each pod, and those proxies negotiate mutual TLS automatically for pod to pod traffic. Because policy is declared on mesh resources, the team can apply authentication and authorization rules uniformly so that every service shares the same security baseline. Traffic features like timeouts, retries, and weighted splitting are likewise expressed in mesh configuration instead of in the services themselves.

The same sidecars collect telemetry on their own, producing detailed metrics, logs, and traces along every request path. The team therefore gains deep observability while the application logic stays untouched.

Cloud Armor operates at the network edge, where it provides DDoS mitigation and web application firewall rules. It neither secures traffic flowing between services inside the cluster nor offers a mesh capable of mutual TLS or mesh-wide telemetry.

Secret Manager exists to hold secrets and to manage their rotation and access. It has nothing to do with encrypting service to service traffic, defining traffic policy, or gathering request telemetry.

Traffic Director is a managed control plane for Envoy and proxyless gRPC aimed at global traffic management. On its own it is not a drop-in service mesh for GKE and it will not silently enforce mutual TLS and shared in-cluster policy unless you pair it with a mesh such as Istio.

questions.question: A consumer app vendor at example.com runs its workload across four namespaces in a single Google Kubernetes Engine cluster. Security wants pods to talk freely with other pods in their own namespace, but pods must never be allowed to open connections to pods sitting in a different namespace. Which mechanism should you adopt?
questions.correct_text: Kubernetes Network Policies
questions.explanation:
Kubernetes Network Policies are the correct mechanism, since they express ingress and egress rules scoped to namespaces. That lets you keep traffic open inside a namespace while forbidding pods from reaching across namespace boundaries.

The pattern is to turn on Network Policy enforcement for the cluster, then apply a default deny on egress along with an allow rule whose selector matches every pod in the same namespace. The result is unrestricted intra-namespace communication and blocked cross-namespace connections, which is exactly the stated goal.

Istio Service Mesh can apply service to service controls at higher layers and brings mutual TLS and routing, yet it is overkill for plain namespace-level isolation and raises operational burden while solving the problem at the wrong layer.

Cloud VPN builds encrypted links between networks for hybrid or VPC to VPC use. It has no influence over how one pod reaches another inside a GKE cluster.

VPC firewall rules act on traffic to and from VM instances and subnets, so they cannot select Kubernetes pods or namespaces. They simply cannot encode a rule that permits traffic only within a namespace and blocks the rest.

questions.question: You are designing a new backend for Crestlane Logistics. The team requires that every change to the cloud infrastructure is versioned and auditable. They want to rely on fully managed Google services for both the application stack and the build and deployment tooling. The application must execute on a serverless compute platform with minimal operational overhead. Which architecture design should you choose?

options.text: Create a Cloud Build pipeline that applies Deployment Manager templates for infrastructure, then build a container from the latest source and deploy it to a Compute Engine instance
Provision Jenkins from Google Cloud Marketplace to run the CI pipeline, fetch the code from a Git repository, and deploy the application to App Engine

Store both application code and infrastructure as code in a Git repository, use Cloud Build to apply Terraform for infrastructure changes, and deploy the application to Cloud Functions within the pipeline
Script infrastructure creation with gcloud commands, set up Cloud Build for application changes that containerize the code, and deploy the container to Cloud Run

questions.correct_text: Store both application code and infrastructure as code in a Git repository, use Cloud Build to apply Terraform for infrastructure changes, and deploy the application to Cloud Functions within the pipeline
questions.explanation:
The right design is Store both application code and infrastructure as code in a Git repository, use Cloud Build to apply Terraform for infrastructure changes, and deploy the application to Cloud Functions within the pipeline.

Keeping both application and infrastructure definitions in Git gives you version history and pull request reviews, which satisfies the requirement for versioning and traceability. Cloud Build is a fully managed Google service for build and deployment, and it produces build history and audit logs that make changes auditable. Terraform provides declarative infrastructure as code with plan and apply steps that are easy to review and automate. Cloud Functions is a fully managed serverless platform, so the application runs without server management and operational overhead stays minimal. Together, Cloud Build and Cloud Functions meet the requirement to rely on fully managed Google services for the tooling and the runtime.

Create a Cloud Build pipeline that applies Deployment Manager templates for infrastructure, then build a container from the latest source and deploy it to a Compute Engine instance is not aligned because Compute Engine is not serverless and you must manage virtual machine instances. Deployment Manager has also been deprecated and is being retired, which makes this choice less suitable for new designs on current exams.

Provision Jenkins from Google Cloud Marketplace to run the CI pipeline, fetch the code from a Git repository, and deploy the application to App Engine does not meet the requirement to rely on fully managed Google services for build and deployment. Jenkins is not a fully managed Google service, and you would still operate and patch it. While App Engine is serverless, the CI tooling is not fully managed by Google.

Script infrastructure creation with gcloud commands, set up Cloud Build for application changes that containerize the code, and deploy the container to Cloud Run uses a serverless runtime for the application, but the infrastructure workflow is imperative scripting. Even if scripts are stored in Git, they do not provide the same declarative, reviewable, and stateful audit trail as infrastructure as code, so this approach falls short of the strong versioning and auditability required.

questions.question: At a regional courier firm, an order-processing service pulls events off a Google Cloud Pub/Sub subscription. You want unit tests that prove your code parses incoming messages and acknowledges them correctly. Those tests have to stay cheap and must never touch a live Pub/Sub topic or subscription. Which approach fits best?
questions.correct_text: Run the Pub/Sub emulator locally to mimic message delivery and acknowledgements
questions.explanation:
The right choice is to run the Pub/Sub emulator locally to mimic message delivery and acknowledgements.

The emulator runs entirely on your workstation or inside your CI runners and needs no live topic or subscription at all. You can publish test messages, consume them in your code, and assert on acknowledgement behavior, which is precisely what makes it suited to cheap, repeatable unit tests.

Standing up a dedicated test subscription in a staging project still leans on real Pub/Sub resources. That brings cost and an external dependency and breaks the rule that no real topic or subscription may be used.

Having Cloud Logging capture production messages for replay does not work because logs are neither a reliable nor a supported way to replay Pub/Sub traffic. It also wires your tests to production data and systems, destroying isolation and creating privacy and security exposure.

Shifting the tests to Pub/Sub Lite in a separate project still consumes real resources, so it misses the requirement. Pub/Sub Lite also behaves differently and is not a drop-in substitute for Pub/Sub, making it a poor basis for unit testing parse and acknowledge logic.

questions.question: A retail startup named Sterling Outfitters is moving its commerce site at sterlingoutfit.io to Google Cloud and must manage ephemeral user sessions and persistent shopping carts in a secure and scalable manner that follows Google guidance. Sessions should expire in about 30 minutes, and cart contents must be durable and quickly retrievable across regions. Which approach should the team adopt?

options.text: Use BigQuery to store both session data and shopping cart records
Write shopping cart objects to Cloud Storage using a unique session token as the object name
Store session state in Memorystore for Redis with expirations and persist shopping cart items in Firestore
Keep sessions and carts in instance memory and rely on cookie based session affinity on a global external HTTP(S) Load Balancer

questions.correct_text: Store session state in Memorystore for Redis with expirations and persist shopping cart items in Firestore
questions.explanation:
The right approach is Store session state in Memorystore for Redis with expirations and persist shopping cart items in Firestore.

This approach cleanly separates ephemeral and durable concerns. The in memory cache supports per key expiration so it can enforce a session lifetime of about thirty minutes with very low latency and high throughput. The document database provides durable storage with strong consistency and multi region availability, which keeps cart contents safe and quickly retrievable even during zonal outages. This pattern keeps the application tier stateless and scales horizontally while following Google guidance for using a cache for sessions and a database for persistent data.

Use BigQuery to store both session data and shopping cart records is not suitable because BigQuery is an analytical data warehouse that optimizes for large scale batch analytics rather than low latency transactional reads and writes. It is not intended for per request session state or frequent cart updates.

Write shopping cart objects to Cloud Storage using a unique session token as the object name is not a good fit because an object store is not a transactional database. It lacks efficient record level updates, queries, and atomic operations for cart changes. It also provides no built in session expiry, and coupling object names to session tokens raises security and access control concerns.

Keep sessions and carts in instance memory and rely on cookie based session affinity on a global external HTTP(S) Load Balancer is risky and not durable. Instance restarts or autoscaling would lose all state, and session affinity only influences routing and does not provide storage or cross region continuity. This design breaks under failures and does not meet durability or scalability goals.

options.text: Put both subs-dev and subs-prod in one environment group called subs-group and register both hostnames on that group
Place subs-dev and subs-prod in a single environment group and bind each hostname straight to the matching environment
Place subs-dev in a dev environment group and subs-prod in a prod environment group, then register each hostname on the corresponding environment group
Skip environment groups and use Cloud Load Balancing URL maps to route api-dev.example.com to subs-dev and api.example.com to subs-prod

questions.question: Using Apigee, you are publishing a Subscriptions API for a digital publishing company. You have built two environments, subs-dev and subs-prod, and you intend to surface them on separate hostnames, api-dev.example.com/v2/subscriptions for one and api.example.com/v2/subscriptions for the other. How should you configure things so that each environment can be reached only on its own hostname?
questions.correct_text: Place subs-dev in a dev environment group and subs-prod in a prod environment group, then register each hostname on the corresponding environment group
questions.explanation:
The correct configuration is to place subs-dev in a dev environment group and subs-prod in a prod environment group, then register each hostname on the corresponding environment group.

In Apigee, inbound hostnames belong to environment groups, and a hostname can only reach the environments that are attached to its group. If subs-dev lives in a dev group that owns api-dev.example.com, and subs-prod lives in a prod group that owns api.example.com, the two are strictly separated. Each hostname resolves only to the environment in its own group, which is exactly the isolation the requirement asks for.

Putting both subs-dev and subs-prod in one environment group with both hostnames registered fails because both hostnames then resolve into the same group. Either hostname could reach any proxy deployed in either environment within that group, so there is no isolation.

Binding each hostname straight to the matching environment is also wrong because hostnames are not configured on environments at all. They are defined on environment groups, so a direct hostname-to-environment binding does not exist.

Using Cloud Load Balancing URL maps instead of environment groups is incorrect because Apigee resolves inbound hostnames through environment groups. You still must use environment groups to tie hostnames to environments, and an external URL map does not remove that requirement.

questions.question: At LakeshoreView Media your team writes receipt files to a Cloud Storage bucket in the production project, and you want every new or replaced object to result in a message on a Pub/Sub topic for downstream processing. You prefer the simplest approach that avoids building and operating custom services. What should you do?

options.text: Create a Cloud Function that triggers on changes in the bucket and publishes a message to the Pub/Sub topic
Deploy a container to Cloud Run and use Eventarc to receive Cloud Storage Audit Logs events, then forward to the Pub/Sub topic
Run a workload on Google Kubernetes Engine that polls the bucket and sends a Pub/Sub message when it finds new files
Configure Pub/Sub notifications on the Cloud Storage bucket so that object changes publish directly to the topic

questions.correct_text: Configure Pub/Sub notifications on the Cloud Storage bucket so that object changes publish directly to the topic
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Configure Pub/Sub notifications on the Cloud Storage bucket so that object changes publish directly to the topic.

This uses the bucket feature that emits object change events and publishes them to a topic without any code to run. It covers object finalization events which occur when new objects are created or overwritten, and it keeps operations simple since you only configure the bucket to publish and ensure the topic IAM is set correctly.

Create a Cloud Function that triggers on changes in the bucket and publishes a message to the Pub/Sub topic is unnecessary for this requirement because it adds code and a runtime to manage when the bucket can publish directly.

Deploy a container to Cloud Run and use Eventarc to receive Cloud Storage Audit Logs events, then forward to the Pub/Sub topic adds more moving parts and still requires you to build and operate a forwarding service. This is more complex than using the native bucket integration.

Run a workload on Google Kubernetes Engine that polls the bucket and sends a Pub/Sub message when it finds new files is not event driven and increases cost and operational overhead. Polling can be inefficient and can miss or duplicate changes.
