questions.question: A SaaS provider named Highridge Analytics runs its customer facing service on Google Kubernetes Engine, and users are seeing intermittent response time spikes between 1 and 3 seconds during peak traffic. As the developer on call, what is the most appropriate first action to diagnose where the latency originates?

options.text: Increase the Deployment's replica count to spread traffic across more pods
Start with Cloud Trace to visualize request paths and locate the latency bottleneck
Review Cloud Logging to look for warnings and error messages that might correlate with slow requests
Upgrade the node pool to a larger machine type with more vCPU and memory

questions.correct_text: Start with Cloud Trace to visualize request paths and locate the latency bottleneck
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Start with Cloud Trace to visualize request paths and locate the latency bottleneck.

Cloud Trace gives end to end visibility into each request across services running on GKE and shows spans with precise timing so you can see exactly where time is spent. During peak traffic, you can compare slow outliers with normal traces and quickly identify whether latency is coming from application code, interservice calls, databases, or external dependencies. Starting with Cloud Trace is the most appropriate first step because it diagnoses the source of latency without changing the system.

Increase the Deployment's replica count to spread traffic across more pods is a scaling change rather than a diagnostic action, and it can mask the issue. If the slowdown is caused by a downstream dependency or a shared resource, adding pods can increase contention and still will not reveal the root cause.

Review Cloud Logging to look for warnings and error messages that might correlate with slow requests can provide context, but logs do not visualize the request path across services and they often cannot pinpoint which hop introduces latency. Use logs to deepen the investigation after you have localized the bottleneck.

Upgrade the node pool to a larger machine type with more vCPU and memory is capacity tuning, not diagnosis. It increases cost and rollout time and may not help if the latency comes from application behavior, a database query, or an external call.

questions.question: Halcyon Retail is preparing to roll out a new set of microservices on Google Cloud. You want to capture latency and error metrics for both the current production version and a new build using real user requests. Before you switch users to the new release you must validate it under the same volume as existing production traffic. Which deployment approach should you choose?

options.text: Perform a blue green cutover with two identical environments
Mirror live production requests and run A/B validation before cutover
Roll out a canary by splitting a small percentage of traffic with Cloud Load Balancing
Apply a rolling update in GKE to gradually replace pods

questions.correct_text: Mirror live production requests and run A/B validation before cutover
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Mirror live production requests and run A/B validation before cutover.

This approach duplicates real user requests to the new build while production continues to serve the only user visible response. It lets you observe latency and error metrics for both versions under the same traffic volume and patterns. You can compare the results and proceed with the cutover only after the new release proves healthy.

Perform a blue green cutover with two identical environments gives you two environments and then switches all traffic to the new one. It does not validate the new build with mirrored live traffic before switching, and you only see full volume after the cutover, which does not meet the requirement.

Roll out a canary by splitting a small percentage of traffic with Cloud Load Balancing sends only a small fraction of users to the new version, which does not provide validation under the same volume as production traffic, and it exposes users during the test.

Apply a rolling update in GKE to gradually replace pods replaces instances behind the service and sends real users to the new pods. It is an in place release method rather than an A/B validation with mirrored traffic, and it cannot keep both versions processing the same full set of requests.

Limited control over the execution environment in App Engine can restrict custom runtimes and system packages
App Engine provides poor integration with CI and CD tooling, which slows automation

questions.question: A team at Riverbend Media uploads application logs to a Cloud Storage bucket every day. Signed in analysts need to review the most recent 18 days of logs frequently, and an external auditor will examine the entire history once per year. Regulations require these logs remain available for at least 7 years. You need a cost efficient storage approach that meets these access patterns and retention needs. What should you do?

options.text: Configure a lifecycle management policy to move objects older than 18 days to Nearline
Create a lifecycle rule that shifts objects older than 18 days into Coldline
Apply Bucket Lock to enforce a 7 year retention policy
Run a scheduled workflow that reclassifies objects older than 18 days to Coldline
Issue short lived JWTs for users who need to read from the Coldline bucket

questions.correct_text: Run a scheduled workflow that reclassifies objects older than 18 days to Coldline
questions.explanation:
The right picks are Create a lifecycle rule that shifts objects older than 18 days into Coldline and Run a scheduled workflow that reclassifies objects older than 18 days to Coldline.

Using Create a lifecycle rule that shifts objects older than 18 days into Coldline aligns the storage class with the access pattern. The newest 18 days remain in Standard for frequent analyst reads while older logs transition to Coldline, where storage is cheaper and data remains available for the annual audit. Coldline is designed for infrequent access, and its minimum storage duration is not a concern because the logs must be retained for seven years.

Run a scheduled workflow that reclassifies objects older than 18 days to Coldline is also valid when teams want orchestration control or need to coordinate transitions across buckets or prefixes. It achieves the same cost optimization by moving infrequently accessed data into Coldline while keeping recent data hot for analysts.

Configure a lifecycle management policy to move objects older than 18 days to Nearline is less cost efficient because Nearline targets monthly access patterns. The auditor only needs the older data once per year, so Coldline provides a better cost fit while still meeting availability needs.

Apply Bucket Lock to enforce a 7 year retention policy is unnecessary because the requirement is to keep data available for seven years rather than to enforce immutability. Bucket Lock makes the retention permanent and cannot be relaxed, which adds operational rigidity without improving cost efficiency for this scenario.

Issue short lived JWTs for users who need to read from the Coldline bucket does not address storage cost or lifecycle strategy. Authentication and authorization are separate concerns and do not influence which storage class best matches the access and retention pattern.

questions.question: When a web application needs to call Google Cloud APIs on behalf of a user who has signed in, which mechanism lets it display a consent screen and ask only for a narrow set of scopes?
questions.correct_text: OAuth 2.0
questions.explanation:
OAuth 2.0 is the correct answer. It is what allows a web app to surface a Google consent screen to a logged-in user and to request just the limited scopes the app needs in order to call Google Cloud APIs for that person.

In this flow the app redirects the user to the consent screen defined in the Google Cloud console. After the user approves the requested scopes, the app receives an authorization code that it trades for an access token and optionally a refresh token. Because the token carries only the granted scopes, least privilege is enforced when the app calls APIs on the user's behalf.

OpenID Connect is about authenticating the user and issuing ID tokens that assert identity. It does not deliver the consent-driven authorization model with granular API scopes that this scenario calls for.

Workload Identity Federation lets external workloads obtain short-lived Google credentials for a service account without keys. It is built for workload to workload exchanges, not for interactive end-user consent, and it never shows a consent screen.

A Service Account Key is a static credential for a service account used in server to server access. It involves no user and no consent screen, and it is discouraged due to the security risk relative to federation or user-driven OAuth.

questions.explanation:
Pick the Local Emulator Suite Firestore emulator, since it lets you test frequently while staying fully isolated from production and keeping cost essentially zero.

Running locally, it makes tests fast and deterministic with no risk of touching production data. You can seed and reset data between runs, validate security rules, and fold it into CI without incurring Firestore charges.

Production Firestore with rollback is risky and slow for frequent runs, because stray writes or botched cleanups can hit live data and you still pay for reads and writes, while rollbacks fail to undo side effects such as triggered functions or consumed quota, so true isolation and low cost are not achieved.

A dedicated staging Firestore project gives isolation but adds operational overhead and ongoing cost, since reads and writes are billed and quotas consumed, and it requires data setup and teardown that slow rapid iteration relative to the local emulator.

options.text: Create one Pub/Sub topic per meter and a push subscription for each topic
Create one Pub/Sub topic and several push subscriptions, each with its own subscription filter, for the processing service
Create one Pub/Sub topic and one pull subscription that every processing instance shares
Create one Pub/Sub topic and one pull subscription per processing instance

questions.question: You are designing a streaming analytics pipeline for MeterFlow Energy that ingests smart-meter telemetry from many cities. Every meter pushes readings into a central processing tier that must scale out on Google Cloud, and you will put Pub/Sub between the meters and the processors to decouple them. The tier needs to sustain roughly 150,000 messages per minute, must avoid processing the same message twice, and you would like to keep the topic layout simple for easy operations. How should you set up the Pub/Sub topics and subscriptions to deliver high throughput with horizontal scaling?
questions.correct_text: Create one Pub/Sub topic and one pull subscription that every processing instance shares
questions.explanation:
The correct option is to create one Pub/Sub topic and one pull subscription that every processing instance shares. This funnels all meter readings into a single stream and lets a pool of workers split the load while sidestepping the fan-out duplicates that come from multiple subscriptions.

With a single shared pull subscription, Pub/Sub spreads messages across the active subscribers of that subscription, so each message lands with only one worker in the group. You scale horizontally simply by adding more subscriber clients, and Pub/Sub balances the load with no extra topics or subscriptions. Pull subscribers also bring flow control and back pressure, which helps the tier hold roughly 150,000 messages per minute without being swamped.

Because delivery is at least once, you should acknowledge only after processing succeeds and make the processing idempotent. With a single subscription, duplicate processing across instances is minimized because you avoid the deliberate duplication that happens once you add more than one subscription on the same topic.

Creating one topic per meter with a push subscription per topic is operationally heavy and does nothing for throughput. It multiplies the topics and endpoints you must manage, and push delivery gives you less control over flow, complicating both scaling and error handling.

Creating one topic with several filtered push subscriptions adds duplication and complexity. Each subscription gets its own copy of matching messages, and overlapping filters cause a message to land on multiple subscriptions, increasing duplicate processing. Push endpoints also add operational overhead and weaker flow control.

Creating one topic with one pull subscription per processing instance means every instance receives every message, since each subscription gets its own copy. That multiplies deliveries, drives up cost, and produces widespread duplicates instead of sharing the work.

options.text: Apply a rolling update within the same namespace that swaps old Pods for new Pods bit by bit while watching metrics and reverting if needed
Bring up the new version in a separate namespace and flip the Ingress so all requests immediately go to the new namespace for evaluation, then delete the old namespace if nothing breaks
Deploy the new release into a parallel namespace and point Kubernetes Ingress at both versions for validation, then switch the Ingress to send all traffic to the new release once checks pass
Use Google Cloud Deploy to run a canary rollout on the GKE cluster, beginning with a small slice of traffic and ramping up after monitoring

questions.question: Meridian Learning Group runs a microservices platform on Google Kubernetes Engine and wants blue green deployments so it can validate new releases with zero downtime and roll back quickly if something breaks. It also wants the cutover to require as little configuration change as possible. Which approach should the team take?
questions.correct_text: Deploy the new release into a parallel namespace and point Kubernetes Ingress at both versions for validation, then switch the Ingress to send all traffic to the new release once checks pass
questions.explanation:
The correct option is to deploy the new release into a parallel namespace and point Kubernetes Ingress at both versions for validation, then switch the Ingress to send all traffic to the new release once checks pass.

This builds two isolated environments running side by side, so you can validate the new Services while the current version keeps serving users. Using GKE Ingress with traffic splitting lets you steer a portion of traffic to the new namespace for verification and health checks. Once validation succeeds, a single Ingress change moves all traffic to the new environment, which keeps the cutover minimal and makes rollback instant by simply pointing traffic back to the original environment.

Applying a rolling update in the same namespace is not blue green because it replaces Pods in place, which complicates rollback and never gives you two fully isolated environments for side-by-side validation.

Bringing up the new version and flipping the Ingress so everything immediately goes to it forces an all-at-once cutover with no safe window where both versions take traffic. That limits validation under real load and raises risk if problems surface right after the switch.

Using Google Cloud Deploy for a canary rollout describes a canary strategy, not blue green. It gradually shifts traffic rather than keeping two fully separate environments for a quick cutover and easy rollback.

options.text: Coldline Storage
Standard Storage
Archive Storage

questions.question: Solstice Benefits must keep policy documents for 15 years to meet regulatory obligations, and the files are written once and almost never read again afterward. Which Cloud Storage class minimizes storage cost for this use case?
questions.correct_text: Archive Storage
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Archive Storage.

This class is tuned for long-term retention at the lowest storage price and is meant for data read less than once a year. It suits write-once workloads well because you only pay retrieval costs when you actually read the data, and the minimum storage duration is a non-issue for multi-year retention. It also works alongside bucket retention policies and object lock, which helps satisfy a 15-year regulatory hold.

Coldline Storage targets data read less than once a quarter and carries a higher storage cost than the archival class. For files written once and held for many years, it will not give you the lowest cost.

Standard Storage is built for frequently accessed, low-latency data, which makes it the most expensive choice for storage and a poor fit for long-term archival.

Nearline Storage is aimed at data read about monthly, so its storage cost exceeds the archival class and it is not ideal when access is rare across many years.

options.text: Enqueue each low-stock alert with Cloud Tasks and invoke a Cloud Run service that calls the email API with retries
Add a Cloud Function that scans Cloud Logging for HTTP 500 errors and resends the failed email requests
Publish low-stock events to a Pub/Sub topic and trigger a Cloud Function subscriber that processes and retries messages automatically
Bump the existing Cloud Function's configured retries and timeout and raise its max instances to absorb the bursts

questions.question: Lumberyard Goods keeps its inventory system on Google Cloud and relies on a Cloud Function to call a third-party email API at api.example.com whenever stock for an item dips below a threshold. During a 45-minute flash sale, several alerts went out late or not at all, and the logs reveal clusters of HTTP 500 errors coming back from the email provider. You need to rework the alert path so notifications are durably accepted and still get processed when traffic spikes or the email API throws transient errors. What should you build?
questions.correct_text: Publish low-stock events to a Pub/Sub topic and trigger a Cloud Function subscriber that processes and retries messages automatically
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is to publish low-stock events to a Pub/Sub topic and trigger a Cloud Function subscriber that processes and retries messages automatically. This design durably accepts the alerts and keeps processing them through spikes and transient provider failures.

The pattern puts a durable buffer in front of the email integration, so alerts are accepted and stored quickly even when the downstream is unstable. Messages are delivered at least once with automatic retry and backoff until they are acknowledged, which absorbs temporary HTTP 500 responses from the email provider. The subscriber scales with load, and you can wire up a dead-letter topic for messages that keep failing so you can inspect or reprocess them safely.

Enqueuing each alert with Cloud Tasks and invoking a Cloud Run service that retries is workable but not the best fit for event distribution and high fan-out. It makes you operate an extra HTTP handler and build your own dead-letter handling and idempotency, whereas the recommended eventing design integrates more simply and scales elastically for bursty publish rates.

Adding a Cloud Function that scans Cloud Logging for HTTP 500 errors and resends them reacts to failures rather than guaranteeing durable acceptance when alerts are created. Logs are not a dependable work queue, so this can drop or duplicate work and add real delay.

Bumping retries, timeout, and max instances on the existing function still lacks a durable buffer. Bursts and provider outages can overwhelm the system and work gets dropped once retries or timeouts run out, since nothing persists the alerts for later processing.

questions.question: A compliance team at WoodMint Finance needs to archive transaction records for long retention. The system must store about 35 TB of structured records that are exported as CSV and JSON, and auditors will access the files about once or twice per month. Regulations require the data to remain available for seven years at the lowest possible cost. Which Google Cloud service should you choose?

options.text: Cloud Spanner
BigQuery
Cloud Storage Nearline class
Cloud Bigtable

questions.correct_text: Cloud Storage Nearline class
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Cloud Storage Nearline class for this requirement.

Cloud Storage Nearline class is optimized for infrequently accessed data and stores objects such as CSV and JSON natively, which matches the format of the exported records. Access roughly once per month fits its intended use pattern, and it provides millisecond access when auditors need the files. It offers significantly lower storage cost than Standard, and when access is only occasional the total cost remains low even with retrieval charges. You can also set a bucket retention policy to enforce seven years so the data remains preserved for compliance while the service scales easily to 35 TB and beyond.

Cloud Spanner is a globally distributed relational database for transactional workloads, and it is not designed to store files as objects. Using it to hold 35 TB for rare access would be costly and unnecessary since it targets low latency OLTP, not archival retention.

BigQuery is a serverless data warehouse for analytical queries. Although you could load CSV or JSON into tables, that would transform the data and introduce storage and query costs that do not align with simple file archiving. Occasional auditor access to original files is better served by object storage.

Cloud Bigtable is a NoSQL wide column database for very low latency and high throughput access patterns. It does not store raw files like CSV and JSON as objects and would be more expensive and operationally unsuitable for a long term archive accessed only a few times per month.

options.text: Turn on Autoclass for the bucket
Set a bucket retention policy with a 12-year duration
Use IAM Conditions to allow access only during the first 12 years after an object is created
Add a lifecycle rule that moves objects to Archive Storage after 5 years
Enable Object Versioning and keep every generation for 12 years

questions.question: You are building a service for Lattice Design Works that keeps confidential design files as objects in one Cloud Storage bucket. Regulators insist every object stay retrievable for at least 12 years after it is created, and access logs show objects older than 5 years are read only very rarely. You want to meet the compliance rule while cutting storage cost on the older files. Which actions should you take?
questions.correct_text: Add a lifecycle rule that moves objects to Archive Storage after 5 years
questions.explanation:
The correct actions are to set a bucket retention policy with a 12-year duration and to add a lifecycle rule that moves objects to Archive Storage after 5 years.

A bucket retention policy guarantees that objects cannot be deleted or overwritten until twelve years have elapsed. That keeps every object retrievable for at least the mandated period and directly satisfies the compliance rule.

A lifecycle rule that transitions objects to Archive after five years lowers spend because Archive is built for long-term retention of data that is read rarely. The objects stay retrievable when needed, and the retention policy together with the lifecycle rule meets both the regulatory and the cost goals.

Turning on Autoclass is not the right fit because it does not guarantee a precise five-year transition point and it does not enforce a minimum retention. Autoclass also cannot run alongside a lifecycle rule that sets the storage class, which would block the exact transition you want.

Using IAM Conditions to allow access only during the first 12 years is wrong because IAM governs authorization, not retention. It could even cut off reads after twelve years, which works against the requirement to keep data retrievable for at least that long.

Enabling Object Versioning and keeping every generation for 12 years is unnecessary and raises cost. Versioning helps you recover from deletes or overwrites, but a retention policy already blocks those actions during the required window.

options.text: Spin up a Compute Engine VM running HAProxy with the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy, then have the app connect via the VM IP
Connect from your laptop to the instance private IP and encrypt each database payload in the app, keeping the decryption key in an App Engine variable
Install the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy on your laptop, run it to reach the Cloud SQL instance, and point the application at 127.0.0.1
Install PostgreSQL on your laptop and point the application at a local database on localhost

questions.question: You are developing a web service for the analytics team at Harborline Apparel that runs on App Engine and uses Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL. Before promoting a build to the team's shared development project, you want to run the service on your laptop. Every connection from your machine to Cloud SQL has to be encrypted in transit and must authenticate to the managed PostgreSQL instance using Cloud IAM. What should you set up locally before you launch the server?
questions.correct_text: Install the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy on your laptop, run it to reach the Cloud SQL instance, and point the application at 127.0.0.1
questions.explanation:
The correct option is to install the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy on your laptop, run it to reach the Cloud SQL instance, and point the application at 127.0.0.1.

This opens a secure TLS tunnel from your workstation to Cloud SQL and authorizes the connection with your IAM credentials. Because the application connects to localhost, no TLS-related code changes are needed and the tunnel still guarantees encryption in transit. When Cloud SQL IAM database authentication is enabled, this setup lets you authenticate to the PostgreSQL instance with IAM, satisfying the IAM-based authentication requirement from your laptop.

Spinning up a Compute Engine VM running HAProxy with the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy is unnecessary and pushes the trust boundary onto a VM instead of your workstation. Your local connection would end at the VM and might not use your IAM identity to authenticate to the database, adding complexity without meeting the requirement to authenticate from your workstation with IAM.

Connecting to the private IP and encrypting each payload in the app, with the key in an App Engine variable, gives no transport encryption by default and depends on error-prone custom payload encryption. It also does not use Cloud IAM to authenticate to Cloud SQL, and stashing keys in an App Engine variable has nothing to do with local development and is not an appropriate control.

Installing PostgreSQL locally and pointing the app at a local database never connects to the managed Cloud SQL instance at all. It therefore provides neither IAM authentication to Cloud SQL nor encryption in transit to the service you must test against.

questions.question: You are building a payments API for brightorbit.io on Google Cloud. The business requires the service to keep operating if an entire zone in the selected region becomes unavailable. Which deployment strategy should you implement to meet this requirement?

options.text: Use Cloud CDN to cache application responses
Place instances behind a global external HTTP(S) Load Balancer while hosting all backends in one zone
Deploy the service across multiple zones in a single region using a regional configuration
Keep all services in one zone and enable automated backups

questions.correct_text: Deploy the service across multiple zones in a single region using a regional configuration
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Deploy the service across multiple zones in a single region using a regional configuration.

A regional deployment distributes compute resources across multiple zones within the same region so the service can continue operating if one zone fails. You can use a regional managed instance group or a regional GKE cluster to spread instances across zones. With health checks and a load balancer, traffic is routed to healthy backends in the remaining zones when a zonal outage occurs.

Use Cloud CDN to cache application responses is not sufficient for high availability of a payments API. A CDN improves latency and offloads cacheable responses, yet dynamic API traffic and writes must reach the origin service. If the backend in a failed zone is unavailable, then the CDN cannot keep the service operating.

Place instances behind a global external HTTP(S) Load Balancer while hosting all backends in one zone does not meet the requirement. A global load balancer helps distribute traffic, however if every backend resides in a single zone, then a zonal failure removes all capacity and the service will be unavailable.

Keep all services in one zone and enable automated backups addresses data protection and recovery objectives rather than availability. Backups do not keep the API running during a zonal outage, and a single zone deployment lacks redundancy.

Stand up a Compute Engine VM to run JMeter, export Cloud Run logs to BigQuery with a log sink, and build reports in Looker Studio

questions.question: Beacon Lending wants to load test a Cloud Run API with Apache JMeter and intends to follow Google's recommended way of running the tests, centralizing log analysis, and building dashboards. How should the team arrange the load generator, the logging, and the reporting so the workflow stays reliable and scalable?

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is to stand up a Compute Engine VM to run JMeter, export Cloud Run logs to BigQuery with a log sink, and build reports in Looker Studio.

This matches Google Cloud guidance for a dependable load generator and for analytics at scale. A dedicated VM offers predictable resources for headless JMeter runs and avoids the variability of developer machines. Routing Cloud Run logs through a Cloud Logging sink into BigQuery yields structured, queryable data with retention controls and SQL analysis. Looker Studio connects directly to BigQuery, so the team can build interactive dashboards with no extra pipeline.

Standing up a VM but exporting logs to a Cloud Storage bucket is not ideal because Cloud Storage stores raw files rather than structured tables. That makes ad hoc analysis and dashboarding awkward and forces extra parsing or ETL before you can visualize anything.

Running JMeter on a developer laptop is neither reliable nor scalable, since a laptop is prone to resource contention and network variability. It also suggests Looker rather than Looker Studio, adding unnecessary modeling overhead for simple log dashboards.

Running JMeter in a GKE Autopilot cluster adds orchestration complexity for a simple load generator and again routes logs to Cloud Storage, which is unsuited to interactive log analytics or dashboards without extra processing.

questions.question: Helios Pay operates a busy Cloud Run service serving roughly 90,000 requests per hour, and the team wants to ship features fast while keeping risk to the broader user base low. Which release strategy lets you try changes on a small slice of users first and then safely expand to everyone?
questions.correct_text: Create a new revision and use Cloud Run traffic splitting to route 5 percent of requests to it, then gradually increase the share while telemetry stays healthy
questions.explanation:
The correct option is to create a new revision and use Cloud Run traffic splitting to route 5 percent of requests to it, then gradually increase the share while telemetry stays healthy.

This is a canary-style rollout on Cloud Run that sends a small fraction of live traffic to a new revision. You can watch errors, latency, and business metrics with real users while keeping the blast radius small. If everything looks healthy, you raise the share until all traffic is on the new revision, and if trouble appears you stop or roll back fast.

Doing a blue green release that cuts 100 percent of traffic after basic checks is a full cutover and does not validate the change on only a small slice of users. Even though rollback is easy, it exposes everyone at once, which does not meet the requirement.

Running weekly production load tests can help with capacity and regression checks, but it is not a deployment method that governs how much live traffic sees the new version. It does not give you a gradual production rollout.

Deploying to a staging project and stress testing there improves preproduction quality but does not reduce production risk, because once you promote, every user is affected simultaneously.

questions.question: At a fintech startup called Cypress Pay, you run a Cloud Run service that processes confidential customer data only during each request. A new compliance rule states that sensitive content must never be persisted to disk and cannot land on any container filesystem. You need a temporary storage mechanism for this short lived data that satisfies the rule and provides low latency access for the service. What should you choose?

options.text: Write temporary objects to a Cloud Storage bucket with CMEK and a lifecycle rule to delete after 30 minutes
Store ephemeral request state in Memorystore and access it from the Cloud Run service
Keep temporary payloads in Secret Manager and delete versions after processing
Use Firestore native mode with a TTL policy to remove documents after 1 hour

questions.correct_text: Store ephemeral request state in Memorystore and access it from the Cloud Run service
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Store ephemeral request state in Memorystore and access it from the Cloud Run service. It keeps transient data in memory and provides very low latency while ensuring nothing is written to the container file system.

Memorystore is an in memory data store that supports short time to live keys so the service can create and expire values on a per request basis. It delivers millisecond level access over the network and avoids any persistent disk writes, which aligns with the rule that sensitive content must never be persisted and must not touch the container filesystem.

Write temporary objects to a Cloud Storage bucket with CMEK and a lifecycle rule to delete after 30 minutes is incorrect because objects are durably stored on disk even if encrypted and a lifecycle rule only deletes them later. This violates the requirement that the data must never be persisted to disk.

Keep temporary payloads in Secret Manager and delete versions after processing is incorrect because Secret Manager is for managing secrets rather than transient request payloads and stored versions are persisted to durable storage until deletion. This approach also introduces unnecessary latency and quota limits for per request state.

Use Firestore native mode with a TTL policy to remove documents after 1 hour is incorrect because Firestore persists data to disk and TTL removals are not immediate. It also has higher latency compared to an in memory cache for hot request data.

questions.question: You want a web app running on one Compute Engine VM to be reachable by the public over HTTPS, and users should not have to authenticate. What is the right way to do this?
questions.correct_text: External HTTPS Load Balancer with Google-managed certificate
questions.explanation:
The right way is an External HTTPS Load Balancer with a Google-managed certificate.

It provides a global Layer 7 front door that terminates TLS with certificates Google provisions and renews on your behalf. Users reach the app over HTTPS with no authentication prompt, and the load balancer forwards requests to a backend service holding a single instance group that contains your VM. That makes the app public over HTTPS while keeping certificate handling simple.

Publishing static files to a public Cloud Storage bucket only serves static content and cannot run or proxy a VM-hosted app, so it cannot forward dynamic requests to your instance.

Identity-Aware Proxy is built to require authentication, but the question explicitly forbids it, and IAP fronts an existing HTTPS endpoint rather than replacing it.

A Network Load Balancer works at Layer 4, so it neither terminates HTTPS nor supplies managed certificates. You would manage TLS on the VM yourself, which adds complexity and misses the requirement for a clean public HTTPS endpoint.

questions.question: You need to host a gRPC backend that keeps persistent connections open and sees bursty, uneven traffic, and you want both cost and operational effort kept low. Which Google Cloud service should you choose?
questions.correct_text: Cloud Run
questions.explanation:
Choose Cloud Run.

It natively handles gRPC over HTTP/2, bidirectional streaming and long-lived connections included, within its documented limits. It ramps up fast to meet bursty traffic and scales all the way down to zero when idle, holding cost low. You are billed only while requests are served and there is nothing to operate, which keeps the operational burden minimal.

It also permits high concurrency per instance and lets you optionally hold a small minimum instance count to reduce cold starts, all while staying fully managed.

GKE Autopilot can serve gRPC but still expects Kubernetes objects and tuning. Its pods keep running and incur charges even when idle, and they do not scale to zero by default, so it is less cost efficient than serverless for spiky traffic.

App Engine flexible environment keeps VMs alive and frequently needs a minimum instance count. It scales more slowly and carries a baseline cost when idle, working against the aim of low cost for bursty load.

Cloud Functions is not designed for long-lived streaming gRPC and is tuned for short HTTP or event-driven runs. Without first-class gRPC server support, it is a poor fit for a backend built on persistent connections.

questions.question: Which Google Cloud product is purpose-built to store application tokens and passwords centrally and auditably, with versioning and fine grained access control?
questions.correct_text: Secret Manager
questions.explanation:
The product is Secret Manager, which provides centralized, auditable storage for application tokens and passwords with versioning and fine grained access control.

It holds secrets such as API keys and database passwords, exposes versions to support safe rotation, and lets you set fine grained permissions at the project or secret level. It records access through Cloud Audit Logs and offers regional replication choices plus integration with common runtimes via client libraries and environment variables.

Identity and Access Management decides who can act on Google Cloud resources, but it does not store application secrets and offers no secret versioning or retrieval APIs.

Cloud Storage is an object store; you could place sensitive files in it, but it is not built for secret management and lacks native secret retrieval, rotation workflows, and secret-specific auditing despite supporting object versioning.

Cloud Key Management Service manages cryptographic keys and key versions and performs encryption and decryption, yet it neither stores application secrets nor provides secret-access workflows, so it complements rather than replaces a dedicated secrets service.

questions.question: A streaming-media startup has gathered about 110 TB of clickstream logs over the past five years and now needs to run both complex ad hoc and scheduled SQL queries over that historical data, with no online transaction processing in the picture. Which single Google Cloud service should provide both the storage and the analytics?
questions.correct_text: BigQuery
questions.explanation:
BigQuery is the service to choose. As a serverless data warehouse it can hold and analyze roughly 110 TB of historical clickstream logs and run complex ad hoc and scheduled SQL queries with no need for online transaction processing.

BigQuery is built for analytics at scale and keeps storage and compute separate, so you can run interactive analysis over years of data and schedule recurring queries without operating any infrastructure. It handles terabytes to petabytes with standard SQL and gives a cost-effective, fully managed home for both exploration and scheduled reporting.

Cloud Storage is an object store for files with no SQL engine of its own. You would still need a separate analytics service to query, which breaks the requirement to use one service for storage and analytics.

Cloud SQL targets transactional relational workloads and is not tuned to scan tens of terabytes with heavy analytical SQL. It fits OLTP rather than large-scale historical analytics.

Bigtable is a low-latency NoSQL wide-column store for key-based access and time series, and it does not natively support SQL analytics or joins, so it is wrong for ad hoc SQL over clickstream logs.

questions.question: At Pelagic Labs your platform team manages a production application on Google Kubernetes Engine. A separate integration team needs to run their connector alongside your service in the same cluster. You must allow them to deploy and manage only their own resources and you must prevent any ability to change your application. What should you do?

options.text: Grant the Viewer role on the cluster's Google Cloud project by using IAM
Provision a separate GKE cluster and grant the other team the Editor role on the project with IAM
Create a dedicated namespace in the existing GKE cluster and use Kubernetes RBAC to assign the admin role that is scoped to that namespace to the other team
Create a new namespace in the current cluster and grant the other team project wide Editor permissions through IAM

questions.correct_text: Create a dedicated namespace in the existing GKE cluster and use Kubernetes RBAC to assign the admin role that is scoped to that namespace to the other team
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Create a dedicated namespace in the existing GKE cluster and use Kubernetes RBAC to assign the admin role that is scoped to that namespace to the other team.

Namespaces provide isolation of Kubernetes resources within the same cluster, and Kubernetes RBAC lets you scope permissions to that namespace. With namespace scoped RBAC you can bind the built in admin ClusterRole to the integration team using a RoleBinding in only their namespace. They can then create and manage Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, and other namespaced resources for their connector while they cannot change your application or any cluster wide objects. This aligns with least privilege and separates duties while sharing the same GKE cluster.

Grant the Viewer role on the cluster's Google Cloud project by using IAM is insufficient because Viewer is read only and does not permit creating or modifying Kubernetes objects. Project IAM also governs Google Cloud resources rather than granting the namespaced Kubernetes permissions needed to deploy and manage the connector.

Provision a separate GKE cluster and grant the other team the Editor role on the project with IAM does not meet the requirement to run in the same cluster, and it grants overly broad project wide permissions. Spinning up another cluster increases cost and complexity when namespace isolation with RBAC already solves the problem.

Create a new namespace in the current cluster and grant the other team project wide Editor permissions through IAM violates least privilege and still does not provide namespace scoped Kubernetes permissions. Editor affects many Google Cloud resources outside the cluster, and it is not the right mechanism to control access to Kubernetes objects within a single namespace.

questions.question: A community platform you are developing on mcnz.com has to keep structured account and preference records alongside photos and short video clips that members upload. First-year projections are around 100,000 monthly active users and about 16 TB of media. The profile data demands transactional consistency while the media calls for durable, inexpensive storage. Which combination of Google Cloud services should you adopt?

questions.explanation:
The pairing to use is Cloud SQL for structured profiles and Cloud Storage for media content.

Cloud SQL is a fully managed relational database with strong transactional consistency for profile changes, meeting the need for reliable account and preference updates, and it serves around 100,000 monthly active users comfortably while keeping administration light. Cloud Storage offers durable, highly available, low-cost object storage for photos and short clips, scaling well beyond 16 TB and serving static media efficiently.

Firestore plus Filestore is a poor fit, because Filestore is a managed NFS share attached to compute instances rather than an object store, and it is not tuned for large-scale web media storage and delivery.

Bigtable plus Cloud Storage misses the transactional requirement for profiles, since Bigtable lacks the multi-row transactions and relational semantics profile updates need, even though the object store suits media.

Cloud Spanner plus Pub/Sub is unsuitable, because Pub/Sub is messaging rather than persistent media storage, and a globally distributed relational database would be unnecessary and costly at this scale.

options.text: Containerize the service on Google Kubernetes Engine with a horizontal pod autoscaler enabled
Run it on Cloud Run with per-request scaling, deployed across several regions behind a global HTTP load balancer
Deploy it to the App Engine standard environment with automatic scaling for web requests

questions.question: Trailblaze's fitness-tracker app surges to roughly 6,000 requests per second during weekly challenges yet stays almost idle for about 20 hours a day. It needs an HTTP API reachable across multiple continents with p95 latency under 250 ms that can drop to zero instances when idle to save money. Which Google Cloud deployment best fits?
questions.correct_text: Run it on Cloud Run with per-request scaling, deployed across several regions behind a global HTTP load balancer
questions.explanation:
The best fit is to run it on Cloud Run with per-request scaling, deployed across several regions behind a global HTTP load balancer.

Being request driven, Cloud Run ramps up quickly to meet the 6,000 requests per second surge and falls to zero when traffic stops. Per-request scaling with concurrency set to one gives each request its own instance, helping hold p95 latency down during spikes.

Spreading the service across regions behind a global HTTP load balancer routes each client to the nearest healthy region, trimming cross-continent latency and supporting the 250 ms p95 target. Serverless network endpoint groups let the load balancer deliver traffic straight to the Cloud Run service in each region, giving a simple multi-region design with no servers to run.

Containerizing on GKE with a horizontal pod autoscaler is a poor fit, because the cluster keeps running with no traffic and the autoscaler does not reach zero by default, sustaining cost through the long idle windows and adding operational overhead the scenario does not need.

Deploying to App Engine standard is not ideal, because an App Engine app is tied to one region, making low-latency multi-continent delivery awkward without complex multi-project patterns. It can shed instances when idle but does not provide the simple multi-region deployment requested.

A Compute Engine managed instance group autoscaling on CPU is a weak match, because it usually keeps at least one VM up and cannot scale to zero, and it reacts to utilization rather than individual requests, which can lag during sudden spikes and push up latency or cost.

questions.question: Sequoia Outfitters is decomposing a legacy monolith into independently deployable microservices on Google Cloud, and the team wants services to evolve without tight coupling to their clients. Which design considerations should you emphasize for the new architecture?

options.text: Rely on Anthos Service Mesh to absorb interface changes so formal API definitions are unnecessary
Apply explicit API versioning so that future changes that break compatibility can be introduced safely
Implement every microservice using the same programming language as its consumers
Define and publish stable API contracts that clearly separate service implementations from their consumers
Require asynchronous messaging for all calls between services regardless of use case

questions.correct_text: Define and publish stable API contracts that clearly separate service implementations from their consumers
questions.explanation:
The right picks are Apply explicit API versioning so that future changes that break compatibility can be introduced safely and Define and publish stable API contracts that clearly separate service implementations from their consumers.

With microservices that evolve independently, API versioning allows breaking changes to be introduced without disrupting existing consumers. You can publish a new version while keeping older versions available so clients migrate at their pace. This supports safe rollout strategies and independent deployments.

Publishing stable API contracts creates a strong boundary between implementation and consumers. Using well specified contracts such as OpenAPI or protobuf makes interfaces explicit and testable and enables code generation, schema validation, and clear expectations which reduces coupling and supports replaceable implementations.

The option Rely on Anthos Service Mesh to absorb interface changes so formal API definitions are unnecessary is incorrect. A service mesh improves traffic management, security, and observability but it does not make interface changes safe for clients, and you still need clear interfaces and change management practices at the API level.

The option Implement every microservice using the same programming language as its consumers is incorrect. Microservices should be technology agnostic, and teams can choose the best stack for each service because interoperability comes from networked APIs rather than language sameness.

The option Require asynchronous messaging for all calls between services regardless of use case is incorrect. You should choose synchronous or asynchronous communication based on latency, consistency, and workflow needs because a blanket mandate adds complexity and can harm user facing interactions that expect immediate responses.

questions.question: Solstice Labs operates four Google Kubernetes Engine clusters across two regions, each running a Deployment named cart-api with ten replicas, and the GKE logging agent ships every container's stdout and stderr to Cloud Logging. You want a single command that returns the merged logs from every replica of this Deployment across all clusters, without signing into each cluster separately. Which command should you run?
questions.correct_text: gcloud logging read "resource.type=k8s_container AND resource.labels.container_name=cart-api"
questions.explanation:
The command to run is gcloud logging read "resource.type=k8s_container AND resource.labels.container_name=cart-api".

Since Cloud Logging collects container stdout and stderr from every GKE cluster in the project, one Logging query can merge the data across clusters and regions. The query filters on the Kubernetes container monitored resource and matches the container name cart-api, returning logs from every replica wherever it runs. You run it once from your workstation, never switching Kubernetes contexts or connecting to a cluster.

kubectl logs deployment/cart-api --all-containers --all-namespaces only acts on the current Kubernetes context, so it shows one cluster at a time and cannot merge across clusters, and it ignores the centralized logs already in Cloud Logging.

gcloud compute ssh my-node --command="sudo journalctl" connects to one VM and reads its system journal, which is not merged container logging across clusters. You would repeat it per node and bypass the centralized Logging service.

kubectl exec -it deploy/cart-api -- journalctl is invalid, because you cannot exec into a Deployment resource, and even on a specific pod you would see only that one container rather than all replicas or clusters, while many containers do not ship journalctl at all.

questions.question: Pathwise Couriers is building an event-driven system on Google Cloud where the application publishes and consumes Cloud Pub/Sub messages for delivery updates, and the team wants send and receive operations to run with the lowest latency they can get. How should the application integrate with Cloud Pub/Sub to keep those operations as fast as possible?
questions.correct_text: Use Google Cloud's official Cloud Pub/Sub client libraries
questions.explanation:
The right integration is to use Google Cloud's official Cloud Pub/Sub client libraries.

They yield the fastest end-to-end behavior because, under the hood, they rely on efficient gRPC streaming and hold long-lived connections. They handle automatic batching and flow control, asynchronous publishers and subscribers, message prefetching, and smart retries with backoff. Collectively these cut per-message overhead and round trips, lowering latency for both sending and receiving.

Hitting the REST endpoints directly on every call is wrong, because synchronous HTTP adds connection and serialization overhead and the REST pull model raises latency, and you forgo the client-side batching and streaming that keep throughput high and latency low.

Invoking gcloud from the application is wrong, because gcloud is an administration and scripting tool. Spawning a process per operation is heavy and unsuited to a low-latency or high-throughput path.

Generating and using raw gRPC stubs is wrong, because while raw stubs can be quick, you would have to reimplement batching, flow control, streaming-pull concurrency, retry logic, and connection management. The official libraries already implement and tune all of that.

questions.question: Cinder Outfitters runs a Kotlin service on a GKE Standard cluster, and it writes structured JSON to standard output. You need those logs in Cloud Logging carrying Kubernetes metadata such as cluster name and node name, and you must achieve it without editing the application code. What should you do?

questions.explanation:
You should enable Cloud Operations for GKE so its built-in collector forwards stdout logs to Cloud Logging with Kubernetes metadata.

Enabling it activates the managed logging pipeline on the cluster. The collector tails container standard output from the node file system and delivers entries to Cloud Logging, enriching each one with Kubernetes resource metadata such as cluster name, node name, namespace, pod, and container, meeting the requirement with no application code change.

When the service writes structured JSON to standard output, Cloud Operations for GKE forwards those lines to Cloud Logging, which parses them as structured logs. The JSON becomes the jsonPayload while the Kubernetes metadata remains available as resource labels and fields, keeping queries and filters simple.

Having the service call the Cloud Logging API and embed cluster and node values is wrong, because it requires code changes and duplicates metadata the platform already supplies, risking inconsistent or missing labels next to the automatic enrichment.

Hand-installing Fluent Bit as a DaemonSet is unnecessary on GKE, since the managed collector ships when you enable Cloud Operations for GKE; running your own adds overhead and configuration to map metadata the managed solution already handles.

Attaching a persistent disk per node and uploading files with a custom script ignores container logging best practices, adding complexity and cost, risking data loss on node changes, omitting Kubernetes metadata, and shifting log shipping into custom scripts instead of the supported managed pipeline.

questions.question: For real-time collaborative editing that must propagate updates to all clients quickly and scale to about twenty thousand simultaneous editors, which Google Cloud data store should you choose?
questions.correct_text: Firestore Native with snapshot listeners
questions.explanation:
Choose Firestore Native with snapshot listeners.

Firestore ships built-in real-time change streams through snapshot listeners that push updates to clients the moment data changes. As a fully managed document database it scales horizontally by itself and sustains large numbers of concurrent connections, which suits collaborative editing where many editors need low-latency updates and consistent document state.

Pub/Sub as a primary store is wrong, because it is messaging rather than a database, offering no queries and no persistent document model for collaborative editing, and it is not meant to be the system of record.

Cloud SQL with polling is wrong, because polling injects latency and load and never delivers instant push updates, and handling many connections with frequent polls at this scale is inefficient and falls short of strict real-time collaboration.

Memorystore for Redis as a primary store is wrong, because Redis in Memorystore is an in-memory cache rather than a durable primary store, lacking the native real-time document synchronization model and durability guarantees these workloads usually need.

questions.question: Migrating a payments ledger from MySQL to Cloud Bigtable, your team at Vellum Payments must settle on an effective row key. In MySQL the table is Customer_Transactions, with columns cust_id INT, event_time DATETIME, txn_type STRING, and amount DECIMAL(19,2), and the composite primary key is cust_id then event_time. You want a Bigtable row key that preserves each customer's activity in chronological order while reducing the risk of hot spotting. Which row key should you choose?
questions.correct_text: Build a composite row key of cust_id followed by event_time
questions.explanation:
The row key to choose is a composite of cust_id followed by event_time.

This aligns with Bigtable row-key best practices. Because Bigtable stores rows in lexicographic order, leading with the customer identifier keeps all of a customer's transactions together, and appending the event time orders them within that customer, making scans by customer and by time efficient. Since customers have different leading keys, write load spreads across tablets, which lowers hot-spotting risk compared with a design that starts with a globally increasing value.

Prefixing with a two-byte hash of cust_id and appending event_time is unsuitable, because it removes the real customer identifier from the key space, interleaving customers under the same short hash, blocking efficient single-customer range scans, and not guaranteeing per-customer time order.

Leading with event_time then cust_id will likely hot spot, because new events share a monotonically increasing leading key, and it scatters a customer's transactions across many ranges rather than keeping them contiguous.

Using cust_id alone collapses a customer's transactions into one very large row, a poor fit for per-event access and time-range scans, with no natural ordering of individual events and a risk of uneven load on large rows.

questions.question: Northwind Athletics is launching a social feed service with intense reads and writes on user profiles and posts, peaking near 50,000 writes per second across two regions. Whichever region serves a request, users must immediately see the latest committed change right after it is made. Which Google Cloud storage service meets these consistency and scale demands?
questions.correct_text: Cloud Spanner
questions.explanation:
Cloud Spanner is the choice, since it provides global external strong consistency together with horizontally scalable throughput, so users read the latest committed update from any region even at peaks near 50,000 writes per second.

Spanner replicates synchronously across multi-region configurations and uses a globally synchronized clock to guarantee read-after-write consistency from any region, and it scales linearly as you add processing units or nodes, sustaining very high read and write rates with transactional guarantees intact.

Cloud SQL uses a single primary with asynchronous replicas for cross-region reads, so a user elsewhere may not see a fresh write right away, and it does not scale to sustained tens of thousands of writes per second without heavy sharding and complexity.

Cloud Bigtable handles enormous throughput, but its multi-cluster replication is eventually consistent across regions, so it cannot guarantee immediate cross-region read-after-write, and it lacks the multi-row transactions strongly consistent profile and feed updates often need.

Cloud Firestore offers strong consistency for single-document reads and queries but is not intended for very high sustained multi-region write rates at this scale, and its index and hot-spot limits can constrain it, while it also lacks global relational transactions for cross-document consistency a feed often requires.

questions.question: Your team at a logistics startup runs production workloads on Google Kubernetes Engine, and you must prevent any deployment unless the container image originates from your approved registry and meets your organization's vulnerability policy. Which Google Cloud service can enforce an admission policy so only trusted images are allowed to run in the cluster?

options.text: Artifact Registry vulnerability scanning
Cloud Identity-Aware Proxy
Binary Authorization
Cloud Audit Logs

questions.correct_text: Binary Authorization
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Binary Authorization because it provides an admission controller for Google Kubernetes Engine that enforces policies so only trusted images from approved registries and with required attestations are allowed to deploy.

Binary Authorization lets you define a policy that restricts images to specific registries and requires attestations such as vulnerability checks before admission. It evaluates each deployment request at admission time and blocks any image that does not meet your organization's requirements. It integrates with scanning results so you can enforce vulnerability thresholds rather than only detecting issues.

Artifact Registry vulnerability scanning identifies vulnerabilities in images stored in the registry, yet it does not act as an admission controller in the cluster. On its own it cannot block pods from being deployed.

Cloud Identity-Aware Proxy controls access to web applications and resources behind HTTPS. It does not evaluate container images or enforce Kubernetes admission policies.

Cloud Audit Logs records administrative and data access events for auditing. It provides visibility but cannot prevent deployments or enforce policy at admission time.

Keep the secret in Secret Manager, grant a Google service account access, and use Workload Identity so a Kubernetes service account impersonates it, letting Pods retrieve the secret without going through the Kubernetes Secrets API

questions.question: Riverton Media runs roughly 24 microservices across two regional Google Kubernetes Engine clusters. A database password must never be obtainable by reading Kubernetes API objects, and the team also wants to steer clear of distributing long-lived service account keys. Which approach best meets both constraints?
questions.correct_text: Keep the secret in Secret Manager, grant a Google service account access, and use Workload Identity so a Kubernetes service account impersonates it, letting Pods retrieve the secret without going through the Kubernetes Secrets API
questions.explanation:
The best approach is to keep the secret in Secret Manager, grant a Google service account access, and use Workload Identity so a Kubernetes service account impersonates it, letting Pods retrieve the secret without going through the Kubernetes Secrets API. That both blocks retrieval via Kubernetes API object reads and avoids handing out long-lived service account keys.

Workload Identity ties a Kubernetes service account to a Google service account, so Pods automatically obtain short-lived credentials. The application reads the password from Secret Manager at runtime, meaning there is no Kubernetes Secret object anyone could read. IAM governs the access, and you pick up Secret Manager features like versioning and audit logging that work uniformly across clusters.

Enabling GKE application-layer secrets encryption with a Cloud KMS key only encrypts Secret resources at rest and does nothing to stop authorized API clients from reading those Secret objects, so the password stays retrievable through Kubernetes API reads, violating the constraint.

Using the Secret Manager CSI driver with a mounted JSON key in a Kubernetes Secret relies on a long-lived key stored inside a readable Kubernetes Secret. The CSI driver can be secure with Workload Identity, but this option specifically uses a JSON key, failing the key-management constraint.

Storing the secret in Cloud KMS and mounting a JSON key via a ConfigMap uses a long-lived key and puts sensitive material in a ConfigMap, which is not for secrets. Cloud KMS manages keys rather than storing secrets, so the app would handle ciphertext storage and decryption, adding complexity and missing the constraints.

questions.question: A team at Brookbend Analytics plans to launch a new service on Cloud Run without providing a Dockerfile, and company policy requires every container image to be stored in a centrally managed Artifact Registry repository. Which actions will let you build the container image without a Dockerfile and ensure it is stored in the central registry?

options.text: Set up a Cloud Deploy pipeline to build and push an image to Artifact Registry
Run gcloud run deploy with the --source flag so Cloud Build uses buildpacks and stores the image in Artifact Registry
Use the pack CLI to run pack build and push the resulting image to Artifact Registry
Upload your application source tree to Artifact Registry and let Cloud Run build from there
Add the --platform=kubernetes option to gcloud run deploy and rely on that to create the image

questions.correct_text: Use the pack CLI to run pack build and push the resulting image to Artifact Registry
questions.explanation:
The right picks are Run gcloud run deploy with the --source flag so Cloud Build uses buildpacks and stores the image in Artifact Registry and Use the pack CLI to run pack build and push the resulting image to Artifact Registry.

Using gcloud run deploy with the --source flag lets Cloud Build invoke Google Cloud Buildpacks to detect your application and build a container image without a Dockerfile. The resulting image is automatically pushed to Artifact Registry which satisfies a policy that images must be stored in a centrally managed registry. This path also streamlines source to service deployment for Cloud Run.

Using the pack CLI with Google Cloud Buildpacks also builds a container image from source without a Dockerfile. You can configure the image name to point to your centrally managed Artifact Registry repository and push the built image there, which fulfills the storage requirement before deploying the image to Cloud Run.

Set up a Cloud Deploy pipeline to build and push an image to Artifact Registry is incorrect because Cloud Deploy is for continuous delivery and release orchestration, and it expects artifacts such as container images to be built by another system like Cloud Build or pack.

Upload your application source tree to Artifact Registry and let Cloud Run build from there is incorrect because Artifact Registry stores built artifacts such as container images and language packages, and it does not store raw source trees or perform builds. Cloud Run does not build directly from a source tree stored in Artifact Registry.

Add the --platform=kubernetes option to gcloud run deploy and rely on that to create the image is incorrect because that option targets the Kubernetes based variant and it still requires a prebuilt container image and does not create one from source. This variant has also been de emphasized in favor of fully managed Cloud Run on newer exams.

questions.question: Skyport Analytics operates a trading platform that uses Cloud Spanner as the source of truth. You want to detect performance regressions by running automated performance benchmarks on every commit that Cloud Build triggers. As many as six commits may be tested at the same time, and the test runs must not interfere with each other. What should you do?

options.text: Run the Cloud Spanner emulator inside the Cloud Build pipeline, load the test dataset, execute benchmarks, and stop the emulator when finished
Create a new Cloud Spanner database for each build in a shared instance, seed schema and data, run tests, then drop the database
Provision a fresh Cloud Spanner instance for every build, apply schema and fixtures, run performance tests, then delete the instance
Use a single long lived Cloud Spanner instance with preloaded data and have the pipeline restore the dataset after each run

questions.correct_text: Provision a fresh Cloud Spanner instance for every build, apply schema and fixtures, run performance tests, then delete the instance
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Provision a fresh Cloud Spanner instance for every build, apply schema and fixtures, run performance tests, then delete the instance. This gives each concurrent benchmark its own dedicated capacity which prevents interference and produces consistent and comparable performance results.

Cloud Spanner allocates compute and storage at the instance level. Databases inside a single instance share those resources, so only a separate instance provides the strong isolation that performance tests require. Creating a temporary instance per commit lets you size capacity to mirror production and lets Cloud Build create and delete these instances programmatically to control cost while maintaining test fidelity.

Run the Cloud Spanner emulator inside the Cloud Build pipeline, load the test dataset, execute benchmarks, and stop the emulator when finished is incorrect because the emulator does not replicate real Spanner performance characteristics and is not suitable for performance benchmarking.

Create a new Cloud Spanner database for each build in a shared instance, seed schema and data, run tests, then drop the database is incorrect because databases in the same instance share compute and storage, so concurrent tests would contend for the same resources and influence each other.

Use a single long lived Cloud Spanner instance with preloaded data and have the pipeline restore the dataset after each run is incorrect because simultaneous runs would still share the same instance resources and interfere, and resetting data does not provide the isolation needed for reliable performance measurements.

questions.question: A digital learning platform run by Cypress Labs is hosted on Google Cloud and relies on Firebase Authentication to handle user identities. The team needs users to remain signed in when they open a new tab and when they close the browser and return later. What should you implement to keep the sign in state persistent across visits?

options.text: Manage sessions using HTTP cookies that you create and set from the application server
Use Cloud Memorystore to keep user session tokens and retrieve them when the user returns
Configure Firebase Authentication with local persistence so the sign in state is stored in the browser's local storage
Save session information in Firebase Realtime Database and load it on every request

questions.correct_text: Configure Firebase Authentication with local persistence so the sign in state is stored in the browser's local storage
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Configure Firebase Authentication with local persistence so the sign in state is stored in the browser's local storage.

This configuration uses Firebase on the web to store the authentication state in the browser's local storage, which survives tab opens and browser restarts. When you enable local persistence, Firebase saves the credentials in a storage area that is shared across tabs for the same origin, so users remain signed in when they open a new tab and when they return later.

Manage sessions using HTTP cookies that you create and set from the application server is not appropriate because Firebase Authentication already manages client side session persistence and token refresh, and custom cookies add unnecessary complexity and security risk for a web client flow.

Use Cloud Memorystore to keep user session tokens and retrieve them when the user returns is incorrect because Memorystore is a server side cache and does not maintain client side sign in state. Storing tokens there would not automatically restore a user session in the browser and would complicate security.

Save session information in Firebase Realtime Database and load it on every request is not advisable because authentication secrets should not be stored in a database, and this approach bypasses the built in, secure persistence provided by Firebase Authentication on the client.

Create an Eventarc trigger on the bucket with attribute filters for an exact object name and route the events to Cloud Run

questions.question: A service at Zephyr Retail should fire only on updates to one specific Cloud Storage object, reports/daily.csv. Across the coming 120 days the team expects to flip among various object event types and may layer on a metadata-based filter as well. The arrangement needs to be simple and declarative so that multiple engineers can revise or swap out these triggers without ever redeploying the app. Which approach fits?
questions.correct_text: Create an Eventarc trigger on the bucket with attribute filters for an exact object name and route the events to Cloud Run
questions.explanation:
The approach to use is to create an Eventarc trigger on the bucket with attribute filters for an exact object name and route the events to Cloud Run. Eventarc can target only reports/daily.csv by filtering on the CloudEvents subject, and it can switch between object finalized and metadata updated events when you edit the trigger. Teammates manage those filters declaratively and apart from the service, so the Cloud Run deployment never needs to be redeployed.

Because Eventarc triggers are resources separate from the application, you can add or change attribute filters such as bucket and subject to match a single object path, and you can update the event type as needs shift. That leaves the application immutable while the trigger configuration evolves across the 120 days.

Configuring a Cloud Function on object change events is not the best fit, because its trigger is bound to the function deployment. Changing event types or adding an exact object filter usually forces a redeploy or filtering logic in code, which works against simple declarative updates by several teammates.

Having Cloud Scheduler hit a Cloud Run endpoint on an interval is polling rather than event driven. It fires needless runs when nothing changed, adds latency, and offers no trigger-level filters for event types or an exact object name.

Forwarding Cloud Storage notifications to Pub/Sub to launch a Cloud Build job is heavy and operationally complex. Cloud Build is built for builds and CI, not for repeatedly running application code, and this path lacks straightforward attribute filters and easy updates without retooling the pipeline.

questions.question: A stateless API for scrumtuous.com runs on Google Kubernetes Engine with a handful of replicas in one deployment. You have 14 days to deliver automatic scaling, you want to touch the manifests as little as possible, and you would rather use default metrics than wire up custom integrations. Which approach should you take?
questions.correct_text: Create a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler that targets average CPU utilization
questions.explanation:
The approach to take is to create a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler that targets average CPU utilization.

It rides on the built-in CPU utilization metric that Kubernetes already exposes for Pods through the metrics server and Cloud Monitoring. All it takes is a small HorizontalPodAutoscaler manifest, with no custom metric adapters and no code changes. It scales the replica count horizontally, which suits a stateless API and can be stood up quickly.

Creating an HPA driven by a custom application metric is not ideal, because it means publishing custom metrics into Cloud Monitoring and configuring the custom or external metrics pipeline, adding integration effort and time the team wants to avoid.

Switching on the cluster autoscaler while holding the Pod count fixed is wrong, because the cluster autoscaler scales nodes, not Pods. Fixing the Pods provides no automatic scaling of the application replicas.

Adding a Vertical Pod Autoscaler does not meet the goal, because VPA adjusts CPU and memory requests rather than the replica count. It can also restart Pods, and while it complements horizontal scaling it does not deliver the replica scaling required.

questions.question: PulseWave, a media-analytics startup, runs a Python service on Cloud Run that fields about 4,500 API calls a minute. The team wants both application messages and error stack traces to appear in Cloud Logging, and they want the code to remain portable so it can move to other platforms without depending on cloud-provider-specific libraries. What is the simplest way to satisfy both goals?
questions.correct_text: Set up the Python logging module to emit messages and exceptions to standard output and standard error
questions.explanation:
The simplest path is to set up the Python logging module to emit messages and exceptions to standard output and standard error.

Using the built-in Python logging module to send messages and exception tracebacks there keeps the service portable, since it depends on standard runtime behavior rather than provider-specific libraries. It is the most direct way to land both application messages and stack traces in Cloud Logging on Cloud Run.

Pulling in the Cloud Logging client library would work but couples the code to Google Cloud and undercuts portability, and it is redundant on Cloud Run where stdout and stderr are ingested automatically.

Writing logs to files in the temporary directory and uploading them to Cloud Storage does not feed Cloud Logging by default, and the container filesystem is ephemeral. That delays visibility and complicates operations versus simply writing to standard output and standard error.

Jib produces Java container images straight from source using Maven or Gradle. It does not lift an existing VM into a container or pick up the OS-level dependencies that reside on that VM.

Cloud Buildpacks convert source code into container images with no Dockerfile, which assumes you build from source rather than migrating a running VM environment.

A Compute Engine custom image yields a reusable VM image for spinning up more virtual machines. It produces neither a container nor any GKE deployment artifacts.
