questions.question: Crestline Media keeps a large monorepo on Google Cloud and drives CI and CD through Cloud Build. On a typical day under 4 percent of the code changes per commit, yet every build runs for a long time. You want shorter builds without rearchitecting the app, and you want previously built artifacts reused whenever you can. What should you do?

options.text: Move to a larger machine type for Cloud Build
Turn on layer caching in Cloud Build using Kaniko caching with Artifact Registry
Break the monorepo into individual microservices, each with its own pipeline
Append the --no-cache flag to every container build step

questions.correct_text: Turn on layer caching in Cloud Build using Kaniko caching with Artifact Registry
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to turn on layer caching in Cloud Build using Kaniko caching with Artifact Registry.

This lets the builder push and pull cached image layers from Artifact Registry, so unchanged layers are reused and only the minimal set is rebuilt. It is ideal for a monorepo where each commit touches a small slice of code, and it shortens builds without restructuring the repo. It also directly meets the requirement to reuse previously built artifacts.

Moving to a larger machine type for Cloud Build is not the best pick because it may speed individual steps but does not reuse prior artifacts. Without a layer cache the build still rebuilds unchanged layers, so you mostly just pay more.

Breaking the monorepo into separate microservices with their own pipelines violates the no rearchitecture constraint. It can help some organizations, but it is unnecessary here since caching already addresses the slowness.

Appending --no-cache to every build step does the exact opposite of what you want by disabling caching and forcing a full rebuild every run, which lengthens builds.

questions.question: At Meridian Freight you are writing unit tests for a microservice that publishes about 100 small Pub/Sub messages and a subscriber consumes them. You must verify the subscriber processes messages in the order they were published while keeping the tests cheap and reproducible both on developer laptops and in continuous integration. What should you do?

options.text: Set up a dedicated Pub/Sub topic and subscription for each developer
Stub the Pub/Sub publisher and subscriber clients with a mocking library
Execute the tests against the Pub/Sub emulator in both developer and CI environments
Stand up real Pub/Sub resources in a dedicated test project and run the tests there

questions.correct_text: Execute the tests against the Pub/Sub emulator in both developer and CI environments
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to execute the tests against the Pub/Sub emulator in both developer and CI environments.

The Pub/Sub emulator runs locally and in CI, so tests stay fast, free, and repeatable. It exercises the real client libraries and APIs, letting you validate integration behavior while you control concurrency and timing. You can publish your batch of messages and confirm the subscriber processes them in the intended order without cloud charges, quotas, or network jitter.

Setting up a dedicated topic and subscription per developer raises overhead and cost and still depends on real cloud resources, which makes tests slower and less deterministic. It also does nothing inherent to verify ordering on laptops or in CI.

Stubbing the publisher and subscriber clients with a mocking library only checks your own code paths, not real Pub/Sub semantics. Mocks cannot prove ordering or flow control because they bypass the service behavior your subscriber must contend with.

Standing up real Pub/Sub resources in a dedicated test project adds cost and setup and can be flaky due to quotas, network, and multi tenancy. It is slower and less repeatable than the local emulator.

questions.question: You are an engineer at a digital payments startup called PactPay, and you need to deploy a feature rich web application onto a serverless platform. The app makes many HTTP calls to internal microservices and has to stay low latency even when traffic spikes suddenly. Which Google Cloud service fits best?

options.text: Google Kubernetes Engine
App Engine Standard environment
Cloud Functions
API Gateway

questions.correct_text: App Engine Standard environment
questions.explanation:
The right pick is the App Engine Standard environment because it is a fully managed serverless platform for web apps that scales fast during spikes and can keep latency low while calling internal microservices over HTTP.

App Engine Standard automatically scales and manages instances, adding capacity quickly when requests surge. Setting minimum instances keeps instances warm to cut cold starts and sustain low latency. It is built for HTTP apps, can call other services over HTTP, and when private connectivity is needed it can reach internal services securely through a VPC connector.

Google Kubernetes Engine is capable and can be low latency, but it is not serverless and requires you to run clusters, nodes, and scaling configuration, which fails the serverless requirement.

Cloud Functions is serverless and supports HTTP triggers, yet it is geared to single purpose, event driven functions and can suffer worse cold start impact for a complex web app that aggregates many microservice calls, making it a weaker fit for strict low latency needs.

API Gateway secures and routes API requests but runs no application code, so it is not a compute platform for hosting the web app.

questions.question: A specialty footwear retailer at mcnz.com runs its storefront on Cloud Run backed by Firestore in Datastore mode. The home page lists in stock items and shoppers must be able to browse the full catalog. During the pilot you simply returned the entire catalog from Firestore. After going public at about 1,100 requests per second you start seeing HTTP 500 responses from Cloud Run at peak, and logs show the container being killed when memory spikes, coinciding with bursts of Datastore reads. You want a fast change that stops the crashes while you plan deeper query and caching work. What should you do?

options.text: Paginate the product listing using Datastore cursors
Raise the Cloud Run service memory allocation to a larger tier
Add integer offsets to the product query
Introduce Memorystore for Redis to cache the catalog

questions.correct_text: Raise the Cloud Run service memory allocation to a larger tier
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to raise the Cloud Run service memory allocation to a larger tier.

Your container is terminated when memory spikes during large Firestore in Datastore mode reads. Increasing the memory limit gives each instance more headroom so the process is less likely to be killed for exceeding its allocation. This is a quick configuration change that ships without code edits and stabilizes the service while you work on better queries and caching.

Paginating with Datastore cursors is a strong long term improvement since it shrinks result sizes and read bursts, but it needs application changes and testing. It will not immediately stop the out of memory crashes in production.

Adding integer offsets to the query is inefficient in Datastore because the service still reads and skips preceding entities, raising latency and read cost. It does nothing for memory pressure from large result sets and is discouraged versus cursors.

Introducing Memorystore for Redis can help later but requires provisioning, a Serverless VPC connector, and code to implement caching. It is not a quick stabilization step and does not address the immediate memory limit killing the container.

questions.question: You are designing a Cloud Bigtable schema that captures telemetry for a smart home platform at AeroNest Labs. Every device reports a reading every 3 seconds, and your current row key is the device ID followed by the event timestamp. In a pilot you see read and write hotspots because a handful of devices emit far more data than the rest, producing uneven load across tablets. You need a new row key that balances traffic yet stays mostly human readable for engineers and support staff. What should you do?

options.text: Lead the row key with an ascending timestamp followed by the device ID
Move the data to Cloud Spanner and key the primary key on timestamp
Prepend a small numeric shard derived from a consistent hash of the device ID, then append the device ID and a reversed timestamp
Use only a hash such as SHA256 of the device ID and timestamp as the entire row key

questions.correct_text: Prepend a small numeric shard derived from a consistent hash of the device ID, then append the device ID and a reversed timestamp
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to prepend a small numeric shard derived from a consistent hash of the device ID, then append the device ID and a reversed timestamp.

This spreads reads and writes across tablets because the small hash based shard prefix splits keys from one high volume device into different key ranges. Keeping the device ID in the key preserves readability and supports device focused troubleshooting and scans. A reversed timestamp gives efficient access to a device's recent data while avoiding a monotonically increasing prefix that would create hotspots. Together they balance traffic and keep keys understandable.

Leading with an ascending timestamp followed by the device ID is wrong because a monotonic timestamp at the front drives sequential writes onto the same tablet, causing severe hotspotting, and it scatters a device's data across wide ranges, making device centric scans inefficient.

Moving to Cloud Spanner with a timestamp primary key is wrong because this is a Bigtable schema problem and Bigtable is the right fit for high throughput time series telemetry. Spanner adds cost and complexity without fixing hotspotting if the key still leads with a timestamp, and it ignores the requirement to keep keys mostly human readable in Bigtable.

Using only a SHA256 hash of device ID and timestamp is wrong because a fully hashed key destroys readability and useful locality for per device range scans. It distributes load but at the expense of operability and efficient device queries.

questions.question: You want a single developer workspace that is centrally governed by policy, can connect to private resources inside a VPC, and still lets engineers add their own tools. Which Google Cloud option provides this?

options.text: Cloud Code paired with Identity-Aware Proxy
Cloud Workstations using curated base images plus custom images rebuilt every 28 days
Per developer Compute Engine VMs with OS Login
Cloud Workstations without any centralized image governance

questions.correct_text: Cloud Workstations using curated base images plus custom images rebuilt every 28 days
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Cloud Workstations using curated base images plus custom images rebuilt every 28 days.

Cloud Workstations provides a centrally managed developer environment where admins set workstation configurations, decide which images are allowed, and enforce organization policies. It supports private networking so workstations reach services over private IP in your VPC, meeting the private VPC access requirement. Teams can install custom tooling by building custom container images or using startup scripts. Combining Google curated base images with regularly rebuilt custom images aligns with the need for a policy enforced, consistently patched environment.

Cloud Code paired with Identity-Aware Proxy is not a unified developer environment because Cloud Code is an IDE extension running on a developer's own machine and IAP guards web applications. Together they provide no centralized image control, consistent toolchains, or managed private workspace networking.

Per developer Compute Engine VMs with OS Login can reach private VPC resources and allow tool installs, but they are not a managed, uniform developer platform. They lack standardized image policy and workspace features and impose heavy operational overhead for patching, lockdown, and consistency across users.

Cloud Workstations without centralized image governance fails the policy requirement. Without image governance you cannot reliably control which images or toolchains run or keep them refreshed on a predictable cadence, undermining the unified, compliant experience the question wants.

questions.question: Vellum Outfitters ingests about 75 Pub/Sub messages each second from point of sale systems, and you must use Cloud Run so every message is saved to a Cloud Storage bucket and also to a BigQuery table while keeping operational effort low. Which architecture should you choose?

options.text: One topic, one Cloud Run service, one push subscription that writes to both sinks
Two topics, two subscriptions, two Cloud Run services
One topic, two subscriptions, two Cloud Run services each bound to a different subscription and each dedicated to one sink
One topic, one subscription, two Cloud Run services attached to the same subscription

questions.correct_text: One topic, two subscriptions, two Cloud Run services each bound to a different subscription and each dedicated to one sink
questions.explanation:
The right answer is One topic, two subscriptions, two Cloud Run services each bound to a different subscription and each dedicated to one sink.

This approach uses a Pub/Sub fan out pattern so one topic feeds two independent subscriptions. Each subscription pushes to its own Cloud Run service which lets each service write to a single sink such as Cloud Storage or BigQuery. This cleanly separates failure domains and allows independent retries and autoscaling which keeps operational effort low while ensuring every message reaches both sinks.

By isolating each sink in its own service you avoid coordinating cross sink transactions inside one process. If one sink has a transient failure, then only that service retries while the other sink remains unaffected. This matches Pub/Sub at least once delivery and encourages simple idempotent logic per sink.

One topic, one Cloud Run service, one push subscription that writes to both sinks couples both sinks in one execution. A failure when writing to one sink would lead to a non success response which causes Pub/Sub to retry the entire delivery and can duplicate writes to the other sink. You would need custom deduplication and complex error handling which increases operational effort.

Two topics, two subscriptions, two Cloud Run services requires publishing the same message twice or adding extra fan out logic which raises complexity and cost. Pub/Sub already provides fan out with multiple subscriptions on a single topic so extra topics are unnecessary.

One topic, one subscription, two Cloud Run services attached to the same subscription does not meet the requirement. A push subscription has a single push endpoint so it cannot target two services. With pull delivery the services would compete for messages and each message would be processed by only one service rather than both sinks.

questions.question: Beacon Live, a ticketing platform, runs microservices on Google Kubernetes Engine that talk to each other through Cloud Pub/Sub. Security requires that only authenticated and authorized workloads be allowed to publish to the topic order-events while every other caller is rejected. What should you implement?

options.text: Use VPC Service Controls to put Pub/Sub and the publishing services in one service perimeter
Turn on Firebase Authentication for each microservice and validate tokens before calling the publish API
Grant only the required service accounts the Publisher role through IAM on the Pub/Sub topic and leave everyone else without it
Encrypt the topic with a customer managed encryption key and limit Cloud KMS permissions to trusted services

questions.correct_text: Grant only the required service accounts the Publisher role through IAM on the Pub/Sub topic and leave everyone else without it
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to grant only the required service accounts the Publisher role through IAM on the Pub/Sub topic and leave everyone else without it. This ensures only the authenticated GKE workloads mapped to those accounts can publish, and all other callers receive permission denied.

This uses Pub/Sub resource level IAM, evaluated on every publish request. With GKE Workload Identity the pods authenticate as their Google service accounts, and Pub/Sub authorizes the call only if the account holds the Publisher role on the target topic. Any identity lacking that role is denied, which directly meets the requirement to permit only authorized workloads and block the rest.

Putting Pub/Sub and the publishers in one VPC Service Controls perimeter is not enough because perimeters reduce data exfiltration risk across boundaries but do not provide per caller authorization to a topic. Principals inside the same perimeter can still call the API if IAM allows, so it does not control which workloads may publish.

Turning on Firebase Authentication and validating tokens does not meet the requirement because Pub/Sub relies on Google Cloud IAM with OAuth 2 service account credentials for server to server access. Validating Firebase ID tokens in your app does not make Pub/Sub authorize the request, and you still need topic level IAM to govern who can publish.

Encrypting the topic with a customer managed encryption key and limiting KMS permissions controls encryption at rest, not who may call publish. Pub/Sub uses its service agent to reach the key, and restricting KMS to workloads does not enforce per publisher authorization on the topic.

questions.question: On premises, Summit Analytics hosts a containerized Python 3.12 web service that may only serve users in the United States. It is busy through the working day and idle for about 10 hours each night. After moving it to Google Cloud you want application errors flowing into Error Reporting, and you want to hold down both cost and setup effort. What should you do?

options.text: Host the service on the App Engine flexible environment and depend on Cloud Logging to feed errors into Error Reporting
Deploy the container to a GKE Autopilot cluster and ship error output to a Cloud Storage bucket
Run the service on Cloud Run and write errors to standard error so Error Reporting collects them
Create a Compute Engine managed instance group for the service and write errors to a file on a persistent disk

questions.correct_text: Run the service on Cloud Run and write errors to standard error so Error Reporting collects them
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to run the service on Cloud Run and write errors to standard error so Error Reporting collects them. This captures application errors while keeping cost and setup low, and you can limit access to United States users by fronting the service with an external HTTP load balancer using Cloud Armor geo based rules.

Cloud Run runs your containerized Python 3.12 service with no servers to manage and scales on requests. It also scales to zero during the roughly 10 hour idle window, cutting cost. When the app writes errors to standard error, Cloud Run forwards them to Cloud Logging and Error Reporting automatically extracts and groups them, giving you error groups and alerts without extra instrumentation.

Hosting on the App Engine flexible environment and relying on Cloud Logging is not the best fit for these priorities. Error Reporting can work, but the flexible environment usually keeps at least one instance running, raising idle cost, and custom runtimes here often mean more setup than Cloud Run.

Deploying to GKE Autopilot and sending errors to a Cloud Storage bucket fails the Error Reporting requirement because Error Reporting consumes from Cloud Logging or its API, not from Cloud Storage. It also adds more cluster and logging configuration than Cloud Run.

Creating a Compute Engine managed instance group and writing errors to a file on a persistent disk would not surface errors to Error Reporting since local files are not ingested. It also adds management overhead and cannot scale to zero while idle, conflicting with the cost goal.

questions.question: Compute Engine VMs sit in the same VPC as a Cloud SQL for MySQL instance. Without exposing the database publicly and without maintaining any IP allowlists, how should those VMs reach it?

options.text: Run the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy against a public IP
Set up VPC peering to the Cloud SQL service network
Enable Cloud SQL private IP and connect over the VPC
Build Cloud VPN and route traffic to Cloud SQL

questions.correct_text: Enable Cloud SQL private IP and connect over the VPC
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to enable Cloud SQL private IP and connect over the VPC.

With private IP enabled, the Cloud SQL instance gets an internal address in your VPC through a private service connection, so Compute Engine VMs on the same network connect using internal addressing. This keeps the database off the public internet and removes any need for authorized networks, because access is governed by VPC routing, firewall rules, and IAM. You can use standard MySQL clients or Cloud SQL connectors and all traffic stays private inside the VPC.

Running the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy against a public IP is unacceptable because it still exposes the instance on a public address, even though the proxy removes IP allowlists. The requirement bars public exposure and this option keeps a public IP.

Setting up VPC peering to the Cloud SQL service network is not supported for Cloud SQL. The service uses a private service connection rather than direct VPC peering, and the supported path is enabling private IP on the instance.

Building Cloud VPN and routing to Cloud SQL is unnecessary because the VMs already share the VPC. VPN is for hybrid or cross network connectivity, it does not make a public instance private, and Cloud SQL still needs private IP for internal access.

questions.question: PathPilot, a mobility startup, uses Cloud Bigtable to drive a near real time insights service. The trip_events table holds ride transactions and the current row key is just the user ID. The three busiest metro areas account for most of the writes, which creates hotspots and uneven tablet usage. You need to redesign the row key so traffic spreads evenly while you can still retrieve rows for a given user ID without scanning the table. What should you do?

options.text: Prepend a region code to the user ID
Turn on multi cluster routing with an app profile and keep the existing user ID row keys
Prefix each row key with a short deterministic hash of the user ID and then append the user ID
Take the first three characters of the user ID followed by the reversed user ID

questions.correct_text: Prefix each row key with a short deterministic hash of the user ID and then append the user ID
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to prefix each row key with a short deterministic hash of the user ID and then append the user ID.

This hash prefix spreads sequential keys for popular users across different tablets, evening out write load even when a few metro areas dominate. Because the hash is deterministic, you can recompute it for any user and read a tight key range or a point key without scanning. Appending the original user ID after the hash keeps a user's rows contiguous, supporting efficient range reads such as by timestamp if you add time as a suffix.

Prepending a region code concentrates writes for the busiest regions under a small set of prefixes, worsening hotspots rather than easing them, and it does not distribute traffic evenly when a few regions dominate.

Turning on multi cluster routing with an app profile and keeping the existing keys does not change key distribution within a cluster, so tablet hotspots remain. Multi cluster routing is mainly for availability and global reads and will not fix a key design that concentrates writes.

Using the first three characters of the user ID followed by the reversed user ID does not guarantee even distribution because many users can share the same starting characters. Reversing helps with monotonically increasing values like timestamps but not with skew from shared prefixes, so clustered writes can persist.

questions.question: Verdant Apparel runs its customer website on Compute Engine VMs, and the growth team wants to compare conversion across four redesigned landing page variants while keeping operations simple and latency low. Which approach runs this experiment with controlled traffic distribution?

options.text: Serve the site from Cloud Functions and split traffic across four functions
Migrate the site to App Engine and use version based traffic splitting to send fixed percentages to four versions
Run the variants on Google Kubernetes Engine and rely on the default Ingress for weighted routing across four Services
Deploy each variant as its own App Engine service and shift traffic by editing DNS records every few minutes

questions.correct_text: Migrate the site to App Engine and use version based traffic splitting to send fixed percentages to four versions
questions.explanation:
The right approach is to migrate the site to App Engine and use version based traffic splitting to send fixed percentages to four versions.

This gives precise control over request percentages across multiple versions of one service and is fully managed, keeping operations simple. It supports gradual rollouts and A or B or multivariate experiments while staying low latency through autoscaling and regional serving. You can set stable weights across four versions and adjust or roll back quickly without reconfiguring infrastructure.

Serving from Cloud Functions and splitting across four functions is wrong because Cloud Functions is built for event driven functions rather than hosting a full website, and it has no built in request level weighted splitting across multiple functions. Achieving that needs extra load balancing setup, adding complexity.

Running on GKE with the default Ingress for weighted routing is wrong because the default GKE Ingress has no simple configuration for weighted request splitting across Services. You would need a custom ingress controller or a service mesh to get canary or weighted routing, which conflicts with keeping operations simple.

Deploying each variant as its own App Engine service and rotating traffic via DNS edits is wrong because DNS rotation cannot deliver consistent, precise percentages due to client and resolver caching and TTL behavior. It changes slowly and unpredictably and does not meet the need for controlled distribution.

questions.question: You are building an internal reporting dashboard on Compute Engine for the finance team at Cypress Trading. Users must sign in with their corporate Google accounts, and you have to confirm that each user belongs to the finance Google Group; the company runs Google Workspace. What should you implement?

options.text: Configure Cloud Armor to allow traffic only from the company office IP ranges and have the application validate a JSON Web Token the client presents
Set up Cloud VPN between the corporate network and the project VPC and depend on private connectivity to limit who can reach the service

Enable Identity-Aware Proxy on the HTTPS load balancer, restrict access to the finance Google Group, then issue client certificates to finance users and have the application authenticate those certificates
Enable Identity-Aware Proxy on the HTTPS load balancer, restrict access to the finance Google Group, then have the application verify the IAP signed JWT on every request

questions.correct_text: Enable Identity-Aware Proxy on the HTTPS load balancer, restrict access to the finance Google Group, then have the application verify the IAP signed JWT on every request
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to enable Identity-Aware Proxy on the HTTPS load balancer, restrict access to the finance Google Group, then have the application verify the IAP signed JWT on every request.

Putting Identity-Aware Proxy in front of the external HTTPS load balancer enforces sign in with corporate Google accounts and lets you authorize a specific Google Group. That directly satisfies authenticating users with Google Workspace identities and confirming finance team group membership.

Once IAP grants access, the application should verify the JSON Web Token IAP adds to each request. Checking the token signature and audience ensures the backend trusts the asserted identity and blocks header spoofing. You get both perimeter authorization through IAP and application level assurance of the caller's identity on every request.

Configuring Cloud Armor to allow only office IP ranges plus a client supplied JWT is wrong because IP allow lists control where traffic originates, not who the user is, and a client supplied token does not prove the user is a corporate Google account or a finance Google Group member.

Setting up Cloud VPN and relying on private connectivity is wrong because network access does not authenticate individual users or verify Google Group membership. Anyone on the network could reach the service without user level checks.

Enabling IAP and the finance group but adding client certificates for the application to authenticate is wrong because client certificates are unnecessary and do not integrate with Google Groups for authorization. IAP already authenticates users and enforces group based access, and the app should trust the IAP signed token rather than separate certificate based authentication.

questions.question: Sentinel Assurance, an insurance carrier, is relocating several internal web applications from its own data center to Google Cloud. The team wants these services to authenticate and authorize through Google Cloud IAM and to avoid touching any application code. Which Google Cloud service should they place in front of the applications to satisfy this?

options.text: Use Cloud VPN to link the data center network to the VPC
Adopt Identity Platform to provide sign in for the applications
Enable Identity-Aware Proxy in front of the migrated services to enforce IAM based access without code changes
Configure Cloud Directory Sync to replicate users into Cloud Identity for app access
Set up Workforce Identity Federation so the enterprise IdP can access Google Cloud resources

questions.correct_text: Enable Identity-Aware Proxy in front of the migrated services to enforce IAM based access without code changes
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to enable Identity-Aware Proxy in front of the migrated services to enforce IAM based access without code changes.

It is the only option that natively enforces Google Cloud IAM authentication and authorization for web apps without any code edits. Identity-Aware Proxy sits in front of your HTTPS load balancer and checks user identity and IAM permissions before requests reach the backend. That meets the requirement to rely on IAM while leaving the applications unchanged.

Using Cloud VPN to link the data center to the VPC only supplies secure network connectivity between sites. It does not authenticate users or enforce IAM policies for application access, so it cannot protect the apps on its own.

Adopting Identity Platform is a customer identity product that requires application integration and usually code changes. It does not apply IAM role checks to protect backend services the way this scenario needs.

Configuring Cloud Directory Sync replicates users and groups into Cloud Identity but does not act as a proxy in front of applications, so it cannot enforce per request access.

Setting up Workforce Identity Federation lets external identities access Google Cloud resources with IAM, but it does not front end web applications to enforce access the way Identity-Aware Proxy does.

questions.question: A microservices app at FleetBridge spans Cloud Run and GKE and calls Google Cloud APIs such as Pub/Sub, Cloud Storage, and Secret Manager. You must pick an authentication scheme that limits every service to only the access it requires. What should you use?

options.text: OAuth 2.0 with user consent
A single shared service account holding the Project Owner role
Service accounts with narrowly scoped IAM roles
Application Default Credentials granted the Project Editor role

questions.correct_text: Service accounts with narrowly scoped IAM roles
questions.explanation:
The right answer is service accounts with narrowly scoped IAM roles.

This model enforces least privilege for service to service calls on Cloud Run and GKE. You give each microservice its own service account and grant only the permissions that service actually needs. On Cloud Run you run the service as a chosen service account, and on GKE you use Workload Identity to map a Kubernetes service account to a Google service account. You then attach narrowly scoped roles such as roles pubsub publisher, roles storage objectViewer, and roles secretmanager secretAccessor so each workload holds only the minimum access.

OAuth 2.0 with user consent is built for delegated end user access and requires interactive consent and user tokens. That does not fit automated microservice to Google API calls and does not inherently enforce least privilege per workload.

A single shared service account with Project Owner violates least privilege because Owner is a primitive role granting broad administrative power across the project. One shared identity also widens the blast radius and complicates auditing and isolation.

Application Default Credentials with Project Editor does not guarantee minimum access because Editor is a primitive, overly broad role. ADC is just a mechanism to obtain credentials, not a least privilege strategy, and you still need per workload identities with precise roles.

questions.question: At Vantage Pay, a containerized Java service runs on Cloud Run, and the developer wants every application failure to surface in the Error Reporting console. To make sure the errors are captured, what should the developer check?

options.text: Add the Cloud Monitoring client libraries to the Java service
Replace System.out.println calls with a structured logging framework that writes only to standard output
Confirm the service writes exception stack traces and error messages to the standard error stream
Export logs to a regional Cloud Storage bucket and point Error Reporting at that bucket

questions.correct_text: Confirm the service writes exception stack traces and error messages to the standard error stream
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to confirm the service writes exception stack traces and error messages to the standard error stream.

Cloud Run forwards whatever your container writes to standard output and standard error into Cloud Logging. Error Reporting then analyzes those logs and automatically groups supported language stack traces that arrive with error severity. On Cloud Run, entries written to standard error are recorded as errors, which lets Java exceptions and stack traces be detected and displayed in the Error Reporting console.

Adding the Cloud Monitoring client libraries is unnecessary because Error Reporting ingests error events from Cloud Logging and does not depend on Monitoring client libraries to capture application exceptions.

Replacing System.out.println with a structured logging framework that writes only to standard output is insufficient because standard output is treated as informational by default on Cloud Run. Structured logging helps, but writing exceptions only to standard output does not guarantee error severity and can block Error Reporting's automatic detection.

Exporting logs to a regional Cloud Storage bucket and pointing Error Reporting at it is wrong because Error Reporting reads from Cloud Logging and offers no way to ingest errors directly from Cloud Storage.

questions.question: Your team at Glenmark Textiles pushes container images to Artifact Registry and deploys a microservices workload to a regional GKE cluster in europe-west3. Just after the rollout you notice intermittent failures, and kubectl get pods reports one Pod stuck in CrashLoopBackOff. To investigate this Pod, what should you do first?

options.text: Run kubectl describe pod POD_NAME to inspect events and restart reasons
Run gcloud projects get-iam-policy PROJECT_ID and check that the node pool service account has roles/artifactregistry.reader so images can be pulled
Run kubectl logs POD_NAME --previous to read the logs from the previous container attempt and find out why startup failed
Run kubectl exec -it POD_NAME -- sh and inspect files under /var/log/messages to locate the error

questions.correct_text: Run kubectl logs POD_NAME --previous to read the logs from the previous container attempt and find out why startup failed
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to run kubectl logs POD_NAME --previous to read the logs from the previous container attempt and find out why startup failed.

CrashLoopBackOff means the container starts and then crashes repeatedly. kubectl logs POD_NAME --previous retrieves the logs from the last terminated container instance, which is usually where the startup error appears. This is the quickest way to see the exact failure when the container exits fast and the current logs are empty or partial.

Running kubectl describe pod POD_NAME is not the best first step because it shows events, restart counts, and status details, but not the application stdout or stderr that usually hold the root cause of a startup crash.

Running gcloud projects get-iam-policy and checking for roles/artifactregistry.reader targets image pull permissions. A permissions problem normally shows up as ImagePullBackOff, not CrashLoopBackOff, so this is unlikely to explain a crash that happens after the container starts.

Running kubectl exec -it POD_NAME -- sh and inspecting /var/log/messages is unreliable because a crashing container often cannot be execed into, and Kubernetes container logs go to stdout and stderr rather than system log files inside the container. Reviewing container logs is the right first action.

questions.question: Thornfield Logistics operates a data processing pipeline on Google Kubernetes Engine that pulls about 30 TB of time series records out of Cloud Bigtable on every peak run. During those spikes you want the highest possible read throughput together with the lowest latency. Which action achieves that?

options.text: Restrict Bigtable reads to low traffic hours only
Add more nodes to scale out the Bigtable cluster
Move the workload onto Cloud Spanner
Connect to Bigtable through a public endpoint to take advantage of global routing

questions.correct_text: Add more nodes to scale out the Bigtable cluster
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to add more nodes to scale out the Bigtable cluster.

Bigtable read throughput scales with node count because each node contributes CPU, memory, and IOPS used to serve reads from tablets. Adding nodes spreads tablets across more servers, reducing hotspotting and keeping latency low as the system absorbs a higher read rate. You can raise the node count before or during a peak run and Bigtable rebalances in the background with no downtime.

Restricting Bigtable reads to low traffic hours does not meet the goal because it avoids load rather than adding capacity. The requirement is to maximize throughput and minimize latency during spikes, so you must scale the service, not shift the schedule.

Moving the workload onto Cloud Spanner is inappropriate because Spanner is a strongly consistent relational database for transactional workloads, while Bigtable is built for large scale key value and time series data at very high throughput. A migration would be complex, unnecessary, and would not inherently improve scan performance for this pattern.

Connecting to Bigtable through a public endpoint to use global routing is incorrect because Bigtable serves from regional clusters. A public endpoint adds no global routing benefit and can add network latency. For lowest latency, clients should use private networking in the same region.

questions.question: You support a production microservices platform for a retail analytics company called Cobalt Insights, and you need to instrument the services to emit custom metrics you can watch in real time to track health and performance. Which Google Cloud service should you choose to collect and visualize these custom metrics?

Cloud Pub/Sub
Cloud Monitoring

You define metric descriptors and send time series from microservices through the API or OpenTelemetry, then build dashboards and alerts to track health and performance.

Cloud Trace centers on distributed tracing and latency analysis, following requests across services to find bottlenecks, but it is not a full metrics platform for creating and visualizing arbitrary custom metrics.

Cloud Pub/Sub is a messaging service for asynchronous event delivery between components and provides no metric ingestion, dashboards, or alerting for custom measurements.

questions.question: At Driftwood SaaS the team is building a backend service that uses Firestore for persistence, and the continuous integration pipeline runs about 55 times per day to validate end-to-end reads and writes while avoiding any impact on live environments and costs. What is the best way to run these integration tests?

options.text: Run the tests against the production Firestore instance and roll back the writes afterward
Spin up a temporary Firestore instance in a separate Google Cloud project for each pipeline run
Run the tests against the Firestore emulator in the Local Emulator Suite
Replace Firestore calls with test doubles in your unit tests

questions.correct_text: Run the tests against the Firestore emulator in the Local Emulator Suite
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to run the tests against the Firestore emulator in the Local Emulator Suite. This best meets the need to exercise end to end reads and writes frequently while eliminating risk to production data and avoiding usage costs.

The emulator gives you a local, fully isolated Firestore environment that closely mirrors production behavior. You can validate reads, writes, security rules, indexes, transactions, and listeners without touching live data. Pipelines start quickly, seed and reset state deterministically, and run many times a day with predictable performance and no Firestore billing. It also slots cleanly into CI systems and parallelizes when needed.

Running against production and rolling back is risky and costly. Even with rollbacks there can be side effects from triggers, caches, quotas, or contention with live traffic, plus the chance of data exposure and flakiness, and you still pay for operations.

Spinning up a temporary Firestore instance in a separate project per run is slow, complex, and expensive at this frequency. Firestore is a project level resource, so creating and tearing down projects and databases many times a day brings long setup times, quota management, and needless cost. That is heavy overhead next to a local emulator.

Replacing Firestore calls with test doubles does not satisfy integration testing of real reads and writes. Mocks bypass the real client libraries, network behavior, indexes, and security rules, so they cannot validate the full end to end path.

questions.question: Many containerized workers in an analytics platform at example.com must reach several Google Cloud APIs, and the team forecasts roughly 125,000 requests per minute, each with multi megabyte payloads, while keeping both latency and CPU cost down. To move that much data at that rate efficiently, which approach should they adopt?

options.text: Place Apigee X as a proxy between the application and Google Cloud APIs
Issue the API calls through the gcloud command-line tool
Use the Google Cloud client libraries that use gRPC
Use HTTP JSON REST calls for every Google Cloud service

questions.correct_text: Use the Google Cloud client libraries that use gRPC
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to use the Google Cloud client libraries that use gRPC.

gRPC runs over HTTP2 with multiplexed connections, header compression, and binary Protocol Buffers, which together cut latency and CPU for large request and response bodies. The gRPC based client libraries also offer efficient streaming for uploading and downloading multi megabyte data and manage connection pooling, retries, and authentication for you, helping sustain about 125,000 requests per minute with minimal overhead. Many Google Cloud APIs expose gRPC endpoints natively, so the libraries use the fastest available transport.

Placing Apigee X as a proxy between the application and Google Cloud APIs is not appropriate here because it adds a proxy and policy layer that raises latency and cost. Apigee X is for API management and external exposure, not as a low latency path for internal high throughput calls to Google Cloud services.

Issuing the API calls through the gcloud command-line tool is unsuitable because gcloud is an administration tool, not a high performance client. Spawning processes and parsing output per request would add heavy CPU and latency, so it would not scale to the required rate or payload sizes.

Using HTTP JSON REST for every service works functionally but is less efficient here. JSON encoding and HTTP1.1 patterns raise CPU and bandwidth versus binary protobuf over HTTP2, so they typically mean higher latency and overhead for large payloads at very high throughput.

questions.question: At a startup called Quartz Analytics you created a Pub/Sub topic named device-telemetry to receive IoT events from field hardware. Traffic can burst to roughly 2,600 messages per minute and there are long quiet stretches. Processing must begin the moment an event arrives, the compute must be fully managed, and you only want to be billed while messages are actually handled. How should you design the processing component?

options.text: Run the worker on Google Kubernetes Engine and use the Pub/Sub API with a pull subscription to read from device-telemetry
Use Cloud Functions with a Pub/Sub trigger on device-telemetry so the function runs whenever a message is published
Run a Dataflow streaming job that consumes from a Pub/Sub subscription attached to device-telemetry
Use Cloud Functions that call the Pub/Sub API to pull messages from a subscription on device-telemetry

questions.correct_text: Use Cloud Functions with a Pub/Sub trigger on device-telemetry so the function runs whenever a message is published
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to use Cloud Functions with a Pub/Sub trigger on device-telemetry so the function runs whenever a message is published.

This is event driven, so a new message invokes the function immediately with no polling. It scales automatically to handle bursts around the stated rate and scales to zero during quiet stretches. Billing is per invocation and compute time, so you only pay when messages are processed. It is also fully managed, removing any server or worker administration.

Running the worker on GKE with a pull subscription is not appropriate because a cluster costs money even when idle and you must manage nodes and pods. Pulling also introduces polling, which clashes with the requirement for simple event driven execution.

Running a Dataflow streaming job runs continuously and accrues worker and job charges even when no messages arrive. It can process events with low latency, but it does not scale to zero during long idle periods, so it misses the cost requirement.

Using Cloud Functions that call the Pub/Sub API to pull messages uses a pull model that fits poorly with short lived functions and would need scheduling or long running loops. It does not deliver immediate push based execution and wastes invocations compared with the managed Pub/Sub trigger.

questions.question: For new orders, you want a Google Cloud database that surfaces changes within about four seconds, accepts heterogeneous records under a flexible schema, and can sort and filter on several attributes at once. Which one fits?

options.text: Cloud Bigtable
Firestore Native mode
Cloud Spanner
Firestore in Datastore mode

questions.correct_text: Firestore Native mode
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Firestore Native mode.

It provides near real time visibility because clients can listen for changes and receive updates within a few seconds. Its flexible document model makes heterogeneous order records easy to store without predefined columns. It also supports filtering and sorting on multiple fields through automatic single field indexes and composite indexes, enabling multi attribute queries at low latency.

Cloud Bigtable is a poor fit because it is optimized for large scale key based and time series workloads. It lacks built in secondary indexes for multi attribute filtering or sorting and needs careful row key design for efficient access. It also offers no client real time change listeners for new orders.

Cloud Spanner uses a strongly typed relational schema requiring predefined tables, which is less flexible for heterogeneous records. SQL can filter and sort across many attributes, but it does not push real time updates to clients within a few seconds and is chosen mainly for globally consistent relational workloads.

Firestore in Datastore mode keeps the Datastore API and query model and does not support real time listeners. It offers flexible entities and indexing but lacks the native real time capabilities of the Firestore native experience.

questions.question: You are building a digital receipt service for Brookbend Outfitters where support teams need to view receipts frequently during the first 100 days for refunds and disputes. After that period, access is extremely rare and it can tolerate long retrieval times, and regulations require that each receipt remain immutable for 10 years. You want to lower storage costs while guaranteeing compliance. What should you implement?

options.text: Set a lifecycle rule to move receipts to Nearline storage after 100 days
Enable Bucket Lock with a 10 year retention policy on the bucket
Delete receipts after 100 days and store monthly summaries in BigQuery
Configure a lifecycle rule to transition receipts to Archive storage after 100 days
Keep all receipts in Standard storage for the full 10 years

questions.correct_text: Configure a lifecycle rule to transition receipts to Archive storage after 100 days
questions.explanation:
The right picks are Enable Bucket Lock with a 10 year retention policy on the bucket and Configure a lifecycle rule to transition receipts to Archive storage after 100 days.

Bucket Lock with a 10 year retention policy enforces write once read many immutability for the entire retention period. It prevents deletion or modification of objects until the policy expires, which satisfies the regulatory requirement to keep each receipt unchanged for 10 years and guarantees compliance.

Transitioning to Archive storage after 100 days aligns cost with the access pattern. The first 100 days favor the standard class because support teams access receipts frequently. After that, access is rare, so Archive storage minimizes ongoing storage cost while keeping data available when needed. These two settings work together because a retention policy does not block storage class transitions, so objects can move to Archive storage while remaining immutable under Bucket Lock.

Set a lifecycle rule to move receipts to Nearline storage after 100 days is not sufficient because it does not enforce immutability, and Nearline is optimized for data accessed about once a month, whereas access after 100 days is even rarer. Archive storage better matches the access pattern and lowers cost.

Delete receipts after 100 days and store monthly summaries in BigQuery violates the requirement to keep each receipt immutable for 10 years, so it is not compliant.

Keep all receipts in Standard storage for the full 10 years is unnecessarily expensive for rarely accessed data, and it does not ensure immutability without a retention lock.

questions.question: Lumen Forge Studios, a gaming subsidiary, builds Docker images across a mix of open source Linux distributions and pushes around 60 of them daily to Google Cloud. They want each stored image scanned for known CVEs while the pipeline stays fast, and they prefer managed features over homegrown tooling. What should they do?

options.text: Use Cloud Monitoring to parse Cloud Build logs for vulnerable version strings
Enable vulnerability scanning for container images in Artifact Registry
Build a Cloud Function that triggers on repository commits to scan source code for CVEs
Add a custom Cloud Build step that runs an open source image scanner such as Trivy

questions.correct_text: Enable vulnerability scanning for container images in Artifact Registry
questions.explanation:
The right answer is to enable vulnerability scanning for container images in Artifact Registry.

This managed feature automatically analyzes container images for known CVEs as they are pushed and keeps findings current as new vulnerabilities are published. It covers common Linux distributions used in Docker images and integrates right where the team stores images, removing the need to maintain scanners or signatures. Because scanning happens in the registry and can run asynchronously, it minimizes impact on build times and keeps delivery fast while centralizing security visibility.

Using Cloud Monitoring to parse Cloud Build logs for vulnerable version strings is wrong because Monitoring is not a vulnerability scanner and log parsing is brittle and incomplete. It would miss many CVEs, demand custom pattern upkeep, and add overhead without authoritative findings.

Building a Cloud Function that triggers on commits to scan source code for CVEs is wrong because CVE exposure in container images often comes from OS packages and base images, not just source code. Scanning the repo does not guarantee coverage of the built image and adds custom tooling the team wants to avoid.

Adding a custom Cloud Build step that runs an open source scanner such as Trivy is wrong because it introduces custom maintenance and extra build time. Although effective, it conflicts with the preference for managed capabilities and a fast pipeline, whereas managed registry scanning meets the goal with no added build steps.

questions.question: After scaling a Cloud Spanner cluster from 5 to 15 nodes, write throughput stays flat and recent inserts exhibit high tail latency. Among the following, which schema or key decision is the most probable cause of a write hotspot?

options.text: Several secondary indexes on frequently updated tables
Using LIKE predicates rather than STARTS_WITH in filters
Monotonic UUIDv1 primary keys that cluster new inserts into one range
Change streams enabled on high write tables

questions.correct_text: Monotonic UUIDv1 primary keys that cluster new inserts into one range
questions.explanation:
The right answer is monotonic UUIDv1 primary keys that cluster new inserts into one range.

This is a classic Cloud Spanner hotspot because new rows arrive in increasing key order and land at the end of the keyspace on one or a few adjacent ranges. Spanner partitions data by key ranges and assigns a leader per range. When inserts all hit the same hot end range, one leader and its serving replicas get overloaded. Adding nodes does not help because the bottleneck stays on that hot range, which explains flat write throughput and rising tail latency during bursts.

Several secondary indexes on frequently updated tables increases write amplification since each write also updates affected indexes. But the load still spreads across index key ranges, so write capacity scales with more nodes unless the index key itself is monotonic. This raises per write cost, not a single range hotspot.

Using LIKE rather than STARTS_WITH affects read query planning and execution. It does not change how data is keyed or partitioned for writes, so it cannot create a write hotspot or block write throughput from scaling with nodes.

Change streams enabled on high write tables add extra write and storage work to capture changes, but the feature is built to scale with the underlying partitions. It can raise write latency modestly but does not concentrate inserts into one range, so it does not explain the hotspot symptoms.

Connect Cloud Build to Cloud Monitoring to log dependency versions and review them manually for CVEs
Enable the Container Analysis API and configure Artifact Registry vulnerability scanning to run on image push

questions.question: A mobile app at QuillNest has to keep nested documents, function offline with automatic sync once reconnected, grow with traffic, and run its service account under least privilege. Which combination of database plus IAM role meets all of that?

options.text: Use Cloud Bigtable and assign the service account roles/bigtable.viewer
Use Cloud SQL and grant the service account roles/cloudsql.editor
Choose Firestore in Native mode and grant the service account roles/datastore.user
Choose Firestore in Datastore mode and assign the service account roles/datastore.viewer

questions.correct_text: Choose Firestore in Native mode and grant the service account roles/datastore.user
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Firestore in Native mode with the service account granted roles/datastore.user.

This database stores hierarchical documents and collections, directly addressing the nested documents requirement. Its mobile SDKs offer offline persistence with automatic sync once connectivity returns, satisfying the offline need. It is fully managed and scales transparently as traffic grows.

The chosen IAM role suits an application service account because it permits data reads and writes without granting administrative control. That follows least privilege by enabling normal database operations while avoiding broad instance or project level permissions.

Using Cloud Bigtable with roles/bigtable.viewer is unsuitable because Bigtable is a wide column store, not a document database, and offers no mobile offline sync. The viewer role is read only and would block writes.

Using Cloud SQL with roles/cloudsql.editor does not fit because Cloud SQL is relational and lacks native nested document storage and offline sync. The editor role manages instances rather than granting fine grained data access and is broader than needed.

Choosing Firestore in Datastore mode with roles/datastore.viewer is wrong because Datastore mode targets server workloads and does not provide the client SDK features for offline sync. The viewer role is also read only and would prevent writes.

questions.question: BirchView Media is building a Go web service that lets customers upload project files up to 20 GB directly to a Google Cloud Storage bucket. Users must sign in with their Google accounts, and the team needs a solution that blocks anonymous uploads and scales without proxying file data through the application servers. Which approach should they use?

options.text: Have the application prompt users for their Google username and password and exchange the credentials for an access token, then upload the file to the bucket
Protect the bucket with Cloud Identity Aware Proxy and require Google sign in before allowing users to upload to the storage endpoint
Authenticate users with Google OAuth and have the backend mint a short lived V4 signed URL for the target object so the browser can upload straight to Cloud Storage
Use Firebase Authentication and let the client present the Firebase token to Cloud Storage to perform the upload

questions.correct_text: Authenticate users with Google OAuth and have the backend mint a short lived V4 signed URL for the target object so the browser can upload straight to Cloud Storage
questions.explanation:
The right pick is Authenticate users with Google OAuth and have the backend mint a short lived V4 signed URL for the target object so the browser can upload straight to Cloud Storage.

This approach first authenticates the user with Google OAuth which satisfies the requirement for Google sign in. After the user is authenticated, the backend authorizes the request and issues a short lived V4 signed URL that is limited to the target object and the intended HTTP method. The browser then uploads directly to Cloud Storage using that signed URL, which removes the application servers from the data path and allows the solution to scale for large files. Short expirations and object specific scope prevent anonymous or arbitrary uploads because only authenticated users receive a fresh signed URL from the backend.

For large files such as 20 GB, the team can use a resumable upload initiated with a V4 signed URL, and they should configure CORS on the bucket so the browser can call the Cloud Storage endpoint from the application domain.

Have the application prompt users for their Google username and password and exchange the credentials for an access token, then upload the file to the bucket is insecure and not supported. Applications must not collect Google passwords and should use OAuth for sign in. It also risks forcing the servers to proxy uploads which fails the scalability requirement.

Protect the bucket with Cloud Identity Aware Proxy and require Google sign in before allowing users to upload to the storage endpoint is not viable because Identity Aware Proxy protects apps behind Google Cloud HTTP load balancing and does not sit in front of Cloud Storage APIs. It would not provide gated access to direct browser uploads to the storage endpoint.

Use Firebase Authentication and let the client present the Firebase token to Cloud Storage to perform the upload does not work with the raw Cloud Storage JSON or XML APIs. Firebase ID tokens are evaluated by Cloud Storage for Firebase through the Firebase SDK and its Security Rules, and they are not accepted directly by standard Cloud Storage endpoints.

questions.question: The team at mcnz.com launched a service on App Engine that behaves correctly, yet over the past 48 hours customers have reported occasional response time spikes during normal traffic. You want to find the root cause of these intermittent delays while changing as little code as possible. What should you do?

options.text: Start Cloud Profiler to sample CPU and heap usage in the service
Enable verbose application logging and review per request entries in Cloud Logging
Turn on Cloud Trace and review distributed traces to find the slowest spans and endpoints
Redeploy the application to a different App Engine region to lower latency

questions.correct_text: Turn on Cloud Trace and review distributed traces to find the slowest spans and endpoints
questions.explanation:
The only correct choice is to turn on Cloud Trace and review distributed traces to find the slowest spans and endpoints.

Cloud Trace provides request level latency data with spans across services, so you can see exactly where time is spent on the slow requests. On App Engine, basic tracing can often be enabled with little or no code change, which matches the goal of minimizing changes while investigating recent spikes. You can filter traces by latency, compare normal and slow requests, and pinpoint slow endpoints or downstream calls.

By reviewing spans in Cloud Trace you can tell whether latency comes from application code, RPCs, database queries, or external calls. You can also visualize percentile distributions over the last 48 hours to focus on intermittent tail latency rather than average behavior.

Starting Cloud Profiler to sample CPU and heap usage is better for finding ongoing CPU or memory hotspots and samples rather than tracing individual requests. It does not give end to end request timing with spans, so it is weaker for diagnosing intermittent latency spikes across dependencies.

Enabling verbose application logging and reviewing per request entries can create noise and overhead, and logs alone lack automatic end to end timing and cross service correlation. Without distributed spans you may miss where time is actually spent on a slow request.

Redeploying to a different App Engine region changes geographic latency but does not explain or diagnose intermittent spikes during normal traffic. You should identify the cause with traces before considering a regional move.

questions.question: Crestpoint Insurance is building the backend for a claims-portal IVR. One persistent gRPC connection backs each caller's distinct session, and a dropped connection forces a reconnect that briefly delays the caller. Calls run 2 to 45 minutes, concentrate in business hours, and spike sharply at open enrollment and major policy releases. Aiming to keep cost, effort, and operational overhead low, where should the backend run?

options.text: Cloud Functions
Google Kubernetes Engine Standard mode
Cloud Run
App Engine flexible environment

questions.correct_text: Cloud Run
questions.explanation:
The right answer is Cloud Run.

Cloud Run is a fully managed, container based service that supports HTTP and gRPC over HTTP 2, so it can hold a persistent gRPC connection for the length of each IVR session. Typical call lengths of 2 to 45 minutes fit within the configurable request timeout, and it scales automatically to absorb sharp spikes during open enrollment or policy updates while scaling to zero outside business hours to save cost. You can also set minimum instances to keep a few containers warm during peaks to reduce reconnect delays, which keeps effort and operational overhead low.

Cloud Functions is a poor fit because it is built for short lived stateless invocations and HTTP style requests rather than hosting client facing persistent gRPC services. Maintaining long lived bidirectional streams to individual callers is not what functions are designed for, and the platform lacks the gRPC server capabilities Cloud Run provides.

Google Kubernetes Engine Standard mode could host gRPC services and long connections, but it requires managing clusters, node pools, upgrades, and scaling policies. That operational burden and baseline cost run against the goal of minimizing cost, effort, and overhead, while Cloud Run removes most of that management.

App Engine flexible environment can handle longer requests but keeps instances running, raising baseline cost, and it scales more slowly for spiky workloads. It is also less straightforward for modern gRPC serving than Cloud Run, so it is not the most cost effective or low effort choice here.

questions.question: Nexus Pharma runs a group of microservices on Google Kubernetes Engine that need to pull a private container image hosted in Artifact Registry, and you must allow the pods to retrieve the image securely without distributing long lived credentials inside the cluster, so which step should you take?

options.text: Configure the node pool to use the default Compute Engine service account with broad cloud platform scope so the kubelet can pull the image
Create a Kubernetes Secret of type docker registry that holds a service account key and reference it with imagePullSecrets in the pod manifest
Enable Workload Identity and map a Kubernetes service account to a Google service account that has read access to the Artifact Registry repository
Grant allAuthenticatedUsers the reader role on the Artifact Registry repository

questions.correct_text: Enable Workload Identity and map a Kubernetes service account to a Google service account that has read access to the Artifact Registry repository
questions.explanation:
The best answer is Enable Workload Identity and map a Kubernetes service account to a Google service account that has read access to the Artifact Registry repository.

With Workload Identity, pods use a Kubernetes service account that is bound to a Google service account, which allows short lived federated credentials to be issued automatically. The Google service account needs only the minimum permissions including reader access on the Artifact Registry repository, so the pods can pull private images without embedding secrets or keys.

Configure the node pool to use the default Compute Engine service account with broad cloud platform scope so the kubelet can pull the image is one poor match since it relies on broad and node scoped credentials, which violates minimal privilege and exposes more permissions than needed. It also does not supply pod level identity.

Create a Kubernetes Secret of type docker registry that holds a service account key and reference it with imagePullSecrets in the pod manifest is insecure because it relies on long lived service account keys persisted in the cluster. The scenario explicitly asks to stop distributing long lived credentials.

Grant allAuthenticatedUsers the reader role on the Artifact Registry repository would in practice make the repository accessible to anyone with a Google account, which removes proper access control and is not secure for private images.

questions.question: Within loomwright.io the engineering team adopted Google App Engine as a managed PaaS to accelerate releases. During the last 53 days they observed that getting new features into production takes longer even though build durations remain unchanged. Which inherent trade-off of App Engine could be contributing to the slower rollout?

options.text: Limited ability to handle high traffic loads
Inadequate support for CI or CD
Less control over the underlying runtime and system configuration
No support for traffic splitting or canary strategies

questions.correct_text: Less control over the underlying runtime and system configuration
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Less control over the underlying runtime and system configuration. This managed PaaS abstraction can slow the path to production when features require system level changes or custom runtime tweaks that the platform does not expose.

App Engine owns the operating system and language runtimes, which means teams cannot install arbitrary system packages or run custom daemons or pin unsupported runtime versions. When a new feature needs a specific native library, kernel capability, custom networking, or startup configuration, engineers must rework the design to fit the platform or move to a different environment. That extra adaptation increases release lead time even though the build itself has not changed.

Limited ability to handle high traffic loads is not an inherent issue for App Engine. The service is built to autoscale and absorb bursts, so traffic capacity would not explain a slower rollout of features.

Inadequate support for CI or CD is incorrect. App Engine integrates well with Cloud Build, Cloud Deploy, and common Git based pipelines, so automated delivery is supported.

No support for traffic splitting or canary strategies is wrong. App Engine offers built in versioning and traffic splitting which allows gradual rollouts and canary releases.

questions.question: Elderbrook Studios is building a public API for order processing that must store data in a relational schema and will encounter very high write throughput near 102,000 inserts per second during sales campaigns. The team needs low-latency writes with strong consistency and the ability to scale horizontally without managing replicas. Which GCP service should they select?

options.text: Bigtable
Cloud SQL
Cloud Spanner
Firestore in Datastore mode

questions.correct_text: Cloud Spanner
questions.explanation:
The proper option is Cloud Spanner since it offers a relational schema with SQL support, strongly consistent low latency writes, and automatic horizontal scaling without replica management, which matches the 100,000 inserts per second requirement.

With Cloud Spanner you get a fully managed relational database that on its own shards data and uses synchronous replication to preserve strong consistency while delivering high availability. It scales write throughput by adding nodes so it can handle very high sustained insert rates during sales campaigns while keeping latency low. The service distributes writes across partitions on its own so there is no need to create or manage replicas to scale writes.

Although Bigtable can provide massive throughput and low latency, it is a wide column NoSQL database and does not support a relational schema, joins, or multi row transactions. Since the service needs a relational model, it is not a fit.

Cloud SQL is relational and strongly consistent but it primarily scales vertically and read replicas do not increase write capacity. At 105,000 inserts per second the single primary would become a bottleneck and you would still need to manage replicas, which does not satisfy the requirement for horizontal write scaling without replica management.

Firestore in Datastore mode is a document database and not relational. It lacks joins and traditional relational constraints, and its transactional model focuses on entity groups that limit relational patterns, so it does not meet the need for a high throughput relational store.

questions.question: Catalyst Health uses a BigQuery analytics workspace to deliver insights to more than 100 employees. A data scientist wants to run queries that must not disrupt critical reporting workloads, and they do not care if their queries complete much later. You want to meet this request with the least cost and minimal administrative effort. Which approach should you take?

options.text: Purchase a small dedicated BigQuery Reservations slot commitment for the analyst and assign their jobs to that reservation
Submit the queries as BigQuery batch jobs so they are queued and executed only when idle capacity is available
Move the analyst to a separate Google Cloud project and have them run all work there to isolate impact
Allow the analyst to run jobs only during off peak hours by agreeing on a manual schedule

questions.correct_text: Submit the queries as BigQuery batch jobs so they are queued and executed only when idle capacity is available
questions.explanation:
The proper option is Submit the queries as BigQuery batch jobs so they are queued and executed only when idle capacity is available.

This strategy aligns with the requirement to stop disrupting critical workloads since it queues the scientists queries and runs them when resources are not in use by higher priority work. It also involves almost no administration since it is a per job setting and it avoids extra infrastructure or configuration. It meets the least cost requirement because it does not require purchasing dedicated capacity or building and managing new projects.

Purchase a small dedicated BigQuery Reservations slot commitment for the analyst and assign their jobs to that reservation is not the least cost option because it introduces ongoing flat rate spend and added administrative work to size, manage, and monitor a separate reservation. It is unnecessary when the scientist is comfortable with delayed completion.

Move the analyst to a separate Google Cloud project and have them run all work there to isolate impact adds overhead for IAM, billing, and dataset sharing while it still does not guarantee isolation from shared capacity contention. It also does not meet the minimal effort requirement compared to just changing query priority.

Allow the analyst to run jobs only during off peak hours by agreeing on a manual schedule relies on manual coordination and offers no enforcement or guarantee that capacity will be idle. It increases operational burden and is less dependable than letting the service queue and start work when resources are available.

questions.question: Lighthouse Realty wants to validate a new production release with a small cohort of real users and they need to target the rollout by operating system using request metadata while maintaining the ability to revert instantly if problems occur and they plan to start with roughly 24% of eligible traffic going to the new build. What should they implement to meet these requirements?

options.text: Compute Engine with Traffic Director and configure weighted routing to send a small portion to a canary Managed Instance Group
Cloud Run with traffic splitting by revision tag and send about 20% to the new revision
Google Kubernetes Engine with Anthos Service Mesh and use user agent header based routing to direct about 20% of the selected operating system traffic to the canary
App Engine with traffic splitting based on client IP address ranges

questions.correct_text: Google Kubernetes Engine with Anthos Service Mesh and use user agent header based routing to direct about 20% of the selected operating system traffic to the canary
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Google Kubernetes Engine with Anthos Service Mesh and use user agent header based routing to direct about 16% of the picked operating system traffic to the canary.

This selection accommodates matching on request headers including the User-Agent so developers can pick only traffic from specific operating systems. It also handles weighted routing so you can send roughly 25 percent to the new revision while the rest continues to the stable version. Developers can revert instantly by updating the routing weights back to the stable version which does not require a redeploy and takes effect quickly.

Compute Engine with Traffic Director and configure weighted routing to send a small portion to a canary Managed Instance Group is suboptimal because while Traffic Director can distribute traffic, achieving header based targeting by operating system for end user HTTP traffic needs deploying and managing Envoy proxies in front of the instances. This adds significant complexity compared to a service mesh on GKE that already offers header matches and percentage based canary rules.

Cloud Run with traffic splitting by revision tag and send about 25% to the new revision does not meet the requirement because Cloud Run traffic splitting is percentage based only and does not natively route to revisions based on request headers such as user agent. You cannot target specific operating systems without custom routing outside the platform or application level logic.

App Engine with traffic splitting based on client IP address ranges fails the requirement because IP based splitting does not align with targeting by operating system and it does not supply header based matching to select only the desired cohort.
