questions.question: You are upgrading eight stateful services that run on Google Kubernetes Engine and they must keep data on durable volumes and allow rolling updates without any service interruption. Which configuration meets these goals?

options.text: Run each service as a single Pod that uses a PersistentVolumeClaim and switch traffic with a blue green strategy by updating the Service selector
Deploy each service as a Deployment that mounts a Compute Engine persistent disk and choose a Recreate update strategy to prevent downtime
Use StatefulSets with PersistentVolumeClaims for storage and configure the updateStrategy as RollingUpdate
Create a DaemonSet for each service that mounts local SSD and manage upgrades by hand during planned windows

questions.correct_text: Use StatefulSets with PersistentVolumeClaims for storage and configure the updateStrategy as RollingUpdate
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Use StatefulSets with PersistentVolumeClaims for storage and configure the updateStrategy as RollingUpdate.

This strategy is designed for stateful workloads that need stable identities and durable storage. PersistentVolumeClaims give each replica its own persistent disk so data survives restarts and rescheduling. The RollingUpdate strategy updates pods in a controlled and ordered way which permits traffic to continue to flow as new versions become ready. With proper readiness probes and at least two replicas per service developers can accomplish rolling updates without interruption while keeping data on persistent disks.

The option Run each service as a single Pod that uses a PersistentVolumeClaim and switch traffic with a blue green strategy by updating the Service selector is not right because a single pod builds a single point of failure and cannot supply zero downtime during updates. Blue green with a ReadWriteOnce persistent disk is also problematic since the same volume cannot be attached to two pods on different nodes at the same time which complicates any cutover and risks interruption.

The option Deploy each service as a Deployment that mounts a Compute Engine persistent disk and pick a Recreate update strategy to stop downtime is incorrect because Deployments target stateless workloads and Recreate deliberately stops all old pods before starting new ones which causes downtime. It also does not provide the stable identity and per replica storage guarantees that stateful workloads require.

The option Create a DaemonSet for each service that mounts local SSD and handle upgrades by hand during planned windows is incorrect because DaemonSets run one pod per node which does not match typical stateful service patterns and local SSD is ephemeral rather than durable so data is lost on node failure. Manual upgrade windows contradict the requirement for rolling updates without interruption.

questions.question: Within Opalwood Furniture, an HTTP-triggered Cloud Function receives POST requests that contain a flat JSON payload with numeric and string fields. After the function completes, analysts across several teams need to run complex queries on the ingested records and they require the data to be queryable within 3 seconds of receipt. How should you persist the incoming data to meet these requirements?

options.text: Transform the JSON and insert the records into a regional Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance
Normalize the incoming JSON and write the rows into BigQuery using the streaming interface
Store each request body as a document in Cloud Firestore
Write each payload to a Cloud Storage object and query via a BigQuery external table

questions.correct_text: Normalize the incoming JSON and write the rows into BigQuery using the streaming interface
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Normalize the incoming JSON and write the rows into BigQuery using the streaming interface. It offers near-realtime availability for queries and accommodates complex analytics for many concurrent users.

Streaming inserts make newly ingested rows queryable within seconds in most cases, which satisfies the requirement to be queryable within three seconds. This strategy is one good fit for flat JSON with numeric and string fields because the records map cleanly to a defined table schema. It also permits several teams run advanced SQL without managing infrastructure or indexes, and a Cloud Function can invoke the client library to stream each record as it arrives.

Transform the JSON and insert the records into a regional Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance is a poor match since it targets transactional workloads and does not scale well for heavy analytic queries across large datasets and many users. Meeting near real time analytical freshness and concurrency would be difficult and would require significant tuning.

Store each request body as a document in Cloud Firestore is unsuitable because its query model is limited and does not support complex ad hoc analytics. Organizations often export this data to a warehouse for analysis, which introduces extra steps and latency that would not meet the three second target.

Write each payload to a Cloud Storage object and query through a BigQuery external table will not meet the freshness requirement because external tables over objects are not designed for low latency discovery of new files. Query performance on many small files is also poor compared with native tables.

questions.question: A hosted analytics platform at api.loomwright.io has operated for eight years and serves about 3.2 million users. Your team plans to introduce a major API redesign, yet many partner integrations still call the existing endpoints. What should you do to roll out the new API while protecting current partner integrations from breaking?

options.text: Replace the existing API with the new API and share updated docs for partners to change quickly
Use App Engine traffic splitting to send some requests to a new deployment while the rest go to the current one
Publish the new API under a new version and keep the current API running as a legacy version until partners migrate
Place an Apigee proxy in front and rewrite old requests so they hit the new API then turn off the old backend

questions.correct_text: Publish the new API under a new version and keep the current API running as a legacy version until partners migrate
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Publish the new API under a new version and keep the current API running as a legacy version until partners migrate.

This versioning strategy permits you to introduce breaking changes safely while preserving backward compatibility. Developers can expose the new surface on a clearly versioned endpoint while leaving the legacy endpoint in place so partners can migrate on their own schedule. This reduces risk, allows staged adoption, and aligns with widely suggested API design practices for managing change.

Replace the existing API with the new API and share updated docs for partners to change quickly is risky since it forces immediate partner changes and will likely break existing integrations. Documentation alone does not stop outages when clients depend on the old contract.

Use App Engine traffic splitting to send some requests to a new deployment while the rest go to the current one does not solve compatibility issues because traffic splitting is for gradual rollout of compatible versions. If the new API is not backward compatible, and splitting requests will create inconsistent behavior and still break clients.

Place an Apigee proxy in front and rewrite old requests so they hit the new API then turn off the old backend is fragile for a major redesign because proxies can map simple changes but cannot dependably translate deeper semantic or behavioral differences. Turning off the old backend removes a stable contract that partners rely on and increases the chance of breakage.

questions.question: Within Aether Networks your platform team is rolling out a containerized HTTP service on Google Kubernetes Engine. Traffic fluctuates with user actions and CPU and memory remain low even when requests spike to about 640 requests per second in the evening. You want the workload to scale based on incoming request rate instead of CPU or memory utilization. Which implementation should you choose?

options.text: Enable the Cluster Autoscaler to grow the node pool when request volume increases
Configure a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler that uses a custom request rate metric from Cloud Monitoring to adjust replica count
Cloud Run
Deploy a Vertical Pod Autoscaler and scale from the CPU utilization of each pod

questions.correct_text: Configure a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler that uses a custom request rate metric from Cloud Monitoring to adjust replica count
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Configure a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler that uses a custom request rate metric from Cloud Monitoring to adjust replica count.

Horizontal Pod Autoscaler is designed to change replica counts based on metrics that reflect service demand. When CPU and memory are low yet request traffic varies, using a request rate metric from Cloud Monitoring allows the HPA to scale pods in response to incoming traffic rather than resource utilization. This aligns with the requirement to scale by requests per second so that the workload can add replicas during evening spikes and reduce them when traffic subsides.

Enable the Cluster Autoscaler to grow the node pool when request volume increases is one poor match because the Cluster Autoscaler only adds or removes nodes when pods are pending owing to insufficient capacity. It does not change the number of pods and it does not react to request rate.

Cloud Run does scale on its own with request load, though it would require moving the service to a different platform and it does not meet the requirement to scale an existing workload on GKE. The question asks for scaling the current Kubernetes deployment rather than migrating it.

Deploy a Vertical Pod Autoscaler and scale from the CPU utilization of each pod is not right because VPA adjusts resource requests for pods and it is driven by CPU and memory usage. It does not scale replica count and it does not use request rate.

questions.question: You are building a module at Carbon Forge Steel that records hourly shift submissions in an internal workforce system and needs to notify several independent payroll, compliance, and analytics services. The design must keep producers and consumers loosely coupled and should allow new processing steps to be added next quarter while handling about 380 submissions per minute. What approach will provide reliable communication with downstream services and keep future additions simple?

options.text: Use Cloud Tasks with a queue for each step to push HTTP requests to every downstream system
Create a separate Pub/Sub topic for every step and have each team subscribe only to its own step
Build a microservice on Google Kubernetes Engine that invokes downstream steps in sequence and waits for each response
Publish a shift.submitted event to a single Pub/Sub topic and let each downstream team create and manage its own subscription

questions.correct_text: Publish a shift.submitted event to a single Pub/Sub topic and let each downstream team create and manage its own subscription
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Publish a shift.submitted event to a single Pub/Sub topic and allow each downstream team create and handle its own subscription.

This strategy implements an event driven fan out model that keeps producers and consumers loosely coupled. The producer emits a single event and each downstream service owns its subscription which permits teams scale independently, set their own acknowledgement and retry behavior, and use dead letter handling without coordinating changes with the producer. Adding a new processing step next quarter stays simple because a new subscription can be created without modifying the publisher.

This architecture easily handles 360 submissions per minute because the service is built for high throughput and offers durable at least once delivery. Independent subscriptions stop one slow or failing consumer from blocking others and backlogs can accumulate per consumer until it catches up.

Use Cloud Tasks with a queue for each step to push HTTP requests to every downstream system is one poor match because that service is tuned for targeted task delivery to a specific handler and rate control rather than broadcast to many independent consumers. Managing many queues also couples the producer to every step and increases operational overhead.

Create a separate Pub/Sub topic for every step and have each team subscribe only to its own step increases coupling because the producer must know every step and publish to several topics. It complicates future additions since new steps require publisher changes, whereas a single topic with multiple subscriptions keeps the producer unaware of consumers.

Build a microservice on Google Kubernetes Engine that invokes downstream steps in sequence and waits for each response introduces tight coupling and synchronous dependencies. It builds a single point of failure, increases latency, and makes adding new steps require code changes and redeployments instead of just attaching another subscription.

questions.question: Westgate Hospitals is preparing to run a payment microservice on Google Kubernetes Engine that must scale out to as many as 17 pods during busy periods, and each instance needs a consistent network identity for peer discovery and it also requires its own persistent disk that remains available after rescheduling. Which GKE workload resource should you use?

options.text: Deployment
StatefulSet
ReplicationController
ReplicaSet

questions.correct_text: StatefulSet
questions.explanation:
The right choice is StatefulSet since it offers stable network identities for each Pod and gives every replica its own persistent volume that persists across rescheduling while still allowing you to scale to the needed number of replicas during busy periods.

This resource assigns stable Pod names and works with a headless Service so each instance has a predictable DNS name for peer discovery. It also uses a volume claim template to create a unique PersistentVolumeClaim per replica so the same disk stays associated with the same logical instance after rescheduling, which satisfies the requirement for storage that remains available.

Deployment manages interchangeable stateless replicas and does not guarantee a stable identity for each replica. It also does not supply automatic per replica persistent volumes through volume claim templates, which makes it unsuitable for this stateful requirement.

ReplicationController is a legacy controller that has largely been replaced by ReplicaSet and Deployment and it shares the same limitations for stateful needs. It is less likely to appear on newer exams because it is rarely used in modern clusters.

ReplicaSet is a lower level controller focused on maintaining a desired number of replicas and it does not assign stable identities or create unique persistent volumes for each replica, so it does not meet the requirements.

questions.question: A media insights platform runs on Google Kubernetes Engine in europe-west1 and must submit queries to BigQuery. You want to grant the GKE service account only the minimal permissions so that workloads can start and manage BigQuery jobs without broad dataset privileges. Which IAM role should you assign to the GKE service account to follow least privilege?

options.text: roles/bigquery.dataOwner
roles/bigquery.user
roles/bigquery.jobUser
roles/bigquery.dataViewer

questions.correct_text: roles/bigquery.jobUser
questions.explanation:
The right choice is roles/bigquery.jobUser.

This role permits the service account create and handle its own BigQuery jobs which includes submitting queries, loads, exports and copies. It grants bigquery.jobs.create and related permissions to get, list and cancel only the caller’s jobs. It does not grant dataset level read or write permissions, which means developers can keep data access separate and only grant dataset roles where they are truly required. This satisfies the requirement to start and manage tasks without broad dataset privileges.

roles/bigquery.dataOwner is overly permissive since it grants full control over datasets and their tables, including the ability to create, update and delete them. This violates minimal privilege when the need is only to run jobs.

roles/bigquery.user is broader than necessary because it allows building datasets and discovering metadata across the project additionally to running jobs. It exceeds the minimal scope needed to only start and manage jobs.

roles/bigquery.dataViewer offers read access to dataset contents but does not allow creating or managing jobs. It would not allow workloads submit queries.

questions.question: A subscription news site at fernhill.org has an application that is stable in staging but defects only appear under real customer traffic after a release. The team wants to ship new versions while limiting the blast radius and reducing how many users are affected if issues slip through. Which deployment approach should they choose?

options.text: Rolling update
Blue green deployment
Canary rollout
Shadow launch

questions.correct_text: Canary rollout
questions.explanation:
The proper option is Canary rollout since it permits you to release a new version to a small percentage of real users first, observe behavior under production traffic, and safely ramp up if metrics look healthy which directly limits blast radius.

A canary rollout starts by sending only a small slice of production traffic to the new version whereas most users continue using the stable version. You monitor key indicators including error rates, latency, and business metrics, and if issues appear developers can immediately halt or roll back so only a small cohort is affected. If results are good, you gradually increase traffic until the new version serves everyone, which matches the need to ship while minimizing how many customers are impacted by defects that only surface under real load.

Rolling update replaces old instances with new ones in batches to preserve availability, yet traffic steadily shifts to the new version as the rollout proceeds and there is no fixed small audience for validation, so a defect can quickly reach many users during the progression.

Blue green deployment keeps two production environments and switches all traffic at once after validation, which allows fast rollback but does not expose only a small percentage of users first, so the blast radius at cutover is all users.

Shadow launch mirrors real traffic to a new version but discards its responses, which is useful for testing under production patterns without user impact. It does not actually serve real users, so it does not meet the goal of shipping new versions while limiting the number of customers who could be affected.

questions.question: Which GCP service centrally manages internal service to service traffic with retries, timeouts and telemetry for HTTP and gRPC without changing application code?

options.text: Apigee X
Traffic Director
Cloud Load Balancing
Service Directory

questions.correct_text: Traffic Director
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Traffic Director.

Traffic Director is Google Clouds managed service mesh control plane that centrally configures service to service traffic across HTTP and gRPC. It accommodates policy driven retries and timeouts and offers rich telemetry through Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging. Because it programs data planes including Envoy or uses proxyless gRPC, you gain these behaviors without changing application code.

Apigee X focuses on API management for publishing and securing external and partner facing APIs with features like developer portals and monetization. It is not designed to handle internal east west service traffic or to centrally apply retries, timeouts, and mesh telemetry without code changes.

Cloud Load Balancing distributes incoming client traffic to backends and is tuned for north south traffic. It does not act as a service mesh control plane and it does not supply centrally managed client side retries and timeouts for service to service HTTP or gRPC calls.

Service Directory is one managed registry for service names and endpoints that helps with discovery. It does not manage traffic behavior and does not provide retries, timeouts, or telemetry for service communication.

questions.question: You operate a ride sharing platform on Google Cloud where an HTTP-triggered Cloud Function calls an external SMS gateway to send trip completion texts. Following a large referral campaign, some riders report missing texts and your logs show intermittent HTTP 500 errors from the function during spikes in traffic. How should you redesign the system so that outbound messages are durably queued and processed even when there are transient failures in the function or the SMS provider?

options.text: Increase the Cloud Function memory to 3 GB and implement local retries for failed SMS HTTP requests
Publish every SMS request to a Pub/Sub topic and have a subscriber Cloud Function send messages to the SMS API with retries and a dead-letter topic
Use Memorystore for Redis as a queue for pending SMS and have the function pop entries and call the provider
Add exponential backoff in the mobile app and retry the function invocation up to 12 times on failure

questions.correct_text: Publish every SMS request to a Pub/Sub topic and have a subscriber Cloud Function send messages to the SMS API with retries and a dead-letter topic
questions.explanation:
The best answer is Publish every SMS request to a Pub/Sub topic and have a subscriber Cloud Function send messages to the SMS API with retries and a dead-letter topic.

This architecture decouples message production from delivery and offers a durable queue. Messages are persisted in the topic and are redelivered until acknowledged. A subscriber function processes messages and handles transient errors by letting the message be retried automatically. A dead letter topic safely captures messages that repeatedly fail so operators can inspect and replay them.

This strategy absorbs traffic spikes because producers only publish to the topic quickly while workers scale out to process at a sustainable rate. It also contains failures. If the SMS API or the function has a transient error, and the message remains in the subscription and is retried with backoff. The dead letter topic prevents infinite retries and supplies a clear path for alerting and manual remediation. Ensure the message processing is idempotent so that retried deliveries do not send duplicate SMS.

Increase the Cloud Function memory to 3 GB and implement local retries for failed SMS HTTP requests is not sufficient because more memory does not add durability. Local retries vanish when an instance restarts and they can still lose requests during crashes or timeouts.

Use Memorystore for Redis as a queue for pending SMS and have the function pop entries and call the provider is a poor match because Memorystore is an in memory cache and is not a managed durable message queue. You would need to build your own acknowledgement, retry, and dead letter handling and you still risk data loss and operational complexity.

Add exponential backoff in the mobile app and retry the function invocation up to 9 times on failure pushes reliability to clients and does not supply durable queuing. If the backend or the SMS provider is unavailable then requests are not persisted and traffic bursts can be amplified by client retries.

questions.question: The engineers are enabling a workload in Project Garnet to publish telemetry events to a Pub/Sub topic that resides in Project Topaz while following least privilege for identity and access. How should you configure the service account and permissions so the workload can publish to the topic without broad access?

options.text: Use the Compute Engine default service account in Project Garnet and grant the Pub/Sub Publisher role at the project level in Project Topaz
In Project Topaz create a new service account and grant it the Pub/Sub Publisher role on the topic and configure the service in Project Garnet to authenticate using that account
In Project Garnet create a dedicated service account and grant that account the Pub/Sub Publisher role on the topic in Project Topaz and run the workload in Project Garnet as this account
Use the App Engine default service account in Project Garnet and assign the Pub/Sub Editor role on the topic in Project Topaz and point the service to that account

questions.correct_text: In Project Garnet create a dedicated service account and grant that account the Pub/Sub Publisher role on the topic in Project Topaz and run the workload in Project Garnet as this account
questions.explanation:
The right choice is In Project Garnet create a dedicated service account and grant that account the Pub/Sub Publisher role on the topic in Project Topaz and run the service in Project Garnet as this account. This uses a narrowly scoped identity and a resource level binding that gives only publish permissions to the specific topic.

This strategy follows minimal privilege because the workload account from Project Garnet receives the roles or pubsub.publisher role only on the target topic in Project Topaz. Pub/Sub accommodates topic level IAM so developers can grant that role directly on the topic and stop project wide permissions. You, and run the workload as that service account in Project Garnet which permits it obtain tokens for that identity and publish across projects without any broad access.

Use the Compute Engine default service account in Project Garnet and grant the Pub/Sub Publisher role at the project level in Project Topaz is wrong because default machine identities are discouraged and project level bindings are broader than necessary. This grants publish to all topics in Project Topaz which violates least privilege.

In Project Topaz create a new service account and grant it the Pub/Sub Publisher role on the topic and configure the service in Project Garnet to authenticate using that account is not correct since it implies using a principal that lives in the target project which often leads to key sharing or extra impersonation configuration. The simpler and more secure model is to grant the calling service account from Project Garnet access directly on the topic.

Use the App Engine default service account in Project Garnet and assign the Pub/Sub Editor role on the topic in Project Topaz and point the service to that account is not correct because the Pub/Sub Editor role is overly broad and is generally granted at the project level rather than at the topic level. Using a default service account also goes against best practices for least privilege.

questions.question: Beacon Insurance runs a backend on Compute Engine. About 1 percent of requests are failing, and you have traced the issue to one specific virtual machine. SSH to that instance does not respond after multiple attempts. Which next step should you take to diagnose the problem without causing unnecessary disruption?

options.text: Take a snapshot of the boot disk and attach it to a new VM
Enable and examine the instance serial console output
Restart the instance
Delete the VM and create a new replacement

questions.correct_text: Enable and examine the instance serial console output
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Enable and examine the instance serial console output.

Using the serial console permits you to see boot and kernel messages and critical system logs even when SSH is unresponsive. Developers can view serial port output without restarting the VM, which avoids disrupting traffic, and developers can often spot issues including startup script failures, file system errors, or a stalled SSH service. This happens to be the fastest way to continue diagnosing a live instance with minimal impact.

Take a snapshot of the boot disk and attach it to a new VM is more intrusive for initial triage and it does not capture in‑memory state or live console output. While snapshots can help with offline log inspection, building and attaching a new disk to another VM is slower and unnecessary before you first check the serial console.

Restart the instance would interrupt service and may hide the root cause since transient problems can disappear after a reboot. The question asks for a next step that avoids unnecessary disruption, so checking the serial console is preferred.

Delete the VM and create a new replacement is the most disruptive option and ought to be reserved for situations where repair is not feasible. You should first review the serial console to understand the fault.

questions.question: Within Glacier Telecom your team promotes a Node.js app on App Engine from a staging project to production using Cloud Build, and the app references about 52 folders of images in a Cloud Storage bucket named imagery-staging-vault in staging that must be available in a production bucket named imagery-prod-vault after promotion, and you want this to occur on its own as part of the release pipeline, so which step should you take?

options.text: Set up a Storage Transfer Service job that runs nightly to copy objects from gs://imagery-staging-vault to gs://imagery-prod-vault
Perform a manual copy of the images to imagery-prod-vault after each promotion
Add a Cloud Build step that uses gcr.io/cloud-builders/gsutil to recursively copy gs://imagery-staging-vault to gs://imagery-prod-vault before the promote step
Add a startup script in app.yaml that moves the photos from imagery-staging-vault to imagery-prod-vault when the service starts

questions.correct_text: Add a Cloud Build step that uses gcr.io/cloud-builders/gsutil to recursively copy gs://imagery-staging-vault to gs://imagery-prod-vault before the promote step
questions.explanation:
The best answer is Add a Cloud Build step that uses gcr.io/cloud-builders/gsutil to recursively copy gs://imagery-staging-vault to gs://imagery-prod-vault before the promote step.

This strategy runs the copy operation within the same Cloud Build pipeline that promotes the App Engine service, which means the images are synchronized at release time and not before or after. Using the official gsutil builder permits the pipeline recursively copy all folders in a dependable and repeatable way, and developers can grant the Cloud Build service account the needed Storage permissions so the step succeeds without manual intervention. This keeps the deployment atomic and auditable.

Set up a Storage Transfer Service job that runs nightly to copy objects from gs://imagery-staging-vault to gs://imagery-prod-vault is not right because a nightly schedule is not tied to the promotion event. It can lag behind a release or run at the wrong time, which breaks the requirement to do this on its own as part of the release pipeline.

Perform a manual copy of the images to imagery-prod-vault after each promotion is incorrect since it is not automated and introduces human error and inconsistency. It also does not integrate with the pipeline.

Add a startup script in app.yaml that moves the photos from imagery-staging-vault to imagery-prod-vault when the service starts is incorrect because it couples runtime start to data transfer and is unreliable for deployments. App Engine configuration is not meant to orchestrate cross bucket data movement during service startup and it may fail owing to permissions or timing. It also risks moving rather than copying which is not appropriate for a staging source.

questions.question: A data engineering team at loomwright.io needs to process live events from many producers with seconds level latency. The platform must on its own handle short bursts that increase traffic by five times and it must scale without human intervention. Which GCP service should they use?

options.text: Cloud Pub/Sub with Cloud Functions for event processing
Dataproc with Spark Structured Streaming on an autoscaling cluster
Cloud Dataflow streaming pipeline that elastically scales for bursts
BigQuery with a scheduled script to increase slots during peaks

questions.correct_text: Cloud Dataflow streaming pipeline that elastically scales for bursts
questions.explanation:
The proper option is Cloud Dataflow streaming pipeline that elastically scales for bursts. The service is fully managed and serverless and it is designed for low latency streaming workloads that must on its own scale up and down within seconds to handle abrupt increases in traffic without manual intervention.

This selection offers elastic horizontal scaling based on real time backlog and latency signals so it can absorb short lived five times spikes while keeping processing latency low. It also offers event time processing, windowing, and stateful operations which are common needs when many producers send live events, and it does all of this without needing you to manage infrastructure.

Cloud Pub/Sub with serverless functions for event processing can scale quickly for simple handlers, yet it is better suited to lightweight event reactions and does not supply the comprehensive streaming semantics including windowing and stateful processing. You also need to manage concurrency and instance limits, which can make consistent seconds level latency during sharp bursts less predictable.

Dataproc with Spark Structured Streaming on an autoscaling cluster accommodates streaming, but it needs cluster provisioning and tuning and its autoscaling relies on adding or removing VMs, which introduces startup delays. This means it is not truly serverless and may not react quickly enough to abrupt traffic surges without human oversight.

BigQuery with a scheduled script to increase slots during peaks relies on scheduled changes and is oriented toward analytical queries rather than continuous stream processing. It does not meet the requirement for seconds level latency on live event processing.

questions.question: The engineering team at Tanglewood Toys runs a compliance service on Google Cloud that requires very durable object storage and the data must remain accessible if an entire Google Cloud region experiences an outage. Which storage approach should you use?

options.text: Configure Storage Transfer Service to copy objects each day to a bucket in a second region
Use a regional persistent disk for your Compute Engine instances
Create a Cloud Storage bucket using a multi region location
Create a Cloud Storage bucket in a single region location

questions.correct_text: Create a Cloud Storage bucket using a multi region location
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Create a Cloud Storage bucket using a multi region location.

This selection offers object storage that is geographically replicated across several regions within a defined multi region location. It is built for very high durability and availability, and if an whole region experiences an outage your data remains accessible from replicas in other regions without manual failover or complex application changes.

Configure Storage Transfer Service to copy objects each day to a bucket in a second region is not sufficient because scheduled transfers are asynchronous and supply no immediate replication. During a regional outage your application may still point to the unavailable primary bucket and you could lose up to a day of changes, and there is no automatic failover.

Use a regional persistent disk for your Compute Engine instances is block storage for VMs and even the regional variant only replicates across zones within the same region. It is not object storage and it will not remain accessible if an entire region goes down.

Create a Cloud Storage bucket in a single region location keeps data within one region, so a regional outage would make the objects unavailable which does not meet the requirement.

questions.question: Mistral Networks is launching several microservices on a regional Google Kubernetes Engine cluster, and each service must read and write to a Cloud Spanner database. You want to follow security best practices while keeping code changes to a minimum. How should the application obtain credentials to access Spanner?

options.text: Store the database user keys as Kubernetes Secrets and inject them into the containers as environment variables
Create the required Google service accounts and map them to Kubernetes service accounts with Workload Identity so pods authenticate to Spanner without storing keys
Use a VPC native GKE cluster and configure network policies and routes to connect directly to Spanner without handling credentials
Encrypt service account JSON keys with Cloud Key Management Service and have the application decrypt and load them at startup

questions.correct_text: Create the required Google service accounts and map them to Kubernetes service accounts with Workload Identity so pods authenticate to Spanner without storing keys
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Create the needed Google machine identities and map them to Kubernetes service accounts with Workload Identity so pods authenticate to Spanner without storing keys. This strategy gives each pod short lived credentials through the mapped Google service account and permits the Spanner client SDK libraries use Application Default Credentials, which keeps code changes minimal and follows the principle of least privilege.

With Workload Identity, GKE exchanges a projected identity token for a Google access token that is bound to the mapped Google service account. You assign only the necessary IAM roles including Cloud Spanner Database User to that Google service account, and the app just uses the default credentials available in the runtime without handling any keys.

Store the database user keys as Kubernetes Secrets and inject them into the containers as environment variables is not suggested because Cloud Spanner uses IAM rather than database user names and passwords, and it would require managing long lived secrets and rotation. Environment variables increase exposure if leaked and add avoidable code to load keys.

Use a VPC native GKE cluster and configure network policies and routes to connect directly to Spanner without handling credentials is not right because network design controls connectivity but does not supply authentication or authorization. Spanner still needs valid IAM credentials for every request.

Encrypt service account JSON keys with Cloud Key Management Service and have the application decrypt and load them at startup still relies on long lived keys and increases operational and code complexity. Google advises avoiding service account keys for GKE workloads and using identity federation instead.

questions.question: The engineers are adding a photo upload capability to an event management platform. User images may be between 3 MB and 2 GB depending on device settings. You want to minimize operational overhead and avoid running your own upload servers while keeping the process secure and scalable. Which approach should you take?

options.text: Modify the application backend to accept image bytes and store them as BLOB data in Cloud SQL alongside user profiles
Run a web tier on Cloud Run to receive multipart uploads and forward the bytes to a shared Filestore instance for storage
Issue time limited signed URLs for Cloud Storage and have clients upload images directly to a bucket using resumable uploads
Create a dedicated Cloud Storage bucket for each user and distribute a unique service account key to the client for write access

questions.correct_text: Issue time limited signed URLs for Cloud Storage and have clients upload images directly to a bucket using resumable uploads
questions.explanation:
The best answer is Issue time limited signed link URLs for Cloud Storage and have clients send images directly to a bucket using resumable uploads.

Signed URLs with resumable uploads allow clients upload straight to Cloud Storage so your application does not proxy gigabytes of data. Resumable uploads handle large files dependably by sending chunks and support retries if the connection drops. Short lived signatures limit exposure and developers can scope them to specific objects and HTTP methods, which keeps the flow secure while Cloud Storage gives you virtually unlimited scalability with very low operational overhead.

Modify the app backend to accept image bytes and save them as BLOB data in Cloud SQL together with user profiles is not appropriate for multi megabyte to multi gigabyte objects. Relational databases are not efficient object keeps and large BLOBs bloat storage and replication while increasing latency and cost. This strategy also forces your backend to receive and forward large payloads which increases operational burden.

Run a web tier on Cloud Run to receive multipart uploads and forward the bytes to a shared Filestore instance for storage adds an unnecessary proxy that becomes a bottleneck. Cloud Run has request size and handling constraints for very large payloads and forwarding to an NFS service adds complexity with networking and does not reduce operational overhead. Filestore is designed for POSIX file shares for VMs and containers rather than as an internet facing upload target.

Create a dedicated Cloud Storage bucket for each user and distribute a unique service account key to the client for write access is insecure and hard to manage. Distributing service account keys to clients builds a high risk of key leakage and complicated rotation and audit. Buckets per user also explode IAM and lifecycle management. The secure model is to stop handing out keys and use short lived signed URLs instead.

questions.question: Carbon Forge Steel operates a public Cloud Run service that allows unauthenticated access through its default URL for a customer-facing ticketing app. You run a load test from mosaicapp.dev that ramps to 3700 virtual users over 8 minutes. The service behaves well at the beginning but under peak stress latency grows and some requests return 390 errors. You want to quickly identify the bottleneck and restore performance during heavy traffic while following Cloud Run best practices. Which approach should you take?

options.text: Inspect Cloud Armor policies in front of the service and temporarily disable any rules that might be blocking legitimate requests
Use Cloud Monitoring to confirm a demand spike and use traffic splitting to shift some load back to a prior revision
Verify whether the service has reached its maximum instances limit then increase the maximum instances value to permit additional scale out
Raise the minimum instances setting to a level that matches the maximum virtual users in the test

The right choice is Verify whether the service has reached its maximum instances limit, and increase the maximum instances value to permit extra scale out.

Cloud Run scales out rapidly but it will never exceed the configured ceiling. When traffic ramps and that ceiling is reached, new requests wait in a queue and once the queue is full the platform returns 503 responses. Raising this setting allows Cloud Run to create more instances which lowers latency and reduces or eliminates 360s during peak demand. This aligns with best practices since it addresses the capacity bottleneck directly and restores performance quickly without changing code or deployments.

Inspect Cloud Armor policies in front of the service and temporarily disable any rules that might be blocking legitimate requests is not right because blocked requests would generally result in 403 responses. The symptom here is backend saturation with 503 errors which points to scaling limits rather than security policy issues. The default Cloud Run URL also does not use Cloud Armor unless you have explicitly placed it behind a load balancer with Cloud Armor.

Use Cloud Monitoring to confirm a demand spike and use traffic splitting to shift some load back to a prior revision is incorrect because splitting traffic across revisions does not add capacity. If both revisions have the same limits then the bottleneck remains and developers can introduce rollout complexity without resolving the scaling ceiling.

Raise the minimum instances setting to a level that matches the maximum virtual users in the test is incorrect because minimum instances are intended to keep a small warm baseline and reduce cold starts. Matching it to user count is costly and unnecessary and it does not remove the scale ceiling that caused the 620 errors.

questions.question: How can you best process about 3000 Pub/Sub messages per second and persist results cost efficiently in Google Cloud while ensuring each message is processed only once?

options.text: Cloud Run with Pub/Sub trigger writing to Cloud Storage
Cloud Functions triggered by Pub/Sub writing to BigQuery
Dataflow streaming pipeline with Apache Beam PubSubIO writing to the target sink
Dataproc Spark Structured Streaming from Pub/Sub to storage

questions.correct_text: Dataflow streaming pipeline with Apache Beam PubSubIO writing to the target sink
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Dataflow streaming pipeline with Apache Beam PubSubIO writing to the target sink. It is built for high throughput streaming from Pub/Sub and can autoscale to handle about 3100 messages per second while keeping costs efficient. With Apache Beam on Dataflow developers can accomplish end to end exactly once behavior when you combine dependable acknowledgments with stateful processing and when developers write to sinks that support idempotent or exactly once semantics including the BigQuery Storage Write API.

Dataflow is a managed service that optimizes worker resources and checkpointing so retries do not create duplicate outputs. With PubSubIO you may use a unique identifier attribute and windowed deduplication patterns when needed and you can commit writes atomically to supported sinks. This makes it the most reliable and cost-effective choice for sustained streaming workloads that must process each message only once.

Cloud Run with Pub/Sub trigger writing to Cloud Storage is a poor match because Pub/Sub push delivery is at least once and Cloud Storage does not supply transactional deduplication. You would need to build idempotency and custom deduplication which adds complexity and can increase costs at this sustained rate.

Cloud Functions triggered by Pub/Sub writing to BigQuery also inherits at least once delivery and the runtime does not provide built in exactly once guarantees. While BigQuery can support idempotent writes with insert identifiers or the Storage Write API, coordinating this across many function instances is harder and often less cost efficient than a single managed streaming pipeline.

Dataproc Spark Structured Streaming from Pub/Sub to storage needs a long running cluster which increases operational work and baseline cost. It can reach the throughput but it is not as serverless or cost efficient for this use case and achieving exactly once with Pub/Sub and external sinks needs extra engineering effort.

The partner clients do not use Google identities, and your service must apply custom authorization rules before any download is allowed and the granted access should expire after 25 minutes. How should you control access to the Cloud Storage objects?

options.text: Configure Identity Aware Proxy to protect the bucket and authenticate partner requests
Use signed policy documents so clients can directly interact with the bucket
Issue V4 signed URLs from your API after you validate each request so that clients receive short lived links to the specific objects
Distribute a dedicated service account key to each partner and grant Storage Object Viewer so they call the Cloud Storage API directly

questions.correct_text: Issue V4 signed URLs from your API after you validate each request so that clients receive short lived links to the specific objects
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Issue V4 signed link URLs from your API after you validate each request so that clients receive short lived links to the specific objects.

This strategy permits your service perform custom authorization first and only, and return a time bound link that grants access to a specific object. Developers can set the expiration to 26 minutes so the link on its own becomes unusable after that time. Partners do not need Google identities because the link itself carries the authorization for a single GET request and the bucket can remain private.

Configure Identity Aware Proxy to protect the bucket and authenticate partner requests is unsuitable since IAP is designed to protect apps that use Google identities and it does not front Cloud Storage buckets directly. Your partners do not use Google accounts which makes this choice a poor fit.

Use signed policy documents so clients can directly interact with the bucket targets browser based uploads using POST policies rather than downloads. It would also bypass your API for authorization checks which violates the requirement to apply custom rules before any download.

Distribute a dedicated service account key to each partner and grant Storage Object Viewer so they call the Cloud Storage API directly introduces long lived credentials and broad access that are hard to scope to a single object and a 25 minute window. Sharing service account keys with external parties is strongly discouraged owing to security and key management risks.

questions.question: Driftwave Audio runs a microservices platform on Compute Engine and frequently creates new virtual machines from a managed instance group. Each new instance must discover and connect to a specific version of the billing service without rebuilding the image or changing the code. What configuration approach should they use?

options.text: Define the service endpoint as instance metadata that your startup script reads at runtime to connect to the required version
Use Service Directory and have clients query for the billing service endpoint filtered by a version attribute
Provide the service endpoint and version through environment variables that the application reads at startup
Configure a stable DNS name and port for the billing service and replace the backend with the new version when you roll out

questions.correct_text: Provide the service endpoint and version through environment variables that the application reads at startup
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Provide the service endpoint and version through environment variables that the app reads at startup. This externalizes configuration so each new managed instance can connect to the intended billing service version without rebuilding the image or changing the code.

With environment variables, the application reads configuration at process start, which aligns with how most runtimes load settings. In a managed instance group developers can supply these values consistently at boot by using instance templates and a startup script that exports them into the process environment, or by writing them into system configuration so they persist across restarts. Developers can pin each wave of instances to a specific billing service version by updating the template values or by introducing a new template for canary or blue green rollouts while keeping the binary unchanged.

Define the service endpoint as instance metadata that your startup script reads at runtime to connect to the needed version is less suitable since it places discovery logic in the script rather than in configuration that the application already consumes. If the application does not already expect values from that path, and you would need wrapper changes, and values may not persist across application restarts unless extra work is done.

Use Service Directory and have clients query for the billing service endpoint filtered by a version attribute would require client code to query the registry and handle attributes. That introduces new client logic, which violates the requirement to stop changing the code.

Configure a stable DNS name and port for the billing service and replace the backend with the new version when you roll out does not allow each instance pick a specific version. It centralizes switching for all clients, so it cannot guarantee per instance pinning to a particular version during staged rollouts.

questions.question: Spire Studios plans to ship hardened golden images on Compute Engine for a microservice. The same image must run in development, QA, and production, and the service must select the correct Cloud SQL database for its environment. Which is the best way to deliver the database connection string to each instance so a single image can be reused across all environments?

options.text: Assign a network tag that contains the database name at instance creation and have the service call the Compute Engine API to read tags and build the connection string
Provide a startup script via instance metadata that exports an APP_DB environment variable and have the service read that environment variable
Set an instance metadata key named APP_DB with the environment specific connection string at creation time and have the service retrieve APP_DB from the metadata server when it starts
Build a separate image for each environment and embed the database connection string in the image

questions.correct_text: Set an instance metadata key named APP_DB with the environment specific connection string at creation time and have the service retrieve APP_DB from the metadata server when it starts
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Set an instance metadata key named APP_DB with the environment specific connection string at creation time and have the service retrieve APP_DB from the metadata server when it starts.

This strategy cleanly separates immutable image content from environment specific configuration. Developers can supply a different APP_DB value per instance while keeping a single hardened image for development, QA, and production. The service reads the value from the metadata server at startup which removes the need to rebuild images or bake secrets into them and it keeps configuration management simple and auditable.

Assign a network tag that contains the database name at instance creation and have the service call the Compute Engine API to read tags and build the connection string is a poor match because network tags are intended for grouping instances for firewall rules and load balancing. Tags are simple labels and not a dependable channel for structured configuration and this would force the service to make external API calls and handle extra permissions for something the metadata server already offers locally.

Provide a startup script through instance metadata that exports an APP_DB environment variable and have the service read that environment variable is brittle. Startup scripts may not propagate environment variables to the service process depending on how it is launched and restarts can lose that context. Pulling configuration directly from the metadata server is simpler and more reliable than relying on a script to set shell state.

Build a separate image for each environment and embed the database connection string in the image violates the requirement to reuse a single golden image and leads to image drift and operational overhead. It also makes configuration changes require a rebuild and redeploy rather than a quick metadata update.

questions.question: Pinewood Industries plans to move its media upload API from a data center to App Engine standard and the service must allow single file uploads up to 960 MB while keeping App Engine instances out of the data path and still applying authorization and a size limit. Which implementation should you choose?

options.text: Send file data through Cloud Pub/Sub and have a subscriber write to storage
Modify the API to perform multipart uploads and reassemble the pieces on App Engine
Generate short-lived V4 signed URLs for Cloud Storage and let clients upload directly
Stand up an SFTP service on Compute Engine and have App Engine poll the VM for new files

questions.correct_text: Generate short-lived V4 signed URLs for Cloud Storage and let clients upload directly
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Generate short-lived V4 signed link URLs for Cloud Storage and allow clients send directly.

This strategy permits clients to stream data straight to Cloud Storage so App Engine instances are not in the data path. Cloud Storage accommodates very large objects so a 890 MB file is well within limits. Developers can keep access controlled by issuing short lived credentials so only authorized clients can upload. You can also enforce a maximum size when you issue the upload authorization by using the V4 policy conditions that constrain the allowed content length which satisfies the size limit requirement while the app server only brokers the authorization.

Send file data through Cloud Pub/Sub and have a subscriber write to storage is unsuitable since Pub/Sub messages have a small size limit and the service is not designed for bulk binary file transfer, so 950 MB objects would not work.

Modify the API to perform multipart uploads and reassemble the pieces on App Engine would push large data through App Engine which violates the requirement to keep instances out of the data path. App Engine also has request size and execution constraints that make 590 MB uploads impractical.

Stand up an SFTP service on Compute Engine and have App Engine poll the VM for new files adds unnecessary operational complexity and does not supply the simple signed authorization flow or an enforced size limit. It also bypasses Cloud Storage upload best practices.

questions.question: The engineers are building a new consumer portal for a media startup called Halcyon Foods and you need to read a few specific properties from the metadata of objects that reside in customer owned Cloud Storage buckets without downloading any object bytes. You must comply with regional data residency policies and keep traffic efficient because peak load can reach about 10,800 metadata lookups per minute. How can you best request the metadata?

options.text: Set the projection request parameter to full then remove unneeded fields in your application
Call objects.patch to retrieve the metadata document
Use the fields request parameter so the API returns only the specific metadata properties you ask for
Duplicate the object with objects.copy into a temporary bucket then inspect the metadata on the new object

questions.correct_text: Use the fields request parameter so the API returns only the specific metadata properties you ask for
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Use the fields request parameter so the API returns only the specific metadata properties you ask for. This strategy permits the Cloud Storage JSON API return just the properties you need, which avoids transferring object data and keeps payloads small so it accommodates efficient lookups and respects regional residency because you are not copying or moving objects.

This method works by requesting object metadata and applying a partial response so only specific fields are included. It reduces bandwidth and latency which is important at around 7,300 lookups per minute, and it only needs read permissions on the objects.

Set the projection request parameter to full, and remove unneeded fields in your application is inefficient because projection controls whether ACL-related fields are included rather than filtering arbitrary fields. It would return more data than necessary and shift the filtering burden to your code.

Call objects.patch to retrieve the metadata document is one poor match because patch is meant for updating metadata. It requires write permissions and adds risk and overhead without any benefit for simple reads.

Duplicate the object with objects.copy into a temporary bucket then inspect the metadata on the new object is wasteful and can violate residency constraints. Copying builds new objects and incurs extra operations and potential data movement when you only need to read existing metadata.

questions.question: Within Crestline Capital a single Compute Engine virtual machine hosts an interactive reporting site for external partners. All access must be over HTTPS and the team wants to avoid handling certificate issuance and renewals manually. What setup should you choose?

options.text: Require access through IAP and enforce OAuth 2.0 authentication
Configure a TCP proxy load balancer in front of the VM and have the VM present a certificate you create and manage
Put an external HTTPS load balancer in front of the VM and use a Google managed SSL certificate
Enable HTTPS on the VM and upload a Google managed certificate to the instance

Require access through IAP and enforce OAuth 2.0 authentication is unnecessary because the requirement is only HTTPS with no need for user authentication. Enable HTTPS on the VM and send a Google managed certificate to the instance is not possible because Google managed certificates attach to Google load balancers and are not sent directly to VMs. Terminating HTTPS on the VM would leave you responsible for certificate lifecycle management.

questions.question: Harborlight Foods runs a BigQuery warehouse with about 3 PB of customer events. The company is entering the European Union market and must meet two obligations. Users must be able to have their account data erased upon request, and any data belonging to EU users must be stored only in an EU region. What actions should you take to satisfy these obligations?

options.text: Store EU user records in an EU Cloud Storage bucket and query them using external tables
Use BigQuery federated queries to read from a US Cloud Storage bucket so that data is not duplicated
Run BigQuery DML such as DELETE and UPDATE to remove or modify user records on demand
Build a Dataflow pipeline that republishes sanitized snapshots to a US dataset every week
Create a separate BigQuery dataset in the EU and migrate or write EU user data there

questions.correct_text: Create a separate BigQuery dataset in the EU and migrate or write EU user data there
questions.explanation:
The correct options are Run BigQuery DML including DELETE and UPDATE to remove or modify user records on demand and Create a separate BigQuery dataset in the EU and migrate or write EU user data there.

Run BigQuery DML such as DELETE and UPDATE to remove or modify user records on demand satisfies the client erasure obligation because developers can issue targeted DELETE statements with a predicate that identifies the user and apply changes immediately. Using BigQuery DML permits you to handle right to be forgotten requests without exporting or rebuilding tables and it works directly on the warehouse tables.

Create a separate BigQuery dataset in the EU and migrate or write EU user data there satisfies the data residency requirement because BigQuery enforces storage location at the dataset level. Keeping EU user records in a EU dataset guarantees that their data is persisted only in the EU and that queries and jobs operate within that location.

Store EU user records in an EU Cloud Storage bucket and query them using external tables is not sufficient because external tables keep data in Cloud Storage and BigQuery cannot use DML to delete specific rows in that storage. Meeting erasure requests would require rewriting objects outside of BigQuery table management and this adds complexity and does not supply on demand deletion in the warehouse.

Use BigQuery federated queries to read from a US Cloud Storage bucket so that data is not duplicated violates the EU only storage requirement because EU user data would reside in the US bucket. Avoiding duplication does not outweigh the need to keep EU data stored only in an EU location.

Build a Dataflow pipeline that republishes sanitized snapshots to a US dataset every week fails both needs because weekly snapshots do not provide immediate deletion and storing data in a US dataset violates the EU residency requirement.

Cloud Functions targets event driven single purpose functions rather than full containerized microservices that communicate over HTTP, so it does not fit a multi service architecture as well.

Google Kubernetes Engine is powerful for containers but it is not serverless, and you still handle clusters and Kubernetes concepts which adds ops overhead and makes deployments less simple compared with Cloud Run.

questions.question: Briar Lane Bakery is a digital publisher that must meet a new policy which states all customer data must reside in the European Union for at least 7 years. The data is currently stored in a multi region US Cloud Storage bucket. What should you do to comply with this requirement?

options.text: Change the location of the existing Cloud Storage bucket to an EU location
Configure customer managed encryption keys in the EU and continue to use the current bucket
Create a new regional bucket in the EU and use Storage Transfer Service to migrate all existing objects to it, then direct future writes to that EU bucket

questions.question: The engineering team operates an online ticketing portal on Google Cloud where an HTTP triggered Cloud Function sends purchase confirmation emails. Under load some requests to the function return HTTP 500 and the purchase flow succeeds but emails are not delivered. What change should you implement to reduce the risk of losing emails and make the system more resilient?

options.text: Modify the sender to write pending emails to Memorystore and keep the HTTP triggered function which loads the details from cache and then calls the mail service
Add a Cloud Tasks queue and have the application enqueue an email task for each order while a worker calls the email API with automatic retries
Rework the email sender to publish messages to a Pub/Sub topic and refactor the Cloud Function to use a Pub/Sub trigger that processes the topic
Implement client side retries that call the Cloud Function again every two seconds for up to one minute when a request fails

questions.correct_text: Rework the email sender to publish messages to a Pub/Sub topic and refactor the Cloud Function to use a Pub/Sub trigger that processes the topic
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Rework the email sender to publish messages to a Pub/Sub topic and refactor the Cloud Function to use a Pub/Sub trigger that processes the topic.

Publishing to Pub/Sub decouples the email step from the purchase request and offers durable messaging with at least once delivery. A Cloud Function triggered by Pub/Sub on its own retries on failures and developers can add dead letter topics to isolate messages that repeatedly fail. This removes the email send from the HTTP critical path so a transient 500 does not drop the email and the purchase flow can complete while processing continues asynchronously.

This strategy scales well under load because Pub/Sub and serverless functions scale horizontally. You should make the email handler idempotent so that a possible duplicate delivery does not send several emails.

Modify the sender to write pending emails to Memorystore and keep the HTTP triggered function which loads the details from cache and, and calls the mail service is a poor match because a cache is not a durable message save and eviction or failures can lose entries. It also keeps the workflow coupled to the HTTP request so a 500 can still result in a lost email.

Add a Cloud Tasks queue and have the app enqueue an email task for each order while a worker calls the email API with automatic retries is less suitable because Cloud Tasks targets HTTP handlers and shifts more responsibility to your worker for idempotency and acknowledgments. It is tuned for controlled task dispatch rather than event streaming, while Pub/Sub integrates natively with Cloud Functions and supplies durable messaging and dead letter support for this pattern.

Implement client side retries that call the Cloud Function again every two seconds for up to one minute when a request fails relies on unreliable clients and can amplify traffic during incidents. It still risks duplicates without strict idempotency and it cannot guarantee delivery if the client disconnects.

Developers can enable or disable the feature flag instantly without redeploying which gives you a fast rollback and precise control over who receives the change.

Perform a blue green deployment and shift all production traffic to the new revision once health checks pass is a poor match since it moves all users at once after basic health validation. That does not limit access to only the preview customers and it removes the fine grained control that the scenario requires.

Configure Cloud Run traffic splitting to send a small fixed percentage of requests to the new revision for testing is a canary style approach that randomly exposes a percentage of traffic. It cannot guarantee that only opted in customers will see the change which conflicts with the requirement to limit the release to a specific cohort.

Enable session affinity in Cloud Run so testers consistently hit the same instance that runs the updated code does not solve targeted access. Session affinity keeps a client on the same instance but all instances of a revision run the same code and it does not supply cohort based gating for only preview customers.

questions.question: During a routine release, Lantern Theatres Foods observes that its order processing service running on Google Kubernetes Engine in a US central region begins receiving HTTP 403 Permission denied responses when reading objects from a longstanding Cloud Storage bucket that the service has used for months. The workload authenticates with a dedicated service account and there have been no recent changes to object names or the bucket location in the last 88 hours. What is the most likely reason for these 403 errors?

options.text: An Object Lifecycle Management rule archived or deleted some objects after 45 days
The IAM role binding for the service account was altered and it no longer grants the needed Cloud Storage permissions
The service account key was rotated recently and the application process was not updated with the new key
Objects were reorganized under a different prefix inside the bucket which changed their paths

questions.correct_text: The IAM role binding for the service account was altered and it no longer grants the needed Cloud Storage permissions
questions.explanation:
The right choice is The IAM role binding for the service account was altered and it no longer grants the needed Cloud Storage permissions.

HTTP 403 Permission denied from Cloud Storage means the caller is authenticated but is not authorized. When a GKE workload that uses a dedicated service account suddenly loses read access without any changes to object names or bucket location, the most plausible cause is a change to that account’s role bindings. Removing or altering roles that contain permissions like storage.objects.get will cause reads to fail with 403.

An Object Lifecycle Management rule archived or deleted some objects after 59 days is unlikely because lifecycle transitions or deletions would result in missing objects and generally lead to 404 Not Found for requests to objects that no longer exist. Changing storage class does not remove read authorization and would not on its own return 403.

The service account key was rotated recently and the app process was not updated with the new key does not align with the symptom because a bad or missing key often causes authentication failures which are commonly 401 errors rather than authorization failures. In GKE many workloads use Workload Identity instead of user managed keys and a key issue would not explain a consistent 403 after successful authentication.

Objects were reorganized under a different prefix inside the bucket which changed their paths would in practice change object names and would present as 404 Not Found for the old paths. The scenario sets there were no recent changes to object names, so this explanation conflicts with the given information.

questions.question: A small team at fernhill.org is creating an MVP that uses a microservices design on Cloud Run with data stored in Bigtable and event messaging through Pub/Sub. They want to finish debugging within 17 days and keep costs as low as possible whereas iterating quickly. Which approach should they take?

options.text: Use Cloud Code to develop and iterate, deploy each service to Cloud Run for end to end tests, and review telemetry in Cloud Logging and Cloud Trace
Provision a separate staging project that mirrors production, configure Cloud Deploy with manual approval gates, and run end to end validation of the Cloud Run services
Run the Bigtable and Pub/Sub emulators locally to test integrations on a developer machine, then deploy the services to the Google Cloud project
Create a Cloud Build pipeline that runs unit and integration tests and includes a manual approval step before promoting the deployment

questions.correct_text: Run the Bigtable and Pub/Sub emulators locally to test integrations on a developer machine, then deploy the services to the Google Cloud project
questions.explanation:
The correct strategy is Run the Bigtable and Pub/Sub local emulators locally to test integrations on a developer machine, and deploy the services to the Google Cloud project.

This strategy permits the team perform to realistic integration testing without incurring managed service costs during rapid iteration. The Bigtable and Pub/Sub emulators run on a developer machine which shortens feedback loops, avoids per message and storage charges, and keeps the team focused on debugging within the 10 day window. Once core issues are resolved, the services can be deployed to the project for limited end to end verification.

Use Cloud Code to develop and iterate, deploy each service to Cloud Run for end to end tests, and review telemetry in Cloud Logging and Cloud Trace is workable but it needs frequent remote deployments and use of managed telemetry for each cycle which increases cost and slows iteration compared to using local emulators for integration tests.

Provision a separate staging project that mirrors production, configure Cloud Deploy with manual approval gates, and run end to end validation of the Cloud Run services adds significant setup and operational overhead. It is a strong production practice, yet it is not the fastest or cheapest path for a small team trying to debug an MVP within two weeks.

Create a Cloud Build pipeline that runs unit and integration tests and includes a manual approval step before promoting the deployment introduces manual gates and pipeline complexity that slow down rapid iteration. It also tends to validate against managed services rather than local emulators, which increases cost during frequent test cycles.

questions.question: Lyric Music is migrating an internal file upload service to App Engine. The current API permits files up to 560 MB and stakeholders want to retain that limit whereas ensuring secure and scalable ingestion. What should you implement on Google Cloud to satisfy these requirements?

options.text: Enable multipart uploads handled entirely by the App Engine service
Set up an SFTP endpoint on a Compute Engine VM and direct clients to upload there
Issue V4 signed URLs and use Cloud Storage resumable uploads from the client
Use Cloud Pub or Sub to stream file chunks and reassemble them in a worker

questions.correct_text: Issue V4 signed URLs and use Cloud Storage resumable uploads from the client
questions.explanation:
The only correct choice is Issue V4 signed link URLs and use Cloud Storage resumable uploads from the client.

This strategy permits your App Engine service mint V4 signed URLs so clients send directly to the object save using resumable uploads. Direct to storage uploads bypass App Engine request size and instance constraints, support large files and unreliable networks, and scale because your service performs only lightweight URL signing while storage handles the data path. Security is preserved because the signed URL is time bound and scoped to specific objects and methods, and developers can enforce content type and other conditions.

Enable multipart uploads handled completely by the App Engine service is not viable for 920 MB files because App Engine has strict HTTP request size limits, and proxying large bodies through the service would be resource intensive and scale poorly.

Set up an SFTP endpoint on a Compute Engine VM and direct clients to upload there needs you to handle servers, capacity, and credentials. It is not serverless or autoscaling, and it still leaves you moving data into Cloud Storage after the fact which adds cost and operational risk.

Use Cloud Pub or Sub to stream file chunks and reassemble them in a worker misuses the messaging service. Pub/Sub messages have a small size limit and are not intended for bulk file transfer, so chunking and reassembly would be complex, inefficient, and unreliable for hundreds of megabytes.

questions.question: Which GCP service should you use to run a Python 3.12 web API with request based autoscaling, fast rollouts several times per day, and low operational cost?

options.text: GKE Autopilot
Cloud Run
App Engine flexible

questions.correct_text: Cloud Run
questions.explanation:
The right choice is Cloud Run. It runs a Python 3.12 web API with request based autoscaling, accommodates fast rollouts several times per day, and keeps operational cost low.

Cloud Run is a fully managed request driven container service that on its own scales instances based on concurrent requests and can scale to zero when idle, which minimizes cost. It handles quick deployments, revisions, traffic splitting, and instant rollbacks so developers can release many times per day with minimal risk. Because you supply a container image you may use Python 3.12 without extra runtime setup and you stop server management.

GKE Autopilot still needs Kubernetes manifests and ops overhead and generally uses metric based pod autoscaling rather than simple request based scaling. It does not scale to zero as seamlessly and there is a baseline cost for the cluster resources, so it does not meet the low operational cost and simplicity needed here.

App Engine flexible has slower deployments and longer instance startup times and often keeps at least one instance running, which increases cost. It lacks the rapid rollouts and scale to zero behavior desired for a request driven web API, so it is suboptimal.
